News.title: US removes all bombers from RAF Fairford base
News.content:
The US has withdrawn all of its bombers from RAF Fairford, the British military base at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter terror police.

A statement from a US department official confirmed on Sunday it had removed all of its bombers from the base back to their home stations in America.

The US did not give a reason for the withdrawal, but it follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire.

Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences near the base and subsequently released on police bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.

Whitehall sources have not disputed the decision from Washington was in response to the incident at RAF Fairford.

The BBC has also been told it was a military rather than a political decision - taken at an operational level - and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts.

The UK's Ministry of Defence has not commented.

Days after the incident, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but did not provide further details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

Initially, five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF). All five were UK nationals from London.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

The sixth man, aged 25, was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts. Counter terror police confirmed on Saturday he had also been released on bail.

RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

Days after the incident, and before the arrest of the sixth man, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Fox News that it "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor".

Rubio did not provide further details - saying at the time he was limited on what he could say on air.

US President Donald Trump separately said he was "surprised" the five men had been released on bail.

"We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this.

News.title: Green Party members back 'Zionism is racism' motion
News.content:
Green Party members have adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism, in a move that has divided senior figures at the top of the party.

The party's joint deputy leaders have been at odds over the subject, with Mothin Ali backing the move, and Rachel Millward describing the wording as "problematic".

Activists endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of members at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1022 votes to 813.

Discussion about the vote has dominated the conference, and exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under leader Zack Polanski and its MPs elected at the last election.

The motion adopted by Green members defines Zionism as an ideology in support of "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".

"The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it says.

It has attracted criticism from some Jewish groups, including the Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council who wrote a letter to the party ahead of the vote.

In a statement on Sunday evening, the organisations called the motion an "attack on the Jewish community".

"Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it," it said.

"Branding most British Jews and Jewish institutions 'racist' stokes anti-Jewish hatred after a year in which British Jews have been murdered attending their synagogue, stabbed in the streets, and seen their community buildings firebombed."

Israel's Foreign Ministry said the motion went beyond "the boundaries of legitimate political debate" and was "a stain on the history of the United Kingdom".

Later on Sunday, it said Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar had banned Polanski from entering Israel in response.

Debate about the motion, as well as the conflict in Gaza, has featured heavily during the conference, which is taking place after a surge in its membership in the wake of Polanski's election as leader in September last year.

Speaking after the vote, Lubna Speitan, the Green member behind the motion, argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression".

"We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions," she added.

Polanski himself did not vote in the debate, having left the conference early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing to be the MP. A full list of candidates in the contest can be found here.

News.title: I'm a classic old school Conservative, says Kemi Badenoch
News.content:
Kemi Badenoch has declared herself a "classic old school Conservative" as she begins her party's annual conference with a string of policy pledges and a 100 page statement on her guiding principles., external

"I believe in common sense, people working hard and being rewarded for that effort," she told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.

She added that welfare should be a "safety net, not a lifestyle".

The Tory leader is trying to ensure her party stands out in a crowded political field. The Conservatives are trailing Labour and Reform UK in the opinion polls and have yet to recover from their historic defeat at the 2024 general election.

Badenoch, whose personal poll ratings are higher than that of her party, has characterised Reform leader Nigel Farage as a "grumpy grandpa" and she told Laura Kuenssberg that Labour leader Andy Burnham is "the cheesy uncle who does all the dad jokes".

She described herself as a "no-nonsense mum".

Asked if her plan for benefit cuts and a massive increase in prison places was a return to the "nasty party" of the past, she said: "It's the common sense party. That's what we're doing.

"And, quite frankly, if we were doing so well the old way, then why did we have such a terrible issue in 2024?"

In her essay The Right Way - a deliberate echo of an essay written by Margaret Thatcher in 1976, external entitled The Right Approach - Badenoch says the last Conservative government failed because it did not know what it stood for.

Despite the party's rhetoric during its 14 years in power, she said: "We did little to reverse the structural changes Labour had made which took the country in the wrong direction.

"The result was that the state grew by stealth."

The essay says the "next Conservative government will have one central principle: business, not government, creates growth".

The Tories would achieve growth through tax cuts, cutting red tape and reducing the size of the civil service back to pre-pandemic levels, the essay says.

And it adds: "What is really missing from politics and government today is people prepared to say no.

"Political parties now need to recruit those who have the stomach to say no to good causes when the resources simply are not there to do everything."

News.title: British Museum announces changes to ease Bayeux Tapestry queues
News.content:
The British Museum has announced changes to how visitors see the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition after concerns over long queues and overcrowding.

The measures include plans for longer opening hours, as well as an audio guide, additional seating and clearer signage.

A museum spokesperson said the public response to the 11th Century embroidery had been "extraordinary", but acknowledged that some visitors had waited longer than they would have wanted.

Some people reported waits of up to two hours, while hundreds of ticket holders were reportedly turned away due to backlogs when the museum closed early last week due to a private event.

Some ticket holders took to social media to complain about the disruption.

One disappointed visitor said the trip had been a "big event" they had looked forward to, while another wrote she had been waiting since she was seven to see the Bayeux Tapestry, and bought tickets only to be turned away after queuing.

The museum later apologised to those who had been unable to enter and said they would be issued refunds and priority booking slots for a rearranged time.

From Monday, visitors will be offered an audio guide with more information about the embroidery, while additional signage and seating will be provided for those queuing to reach the main exhibition.

The museum said it planned to introduce longer opening hours to prevent queues building during the day and allow people with later bookings more time to view the exhibition.

Details of the extended hours have not yet been disclosed.

News.title: Protesters gather as migrants brought ashore on south coast
News.content:
Protesters have gathered in a south coast town as more than 100 people believed to be migrants were brought ashore after crossing the Channel in a small boat.

A number of people were seen arriving at a marina in Gosport, Hampshire, having been transported aboard two RNLI boats late on Sunday. Their dinghy appeared to have set off from near Utah Beach in Normandy during the morning, according to ship tracking data.

French media reported there were about 120 migrants on board.

Hampshire Police said it deployed officers to "support our partners in the event of an emergency at sea". The force imposed conditions under the Public Order Act as well as powers prohibiting the wearing of face coverings.

News.title: Shadow chancellor to unveil Tory plans to cut taxes and regulations
News.content:
Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith is to outline his plans for the UK economy, including hopes to cut taxes, red tape and house-building costs.

Griffith and his colleagues will use day two of the party's conference in Birmingham to also explain how they would want to reduce food costs, support Heathrow Airport expansion and abolish Natural England and the Environment Agency.

Another prospective policy is replacing agreements designed to compel developers to fund community projects and services in areas they want to build.

Griffith will describe his approach as the "most ambitious deregulation project in a generation". Reform UK suggested the Tories were "copying our policies".

Griffith's speech comes after Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch published a 100-page document, external explaining her guiding principles and how her party would act should it return to government by winning the next general election.

Following their historic defeat in the 2024 general election, the Conservatives have been trying to rebuild and convince voters that they can be trusted again.

The Tories have faced repeated attacks from their opponents for their record in government, including on the economy, between 2010 and 2024.

Griffith is expected to say: "No-one else is coming to save our economy. Only we can inject reality, tell the hard truths and make this a country we are proud to hand on to the next generation."

He will accuse Prime Minister Andy Burnham of wanting to pursue a "socialist fever dream of the 1970s", adding the Tories want to deliver "cheaper homes, lower taxes, and less red tape".

Chancellor John Healey last week said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" and the Budget on 28 October would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space".

During a series of speeches on Monday, Conservative shadow ministers will continue to make their case and provide more details of their proposals.

This will include ditching environmental and energy efficiency regulations, including the future homes standard.

The Tories believe their changes could cut the cost of delivering a new home by up to Â£50,000, which in turn they expect could save money for buyers.

A single levy for developers would be implemented in place of section 106 agreements and the Community Infrastructure Levy, which fund projects in the community when building plans are progressed.

The Conservatives argue this new charge would remove delays and improve how the funds are spent to the benefit of residents.

The party has been critical of the roles of Natural England and the Environment Agency in relation to house building and flood prevention work respectively, and wants to abolish both. Their functions would be looked after by the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra).

The Extended Packaging Responsibility (EPR) scheme, which requires firms to cover the cost of collecting, recycling and disposing of packaging it produces, would also be scrapped by the Conservatives.

The party believes this would help lift a "burden" from businesses and in turn could cut the cost of the weekly shop.

On Heathrow, Griffith is expected to say the next Conservative government would do "whatever it takes to end the delays and boost capacity by backing the third runway".

Plans for expansion were scrapped by the Tory-led coalition government in 2010.

Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves championed the runway to boost the economy after Labour won power, although Burnham has refused to say whether he backs the project since becoming prime minister.

Burnham has described it as "principally... a matter for London and Londoners".

Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the Conservatives have "cemented their position as a pointless anti-growth anti-business party" by rejecting closer ties with Europe.

She added: "No-one can take anything the Conservatives say on the economy seriously given their litany of fantasy-land financial pledges."

Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick accused the Conservatives of "once again copying our policies".

He added the Tories were unable to match Reform's pledge to raise the tax-free personal allowance to Â£15,000.

News.title: Glastonbury 2027 tickets sell out in 42 minutes
News.content:
Tickets for Glastonbury Festival 2027 sold out in 42 minutes, organisers have said.

Thousands of people joined the online queue at 09:00 BST in the hope of securing tickets to the festival at Worthy Farm in Somerset, which returns from 23 to 27 June after a fallow year.

Organisers confirmed last month that tickets for the weekend were at their highest price ever - Â£408, including a Â£5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of Â£29.50 from the last event in 2025.

Headliners have yet to be announced but organiser Emily Eavis previously said the team was "very excited" and things were "coming together really well".

Glastonbury posted on Instagram shortly after 09:40 to announce that tickets had sold out, and notified those who were in the queue.

"Thank you to everyone who bought one and we're sorry to those of you who missed out on a morning where demand greatly exceeded supply," the post said.

"There will be a resale of any cancelled or returned tickets in Spring 2027."

News.title: France to close up to 500 schools on Monday over student protests
News.content:
Up to 500 schools across France will be partially or totally closed on Monday after clashes between riot police and student protesters in recent days, the French education minister said on Sunday.

Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some "400 to 500" high schools as security conditions "have not been fulfilled", Ãdouard Geffray said.

He also said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the start of the protests.

Thousands of students have been demonstrating over education standards and the protests, which started last week, have spread from Paris to other cities, including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille.

High school pupils and others have objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.

On Friday, French Justice Minister GÃ©rald Darmanin said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been affected "one way or another" by violent protests.

The education minister warned the number of schools potentially affected on Monday could be comparable to Friday's figure but promised a "partial, progressive return to lessons".

"There are activists - particularly from the far-left - who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Ãdouard Geffray claimed.

"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he said. Geffray added that 78 staff members in education had been wounded, which he described as "something we have never seen before".

On Friday 1,747 people were arrested, according to French Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez.

News.title: Kneecap visit Garvaghy Road to show support for residents
News.content:
In a statement issued to the Press Association after their visit, Kneecap said they support the residents of Garvaghy Road, and described them as a "determined and strong community".

The group did not perform during their visit.

BreandÃ¡n Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition, told BBC News NI that was a "very deliberate decision".

"Kneecap isn't everyone's cup of tea but they wanted to come down, show a bit of solidarity to the kids in the area. They visited the the gaelscoil and bunscoil (Irish language schools), the youth club and community centre. That was their primary focus," Mac Cionnaith said.

On the expected court hearing on Monday, Mac Cionnaith said he "didn't want to pre-judge any outcomes".

Media reports on Sunday, external suggested that the Orange Order has offered to walk away and never return if they secure one last march along the Garvaghy Road.

Speaking on this, Mac Cionnaith said: "There was an agreement beforehand by the Orange Order that they would have their final march on the Garvaghy Road. They had their final march on the Garvaghy Road, and they threw it back in our community's face and said they would be down the road the following year.

"That's the fact. That's the reality."

He added: "Could we trust that organisation again, or trust any of their representatives?

News.title: Courts backlog will fall despite scrapping of jury trial plan, minister says
News.content:
The courts backlog will still fall despite plans to curb jury trials being scrapped, the justice secretary has told the BBC.

Alex Norris said introducing legislation for judge-only trials "was always going to be the most complicated to implement" and would have slowed down reforms.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's decision abandons proposals introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's government to allow judges in England and Wales to make the sole decision on cases that would lead to a sentence of less than three years.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said only complex fraud and financial offences would be judge-only - and it proposes thousands of medium-level crimes should stay with volunteer magistrates, who sit without a jury.

Norris told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the backlog would start falling "in this Parliament", but would not say by how much.

He said it would fall significantly over the next decade "as a result of the changes we're making".

The Conservatives said it was a "major victory" for those who fought to defend trial by jury, while criminal lawyers welcomed the decision but voiced concern about the implications of abolishing a defendant's right to ask for a jury trial.

The Criminal Bar Association (CBA) warned this would keep more middle-ranking cases before magistrates and shift 25,000 cases a year onto magistrates' courts.

Former justice secretary David Lammy first announced the plans to curb jury trials in December following a recommendation in a major review of the court system in England and Wales.

The series of radical reforms, including scaling back jury trials, were presented as the best way of turning around record backlogs which, in turn, were exacerbating the prison population crisis.

The backlog - which has led to record delays for defendants and victims - currently stands at nearly 81,000 cases, having rocketed largely thanks to cuts before the pandemic and court closures during national lockdowns.

News.title: Daughter of MP murdered five years ago tells BBC politicians still at risk
News.content:
Separately, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch confirmed to the BBC the man who pleaded guilty to sending her threatening messages also sent them to her family.

Kieran Kyle, 43, pleaded guilty to two counts of sending communication of an indecent or offensive nature to Badenoch and her family when he appeared in court in September. He will be sentenced on October 29.

"I just think that whether it's Nigel Farage, or even Keir Starmer who had his home fire bombed, that there is a threat to politicians that is increasing and we just need to crack down on this," she told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

Asked how Badenoch coped with threats to her safety, she replied: "it's really tough, but you just have to get on with it".

Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice, who told the BBC he also experienced threats to his safety, told the programme "this was far from where any of us want to be".

"We have to find the middle ground where we're accessible but we're protected and in the overall scheme of things if that requires a bit of extra taxpayers' money, I think hopefully voters would say 'yes'."

Amess said her father "loved meeting people", saying "he was one of the easier members of parliament to take a meeting with because that's what he lived for - to meet people, shake their hands, smile, help them with their problems. My dad wouldn't have wanted constituency surgeries to stop."

She added that he would have wanted to be alerted to someone being reported as a potential threat.

His killer, Ali Harbi Ali had been referred to the government's counter-terror programme Prevent in October 2014 but his case was closed in 2016.

A review published in February 2025 found Ali's Prevent case was closed too early after "problematic" assessments.

News.title: Missing woman found 'safe and well' after appeal
News.content:
A missing woman has been found safe and well after a police appeal to find her.

Leicestershire Police said Charlie Ryan was reported missing on Friday morning.

The force said the 31-year-old was found in the Leicester area on Sunday.

Officers thanked the public for sharing their appeal and contacting them with information.

News.title: Family of teenager killed in crash to sue acquitted driver
News.content:
The family of a teenager killed in a car crash near Stirling two years ago are launching a civil case against the driver who was cleared of causing death by careless driving.

Kyle Marshall, 19, and Jayden McConnell, 17, died when a car driven by Charles Gray spun out of control and into the path of a lorry on the A91 near Bannockburn Interchange in March 2024.

Gray, who had passed his test a month earlier, was acquitted of causing the deaths of his two friends after a five-day trial at Stirling Sheriff Court last November.

According to the Scottish Sun,, external the Marshall family are now suing Gray for a six-figure sum, alleging negligence.

A spokesman for Digby Brown, the law firm representing the Marshall family, confirmed: "A civil action has now been raised in the Court of Session on behalf of the loved ones of Kyle to help them secure answers, support and recognition.

"It would be inappropriate to comment further at this time however we will continue to support the Marshall family during this time."

News.title: Medieval leprosy hospital uncovered in Lincoln
News.content:
The walls of what is thought to be one of medieval England's earliest and largest leprosy hospitals have been uncovered in Lincoln by Time Team archaeologists.

A three-day dig started on Friday on the South Common at the site of the Hospital of the Holy Innocents, which housed up to 20 people with leprosy around the late 11th to early 12th Centuries.

Time Team's Prof Carenza Lewis said they had found traces of square features where it is thought people were housed, which "haven't been excavated before, anywhere".

The dig marks the beginning of a three-year project backed by the National Lottery Heritage Fund.

The remains of the building were found last year during a Local Landscapes and Hidden Histories project.

More than 100 volunteers were involved in excavating test pits which uncovered what were thought to be the medieval boundary walls of the hospital.

News.title: Train station returning to village after more than 100 years
News.content:
Work is beginning on bringing a train station back to the heart of a Greater Manchester village more than a century after its original station closed.

Cheadle in Stockport had a station just off the high street up until 1917.

Funding for a new hub, which would be built next to Alexandra Hospital, was given the green light in 2022, with planning permission granted in 2023 but concerns about its effect on the timetabling of trains elsewhere on the network led to delays.

Stockport Council said the issue had now been resolved and council leader Mark Roberts said it was "a hugely significant moment for Cheadle and for Stockport".

"For years we've fought for this station because we know the difference it will make to residents, businesses and the future prosperity of the area," he added.

Roberts said he was delighted that the initial highways work could now start on site thanks to the persistence and partnership of all involved.

Services are expected to run from Cheadle into Stockport town, Manchester Piccadilly and Chester, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.

The project had been held up by an unresolved timetabling issue over concerns the new station could impact trains elsewhere on the network, with a previous proposal made to remove services at Ashley and Plumley.

Stockport Council said the latest assessment by Network Rail and Northern Trains concluded that Cheadle Station could be introduced without removing a significant barrier that had put the project at risk and these plans have now been dropped.

News.title: Wales' Elfyn Evans wins his first World Rally Championship
News.content:
Elfyn Evans became Britain's first world rally champion for 25 years after rival Oliver Solberg crashed in a highly dramatic finish to the season in Italy.

Sweden's Solberg was on course to snatch the lead on the final stage of the last round of the World Rally Championship, and thereby deny Evans the title.

But Solberg lost control of his car with a few hundred metres to go in the Rally Italia Sardegna, which meant the glory went to Welshman Evans, a five-time runner-up in the championship.

"It hasn't sunk in," said a shocked Evans.

"I was sure it was over. I feel for Oliver - he had an incredible weekend. I don't know what to say."

The 37-year-old and co-driver Scott Martin had led for much of the 2026 season and took a 21-point advantage into the final round in Sardinia.

But that gap had shrunk to a solitary point by the time the drivers lined up for the last of 17 stages, bringing back painful memories of previous narrow misses for Evans.

Solberg, 25, needed only to beat his Toyota team-mate in the final stage to claim enough bonuses to be champion, but he crashed two corners from the finish.

Evans becomes only the third British man to win the WRC title after Colin McRae in 1995 and Richard Burns in 2001.

News.title: Major study launched to solve mystery of rising bowel cancer cases in young adults
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A quarter of a million volunteers are being sought for a nationwide research project investigating the mystery of why bowel cancer diagnoses are increasing among younger adults.

Historically considered a health issue primarily affecting older generations, data reveals that cases are rising among people under the age of 50.

Medical experts note that instances of early-onset bowel cancer have increased "substantially" across the globe since 1990, with the UK suffering one of the steepest rises.

The precise triggers behind this growth are not yet known, although rising levels of obesity are thought to be a contributing factor.

Scientists from King’s College London, working in partnership with health science company Zoe, are aiming to recruit 250,000 adults from across the UK to participate.

The trial, named Prospect-UK, will follow participants over an extended period to monitor dietary habits and lifestyle patterns.

Those taking part will complete online surveys focused on their diet, daily lifestyle, environment, personal health, and related factors.

open image in gallery The trial, known as Prospect-UK, will track people over time, looking at diet and lifestyle factors ( PA )

Volunteers will also be asked to link their survey responses to their electronic health records, allowing investigators to monitor any future cancer diagnoses.

A smaller subgroup of participants will be selected to provide comprehensive dietary diaries along with blood and stool samples.

"Over just a few generations our lifestyles, diets and environments have changed dramatically," said Professor Sarah Berry, chief investigator of the trial and professor of nutritional sciences at King’s College London.

"But we don’t know which of these changes are increasing people’s risk of bowel cancer or which ones could help reduce it.

"We urgently need large-scale, long-term data to uncover the true causes of early-onset bowel cancer."

Dr Rosiered-Brownson Smith, study research associate at King’s College London, said: "Although rates of early-onset bowel cancer are rising, it remains relatively uncommon, which means we need large groups of people to take part in research to help us understand why we are seeing this worrying trend.

"At the same time, our food environment has become increasingly complex, and this means we need to look at diet in much greater detail.

"In the UK, around 60% of our calorie intake comes from highly processed foods, but these foods are not all the same.

"They can differ substantially in their ingredients, processing methods and nutritional composition, even within the same food category."

Dr Smith added: "For the first time, we are collecting detailed, brand-level information about the foods people actually eat.

"This will allow us to better understand which foods and dietary patterns may be linked to the development of early-onset bowel cancer.

"Combining detailed dietary information with long-term health data, we hope Prospect-UK will help us better understand the complex relationship between what we eat and our risk of disease."

open image in gallery Early-onset bowel cancer has increased globally since 1990 say experts ( Alamy/PA )

Data provided by Cancer Research UK shows that roughly 48,200 people are diagnosed with bowel cancer in the UK every year, with approximately 2,900 of those cases occurring in adults aged between 25 and 49.

The charity stated that between the early 1990s and 2019, overall cancer incidence in 25 to 49-year-olds in the UK increased by 24%.

Main symptoms of bowel cancer

According to the NHS

Symptoms of bowel cancer may include:

changes in your poo, such as having softer poo, diarrhoea or constipation that is not usual for you

needing to poo more or less often than usual for you

blood in your poo, which may look red or black

bleeding from your bottom

often feeling like you need to poo, even if you’ve just been to the toilet

tummy pain

a lump in your tummy

bloating

losing weight without trying

feeling very tired for no reason

Bowel cancer can cause anaemia (when you have fewer red blood cells than usual), which can make you feel very tired, short of breath and have headaches.

Dr David Scott, director of global research initiative Cancer Grand Challenges, said: "Bowel cancer is still much more common in older people, but rising rates in younger adults pose a question we are working to answer.

"Diet and lifestyle may be part of the picture, but we need to understand what else could be contributing and how these factors interact.

"Prospect-UK will help investigate that question as part of the international Prospect team’s work, through Cancer Grand Challenges.

"The global team is working to understand what is driving this rise in younger people and, ultimately, identify new ways to prevent bowel cancer."

News.title: Global action urged over digital media’s harm to young people’s mental health
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Coordinated global action is required to address the links between excessive digital media use, declining mental health, poor sleep and physical inactivity among young people, experts have argued.

Technology companies have been accused by researchers of treating public health as "an afterthought" while creating commercial models focused on capturing user attention and gathering data.

In an effort to build a "healthier digital world" for young people, experts are calling on tech firms to release data showing how platform features affect user wellbeing.

The international team emphasised that functionalities such as infinite scroll and autoplay represent "deliberate design choices" rather than a "matter of individual self-control".

Published in the Lancet, the three-paper series includes a major synthesis of reviews examining nine million people under the age of 25.

The research found that high levels of digital media consumption—described as "problematic" use by authors—was associated with a greater risk of mental health difficulties, sleep disruption and reduced exercise.

open image in gallery Researchers accused technology companies of treating health as "an afterthought" while developing business models that capture attention and collect data ( PA )

However, researchers noted that these connections remain "modest".

Professor Ilona Kickbusch, of the Digital Transformations for Health Lab (DTH-Lab) in Switzerland, said: "Use of digital media is now woven into the fabric of childhood and life as a young adult.

"Governments have let technology companies write their own rules, leading to business models built to capture attention and collect data, with health treated as an afterthought.

"The evidence linking problematic digital media use to poorer mental health, sleep and physical activity, although not conclusive, justifies coordinated, global action.

"With the right governance, a healthier digital world for young people is possible, one that allows them to benefit from online opportunities without substantial risk of harm to health."

Louise Holly, of DTH-Lab UK, said: "The associations between problematic digital media use and health harms identified in our review are modest in size and rest on low-certainty evidence that cannot establish cause and effect.

"Meanwhile, the most valuable data on how these platforms actually affect users are hidden within technology companies, limiting independent scrutiny and slowing scientific progress."

The researchers calculate that spending over two hours of daily screen time could be linked globally to around 2.8 million healthy years of life lost to depression, alongside 240,000 lost to obesity each year.

Dr Falk Muller-Riemenschneider, of the National University of Singapore, said the estimates "are intended to be illustrative of the possible scale of harm" and should "not be taken as an accurate measurement of harm".

The series advises that governments should require technology firms to evaluate new products or features for potential harm before release, and to share data with independent researchers.

It also recommends setting up an international panel to monitor potential harms from artificial intelligence among children and young people, alongside a global governance treaty under the World Health Organisation to establish baseline standards and prevent weak regulation.

Professor Barbara Prainsack, of the University of Vienna, said "technology companies are borrowing a playbook well known from tobacco and fossil fuels: manufacture doubt, discredit critics, frame regulation as a threat to freedom".

open image in gallery Link between excessive use of digital media and poor mental health, poor sleep and a lack of exercise among young people "justifies coordinated global actio n ", experts have said. ( Alamy/PA )

"A public health approach counters this by looking at what the evidence suggests about harm across the whole population, not just what any single case can tell us.

"Seen that way, good regulation isn’t the enemy of innovation – it’s a driver of good innovation, channelling it toward safety and trust."

Dr Jay Shaw, of the University of Toronto in Canada, also urged further research into the specific design features implemented by tech platforms.

He said: "Most digital platforms are designed by companies to capture attention and collect data, not to protect health: features such as infinite scroll, autoplay and personalised recommendation feeds are deliberate design choices, not simply a matter of individual self-control

"We need much more research into how these specific design choices in digital media influence the way people use the technology, instead of only investigating the impact of how long people spend online."

The release of the series follows one of the largest studies into pediatric screen time, which concluded that higher usage can affect multiple aspects of wellbeing.

That review, published in the journal JAMA Pediatrics last month, analysed findings involving more than 2.8 million children across 64 countries.

It indicated that increased screen time for gaming, social media and video streaming can lead to reduced academic performance and language development delays, with children spending more time on screens demonstrating higher "socioemotional" and mental health issues.

News.title: Russian lab worker dies of ‘unknown’ virus as hundreds placed in quarantine
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Russian health authorities have reportedly placed hundreds of people in quarantine in Siberia following the death of a laboratory worker who was exposed to an “unknown” virus.

The 28-year-old victim was an employee at the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov, a town near the regional capital of Irkutsk, according to reports.

Prior to her death, she reportedly told medical personnel that she had accidentally broken a test tube containing live biological samples while working inside the facility.

She was subsequently hospitalised with severe pneumonia of "unknown origin," placed on a ventilator, and died shortly after on Thursday.

Daria Sh. is believed to have died after being exposed to an “unknown” virus ( AFP/Getty )

State consumer safety watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said that emergency sanitary protocols were immediately enacted following a case involving "pneumonia of unknown etiology" at the facility.

Since, Rospotrebnadzor has maintained that the broader situation in the Irkutsk region remains stable.

At least 197 people suspected of having direct or indirect contact with the technician have been placed under medical isolation, according to independent regional news outlet Liudi Baikala. More than 100 of those individuals are currently being monitored in hospital wards.

At the same time, local authorities have instituted strict quarantine measures across the district, targeting the Shelekhov District Hospital, a nearby maternity facility, and a local aluminium plant.

Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev urged residents to remain calm, writing on Telegram that an anti-epidemic commission convened to address a "suspected case of a particularly dangerous infection."

While his public statement did not acknowledge the worker's death, Kobzev stated that all identified close contacts remain asymptomatic and have tested negative.

Russian law enforcement agencies have reportedly opened a criminal investigation into potential workplace health and safety violations resulting in the lab worker’s death.

Former Rospotrebnadzor head Gennady Onishchenko downplayed the threat in comments to state news agency TASS, stating that the infection in the Irkutsk region is "most likely not the plague, but even if confirmed, there will be no spread of this disease."

He added that widespread transmission remains unlikely, noting that cooler seasonal temperatures would help contain potential spread.

Because the facility specialises in dangerous pathogens, the incident has drawn speculation it could be pneumonic plague – one of three variants caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.

Unlike bubonic and septicemic plagues, which generally pass to humans via flea bites or contact with infected animals, pneumonic plague attacks the lungs directly and can easily spread from person to person through airborne respiratory droplets.

According to guidelines from the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, patients infected with pneumonic plague typically experience rapid onset fever, headaches, and physical weakness, alongside severe respiratory distress such as shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing, and watery or blood-tinged mucus.

While the World Health Organisation (WHO) warns that the disease carries a high mortality rate if untreated, it remains highly manageable with early antibiotic administration and standard infection control measures.

News.title: Anti-migrant protesters gather in seaside town as dinghy crossing the Chanel arrives
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Migrants have arrived in Hampshire after crossing the Channel from France by dinghy, landing at Haslar Marina in Gosport aboard two RNLI lifeboats late on Sunday evening.

French media reported there were around 120 migrants on board the vessel, which appeared to have set off from near the Utah Beach area of Normandy on Sunday morning. Departures so far west have been rare in recent years, but this marks the third such crossing from the area in the space of a month.

Around 100 anti-migrant demonstrators gathered in the seaside town following reports that authorities were preparing for the arrival of the vessel. The dinghy was shadowed by French rescue vessels until it entered English waters, where it was met by RNLI boats, according to ship tracking data.

While understood to have started as a largely peaceful demonstration, six people have been arrested by police officers, according to reports.

open image in gallery Anti-immigrant demonstrations have broken out across the coastal town of Gosport ( Getty )

Footage capturing scenes by Gosport’s Haslar Marina shows crowds gathered around police vans chanting “shame on you” and “deport the lot”.

The demonstration follows heightened scrutiny over migrant arrivals to the UK, where similar anti-immigration protests have flared up across coastal towns including Dover and Portsmouth.

Earlier today, the Reform leader of Hampshire council George Madgwick, said on X:“I hate to report that Gosport is the planned landing point for today’s migrant boat.

“This is an absolute shambles,” he said, “But there is hope. Last time they planned to dock there they changed course. Let’s hope they do the same today.

“If you’re heading there stay peaceful and calm.”

open image in gallery Demonstrators are hoping to deter the arrival of a vessel understood to be hosting immigrants ( PA Wire )

Similar scenes unfolded in Gosport last month when protesters gathered expecting a landing after coaches and ambulances were spotted nearby.

On that occasion, the passengers – 51 migrants who refused help from the French coastguard, arrived in Dover after being transferred to Border Security Command boats.

A government spokesperson said: “The Border Security Command works around the clock to monitor the Channel and protect our border. It is vital we continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival.”

The provisional total for Channel crossings this year is 19,451.

This is down 43% on this time last year and 23% below the figure at this stage in 2024.

Authorities have since placed a dispersal order under Section 34 of the Anti-Social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014 to cover the town of Gosport.

This order is in place until 7am on Tuesday, 6 October. Those who refuse to comply with the order are committing a criminal offence and are liable for arrest.

More follows on this breaking news story. Subscribe here to get the latest updates from The Independent

News.title: Brazil's Bolsonaro takes early lead as results trickle in for high-stakes election
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Senator Flavio Bolsonaro took an early lead as Brazil began reporting results on Sunday afternoon in the first round of a tight presidential election, following a campaign dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling.

The field of 13 candidates has been led by two clear frontrunners — leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, 80, who is seeking a fourth term, and Flavio, the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who hopes ⁠to return his father's right-wing movement to power.

With about 32% of votes reported, Flavio led Lula with 50.74% of the votes to the president's 41.14%.

Early results showed southern states that lean to Bolsonaro reporting faster, while votes from Lula's northeast stronghold are tallied slower.

If no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes, the top two will face off on October 25. Surveys show Lula and Flavio polling roughly even in a likely runoff.

A victory for the senator would extend a wave of wins across Latin America by right-wing candidates aligned with US President Donald Trump, while Lula's reelection could create a headache for Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.

Despite growing worries over Brazil's public finances and sluggish economic growth, the campaign ⁠offered meager policy debate, as both leading candidates skipped the major TV debates.

open image in gallery Supporters of Brazil's President and presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva react after the first results of the presidential election in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 4, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

While polls right up until Saturday showed ​Lula would ⁠likely lead the first round but not avoid a runoff, Flavio told journalists in Rio de Janeiro he was confident he could win the presidency in the first round, citing voters' frustration with his chief opponent.

Flavio was counting on "a protest vote from people who would otherwise vote for another candidate but are opposed to Lula," he said. "I hope it’s enough to secure a victory in the ⁠first round."

Thaise Lima, a 41-year-old lawyer on her way to vote in Sao Paulo, said her main goal was to get Lula's Workers' Party out of office.

"I don't think Flavio is the best candidate, ​but I might decide to ⁠vote for him in the next few minutes," she said, adding that she ‌wished psychiatrist and author Augusto Cury were a more viable candidate.

Fernando Tempel, 49, a management consultant, told Reuters he was voting for Flavio despite initially planning to vote for Romeu Zema, the former governor of Minas Gerais state.

open image in gallery Supporters of Brazil's right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro react as they wait for the first results in in Porto Alegre, Brazil, on October 4, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

On the other hand, Lula's allies have warned that the Trump administration might refuse to recognize election results if he wins, pointing to an aborted effort to send US officials to Brazil.

"What is at stake ‌is the future of Brazil," Lula said after voting in Sao Bernardo do Campo, in Sao Paulo state.

Trump has not formally ‌endorsed a candidate, though he hosted Senator Flavio Bolsonaro at the White House and praised him publicly.

"I'm a little worried about everything that's been happening recently, including internationally. I feel this election has had a lot of outside influence, more than in previous elections," said Cristiano, 34, a doctor in Brasilia who voted for Lula and preferred to withhold his surname.

"We are confident in our President Lula, who will fight for national sovereignty," said Pedro Palacio, 45, who was voting in Brasilia alongside his wife, Andreia, and their two sons and two dogs, all of whom wore ⁠outfits supporting the president.

As of Sunday afternoon, the election was proceeding normally, Brazil's electoral court chief Kassio Nunes Marques said in a press conference.

“Teams monitoring international risks have not identified any risks whatsoever," he said.

Reuters reported on Wednesday that Brazilian intelligence officials briefed a French and German delegation on alleged US and Russian interference before the election. The US has rejected claims of interference in Brazil's affairs.

open image in gallery Supporters of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for presidential re-election, react as they wait for results at Paulista Avenue in Sao Paulo, Brazil October 4, 2026. REUTERS/Alexandre Meneghini ( Reuters )

Despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over voters grappling with high living costs, heavy household debt and the threat of street crime and more pervasive gang activity.

Flavio Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns, while Lula has moved to ban online gambling and, as the race tightened, expanded welfare and proposed fresh debt relief for families.

Rising spending and public debt above 82% of GDP have stoked fiscal concerns that Brazil's next president will need to address. The government lowered its economic growth forecasts for this year and next to 2.0% and 2.3% respectively.

"I voted for Brazil to start growing again," said Marciano de Souza e Silva, a 52-year-old public servant in Brasilia and former Lula voter who ‌moved right, voting for Jair Bolsonaro in 2018 and 2022 and Flavio on Sunday.

"The best social program is one that encourages people to start businesses, to actually produce real wealth," he said.

open image in gallery A supporter of Brazil's right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro await for the first results of the presidential election in Porto Alegre, Brazil, on October 4, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Overshadowing the policy debate, a scandal surrounding the now-defunct Banco Master has engulfed much of Brazil's political class and renewed public anger over corruption.

Daniel Vorcaro, who ran the bank, was arrested earlier ‌this year and accused of a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme. The investigation has probed the banker's ties to ⁠figures from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes to Flavio Bolsonaro, who is being investigated for money laundering tied to the case by the federal police.

The candidate has denied any wrongdoing, although ⁠he confirmed raising millions of dollars from Vorcaro to make a movie about his father.

The banker's connections to Moraes, widely perceived as a Lula ally, plunged the court into crisis a month before the vote, creating fresh problems for the president. Moraes has said the case against him is ‌politically motivated for his role in the conviction of the elder ​Bolsonaro.

On Sunday, voters will also elect all 513 lower house members and two-thirds of the Senate, where some lawmakers ‌have pushed to impeach Moraes.

Congress has gained greater influence in Brazilian politics since the impeachment of ​former President Dilma Rousseff, a Lula ally, in 2016, raising the stakes of those legislative races.

News.title: As Trump spirals with midterms, it seems his go-to safe spaces are becoming less welcoming
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

On Sunday, President Donald Trump raged at Fox News for not broadcasting his rallies.

It was a surprising turn given that Fox remains the most-watched news outlet in the United States and many of Trump’s most devoted fans still watch it.

“Sad to see that Fox & Friends (Sunday) is not covering our packed house and incredibly enthusiastic (beyond!),” he said. “These Election Rallies were representative of what is really happening with our great Republican Party.”

On one hand, Trump griping about Fox News is not that surprising. He’s clashed with Fox News ever since his first campaign for president when he famously criticized debate moderator Megyn Kelly, saying “you could see there was blood coming out of her eyes, blood coming out of her wherever.” He recently criticized host Shannon Bream for displaying outdated photos of his planned ballroom. And Trump understands something about the id of the Fox viewer more than the executives of the network do.

In the grand scheme of Trump’s attacks on the press, this appears, to borrow a Trumpism, like “small potatoes.” Trump banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House premises and is still trying to stiff-arm their coverage.

But a look at the data shows that Trump is in real trouble, including in the states where he’s barnstorming. And the more Trump becomes unpopular, the more he is likely to lash out at Fox since he feels he can influence it the most.

On Saturday, he visited Ohio. On paper, this should be a bank shot for Trump. He turned it from a perpetual swing state to a solid red state. His endorsement of JD Vance in the 2022 primary paved the way for him to become a senator and his running mate in 2024.

open image in gallery US President Donald Trump gestures during a rally at Butler High School in Vandalia, Ohio, US, October 3, 2026. ( Reuters )

Now? Vance’s replacement in the Senate, Jon Husted, is floundering. A New York Times/Siena College poll released Saturday showed former Sen. Sherrod Brown beating Husted by three points. And the Republican candidate for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, is not doing much better. The same poll shows Democratic Amy Acton beating Ramaswamy by four points in the Buckeye State.

Then there is Texas. This might be where Trump’s hubris could cost him more than anything. In May, he chose to endorse ultra-MAGA Attorney General in the primary runoff against incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn.

But Paxton’s numerous scandals, which led to the Texas state House impeaching him before the state Senate acquitted him, have proven to be an albatross. Paxton’s estranged wife, whom he allegedly cheated on, had to cut an ad this week saying “it’s about getting the whole team across the finish line,” and “that’s why I am voting the Republican ticket on November 3rd.”

And despite pouring millions of dollars into Texas, Democrat James Talarico has a slight lead. If he wins, Talarico would be the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Texas since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988. Even more alarming, polling is now showing that Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who is seeking a fourth term, is now in a competitive race with Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

Even in blood-red Kansas, incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall is in a competitive race.

Trump continues to say this is all a matter of branding, rather than actual anger about his policy on tariffs and the war in Iran, which has only driven prices up.

open image in gallery Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico is leading multiple polls in the Texas Senate race ( Reuters )

Furthermore, Trump’s ability to touch on subjects that anger voters has dulled. He’s pushed back on voters’ anger about data centers and AI, fully embracing both and attempting to dub the latter “Super Intelligence.”

But people aren’t buying it. Trump continues to bleed support, and surveys show Democrats are more motivated to turn out than Republicans, as is usually the case in midterm elections with the minority party.

And as time progresses and Trump enters the twilight of his time in politics, expect Fox to be more forward-looking. It will likely have to begin focusing on whatever outrageous comments from Democrats they can amplify while also giving special attention to the 2028 Republican candidates.

Trump may not like it, but the currents of politics are moving away from him. And they are forces stronger than him. Not even Fox can defy them.

News.title: US Air Force removes all bombers from British air base targeted by a suspected terror attack
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The U.S. Air Force has brought home its bombers stationed at a U.S.-run military air base in England used to strike Iran following an investigation into a planned terror attack at the RAF Fairford base.

The bombers were redeployed to their home bases in the United States, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorized to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke Sunday on condition of anonymity.

Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war. Observers noticed a host of B-1 bombers fly out of the base on Sunday.

The move comes as President Donald Trump weighs options for his war on Iran — including new strikes — despite his initial promises to Americans that the campaign would last a matter of weeks.

“We have decisions that I’ll make about Iran. Iran’s been decimated. So the only question is — it’ll either be the easy way, or the hard way,” Trump told reporters on Saturday as he left the White House for a rally in Ohio.

A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and then released on bail during the investigation.

British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement, but it has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

U.K. officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.

RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.

The U.S. military still maintains a sizable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a U.S. official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier, as well as the USS Malkin Island amphibious readiness group — a group of ships that together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines — are heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers in the region as early as the end of October.

___

AP writer Melissa Goldin contributed from New York.

News.title: Texas woman accused of allowing doctor to sexually assault child in exchange for Adderall
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A woman in Texas allegedly allowed a doctor to sexually assault a child in exchange for Adderall, according to police.

Alicia Evonne Sanchez, 37, was arrested on Wednesday and has been charged with sexual assault of a child under 14.

Police say she took a child to Dr. Kenneth Donald Haygood's office on numerous occasions, allegedly allowing the doctor to sexually assault the child on at least 10 occasions.

Investigators said that Sanchez stayed in the room during the alleged assaults. The child reportedly pleaded and cried for the doctor to stop, but was ignored or told that "this is what doctors do."

Following the assaults, the child told another adult and a counselor that the doctor would give Sanchez Adderall pills following their visits.

Alicia Evonne Sanchez, 37, left, has been charged with sexual assault of a child under 14 after she allegedly allowed Dr. Kenneth Donald Haygood, right, to sexually assault a child in exchange for Adderall pills ( Smith County Sheriff's Office )

Sanchez allegedly told the child that the pills were for "people who couldn't get them from their doctor" or that there was a medicine shortage.

She is being held on a $3 million bond.

If convicted, Sanchez faces up to 99 years in prison. Investigators have not yet revealed Sanchez's link to the child or the child's gender.

Haywood was sentenced in 2025 to eight years in prison after he pleaded guilty to other sexual assaults. He admitted to two counts of sexually assaulting two female patients in a plea deal that saw six other charges dropped, including sexually assaulting a child.

He had to register as a sex offender for life.

It's unclear if additional charges will be brought against him.

News.title: Jibulu emerges as England World Cup bolter in Sale defeat of Saracens
News.content:
Could Nathan Jibulu, the Sale Sharks hooker, emerge as a bolter for England’s World Cup squad? With Steve Borthwick, the England head coach, watching from the stands, the 23-year-old produced the kind of “wrecking-ball” performance in this surprise victory for the North West side that suggested he is on course to do so.

After their tame defeat by Bristol Bears in the opening round, few had predicted that Alex Sanderson’s side had much hope against Saracens, who were looking to back up their impressive win at Welford Road last weekend. But Jibulu’s powerhouse display on either side of the ball typified their stout and physical resistance, backed up by a masterly display by George Ford.

Given the age and injury profile of England hookers Jamie George and Luke Cowan-Dickie, who both missed this contest, and the fact that Theo Dan has yet to make a forceful challenge for the position in the national side, Sanderson is in no doubt that Jibulu has the X factor required to break into Borthwick’s squad this season.

“This is the player that any time you watch him play, he impacts – he takes metres either side of the ball – and we knew that he had that in him,” Sanderson said.

“It shows he’s of international class. He nailed his line-outs, on the back of that he was a wrecking-ball runner causing havoc around the field.

“This is the person that we knew, this is the player that we knew we had in him. It could be the year where he explodes onto the international scene. I hope it is, but it’s early days.

“He’s that quality, he’s that kind of an athlete. You can get away with being fast and skilful in the Prem, but it’s another level again in terms of the power that’s required at international level. And he’s got that ability, he’s immensely strong.”

Borthwick will have left the StoneX Stadium on Sunday evening with a full notebook. Ben Bamber, Sale’s 6ft 9ins lock, has also been attracting his interest and it was Bamber who crossed for the decisive try, Sale’s third, hitting a great line off Ford to finish like an outside centre.

News.title: Brilliant Hamilton storms to podium despite another Ferrari blunder
News.content:
One of the big talking points heading into the weekend has been the cooling vests drivers wear under their overalls (as opposed to the jacket-like ones they wear when they’re out of their cars). Russell told us in our Brits media session on Thursday that Mercedes had decided to forego the vests here, since the technology was not yet refined. The system works by pumping a coolant through thin tubes stitched into the vest.

Drivers have complained that the connecting valve to the pump, which was originally placed on the side of the vest, proved uncomfortable when combined with the high G-forces experienced in an F1 car. On some vests the connector has been moved to find a more comfortable position, but the thick material and tubing have also proved cumbersome under the driver’s fireproof overalls. There are also concerns over the reliability of some systems and the possibility that a failure will mean the vest will have the opposite effect and work as a heat insulator.preferring to spend that money instead on car upgrades. The money to develop the vests comes out of the budget cap.

But Russell added that the FIA should make the tech mandatory and develop it themselves, describing this race as like being in a “sauna”.The Briton’s comments prompted a sarcastic response from Verstappen - who doesn’t wear the vests either, out of choice - who said Russell “shouldn’t make a fuss”.

“I don’t need it,” Verstappen said. “Maybe I suffer a bit less from the heat.. I find a Finnish sauna at 85 degrees a lot hotter... You shouldn’t make a fuss. Yes, it is hot, but that’s part of it. You have to train for that.”

The Dutchman added: “When I was 18, I had a bit more trouble with these conditions. But after that, I started training more in the heat, such as in the sauna and a steam room, so that I can handle the sweating better and the fact that your head gets very hot. Maybe I should take him (Russell) to the sauna a few times.”

These two have history, of course. They’ve sniped at each other for years. In 2024, in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, it reached a peak when Verstappen described Russell as being “two-faced” and said he had lost all respect for him. Russell responded by saying Verstappen was “a bully”. Earlier this year, the Mercedes driver said Verstappen could always retire from the sport and drive sports cars if he didn’t like the regs.

News.title: Rees-Zammit taunts Pollock as Bristol outplay Northampton
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Bristol Bears vs Northampton Saints from the Gallagher Prem, with both teams looking to build on winning starts following the opening weekend of action.

Last season’s champions Northampton kicked off their title defence with an emphatic 59-26 victory over a new-look Newcastle Red Bulls outfit at Franklin’s Gardens.

While Henry Pollock’s new cornrow hairstyle was the centre of attention at kick-off, the limelight was soon stolen by Tommy Freeman and James Pater, who both notched hat-tricks for Phil Dowson’s side.

Of 19-year-old full-back Pater, who starts on the bench today, Dowson said afterwards: “He doesn’t let the occasion get to him. He has an incredible skill set, great speed and ability to manoeuvre away from defenders.”

Bristol, meanwhile, began their season with an impressive 34-24 victory away at Sale Sharks, with Pat Lam’s side ensuring Courtney Lawes’s return to the English game was a disappointing one.

Louis Rees-Zammit was operating in his favoured wing position and got Bristol off to a strong start with two tries in the opening 23 minutes, offering Lam hope of a fruitful campaign from the Welshman.

“When you look at our wingers in the past, they scored a lot of tries and Louis is a world-class finisher,” the Bristol director of rugby said. “You get the ball to him in space and you create the opportunity, there’s a good chance he’ll finish it.”

Northampton will be hoping for a repeat of the meeting between the sides at Franklin Gardens in May when they thumped Bristol 94-33, but they have not won at Ashton Gate since 2021.

Both teams have made a pair of changes following their opening-weekend victories, with England international Ellis Genge among the players to drop out after spraining his wrist against Sale.

News.title: Sublime England thrash Croatia in best performance for a decade
News.content:
We came out of the World Cup wondering if Tuchel really had an idea of how he can get England over the line. After last Saturday’s defeat by world and European champions Spain, followed by Tuesday’s win over the Czech Republic we still did not know.

But here the standard was set – it was an exhilarating example of the football England are capable of. On display we saw the speed, the movement, the passes under pressure, the ambition, the control and aggression. This was the full package. Bottle it. Bag it. Believe it.

Croatia have an ageing team and are in transition, but they were left looking callow. It looked as though it was men against boys. There were plenty of boys in the stands, with 6,200 children allowed in for what was supposed to be a behind-closed-doors fixture – Croatia’s punishment for crowd trouble.

Their new head coach Slaven Bilic would doubtless have been relieved that the match was not played in front of the usual, passionate, partisan crowd. Even then some of the kids booed and left early. Bilic looked shell-shocked. As well he might.

News.title: Russell must do something wacky now after disappointing Bahrain GP qualifying
News.content:
The screens in the media centre here in Sepang tell me that the air temp right now is 32.8C and the track temp is 58C. It feels even hotter. Lots of chat about cooling vests this week, which are optional. George Russell is among the drivers who isn’t using one, which is interesting a) because Russell has suffered badly from heat in the past (Qatar, Singapore) and b) because he says Mercedes chose to put the development money into car upgrades instead.

It’s an interesting admission. Not everyone is sold on the idea of cooling vests. Ferrari and McLaren will definitely be using them this weekend, for instance. Max Verstappen won’t as he doesn’t like them. Russell thinks the FIA should just develop the tech themselves and it shouldn’t be part of the budget cap.

“Our team have put a lot of emphasis this year on the cockpit temperature,” he said. “We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough. I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say ‘Here’s some money extra in the cost cap or there’s an external company who’s going to develop it for everybody’. Because we should all be wearing it. When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me...look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it...[but at a cost].

He added: “The top itself is not expensive ..you’ve got to effectively make a system where you can fit a block of dry ice or actual ice, and then has the airflow to circulate the cool water throughout. If that system isn’t robust enough, then suddenly you have no circulation, and then you get hot. You get ambient temperature circulating. The vest is one-design, but the system that circulates the water is different [at different teams].”

News.title: Bath complete revenge mission on Exeter despite imperious Feyi-Waboso
News.content:
Bath held off a furious comeback from Exeter, led by the irrepressible Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, to avenge their Gallagher Prem semi-final defeat here in June.

It felt as if lightning might strike Bath twice. Once again Exeter overturned a 26-10 half-time deficit, to manufacture a second-half lead thanks to a pair of blistering finishes by Feyi-Waboso. Four months ago, Bath failed to take a drop goal in the closing stages, but this time with the reassuring presence of Finn Russell at fly-half, they kept their cool.

The Scotland playmaker twice sent penalties deep into the Exeter 22 from where Stephen Varney conceded a yellow card and penalty try before Bath replacement Ted Hill powered through a thicket of Exeter tacklers.

“Finn is one of the best 10s in the world and I thought he had a very good game,” Johann van Graan, the Bath head of rugby, said. “His decision making is above most players in the world and I thought that came through tonight.”

Despite the appearance of yet another high-scoring shoot-out, both teams defended with real bite, although Bath struggled to lay a finger on Feyi-Waboso who ended up in a scrap with a fan in the stands here when he was a spectator in May. He exacted a measure of revenge beating eight defenders and carried for 132 metres.

“Manny still needs game time,” Rob Baxter, the Exeter director of rugby, said. “When he’s on the ball, you see something incredible, but it is his ability to get on the ball again. He is just getting his game minutes and match fitness up.”

News.title: FTSE 100 tumbles amid bond market sell-off
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. House prices fell unexpectedly last month as mortgage borrowers prepare for a jump in interest rates.

Typical property values declined by 0.2pc during September, reversing 0.2pc growth in August, according to the Nationwide house price index.

The figure was much worse than analysts had forecasts, with most expecting prices to remain steady.

Over the course of the year to September, the rate of house price growth halved from 1.6pc to 0.8pc, which was the weakest rate since December 2025.

The value of the average home has fallen to £274,251 over concerns the Bank of England is on the cusp of raising interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for mortgage holders.

Money markets indicate there is an 84pc chance policymakers will raise rates from 3.75pc to 4pc in November in an effort to bring down inflation caused by the Iran war energy shock.

Robert Gardner, chief economist at Nationwide, said:“Market activity and house prices have remained subdued in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop.

“Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict in the Middle East exerting upward pressure on energy prices, fanning inflation concerns.

“This in turn has led to mounting financial market expectations of Bank Rate increases, which has maintained upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Polanski urges Miliband to block Rosebank oil field over Israel links | Green leader claims North Sea project is a test of Foreign Secretary’s proposed sanctions regime

2) Netherlands ditches wealth tax over exodus fears | Dutch PM scraps plan to target paper profits, instead introducing a more convention capital gains levy

3) Diesel crisis deepens as UK’s biggest refinery shuts for 10 weeks | Fears of squeeze on supplies after fuel costs rise higher than £2 per litre

4) Debt-ridden France branded ‘the new sick man of Europe’ | Investors hope the European Central Bank sees the struggling country as ‘too big to fail’

5) Britain blocks foreign lawyers after surge in south Asian applicants | Bar Standards Board halts scheme unless candidates have already secured a position

What happened overnight

The cost of government borrowing edged higher in Asia as soaring energy costs sparked inflation fears.

Bond yields, a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money, surged in September as investors brace for a period where interest rates stay higher for ​longer.

The yield on benchmark US 10-year Treasury notes hit 5.31pc, the ‌highest level since mid-June 2007. The 10-year yield gained 87 basis points in the July-September quarter, the biggest quarterly rise since 1994.

Market focus has been on how long US Treasury yields stay above the psychologically important 5pc level, while some investors even contemplate the possibility of yields breaching 6pc.

Yields in Japan have climbed to multi-decade highs too, while those in Germany, France and Britain have all hit 17 to 19 year peaks.

On Thursday, the benchmark 10-year Japanese government ​bond yield was at 3.11pc, not far from the 30-year high it hit last week.

Asian technology stocks rose after a boost from AI chipmaker Micron, ​although US bonds struggled ‌after their sharpest quarterly sell-off in more than three decades as inflation risks from elevated energy prices linger.

Stalling peace talks between the US and Iran to end the seven-month-long war in the Middle East have kept crude prices aloft.Brent futures surged 42pc in the July-September quarter.

The high-stakes earnings from Micron, a key supplier to AI bellwether Nvidia, signalled strong demand for AI memory chips, with financial commitments under long-term supply agreements at $32 billion, up from $22 billion in June.

That helped push tech-heavy stock markets in Asia higher. Japan’s Nikkei jumped over 3pc, and South Korea’s Kospi reversed earlier losses to gain 1.7pc. Taiwan’s stock benchmark was 0.8pc higher.

News.title: Chewing tobacco killed 250,000 people in one year, study shows
News.content:
Chewing tobacco killed around a quarter of a million people in 2023, with use of the product remaining stubbornly high, according to research.

The smokeless tobacco, which is placed between the cheek and lower gum, is particularly popular in south Asia. It is flavoured and sometimes sweetened, and users often spit out unwanted juices while chewing. It is often viewed as safer than smoking but it is a major cause of stroke, as well as head and neck cancer.

Chewing tobacco is different to white snus or nicotine pouches, which contain no tobacco. These white pouches are also made up of flavourings and sometimes sweeteners, and deliver a hit of nicotine through the lining of the mouth.

Despite a successful fight against smoking over the last few decades, rates of chewing tobacco use have fallen little and it has often been overlooked in tobacco control efforts, researchers point out. In a study published in the Lancet Global Health, researchers from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation in the US estimate that 241 million people aged 15 years and older used chewing tobacco in 2023.
