Researchers looked at data on use in 204 countries between 1990 and 2023 and found that there was no significant decrease in the number of users of chewing tobacco over that period. And in 24 countries there was a significant uptick in the number of people using the product. Researchers estimate that about one in five men and one in 10 women in south Asia chewed tobacco in 2023.

Bangladesh has seen the biggest increase in the number of people using the product with 15 million new users between 1990 and 2023. Nepal, Madagascar and Yemen also saw increases in the number of users.

In India 105 million people chew tobacco regularly, accounting for just over two thirds of users globally. Historically, Indians would chew paan, tobacco in its raw form which was mixed with betel leaf and areca nut, a mild stimulant. But the use of chewing tobacco exploded in the 1980s when manufacturers began grinding these into a powder and selling them in packets known as gutkha. This was banned in 2012 but is still widely available. Chewing tobacco is also popular in Pakistan, China and Vietnam.

Sports.title: Ireland coach makes half-time 'spit' allegation against Israel player
Sports.content:
Ireland coach makes half-time 'spit' allegation against Israel player

The alleged incident took place during the half-time interval between Ireland and Israel during their Nations League clash

View 2 Images Israel and Republic of Ireland players clash in their Nations League encounter. (Image: (Photo by Srdjan Stevanovic/Getty Images))

An Israeli player has been accused of spitting at a member of the Republic of Ireland coaching staff during Sunday's Nations League clash. Fitness coach Damien Doyle was spotted protesting following an incident involving an unnamed Israeli player as both teams made their way towards the tunnel at half-time.

‌



‌



It is claimed he was spat at as tensions boiled over - with the incident unfolding in front of stadium security and local police. The flashpoint triggered a confrontation between the two camps, and Spanish referee Juan Martínez Munuera, who had awarded Troy Parrott a first-half penalty following a VAR review, intervened to separate the feuding players and coaching staff.

‌



He is understood not to have witnessed the spitting incident, reports the Irish Mirror. However, the Irish Independent claims that Serbian security staff did see the incident take place.

‌

FAI officials are currently examining audio recordings from pitchside microphones after Jayson Molumby approached the match official last Sunday to raise concerns about racist abuse directed at Adam Idah and James Abankwah from the Israeli supporters.

Sports.title: Erling Haaland goes off injured for Norway as Man City handed another blow
Sports.content:
Erling Haaland goes off injured for Norway as Man City handed another blow

Manchester City have endured a miserable week after being found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules - and now star striker Erling Haaland has picked up an injury

View 2 Images Erling Haaland asked to be substituted (Image: Miguel RIOPA / AFP via Getty Images)

Manchester City's week may have just got even worse, with star striker Erling Haaland going off injured while playing for Norway.

‌



‌



Haaland gestured to be substituted during Norway's Nations League match against Portugal on Sunday night. The City striker was replaced by Jorgen Strand Larsen in the 67th minute in Porto with the score at 1-1 after signalling to manager Stale Solbakken.

‌



Portugal then netted a second goal through Goncalo Ramos to take the lead. The home side held on to clinch the victory 2-1, despite a red card for Francisco Conceicao in the closing stages.

‌



Haaland had played every minute of Norway's previous three Nations League matches in this international break. He scored twice in the 3-2 win over Denmark before scoring in the 2-1 defeat by Portugal in the first meeting.

The City star went goalless in the 2-1 defeat by Wales before limping off against Portugal on Sunday night. City manager Enzo Maresca will now be concerned ahead of their trip to Anfield to play Liverpool on October 11.

Haaland has scored seven goals in seven games across all competitions for City so far this season. His form has been crucial to their perfect record in the Premier League, with Maresca's side sitting top with five wins from five games.

City will already be without Phil Foden for the Liverpool game, after the midfielder was sent off for kicking Bruno Fernandes in the Manchester City. There are also doubts surrounding Nico O'Reilly, who was forced to leave the England camp with injury, and Antoine Semenyo, who didn't play for Ghana during the break.

‌



City are preparing to return to action in the league following the bombshell news that they have been found guilty on 114 of the 115 charges by an independent commission.

View 2 Images Erling Haaland embraced Stale Solbakken as he went off (Image: Eric Verhoeven/Soccrates/Getty Images)

The club have submitted an appeal, having been found to have used a "disguised funding scheme" between 2009 and 2018 to hide secret funding of more than £830million.

‌



They said in a statement: "The club’s firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.

"The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

"We will continue to respect due process and are necessarily restricted in what we can say further until all proceedings are complete."

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel sends Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham warning to England's rivals
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel sends Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham warning to England's rivals

Thomas Tuchel hailed his talismanic duo after Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham put on a dominant display as England thrashed Croatia 7-0 in the Nations League

View 3 Images England's Jude Bellingham and Harry Kane celebrate vs Croatia

Thomas Tuchel says Jude Bellingham and Harry Kane have formed a “love” affair on the pitch - and they can get even better.

‌



‌



The deadly duo have wiped out England’s World Cup hangover and got the nation dreaming of winning Euro 2028.

‌



Kane and Bellingham inspired England’s record-breaking victory in Croatia as they smashed seven in a win to make the rest of Europe sit up and take notice. Incredibly, Bellingham and Kane have now got ten goal involvements between them in three Nations League games.

‌



Three Lions boss Tuchel has changed their roles to push them further forward together and says England’s front four - including wingers Bukayo Saka and Anthony Gordon - is “on the highest level.”

When asked about Bellingham and Kane, Tuchel said: “They were good in the World Cup. They get better and better. They love playing with each other. They understand each other better.

‌

“We adjusted the positions after the tournament slightly, but it's a front four first of all, and the movements and the counter-movements are on the highest level. It's always a team performance, and it was a team performance on the highest level today.

“I haven't seen too many of the Real Madrid matches but I think Jude almost plays a little bit more offensive for us. That's where I see him in the most dangerous position. We can overload both sides now.

‌



“Like I said, we adjusted their positioning after the World Cup. Jude plays on a high level together with everyone else, and yeah, I'm happy about individual performances, but I'm even more happy about the complexity of the team performance.”

View 3 Images Bellingham and Kane were in on the act again for England

Kane believes England’s record-breaking win in Rijeka - it was Croatia’s worst-ever defeat - shows that they are building towards realising their dream of winning Euro 2028 and they have put their World Cup hangover behind them.

‌



Captain Marvel Kane added: “We spoke about it after the World Cup. It would have been easy to maybe take our foot off the gas in this Nations League and just get ready for the Euros.

"But I think the biggest missing piece in our team at the moment is playing the big nations consistently.

View 3 Images Kane and Bellingham have a staggering 10 goal involvements in three games between them

"If we finish in the top two in this group, we play a quarterfinal against the top nations, a semi final, and a final next year. All great preparation leading into the Euros in a couple of years.

"From our point of view, it's not time to take our foot off the gas. It's time to put our foot down and keep showing not just ourselves but the whole of Europe that we're a real dominant team. Performances like this will definitely show that.”

Sports.title: England new boy Alex Scott sends Thomas Tuchel clear message and hails 'scary' team-mate
Sports.content:
England new boy Alex Scott sends Thomas Tuchel clear message and hails 'scary' team-mate

Alex Scott produced a statement performance on his first start for England, helping the Three Lions thrash Croatia 7-0 to make it back-to-back wins in their Nations League campaign

View 3 Images Alex Scott has broken into the England team (Image: Michael Regan - The FA/The FA via Getty Images)

Alex Scott says his World Cup heartbreak gave him “more hunger” to force his way into Thomas Tuchel's plans. Bournemouth midfielder Scott, 23, went to the pre-tournament training camp in Florida but did not get a cap in the friendlies and also missed out on the squad in the summer.

‌



‌



But Scott has started the season in brilliant form for his club and made his first start for England in Croatia having come on as a substitute in the Czech Republic. Scott now looks made to measure for England's midfield and looked at home straight away even on his full debut.

‌



Scott said: "It gave me more hunger but I've said there's so many top players for this country, it's a tough squad to get into. There was no bad feelings about not going to the World Cup, I went to the prep camp, I wanted to do that and learn as much as I can and it helped me coming into this camp and starting to play games.

‌



"Off the pitch, the stuff that I learned there, being around the group, it's made me feel way more comfortable. It can be challenging but for me it's not been at all. The lads and the group we've got here have made it so comfortable for me.

"Leading up to the game I've been on a few camps now, they make it easy for you and make you feel as comfortable and confident as possible. I just want to go and play my normal football. I spoke to a few of the lads before the game and they said exactly that, 'Go on and do what you do for your club, be confident, be brave'."

England boss Tuchel has described Scott as the most in-form midfielder in the Premier League and admitted it was tough to leave him out in the summer. But Scott says there was no special advice from the England boss after he did not make the cut - but just to keep pushing.

Scott said: "I wouldn't say he said anything, probably just get your head down and keeping playing as well as possible. I've started the season pretty well with Bournemouth - that was important to me and coming into this team and pushing the lads who have been playing well and have been mainstays in midfield, that was what I wanted to do."

‌



Scott also answered the notion that England do not have midfielders with possession and ball retention in their DNA. He also relished the partnership with Elliot Anderson who he knows well from England under-21 duty. Scott added: "First start and they don't come much better than that.

View 3 Images Alex Scott shone on his full England debut (Image: Michael Regan - The FA/The FA via Getty Images)

‌



"Seven goals and we were deadly from the off. That front four we've got and players coming off the bench is frightening. It's an honour to be part of that group and be part of this team.

"Me and Elliot work really well together. We saw that last year at the Euros and we've been speaking about it ever since, playing this midfield together. I thought we did really well out there, of course the result probably shows that.

"I love playing with Elliot, he makes life so easy for me as his partner in there. He's probably one of the best midfielders in the world at the moment. I think we just bounce off each other very well, we both like getting on the ball, aggressive off the ball, we suit each other the way we play so playing next to him is great for me and I know he enjoys it as well.

‌



"We were ruthless off the ball, our counter press and on the break we scored a few goals and had a few chances. That's what we do really well, the players we've got in this team it suits them really well. We did perfectly and everything came together nicely."

Scott also says that “scary” Jude Bellingham is even better in person. The Real Madrid superstar has been in superb form in the Nations League and could easily become one of England’s greatest ever players.

View 3 Images Jude Bellingham is 'the best midfielder in the world', according to Alex Scott (Image: Michael Regan - The FA/The FA via Getty Images)

‌



Scott said: "Honestly, I've never seen anything like it. He's even better in person, seeing it up close and being on the same pitch as him... he's the best midfielder in the world, one of the best players in the world for sure and a great human being.

"Everyone knows that - the fans know that, everyone in the world knows what he's like as a person. On the pitch his ability is scary and that's the benchmark we need to live up to."

Scott says England are now clicking and there seven goal thrashing of Croatia will make the rest of Europe sit up and take notice. He added: "It's hard work, it's the level we've got in our team. The front four were unbelievable and it makes it easy playing behind that. Anthony Gordon is deadly making runs in behind, his pace and ability.

Article continues below

"Jude was everywhere on the pitch, Harry Kane the same and Bukayo Saka was ruthless as well. Playing behind these guys is great for me and Elliot and the backline were excellent with a clean sheet. It feels like the perfect performance.

"I think we've had tough games - Spain was a tough game and we did really well in that one. Unfortunately we didn't get the win. But we beat Czechia and then come here and beat Croatia so we know how good we are and how good we can be so it's important to put these markers down and beat teams like that to scare opposition in the future."

Sports.title: Premier League icon sacked from first managerial role at crisis club after cryptic interview
Sports.content:
Premier League icon sacked from first managerial role at crisis club after cryptic interview

Former Sunderland midfielder Lee Cattermole, 39, has been sacked by crisis-hit Gateshead, having overseen a disastrous start to the season in the National League

View 2 Images Lee Cattermole has been sacked by Gateshead (Image: Ed Sykes/Getty Images)

Lee Cattermole has been sacked by Gateshead after suggesting there were people at the club who didn't want the team to succeed.

‌



‌



Cattermole landed his first managerial role at Gateshead in June and oversaw a disastrous start to the season. The 39-year-old, who spent 10 years playing for Sunderland, managed to record just one win from their 12 league games and departs with the club rock bottom of the National League.

‌



Gateshead were beaten 2-1 by Worthing on Saturday, prompting a fiery post-match interview from Cattermole, who alluded to issues behind the scenes. The club failed to pay their staff and players for September after director Mark Nellist resigned and withdrew his financial support.

‌



"Everyone has to be united, this club is nowhere near that, nowhere near that," Cattermole said after the loss to Worthing. "The club is nowhere near where it should be, it’s been disappointing. Press goes out about the players wages not being paid. That’s disappointing but it happens.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



"But it goes from before that, well before that. We need to figure out who wants to be part of the new regime or whatever you want to call it and find out who wants to be part of it. If we do, we will get the club going because a club like Gateshead has been really competitive in certain spells and that is when everyone is united and everyone is together.

"I’ve been fully aware for the whole time I’ve been here, that isn’t the case. I’ve been managing it, I’ve been dealing with it, I’ve been trying to put a positive spin on it and prepare the team.

"But ultimately, there are people in this building that don’t want the team to move forward and I know that. I can feel it, I see it and the clearer that we can be, that’s staff, players, fans, we might start winning games but it can’t happen, it doesn’t just happen."

‌



View 2 Images Lee Cattermole made 262 appearances for Sunderland (Image: Steven Hadlow/Getty Images)

The club is "appealing to shareholders to continue funding support" in the wake of Nellist's efforts to hand over his shares to fellow shareholder Stephen Paylor.

Gateshead have lost 10 of their 12 league games and are already eight points adrift of safety. Ben Clark has been appointed as interim manager to replace Cattermole.

‌



"There’s been a lot of change and the moment we iron that out and get it going and get everyone aligned, so there’s no hiding place," the former Sunderland star said before the sacking. "Because what happens when you have a struggled, you have people that want to move it forward and other people play hide and seek.

"That happens in every club up and down the country. I’ve been part of it, I’m now trying to lead it and I need every staff member on board so we can go forward. If they are not, the players can feel it, staff members feel it and once we do iron it out, we might have a chance of winning some games."

Sports.title: Ex-Premier League manager claims 'everyone knew' Man City were cheating
Sports.content:
Ex-Premier League manager claims 'everyone knew' Man City were cheating

Manchester City's systematic breaking of the Premier League's financial rules has sent shockwaves through the football world, but Jesse Marsch says it was common knowledge in the game

View 3 Images Jesse Marsch has spoken about Manchester City's guilty verdict (Image: Omar Vega/Getty Images)

Former Leeds manager Jesse Marsch has claimed that "everyone knew" about Manchester City's cheating of the Premier League's financial rules well before their guilty verdict.

‌



‌



City were found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges by an independent commission and could be relegated from the Premier League as punishment. The club was found to have used a "disguised funding scheme" between 2009 and 2018 to hide secret funding of more than £830million.

‌



They have consistently pleaded their innocence and have launched an appeal which will prolong the process significantly. However, the revelation that City used "sham" arrangements to "disguise the true extent of certain club liabilities" has sent shockwaves through the football world.

‌



Marsch is now the Canada manager but previously took charge of Leeds in the 2022/23 season, when they were relegated from the Premier League. City won the Premier League, as well as the Champions League and FA Cup, that season and, despite being well after the years of their financial wrongdoing, Marsch holds a grudge.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



“I think Man City should be punished severely. I think they should have to go down, and by the way, everyone knew about it. Everyone knew,” he told the Guardian.

“That summer [2022], us and Man City were the only teams that said we made money. For us, we did make money, because we sold Raphinha, we sold Kalvin Phillips [to City]. We had a lot left over from what we bought.

"At the time, we weren’t in a position financially to not save. Our ownership didn’t have deep pockets. Whereas when Man City says this, I was literally like, ‘Are you kidding me? Is this some kind of joke?’

‌



View 3 Images Manchester City won the treble in 2022/23 (Image: Catherine Ivill/Getty Images)

“When they said they got Erling Haaland for £52m, it’s like: ‘Yeah, OK, sure!’ So, I knew there were inconsistencies in it, but what can you do? You just put your arms in the air and go, ‘This is football’.”

Leeds' grievances about the 2022/23 campaign goes beyond just City, with the club having finished below both Everton and Nottingham Forest, who were later deducted points for breaching the Premier League's financial rules.

‌



Marsch's comments follow those of Aston Villa manager Unai Emery, who raised eyebrows earlier in the week by claiming "many other clubs have inflated their budgets".

View 3 Images Jesse Marsch was sacked and Leeds relegated in the 2022/23 season (Image: Justin Setterfield/Getty Images)

He told Diario de Sevilla: "It's an issue that was already known. Because we all have our restrictions, we have to sell players to comply with Financial Fair Play, we have to figure out how to draw up contracts with new people.

Article continues below

"Financial Fair Play seeks a financial balance so that what you generate is spent and there isn't inflation. Yes, many other clubs have inflated their budgets, and now it's coming to light, and naturally there's a decline.

"That's something that the courts and those responsible will have to decide. I feel sorry because how that team played. With [Pep] Guardiola, there were times when they were unmatched."

Sports.title: £65m Man City signing hints at return to old club days after 114 charges verdict
Sports.content:
£65m Man City signing hints at return to old club days after 114 charges verdict

A player who signed for Manchester City for £65million in the summer has hinted that he would be keen on a move back to his former club

View 2 Images Iliman Ndiaye signed for Manchester City in the summer (Image: Getty Images)

Manchester City summer signing Iliman Ndiaye has hinted that he would been keen on returning to former club Marseille in the future and admitted: "I don't think the story is over."

‌



‌



Ndiaye, 26, joined City in a £65million deal from Everton in the summer and has made an impressive start to life at the Etihad Stadium. Although the Senegal international hasn't produced a single goal or an assist in his first four appearances, he has helped City continue their winning start and was a standout performer when he came on against Manchester United last month.

‌



But, despite joining City less than five weeks ago, Ndiaye has now revealed that he would like to return to Marseille in the future. The French-born attacking midfielder spent one season at the Stade Velodrome, after joining from Sheffield United for £20m in 2023, before leaving to sign for Everton 12 months later. He scored just four times and provided five assists in 46 games for the Ligue 1 side.

‌



Man City fight back with 'PROOF' government paid sponsorship deals in appeal over 115 charges READ MORE :

When asked about Marseille fans chanting for him to return to the club, Ndiaye said: "The shouts from Marseille supporters asking me to come back? It is nice to hear. I don't think that the story is finished, but we will see. I'm just saying, I never know where it'll lead me, but we'll see anyway.

"I only have positive memories of my time at OM [Marseille], and it was a source of pride for me. I don't miss a single match. It's my club, and it always will be."

Ndiaye is thought to have supported Marseille since he was a child and jumped at the chance to sign for them when he left Sheffield United three years ago. Although it didn't work out during his short time in southern France, it appears he wouldn't say no to giving it another shot.

‌



View 2 Images Iliman Ndiaye in action for Manchester City (Image: Getty Images)

Meanwhile, Ndiaye's comments come just days after the Premier League announced that City have been found guilty of all charges concerning breaches of its financial regulations spanning from 2009/10 to 2017/18. These included artificially inflating revenue by over £900million through "sham" sponsorship agreements.

City, however, have denied any wrongdoing and appealed the decision on Thursday. The club believe they are "innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League" and say they have "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence" to support their case.

‌



"Manchester City Football Club can confirm that at 7pm on Thursday 1st October 2026 the Club lodged its comprehensive Appeal against the opinion of the Premier League Commission, in relation to the Premier League disciplinary matter," City said in a statement on Friday.

"The Club's firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe. The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

Article continues below

"We will continue to respect due process and are necessarily restricted in what we can say further until all proceedings are complete."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Sale defy Vermeulen's first-half red card to beat Saracens
Sports.content:
Sale Sharks won a real battle against Saracens in the Gallagher Prem

Sale defied Jacques Vermeulen's first-half red card to dispatch Saracens 21-17 with Tom O'Flaherty emerging as the star of a slugfest at StoneX Stadium.

Vermeulen was shown a 20-minute red for a dangerous tackle on Tomos Williams at a point in the first half when Alex Lozowski was in the sin bin because of the same offence.

Saracens then took control but it was only temporary and in the 41st minute O'Flaherty produced the match's pivotal moment by racing over for a dynamic solo try.

It was part of a dominant second half from Sale, who capitalised on the hosts' lifeless performance to bounce back after losing to Bristol on the opening weekend with their hooker Nathan Jibulu also outstanding.

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

Referee Joe James and TMO Hamish Smales experienced a busy opening half an hour, issuing two cards and disallowing a Saracens try.

It had started so well for Sale when Jibulu finished a driving maul but soon after centre Lozowski was sent to the sin bin for a high tackle on Alfie Barbeary, who was forced off for an HIA.

Worse was to come when Vermeulen was given his marching orders for a dangerous challenge on Williams as the Sharks looked to press home an attack down the right touchline.

It meant Saracens were given the opportunity to play against 13 for three minutes and Sale's situation would have deteriorated further had Courtney Lawes not seen an attempted deliberate knock go backwards.

Almost immediately the hosts appeared to have taken advantage but a Nick Tompkins try was ruled out because of obstruction by Nick Isiekwe and it was not until Eroni Mawi bundled over in the 34th minute that they were off the mark.

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

For all Saracens' sustained pressure they still trailed 7-5 and a minute into the second half that became 14-5 after O'Flaherty caught a George Ford up and under that went sideways and then slipped through the home defence before sprinting over.

Sale ran out of tacklers to enable Sione Va'enuku to strike back almost immediately but they resumed on the front foot and were frustrated to be penalised just short of the whitewash on two occasions.

They continued knocking on the door and suddenly changed pace with a series of runs gaining yards until Ford sent Ben Bamber galloping over.

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

Sale now led 21-10 and Saracens' dismal afternoon continued when Theo Dan limped off while his fellow hooker Jamie George watched from the stands, sidelined by injury.

Charlie Bracken combined with brother Jack to race over with eight minutes to go and the Sharks then let another commanding position slip away because of a penalty close to the line, but they had already done enough to see off Saracens.

Sports.title: Taylor stars as Colts cruise past Commanders in NFL's return to London
Sports.content:
Jonathan Taylor scored twice as Indianapolis Colts overcame Washington Commanders 30-13 at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium to open this year's triple-header of NFL International Series games in London.

The Commanders initially had the better of things, limiting the Colts offense to 20 total yards in the first quarter as they claimed a 6-0 lead.

But an injury to QB Marcus Mariota when sacked on the play prior to Washington's second field goal proved a turning point, with third-stringer Athan Kaliakmanis - a seventh-round draft pick - unable to lead the Commanders to victory despite a couple of eye-catching plays, including a 47-yard deep-ball TD for his first in the NFL.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Washington Commanders rookie quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis finds Treylon Burks for his first NFL touchdown

Colts quarterback Daniel Jones, who had two turnovers in the first half, ran in Indianapolis' third touchdown of the game early in the fourth quarter to stretch their lead to two scores - and there was to be no way back for Washington.

Image: Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones dives in for the game-clinching touchdown in the fourth quarter

The NFL returns to Tottenham next Sunday for a clash between the Philadelphia Eagles and Jacksonville Jaguars, who are back in action facing the Houston Texans at Wembley a week later, on Sunday October 18.

Stats leaders:

Indianapolis Colts

Passing: Daniel Jones, 19/34, 143 yards, 1 rushing TD, 1 INT

Daniel Jones, 19/34, 143 yards, 1 rushing TD, 1 INT Rushing: Jonathan Taylor, 20 carries, 95 yards, 2 TDs

Jonathan Taylor, 20 carries, 95 yards, 2 TDs Receiving: Laquon Treadwell, 9 catches, 42 yards

Image: Jonathan Taylor scored two rushing touchdowns for Indianapolis Colts

Washington Commanders

Passing: Athan Kaliakmanis, 15/33, 186 yards, 1 TD, 1 INT

Athan Kaliakmanis, 15/33, 186 yards, 1 TD, 1 INT Rushing: Marcus Mariota, 1 carry, 35 yards

Marcus Mariota, 1 carry, 35 yards Receiving: Dyami Brown, 3 catches, 65 yards

The Colts fell behind early when Jones lost the football after he was accidentally tripped by his own team-mate, with the Commanders scoring a field goal after Odafe Oweh recovered the ball at the 20-yard line.

Mariota, filling in for injured starting QB Jayden Daniels, left the game with a knee injury when sacked on the play prior to Washington's second field goal.

Kaliakmanis came in, the 223rd overall pick from the seventh round of the 2026 NFL Draft, and though he found the going tough early on his NFL debut, Colts veteran Jones was similarly struggling and was picked off by Rasul Douglas.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jonathan Taylor runs into the end zone for the Indianapolis Colts' first touchdown in their NFL clash with Washington Commanders in London

But the Colts soon took over again on downs after the Commanders' call to go for it on fourth down from their own 46-yard line. It would prove a poor decision, helping set up Taylor's opening TD for Indianapolis to see them into a lead that they stretched to four by the half with the first of Spencer Shrader's three field goals. Taylor celebrated his score by pantomiming drinking tea in the end zone.

Kaliakmanis threw a costly interception early in the third quarter, with Taylor's second five-yard scoring run of the game then making it 17-6.

Kaliakmanis bounced back on the next drive, though, hitting Treylon Burks on a stunning, 47-yard touchdown pass deep down the left sideline that closed the gap as Burks got past star cornerback Sauce Gardner.

But the Colts (2-2) answered back with further Shrader field goals either side of Jones' touchdown run from four yards out early in the fourth quarter.

Sports.title: Labuschagne hits timely ton as Australia warm up for South Africa Tests
Sports.content:
Marnus Labuschagne scored a speedy, and timely, century in Australia's sole warm-up match before the three-Test series in South Africa from Friday, live on Sky Sports Cricket.

Labuschagne struck 111 from 89 balls, reaching three figures from 76 deliveries and hitting 19 fours, before retiring out against a Cricket South Africa Invitation XI in Potchefstroom.

The 32-year-old will hope to carry that form into the Test arena, starting in Durban this week, having gone 43 innings and over three years without a hundred in the format.

After Labuschagne - who is averaging 25.43 since the 2023 Ashes - made scores of one, 31 and four in the recent 1-1 series draw at home to Bangladesh, ex-Australia captain Ricky Ponting told Sky Sports that the batter's spot in the XI had become "untenable".

However, the Baggy Greens have kept faith with the South Africa-born player and he seems set to line up in his usual No 3 berth at Kingsmead as Australia begin their first Test series in the country since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.

Image: Steve Smith will play Test cricket in South Africa for the first time since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal

Smith scores half-century in Test tune-up

Steve Smith - who along with David Warner and Cameron Bancroft received a ban for the role he played in using sandpaper to alter the condition of the ball - Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and Matt Renshaw are the survivors from that contest eight years ago.

Smith, who followed Labuschagne in retiring out, and Renshaw scored 61 and 32 respectively on the second and final day of the tune-up for this month's Tests, while Alex Carey made 57 as Australia replied to the hosts' 318-7 with 368-6.

On day one, Australia used 11 bowlers in order to manage workload with seven taking a wicket apiece and none of the seamers getting through more than 10 overs.

Image: Josh Hazlewood was one of a plethora of bowlers used by Australia on day one of the tune-up fixture

All-rounder Cameron Green did not feature after picking up an abdominal injury in the final ODI against South Africa last week and appears a doubt for the first Test.

After the series opener in Durban, the teams will meet in Gqeberha from October 18 and then Cape Town from October 27.

South Africa also host Bangladesh and England in Test cricket this winter, with the series against Joe Root's men starting at Wanderers in Johannesburg on December 17.

Sports.title: Let’s stop doubting Thomas Tuchel: England are impressive and Euro 2028 is the target
Sports.content:
Move fast and fix things. It has been a fine week so far for Thomas Tuchel as he attempts the cyclical task of soldering together not just an England team, but a way of looking like one, all the while being battered by the to-and-fro conflicting winds of England managerdom.

There is nothing new here. This is a job that involves not just picking the right players and making high-stakes calculations over your second-half substitutions, but carrying out these basic duties while wrestling with aggrieved members of the Thuggee cult on a collapsing rope bridge outside the Temple of Doom, and simultaneously having your heart ripped out.

No other nation makes quite the same twin-track demands. Manage the games. Yeah, do that obviously. But also tell us who we are and how we should play. This is why the job will always take its pound of mince meat, why these people end up drained and hollowed out, an empty tracksuit resigning in the Wembley toilets, Roy Hodgson in Nice looking like a desiccated vampire, saying “I don’t know why I’m here”.

It is also why it was heartening in Rijeka to see Tuchel gripped with the familiar energies, still whirling about on the touchline in penitent black shoes and black trousers, looking as ever like a famine-ridden earl out taking the hounds for a walk, while simultaneously cracking the Enigma code in his hunting shed.

It feels absurd to say that Tuchel is now safe in the job, if only because the idea he wouldn’t be is so hysterical. Tuchel was never realistically in any trouble. But such is the nature of a role where you’re only ever a few rapid-fire defeats away from the incredible twin feat of a greatest-ever overseas World Cup and a near-instant heaving from the job.

We should of course keep a sense of scale over a couple of Nations League wins against underpowered opponents. The 7-0 steamrollering of Croatia was always a strange affair. From the moment the doors opened the whole occasion felt like a youth club association sports day, where everyone gets a medal at the end and the teachers do a disco dance routine.

It was an atmosphere that seemed to communicate itself to the Croatia players even as they were warming up in a notably fun and jokey way, cheered by shrill groups of junior ultras, and blasted by the Croatian version of We Didn’t Start the Fire through the ear-shredding speaker system.

Croatia played from the first minute like a team recovering from a dose of herbal sleeping tablets. Luka Modric’s every touch was met with the kind of noise more usually associated with an appearance by a Korean boyband at an Apple Store launch event, but one of the great players of the age was simply run over by England’s youthful and hungry midfield.

View image in fullscreen Jude Bellingham was superb in the win over Croatia, as he was during the World Cup. Photograph: Igor Soban/Pixsell/MB Media/Getty Images

These are also the teams you play, however. Croatia were decent enough at the World Cup. Mainly, though this came at an absolutely vital moment in the age of Tuchelism. The next 20 months are basically it, the engine room, the space where Tuchel gets to decide how good his team can be, leading in to a tournament England will never have a better chance of winning.

The only questions that really matter right now are: is there vision of a team and a way to play? And do we have forward progress? The answers to both of which are yes.

England were good in an interesting way in Croatia. We’re used to England teams that seem powerful but also flawed. In Rijeka they looked like a World Cup semi-finalist that has used that experience to improve, strong in every area, physically, technically and in its basic balance.

At times in the current era England have brought to mind the Gareth Southgate team of 2019 into 2020, when some key new players entered a blooming environment, and suddenly they were blowing away mid-range opponents. The Covid break would complicate that arc. An unprovable counter-factual: nudge those first Southgate Euros forward a year and England might have had the momentum to overpower Italy in the final.

There are two aspects to Tuchel’s England this time around. First, the reckoning up with the mistakes of the recent past. Why, oh why didn’t he take Cole Palmer? Well, maybe for the same reason Palmer’s not here now. Well, why of why, then, didn’t he take Phil Foden? This has also answered itself. The same goes for not selecting the back-up striker who is now, it turns out, playing in Saudi Arabia. It is entirely legitimate to still disagree with all these things. But it feels clearer that there was logic and reasoning here.

The past can re-litigate itself. The second key element is the sense of progress. This was always likely to be the case. It takes time to get to know your players. Tuchel had never been to an international tournament before. He was never the knockout specialist some seemed to assume. Just take a look at his record. He’s a process guy. And we are now right in the middle of that process.

View image in fullscreen Lewis Hall has enjoyed a fine international break and looks to be first choice for England at left-back. Photograph: Darko Bandić/AP

So what has changed? Most obviously making Jude Bellingham the hub of this team is an excellent idea, and not just because of his astonishing talent. Rallying around Bellingham is Tuchel’s version of Southgate’s inflatable unicorns, the talk about Spitfires, the away-days with the SAS crawling through an assault course made entirely from Cheddar cheese and Eccles cakes.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

How do you make players want to play for England? Here’s a short cut. Give them aura, brand power, magnetism. Put the big guy right at the centre. Everyone’s turning up if Jude is loving it, and you have a chance for two weeks to exist in his forcefield.

Then there’s the way England have played. There is always talk about “a Premier League style”, which has never been a single thing. But these players are definitely best suited to high-intensity, hard-running, duel-winning football. This wasn’t only there in successfully outmuscling an ageing Mateo Kovacic, who even in his pomp had the air of a frail Victorian child masquerading as an elite modern midfielder, shorts hiked up, skinny legs gamely covering the turf.

England also played like this for half an hour against the world champions, and narrowly lost a game where they went 1-0 down after a minute and missed a late penalty. This felt like an evolved version of the “packet-ball” intensity that blew Croatia away at the World Cup for 20 minutes then could never quite click into gear again. The next Euros are in England. Cancel the heatwave, and they can play like this for longer.

Then there is the issue of balance. Lewis Hall: yes, a proper left-back with a left foot. Jarell Quansah makes lots of sense now, offering something of the Kyle Walker-style recovery athleticism. Alex Scott looked really good in Rijeka, a genuinely smart, head-up, surging midfield presence.

Tuchel is right. He can’t roll into a tournament with two first-choice midfielders. Scott offered something different in the exact area England lose these high-stakes, high-intensity games. He even knows who his back-up centre-forward is now, and it is of course Jude. Ask any question right now. The answer is likely to be the same.

Here is another unprovable counter-factual. England would have beaten that Argentina team in Atlanta with this team in Rijeka. This should not be a source of why-oh-why frustration. It’s forward momentum, learning new patterns, adding new tricks. Stick Bellingham up front in the second half, pack Scott into a three-man midfield, and they’ve got a far better chance of seeing that game out.

The process is also far from done. England need competition on the right wing. Bukayo Saka is an excellent footballer. But he’s not a weapon other teams will fear. Add an England-issue Michael Olise, for example, and this team looks entirely different in its threat levels. Max Dowman is still just a very nice idea at this point. But there’s time. And he doesn’t need to be perfect.

Finally, and back to the key figure in this cycle, there is the total weaponising of Bellingham, whose role in the team is now beautifully clarified. Station him in forward areas and he will still press and harry and add a defensive function. But turning, running, breaking in transitions, making risky creative passes, he is just a supreme footballer. Not to mention a one-man mission statement of the way this team wants to play.

Tournaments aren’t won with a 7-0 win on the Adriatic coast in front of 6,000 over-caffeinated schoolchildren. But there is progress here. And that time will pass in a wink.

Sports.title: Denmark sink Wales as Rasmus Højlund makes Danny Ward pay for blunder
Sports.content:
Only a few days ago Craig Bellamy suggested Wales had blown Nations League A4 wide open with a hand grenade but here Danny Ward detonated it to gift Denmark a penalty and Rasmus Højlund the chance to earn a slender victory from the spot.

Until that moment of madness, after 73 minutes, Ward had kept Wales in the game, his best stop a sublime right-hand save to prevent Gustav Isaksen a headed opener. But after keeping Denmark at bay, he scored an own goal of sorts by taking out Isaksen in the box after a miskick. Bellamy covered his face, using his right hand as a temporary visor while the video assistant referee, Ivan Bebek, reviewed the incident. Then came the unwanted confirmation from the referee and Højlund rippled a pocket of the Wales net with a flawless penalty. A first clean sheet since beating Liechtenstein last November also went out of the window. The life of a goalkeeper, eh?

At the outset, the difficulty for Wales was to trying to replicate the high of Thursday’s victory over Norway, arguably Bellamy’s finest moment in the job, the obvious caveat that their opponents played almost all of the second half with 10 men. The emotions felt after that triumph were always going to be hard to match but despite the awkward 7.45pm kick-off on a Sunday night, the Barry Horns, the brass brand who enthusiastically soundtrack Wales matches, made a racket and contributed to a fine atmosphere. Even without a full house, the prematch anthem was stirring if not spine-tingling. Bellamy stressed the importance of building on the performance in midweek as a minimum, against opposition who last week comprehensively outplayed them in Copenhagen.

Bellamy said it was impossible to name the same XI owing to the toll of four matches across 11 days but in the end Daniel James was the only player to make way, Brennan Johnson taking his place on the wing. Ben Davies, whose only minutes for Tottenham came against a Charlton Athletic B team in the Carabao Cup, started a fourth successive game this window, together with Neco Williams and Ethan Ampadu, whose Leeds team visit Arsenal in Saturday’s early kick-off when the Premier League resumes. Ward continued in goal but had little to do in the first half, Højlund’s weak sixth-minute shot, on the spin, the visitors’ sole shot on target in the opening period. An alert Ward was called into action early in the second half, preventing the Napoli striker Højlund from sweeping in Andreas Skov Olsen’s cross with his left leg.

View image in fullscreen Rasmus Højlund celebrates his second-half winner for Denmark. Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

On the eve of this match Bellamy was effusive in his praise of Pierre-Emile Højbjerg, now of Marseille, describing the former Spurs midfielder as a “coach on the pitch”. After just two touches, a pass and a failed cross, Højbjerg was forced off after seemingly pulling a hamstring. Wales, all in red, had a couple of bright moments but Denmark looked the more dangerous in a low-key game. It was almost as if this was the fourth game in a marathon camp. Isaksen dropped a header wide and Højlund miskicked another decent chance after a speeding Mohamed Daramy beat Davies and Ben Cabango on the flank.

Ward’s first save of the half, to deny Højlund, was smart but his second was phenomenal. Joakim Mæhle raced down the left and before reaching the byline flung into the box a feathery, hanging cross. Isaksen, of Lazio, read the trajectory of the ball all the way and even cleverly adjusted his body position to pick his spot, the target the bottom right-hand corner of Ward’s goal. Isaksen appeared to have directed the perfect header towards goal but Ward got a brilliant right hand to the ball and pushed it on to his right post. At that point, Ward was undoubtedly Wales’s hero.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There were glimpses of quality from Wales but they failed to test Mads Hermansen, a former Leicester clubmate of Ward’s. Thomas was again a threat on the left, intermittently destroying the Denmark right-back Rasmus Kristensen and Liam Cullen, now of Leicester after ending his near two-decade stint at Swansea, was industrious as a playmaker. But then, out of nothing, Ward conceded a clumsy penalty. Cabango shifted the ball across to his goalkeeper, from right to left, but Ward, looking to move the ball on again, inadvertently shovelled a miscued pass straight to Isaksen. A panicked Ward instantly tried to make amends but his desperation got the better of him and he clattered into Isaksen and gave Hojlund the chance to beat him from 12 yards. Hojlund waited for Ward to dive to his left and slotted the ball into the opposite corner.

Sports.title: No handshakes again as Ireland play out tetchy ‘home’ draw with Israel in Serbia
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland were pegged back to a draw by Israel in another tetchy meeting between the sides, this time played without fans at TSC Arena in Backa Topola, Serbia.

Troy Parrott’s first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break in the Group B3 game. Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two ­minutes after the restart.

Ireland players again wore black armbands and bowed their heads ­during the Israeli national anthem before the teams’ second Nations League meeting on Sunday. The Israeli players also wore black armbands in memory of the people killed in the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023.

Ireland’s goalkeeper Caoimhín Kelleher stepped in as captain for Dara O’Shea – who was excused to be with his wife for the birth of their child – and he pointedly avoided shaking hands with Israel captain Peretz, despite completing the usual pre-match formality with the referee and one of his assistants.

Kelleher repeated O’Shea’s actions before the first match in Debrecen, Hungary last week, when O’Shea declined to shake Israel captain Manor Solomon’s hand. Ireland went on to win that game 3-0 through three first-half goals. Solomon was dropped to the bench for yesterday’s match. Israel forward Sayed Abu Farchi was back in the squad after serving a suspension for getting sent off following his goal celebration during Israel’s 3-1 defeat to Austria last month.

Finn Azaz, whose mother has Israeli heritage, was among the Irish substitutes after playing from the start against Austria on Thursday.

The Republic had started to find some fluidity when Jimmy Dunne won a penalty, after arriving at the post to try tucking home a rebound from an earlier saved Parrott effort.

The Israel goalkeeper Assaf Tzur scrambled to smother the ball, and Dunne was brought down under the challenge of Peretz. The Republic were awarded the penalty after a lengthy VAR check.

Peretz levelled the scoring two minutes after the restart. An Oscar Gloukh effort took a favourable deflection off Liam Scales and into the path of the acting Israel captain, who gave ­Kelleher no chance with a low finish.

Sunday’s game was initially supposed to be played in Dublin, but the Football Association of Ireland moved the game to a neutral venue for “operational reasons” in June following widespread calls for a boycott in protest of Israel’s actions in Gaza. The FAI said the game would be played with no fans present.

It followed the FAI’s own motion the previous November calling on Uefa to ban Israel from club and international competitions.

The difficult atmosphere between the sides spilled over during a clash as the sides entered the tunnel at half-time. Officials then broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

Sports.title: Nations League roundup: Haaland limps off in Norway’s loss to Portugal
Sports.content:
Title-holders Portugal maintained their 100% record in the Nations League with a 2-1 home win over Norway on Sunday to seal a place in ⁠the March quarter-finals, while Manchester City’s problems may have got worse after Erling Haaland limped off for the visitors.

Portugal hope their victory at the Estádio Do Dragão shifts the focus further away from Cristiano Ronaldo’s abrupt exit from the squad last week. Gonçalo Ramos netted 11 minutes from time to ensure they secured a top-two ⁠finish in Group A4 as ⁠they moved six points ​ahead of second-placed Denmark, who won 1-0 at Wales.

The home side in Porto were still under a cloud from Ronaldo’s dispute with coach Jorge Jesus, although they were triumphant without him in Denmark ⁠last Thursday after he walked out on the squad, and continued their winning ways on Sunday.

Norway took the lead in ​the 36th minute from centre-back Kristoffer Ajer, who hit a ‌dipping half-volley from the edge of ‌the box. But if that effort was sumptuous, João Cancelo’s thrashing effort to equalise two minutes later was even more awe-inspiring.

Ramos’s ‌winner came off his calf after João Félix had headed across goal for him to score.

View image in fullscreen Gonçalo Ramos knocks down the corner flag in delight after scoring. Photograph: SPP/Shutterstock

Portugal’s win was soured by a red card for Francisco Conceição four minutes from time. He gave the referee a cynical thumbs up after receiving a yellow card and was immediately shown a second.

The Netherlands took over at the top of Group A2, after beating Serbia 2-1 in Eindhoven, but only on goal difference from ⁠Greece, who held on grimly for a goalless draw at home to Germany in Thessaloniki.

With their captain Virgil van Dijk celebrating a 100th cap, the Netherlands went ahead against Serbia when Teun Koopmeiners’s 31st-minute free-kick evaded all in the penalty area and ​crept into the corner. However, the visitors were level within four minutes as Aleksa Terzic crossed for teenager Mihajlo Cvetkovic to rise over Koopmeiners and head in his first international goal.

It took until the 72nd minute to go back ahead when Denzel Dumfries’s low cross was turned back across the goal by Tijjani Reijnders, sliding in at the far post, and tapped in by Joshua Zirkzee, who ⁠received a late call-up to the Dutch squad last week.

Germany dominated away against Greece, but Jürgen ​Klopp’s inexperienced side could not find the net, ​and they have won only one of ​their first four games under the new coach.

Austria needed a late equaliser to draw 1-1 at Kosovo ​but still have a three-point ‌lead at the top ​of Group B3 after the ​Republic of Ireland and Israel drew 1-1 behind closed doors in the Serbian town of Backa Topola.

In Group D2, Abdulakh Khaybulayev’s first-half goal was enough to send Azerbaijan top of the standings with a 1-0 win over previously unbeaten Lithuania, while veteran Teddy Teuma came on as a second-half substitute to hand Malta a 1-0 home win over Andorra in Group D1.

Sports.title: Shaw seals thrilling win over Arsenal to extend Manchester City’s 100% WSL start
Sports.content:
Arsenal’s under-pressure head coach Renée Slegers still believes they will turn their form around, despite falling 10 points behind Manchester City with Sunday’s defeat in an absorbing six-goal thriller against the defending champions.

Arsenal were last season’s runners-up in the Women’s Super League and had high hopes of mounting a strong challenge this term but their chances of lifting a first WSL title since 2019 now appear to be hanging by a thread after five rounds of fixtures, while City maintained their 100% start by coming from behind twice to beat Slegers’ struggling side.

The 37-year-old Dutchwoman, who in January signed a new contract until the summer of 2029, said on Friday that she felt the full support of the club. Asked, after this pivotal 4-2 defeat, whether she would be the one in charge after this month’s international break, she replied: “All I know so far is that the last couple of days we’ve been together as a club, as a team, with support, aligning on the direction. Of course, this result is disappointing, but I’m here, I’m full of energy and I care a lot for the club.”

Slegers added she feels the international break will come at a good time to change environments and that there will be a “big review of our season so far” during the break. She continued: “We see solutions and we see the closeness. It’s not that we’re totally off it. It’s been consistently about margins – when we get them on our side, I think we’re going to be really good.”

The match was the first to be played at the Etihad Stadium since the Premier League published the guilty verdict against Manchester City and there was something of a subdued atmosphere outside the stadium in the buildup to kick-off. That quickly changed once the game started, and was wholly different in the second half as the hosts began to take control and their supporters were thoroughly enjoying themselves.

City had frequently insisted their women’s team were treating this as “business as usual” before their draw with Real Madrid on Thursday. There were very few references to the ongoing saga here on Sunday, aside from some Arsenal fans chanting “same old City, always cheating” during the first half, and one City fan – sitting just in front of the media seats – who defiantly shouted about which part of the anatomy people could “stick your 115 charges”, but nobody else joined in. Matters on the pitch were more interesting.

City will have felt aggrieved about the nature of Arsenal’s opener, as replays showed that Lisa Baum appeared to be offside when Lotte Wubben-Moy headed goalwards. Baum was the quickest to get to the rebound after Ayaka Yamashita’s save and poked home. The visitors could not hold on until the break, however, as Lauren Hemp’s deflected strike found its way into the far corner.

Arsenal went back in front shortly after half-time when Yui Hasegawa lost the ball inside her own area and Alessia Russo pounced, curling a terrific finish into the far corner. It was her first league goal of the campaign. Arsenal appeared to be in control until a triple substitution from Andrée Jeglertz, including the introduction of Kerstin Casparij, changed things.

View image in fullscreen Alessia Russo pounces to make it 2-1 to Arsenal at Manchester City. Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/Reuters

The 26-year-old, playing as an inverted full-back, latched on to a loose ball and curled in a delightful strike to equalise and soon afterwards Hemp tucked a tidy finish through Anneke Borbe’s legs to make it 3-2. Suddenly Arsenal’s body language changed and City were on top. They added a clinical fourth when Shaw latched on to Aoba Fujino’s excellent through-ball and her low finish was superb.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Jeglertz was full of praise for Casparij and his centre-back pairing of Jade Rose and Alex Greenwood. Asked about Arsenal’s woes, he said he still expects them to have a strong campaign, saying: “They have great football players - I’m pretty sure that when we are coming into spring that they will definitely be one of the teams battling.”

Arsenal’s problems were exacerbated by their midfielder Mariona Caldentey going off with a suspected hamstring injury. The Arsenal defender Wubben-Moy said there was unity as she told Sky Sports the players “fought for ourselves, for Renée and for the fans - but ultimately the result didn’t do that justice”, adding: “This is an unprecedented position for Arsenal to be in. It’s up to us to get ourselves out of it.”

Her words may offer some solace to Slegers. So will the sight of the 2,000 travelling fans applauding her after the game. The upcoming “review” will determine whether or not that was a farewell.

Sports.title: Jesse Marsch: ‘We Americans have been inundated with propaganda since we were young’
Sports.content:
Peak leaf hasn’t yet arrived in Montreal but the bursts of gold and butterscotch up on the hill that gave this place its name still mushroom out by the hour.

Sitting in a glass-panelled hotel mezzanine at the foot of Mount Royal, Canada men’s coach Jesse Marsch has his mind on another harvest. When this extended autumnal international window ends, he will decamp to Italy, where the olive crops at his Tuscan villa are ready for reaping.

Flight paths between Canada and Europe have been busy lately, and figurative transatlantic distances are closing fast. As Canada’s relations with the noisiest neighbour to the south stretch and fray, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney is forging alliances with the EU so close that the bloc is apparently inventing new membership categories.

As an American residing in Europe who is also a Canadian leader with robust approval ratings, Marsch is watching. To him, it feels right.

“I’ve always thought Canada was a little bit more European than the US anyway. Right?” Marsch tells the Guardian. “But certainly now there’s enough happening politically and economically that you would say, we’re looking much more like that. There’s talk of [Canada becoming an associate EU member] even actually happening. I like that aspect.

“There’s a uniqueness to Canada in terms of how truly multiethnic this country has become. You can see that Canada is not just a North American country any more, you know? That bodes well for our sport and for the makeup of our team, the makeup of our fans.”

Having led Canada’s men to historic highs at this summer’s World Cup, Marsch is feeling his way into his second act in the job. Some of his sideline displays – we’ll get to that meme – may have irked outsiders, especially in his homeland, during the tournament. Yet, having extended for four more years, Marsch is someone an overwhelming majority of Canadians are happy to have at the helm. There are more than a few cross-points between Marsch and Carney.

“My impression is that first of all, he is a really smart guy, but a really normal guy,” Marsch says of Carney, who attended a number of Canada’s World Cup matches. “Sometimes you meet a US president, and you’re overwhelmed, maybe by their presence, the position itself. I’ve met Clinton, George Bush Sr, Obama, Trump, Biden. Oh, and Carter. Six in person. Carney, compared to all of them, the closest would be Obama. A real air of intelligence, but a real air of being a regular guy. I think that that’s perfect for this country and this moment.

“He has shown great support for us. I made a joke with him that ‘I heard you’re an Everton fan?’ and he goes, ‘Yeah’. And I go, ‘I’m sorry about that’. He replies: ‘Why does everybody say that? Everybody has to pick their team and stick by them.’ I said, ‘I appreciate that you don’t switch from Everton to Arsenal or Liverpool, like everybody else’. There’s something so genuine [about] that. Could a president of the US ever be an Everton fan? No chance.”

View image in fullscreen Canada prime minister Mark Carney greeted Marsch’s team in the locker room after the team’s win over Qatar at the 2026 World Cup. Photograph: Jared C Tilton/Fifa/Getty Images

Circumstances, as well as natural impulses, have led Marsch to play statesman during this prolonged cooling of relations between Canada and his home country. He’s been defiant – lashing out at Donald Trump’s “51st state” barbs – then more deft. Sometimes, especially when it comes to the US Soccer Federation he said led him on with a job offer only to renege, he finds it hard to hide his disdain.

This window is the start of turning the page to the next phase of his Canada project. He admits, with a chuckle, that the four years stretching ahead feel long but there are imminent goals – a first trophy in 25 years, cracking and consolidating inside the world’s top 24.

A win over Chile in Toronto and 2-0 win over Peru here on Saturday afternoon in games billed as The Homecoming made for a solid start. New caps have been handed out. Key players arrived thriving in new surroundings, none more than Jonathan David at Atlético Madrid. Extended injury absences and the awkward non-attendance of captain Alphonso Davies (skipping the window to honeymoon) have been overcome.

But Tuesday’s clash with the US in Saint Paul means more American questions are coming. Looking back, the Folarin Balogun affair feels absolutely tailor-made for a Marschian verdict. He, of course, has thoughts.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“Well, this is a deep conversation,” he says, leaning back. “We, as Americans, have been inundated with propaganda since we were young. We’re the No 1 country in the world, we deserve everything, we dominate everything, No 1 in every aspect of life. This is what we’ve been told. So, when things happen and we don’t feel like we’re in control of it … we feel like we deserve to be treated differently because we’re Americans. That is one of the things that infuriates the rest of the world about Americans. And Americans don’t know that if they don’t ever leave the country.

“So what I feel when the Balogun ruling happens is that would never happen in any other country in the world, and this is why everyone around the world hates America. That was proven to be so. The US had had a good World Cup, was doing well. All that switched in one moment. But do I think that that’s about corruption and unfairness? The problem is, football is inundated with this kind of stuff.”

The meme is another World Cup leftover. “I’ve had all kinds of people ask me what it was, was it a meat slicer?” he says of his sideline gyrations during their match against Qatar. The incident spawned a gif which has been used plenty in the Marsch family WhatsApp since. “I don’t know what I’m doing sometimes. As soon as I’ve done it, I’m like: ‘Why did I do that? I’m such an idiot’.”

He doesn’t feel fooled, however, by the sport’s latest, arguably greatest, modern corruption crisis. Defeats to Manchester City in 2022-23 didn’t help the Leeds United side Marsch had managed when they missed safety by five points. That campaign is not one of the “sham” seasons which were part of the damning verdict against City last week. But he’s adamant the unfairness extended to his time in England.

“I think Man City should be punished severely. I think they should have to go down, and by the way, everyone knew about it. Everyone knew,” says Marsch, who also pointed to Everton and Nottingham Forest later being deducted points for issues in the same season when Leeds were relegated below both.

“That summer [2022], us and Man City were the only teams that said we made money. For us, we did make money, because we sold Raphinha, we sold Kalvin Phillips [to City]. We had a lot left over from what we bought. At the time, we weren’t in a position financially to not save. Our ownership didn’t have deep pockets. Whereas when Man City says this, I was literally like, ‘Are you kidding me? Is this some kind of joke?’

“When they said they got Erling Haaland for £52m, it’s like: ‘Yeah, OK, sure!’ So, I knew there were inconsistencies in it, but what can you do? You just put your arms in the air and go, ‘This is football’.”

Sports.title: Let there be blanks instead of Manchester City’s name on trophies: there was no honour there | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
At half-time in the 2014 League Cup final, Sunderland led Manchester City 1-0. Yaya Touré equalised with a casually brilliant 30-yard clip 10 minutes after the break, and City went on to win 3-1. City, we now know from the independent commission, were at the time involved in a prolonged and calculated act of cheating, while Touré, the leaks in Der Spiegel suggested, was being paid via a dual contract to disguise exactly how much City were spending. Although precise details were left to the appendices, the commission’s report refers to payments “not recorded in an employment contract … but instead recorded in a consultancy agreement”.

Had Sunderland won, they would not merely have ended a 41-year wait for a trophy but would have qualified for the following season’s Europa League. It’s possible, of course, that the strain the extra games placed on the squad would have led to relegation in 2015, rather than the familiar trope of sacking a manager, in this case Gus Poyet, midway through the season, and surviving thanks to a bump under his successor, Dick Advocaat.

But it’s also possible that the greater exposure brought by European football, the surge of positivity engendered by unfamiliar and unexpected silverware, may have led to Premier League consolidation, stability and semi-regular European qualification.

Should Sunderland feel cheated? Of course they should, just as those who came second behind Lance Armstrong should feel cheated; just as Liverpool and Arsenal should feel cheated over the League Cup finals of 2016 and 2018; just as Stoke should feel cheated over the 2011 FA Cup final; just as Manchester United should feel cheated over the Premier League titles in 2012 and 2018 and Liverpool should in 2014; just as every club who played in the same competitions as City between 2009 and 2018 should feel cheated. But does that mean the 2014 League Cup should be taken from City and awarded to Sunderland?

These are two different questions, and it’s probably best to deal with the latter first – and this, unfortunately, is where subjectivity is unavoidable. I can’t speak for other Sunderland fans but, personally, I wouldn’t want it.

Perhaps this comes from never having seen my club win a major trophy. If it happens, I want it to be pure. I want images that will be remembered down the generations, like the highlights of 1973 – Ian Porterfield’s goal, Jim Montgomery’s save and Bob Stokoe’s celebratory skip across the pitch in mac and trilby.

I want the surge of adrenaline when a goal is scored, the agonised wait of injury time, the rush of the final whistle. I want tears and hugs and community and togetherness, all the things my dad’s generation banged on about. I want to get drunk and sing on a train. I don’t want to find out via an alert on my phone 12 years after the fact as I unpack the dishwasher.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City’s Yaya Touré equalises against Sunderland in the 2014 League Cup final. Photograph: Eddie Keogh/Reuters

Others may feel differently but the arithmetic of trophies won seems far less important than the experience of winning and the memories and sense of comradeship it provokes. Glory denied cannot be rectified a generation later by an independent commission, no matter how august.

Awarding rivals league titles seems even less satisfactory. In the 2017-18 season, for instance, the league was effectively over by the end of January with City 15 points clear.

As City went on to amass 100 points, there was little point in the four sides behind them – Manchester United, Liverpool, Chelsea and Tottenham, who were separated by five points – exerting themselves to try to rein City in.

Their priorities changed. United, Chelsea and Spurs all reached the FA Cup semi-finals. Liverpool got to the Champions League final. In those circumstances, why would any of them have prioritised the league? To award United, who finished second, the title, would seem not just empty but arbitrary.

That, though, does not mean City should not be stripped of those titles. They won them unfairly; why on earth should they be allowed to keep them? (And yes, something similar could be said of Chelsea, but that’s an argument for why Chelsea should also have been stripped of titles, not for why City should not be).

How can those trophies be left in the record books for future generations unquestioningly to see? How can City stand as the fourth-most successful side in league history when so much of that success was achieved by cheating?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The argument will be made that City’s players strived hard for those trophies. But so did players for those other teams, the ones who weren’t cheating. And how much easier to win in a deep squad full of high-grade players, drawn to City by the money they were offering, money whose source, the independent commission concluded, had been disguised in contravention of Premier League regulations.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City with the League Cup in 2014, one of seven major trophies won between 2009 and 2018. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Euphoric memories cannot be expunged, but it is for City fans (and players and coaching staff and directors) to decide what to do with them. If they still want to exult in Sergio Agüero’s 94th-minute winner to claim the 2012 Premier League title, nobody can stop them. But the rest of the world knows what it was based on, that as the rest of the Premier League played to regulations voted in by the clubs themselves, City did not.

That would mean that there was no Premier League champion in 2012, 2014 or 2018, no FA Cup winner in 2011 and no League Cup winner in 2014, 2016 or 2018 (and it does not seem unreasonable to wonder, when all this is done, whether there might be more to be investigated after 2018). If there are blanks on the roll of honour, let them be; there was no honour there.

Let the spaces stand as testimony to what those seasons were. Let them stand as a memorial to the years when a foreign entity tried to subvert English football, when a foreign entity took this country’s greatest cultural mode, and all the passion and all the feeling, all the sorrow and all the joy, all the love it has entailed, and tried to twist it for its own political ends. Let them stand as a warning of the dangers of laissez-faire capitalism, when everything, no matter how beloved, could be sold off to the highest bidder.

And let them stand as a monument to a Premier League that finally – belatedly? – took action, to a process that maintained its independence, to an institution that, at no little risk to its own wellbeing – a risk that has not gone away – in the end preferred justice and fairness and decency over grubby deals with the rich and powerful.
