He is facing a tough battle against right-wing senator Bolsonaro, 45, eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his failed 2022 re-election bid.

Little known until a few months ago, Flavio Bolsonaro, who describes himself as more moderate than his firebrand father, has vowed to “rescue” Brazil from Lula, corruption, high taxes and crime.

Oscarina de Oliveira, a 62-year-old caregiver, told AFP she had planned to vote for Lula, as she always has. But “when I got there, I switched to Bolsonaro. Just to see what happens, to see if anything changes.”

Results are expected within a few hours after polls closed, due to the vast nation’s electronic voting system.

Opinion surveys show neither Lula or Bolsonaro were likely to score more than 50 percent — the threshold required to win in the first round. They and are neck-and-neck if the vote goes to a runoff on October 25.

Both candidates have extremely high rejection rates in the deeply polarized nation where a bitter election campaign featured more scandals and mud-slinging than policy and promises.

While all eyes are on the presidential race, Brazilians are also electing lawmakers, senators and governors.

– ‘Flaws and all’ –

Lula is more popular in Brazil’s poor northeast, among low-income voters, Catholics, and women.

“Lula is the only one doing anything for us — at least for us working-class people — flaws and all,” said Sabrina, 34, selling drinks in Rio de Janeiro.

Revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, Lula made a dramatic comeback to office in the 2022 elections after being jailed on a corruption conviction that was later thrown out on procedural grounds.

Riots in Brasilia and the botched coup attempt after his election allowed him to cast himself as guardian of Brazil’s democracy.

In his third term he has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment, but voters complain about a high cost of living.

Lula has also sharply curbed deforestation in the Amazon, while backing oil exploration.

Despite a growing number of extreme weather events in Brazil, climate change has been absent from the campaign.

“It is important to elect a candidate who defends our territory, who defends nature,” said Tainara da Costa Cruz, 22, who lives along the banks of the Rio Negro in Amazonas state and voted for Lula.

– Trump watching –

Buoyed by his father’s legacy, Bolsonaro leads in the south, among wealthier voters and evangelical Christians.

In a cascade of scandals that dominated the campaign, it emerged that Bolsonaro was under investigation for corruption over the financing of the biopic “Dark Horse” about his father.

For many voters, this did little to move the needle.

“Things are truly terrible. As far as I’m concerned, the left just doesn’t work anymore,” said tech worker Joao Batista, 36, in the Rocinha favela, saying he was fed up with the “horrible” expense of basic goods.

Bolsonaro’s rallies featured massive US flags and images of Trump, who has said he is “very closely” watching the election, but did not endorse the candidate.

The US president has wielded tariffs and sanctions to pressure Brasilia over complaints ranging from the trial against his ally Jair Bolsonaro to alleged unfair trade practices.

Lula repeatedly warned him not to “meddle” in the elections.

He also argued that Brazil would retain control over the development of its vast reserves of rare earths, which have attracted interest from Washington and other foreign powers.

Flavio Bolsonaro has pitched Brazil as a “solution” to ease US dependence on China for these critical minerals.

“I support Lula because he stands up for the poor. Flavio will sell our Brazil off to foreigners,” said Victor Jorge Martins, a 25-year-old event planner.

World.title: FHFL Commissions 50 Energy-Efficient Homes for Wives of Fallen Heroes in Ibadan
World.content:
Family Homes Funds Limited (FHFL), in partnership with Post-Service Housing Development Limited (PHDL) and the National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure (NASENI), has commissioned 50 two-bedroom detached, energy-efficient homes for the spouses of Nigeria’s fallen military personnel in Idi-Ape, Akobo, Lagelu Local Government Area of Oyo State.

The commissioning brought together government representatives, military authorities, development partners and other stakeholders to mark the completion of a housing intervention dedicated to families of fallen heroes. The development provides beneficiaries with secure and dignified homes while advancing a housing model that brings together affordability, sustainability, and social impact.

FHFL’s commitment to the beneficiaries extends beyond the provision of homes. Representing the Managing Director/CEO of FHFL, Abdul Mutallab Mukhtar, the Executive Director, Operations, Dr. Henry Inegbu stated: “This initiative is about providing the wives of our fallen heroes with the security and stability that comes with having a home of their own. Their husbands gave their lives in service to Nigeria, and we have a responsibility to ensure that the families they left behind receive meaningful support. Beyond the homes we are delivering today, we are committed to supporting the widows with skills development and livelihood opportunities that can strengthen their capacity for self-sustainability.”

This project aligns with FHFL’s mandate to expand access to housing that improves lives and responds to real needs by combining affordable housing delivery with sustainability and social impact.

Speaking on the importance of partnerships in providing affordable housing and creating impact, Dr. Nnegbu stated: “For these families, the homes provide a stable and dignified environment in which they can build their future, while honouring the sacrifice of the men who served our country. We remain committed to working with credible partners to deliver housing solutions that create lasting value for beneficiaries and communities.”

The housing units were formally commissioned on behalf of the Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, by the General Officer Commanding, 2 Division, Nigerian Army, Major General Auwalu Mahmuda.

Representing the Chief of Army Staff, Major General Mahmuda reaffirms the Nigerian Army’s commitment to initiatives that provide housing and other forms of assistance to the families of fallen personnel: “The Nigerian Army remains committed to supporting initiatives that provide housing and other forms of assistance to the families of our fallen heroes, in recognition of their patriotic service and sacrifice to the nation. We appreciate FHFL for bringing this intervention together with its partners and for providing these families with homes that offer greater security, stability, and dignity. The welfare of the families of our fallen personnel remains an important responsibility, and partnerships of this nature provide practical support to those who have made significant sacrifices for Nigeria.”

The commissioning featured the presentation of keys to the beneficiaries, with the wives of the fallen heroes receiving their homes amid visible excitement and appreciation. For the families, the homes provide a greater sense of security, stability, and hope as they move forward.

The project reinforces FHFL’s commitment to reducing Nigeria’s housing deficit and expanding access to quality, affordable and sustainable housing, particularly for vulnerable households. Through partnerships with institutions across the housing and development ecosystem, FHFL continues to deliver interventions that connect housing provision with broader social and economic outcomes.

World.title: 10 things to know about BBNaija Season 11 winner Temi Nkem
World.content:
Temi Nkem has emerged as the winner of Big Brother Naija Season 11, beating the other finalists to claim the title and the ₦160 million prize package.

The 21-year-old, whose real name is Temitope Chigbue, became one of the most recognisable housemates of the “Show Ya Sef” edition because of her bold personality and outspoken nature.

Here are 10 things to know about the latest BBNaija winner.

1. Her real name is Temitope Chigbue

Temi Nkem’s real name is Temitope Chigbue. She entered the BBNaija house under the name Temi Nkem.

2. She is 21 years old

Temi Nkem was introduced as a 21-year-old contestant when Season 11 began in July 2026.

3. She is a student

Temi Nkem was listed as a student when she joined the reality show.

4. She described herself as bold and vibrant

Before entering Biggie’s house, Temi Nkem described herself as “bold, vibrant, and impossible to ignore.” She said she believed she represented what the show needed.

5. She enjoys golfing, eating and walking

Her listed hobbies include golfing, eating and walking.

6. She considers herself a good listener

One of the qualities Temi Nkem highlighted in her profile was her ability to listen to people and offer advice. She listed being a good listener and giving great advice among her hidden talents.

7. She described herself as egotistical

Temi Nkem did not shy away from describing the less flattering side of her personality. In her BBNaija profile, she said she could be egotistical and arrogant, adding that she does not shrink herself for anyone.

8. She was one of the nine finalists

Temi Nkem made it to the grand finale alongside Aikou, Barry, Bluethopia, Flora, Oyin, Ricky, Sheba and Tram after the season began with 24 housemates.

She survived the successive evictions that reduced the competition before ultimately claiming the crown.

9. She is now the BBNaija Season 11 winner

Temi Nkem was announced as the winner during the Season 11 grand finale on Sunday, October 4, 2026. She succeeds Imisi, who won the previous edition of BBNaija.

10. She intends to go into content creation and blogging after the show

Her victory earns her the ₦160 million grand prize package, which includes ₦90 million in cash, a brand-new SUV and other

sponsored prizes.

Vanguard News

World.title: Kila rejects ‘Fake Professor’ claim, heads to court
World.content:
Professor Anthony Kila has rejected reports describing him as a “fake professor”, saying the characterisation was inaccurate, misleading and damaging to his reputation and professional standing.

Kila, in a statement responding to a publication dated October 3, 2026, said he remained a professor and stood by the academic and professional credentials on which his professorial title was based.

“For the avoidance of doubt, I am a professor, and I stand by the title and the professional and academic credentials on which it is based,” he said.

He argued that the report was based on what he described as an incomplete understanding of the nature, origin and institutional basis of his professorship.

According to him, the matter should be assessed on the basis of the relevant facts and supporting documentation.

Kila, who is Pro-Chancellor of Michael and Cecilia Ibru University, Delta State, and Director of the Commonwealth Institute of Advanced and Professional Studies (CIAPS), said he was prepared to make the relevant facts and documents concerning his professorial status available.

He particularly objected to the description “fake professor”, arguing that the phrase was presented as a factual conclusion that required evidence and carried serious implications for his reputation.

While acknowledging the role of journalism in scrutinising the credentials of people occupying positions of responsibility, Kila said such scrutiny should be conducted fairly and with a proper understanding of the facts.

He said he was “baffled” by the level of attention directed at him, noting that he neither holds political office nor is seeking one, and is not a government official.

Kila also thanked colleagues, friends, students and members of the public who contacted him after the publication to express confidence in his academic and professional credentials.

He disclosed that he had instructed his lawyers to review the publication and any subsequent dissemination of the allegations and advise him on appropriate legal steps to protect his reputation and professional standing.

“The facts and documentation will speak for themselves,” Kila said.

World.title: Breaking: Temi Nkem wins BBNaija season 11
World.content:
Temi Nkem has emerged as the winner of BBNaija Season 11, bringing the reality show’s latest edition to an end.

Temi Nkem was crowned winner during the grand finale on Sunday night after weeks of competition, evictions and intense drama among the housemates.

The victory sees Temi Nkem take home the ₦160 million prize package awarded to the winner of the season.

The season began with 24 housemates before the competition was gradually narrowed down to the finalists.

The finalists were Temi Nkem, Barry, Tram, Oyin, Flora, Sheba, Aikou, Ricky and Bluethopia.

Barry was the first finalist to be evicted during the live finale, followed by Oyin, Ricky and Flora as the show progressed towards its decisive stage.

Temi Nkem ultimately outlasted the remaining contestants to claim the title and become the latest winner of the BBNaija franchise.

The victory marks the culmination of weeks of tasks, nominations, evictions and public support, with Temi Nkem now taking the season’s top prize.

Vanguard News

World.title: NDC 10,000-man march: Ughelli council chairman seals organiser’s property
World.content:
…..Council boss says structure was built under high-tension wire, insists action not politically motivated

By Efe Onodjae

Ambassador Tobore Alex Agbah, organiser of the 10,000-man march for the National Democratic Congress, NDC, in Ughelli, Delta State, has alleged that the Ughelli North Local Government Council Chairman, Olorogun Jaro Egbo, sealed his property following the political rally.

Agbah, who disclosed this in an interview with Vanguard on Sunday, alleged that the action was politically motivated and linked to his role in organising the NDC awareness march held on Saturday.

He said the march, organised by his group, Team Agbah, was aimed at sensitising residents and mobilising support for the NDC and its aspirants.

According to him, the march attracted a huge turnout, which he described as an “organic” mobilisation.

Agbah said he was informed by his wife during the march that officials were coming to inspect his property and possibly demolish it.

He said: “While we were on the march, my wife called me that they were coming to see my property and demolish it. We thought it was a joke.

“But this afternoon, as I was coming from church, before I could get to my house, they called me that the local government chairman had sealed my property.”

Asked whether he was aware of any breach of law that could have led to the sealing, Agbah attributed the action to his political activities.

He said: “The reason is the 10,000-man march against APC. It is political.

“There was no notice. The property has been there for decades. All the local government chairmen who have come and gone have met the property there without any issue.

“Yesterday was Saturday and we did the march. Today, Sunday, they brought a notice and sealed the place.”

Agbah further alleged that the council chairman had threatened to frustrate him because of his political activities.

He appealed to the Federal Government and relevant authorities to intervene, saying political differences should not result in victimisation.

“I am calling on the Federal Government to call the local government chairman to desist from politics of bitterness.

“Politics is not a game of enmity; it is a game of interest. We are not doing politics to hurt ourselves.

“I have known him before now. We have been in the same political struggle before. So why is it that because I am in NDC, he is trying to frustrate me?

“He told my wife openly that I am fighting this party and that, as a result, he would make sure they frustrate me.

“I don’t deserve such treatment just because I led a 10,000-man march for NDC.”

However, reacting to the allegation, Egbo said the property was sealed because it was allegedly built under a high-tension electricity line and that the action had nothing to do with Agbah’s political affiliation.

The council chairman said his officials had written to Agbah several times over the alleged violation of environmental regulations, but that he failed to comply.

Egbo said the council had, since he assumed office, carried out more than 30 demolitions involving structures allegedly obstructing waterways or built under high-tension lines.

He said: “The particular sealed property was built under high-tension wire. As a matter of fact, my officials told me that they have written to him several times, but he refused to obey simple environmental regulations.

“Since I took office, we have carried out over 30 demolitions from those who block waterways and those who build under high tension, like this particular illegal structure.

“Let me reiterate that being in opposition does not make you above the law. Let your man bring his approval for the illegal structure.”

On allegations that the action was connected to the NDC march, Egbo dismissed the claim, insisting that the enforcement was based on alleged regulatory violations.

He also accused Agbah of branding a vehicle without paying the prescribed mobile advertising fee.

Egbo said: “On the branded bus, he branded the vehicle without paying for mobile advert. By the grace of God, I am the Chairman of the Governing Board of Delta State Advertising Agency, DESSAA.”

He warned that the council would enforce the law if Agbah failed to produce approval for the structure or pay the prescribed advertising fees.

“If he fails to bring the approval for the illegal structure or fails to pay the prescribed fees, the law will take its course and heaven will not fall,” Egbo added.

Vanguard also checked photographs and videos posted on social media purportedly showing the sealing of the property.

World.title: INEC to Hold World Press Conference as 2027 Elections Hit 100-Day Countdown
World.content:
The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) will hold a World Press Conference and National Stakeholders’ Meeting on Tuesday to mark 100 days to the 2027 General Election.

According to a statement signed by Adedayo Oketola, Chief Press Secretary/Media Adviser to the INEC Chairman on Sunday night, the Commission will provide updates on preparations for the elections, including the voters’ register, candidate nominations, logistics and critical measures to ensure the integrity of the electoral process.

The statement said event will be addressed by INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, SAN, alongside other key stakeholders involved in the electoral process.

It noted that the national stakeholders’ meeting underlines the Commission’s commitment to “absolute transparency, proactive public communication, and collaborative engagement with key actors in the electoral ecosystem.”

The meeting will bring together political party leaders, security agencies under the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security (ICCES), members of the diplomatic corps, development partners, civil society organisations, observer groups, disability rights advocates, religious and traditional leaders, youth organisations and media executives.

The event is scheduled to hold at 10:00am at the Bola Ahmed Tinubu International Conference Centre (BAT-ICC), Abuja.

The statement added that the event will be broadcast live on major national television networks and streamed on INEC’s official social media platforms.

World.title: Nail-biting Finale to BBNaija S11 as Temi Nkem Is Crowned Winner
World.content:
Vanessa Obioha

The race for the N160 million grand prize package in the 11th season of Big Brother Naija came to a climactic end tonight as 21-year-old Temi Nkem emerged winner of the reality show.

In what proved to be one of the most unpredictable seasons of the show, only nine of the 24 housemates who entered the house in July made it to the finale.

One by one, the nine were reduced to three finalists, all waiting to discover who would be crowned the winner of BBNaija’s ‘Show Ya Sef’ season and walk away with the grand prize.

Barry, who emerged as the first finalist of the season, was the first to take a bow, followed by Oyin and Ricky. Flora and Tram were next to leave, narrowing the field further.

The tension heightened as the final four — Bluethopia, Sheba, Aikou and Temi Nkem — awaited the announcement. Only Aikou, Sheba and Temi Nkem eventually made it to the stage, where host Ebuka Obi-Uchendu waited to reveal their fate.

Chants of Aikou and Temi Nkem filled the studio as fans waited to see who would take the crown. For many, it was still too close to call.

When her name was finally announced, an ecstatic Temi Nkem rolled on the floor before jumping to her feet, celebrating in disbelief. Her reaction was as vibrant as the personality that had made her difficult for viewers to ignore throughout the season.

Temi Nkem goes home with N90 million in cash, an SUV and other prizes.

World.title: Heirs Insurance Boss Challenges Operators on Rebuilding Confidence
World.content:
Ebere Nwoji

The Managing Director Heirs General Insurance, Mr Wole Fayemi, has challenged insurance operators to rebuild public confidence and deepen insurance penetration through prompt claims payment, customer-focused innovation and easier access to insurance solutions.

Fayemi stated this while speaking as one of the panel of discussants at the Business Day Insurance Conference in Lagos.

Fayemi said the industry’s growth ambitions would depend not only on stronger capital positions but also on its ability to consistently deliver on its promises to customers.

“Customers must be confident that insurers will fulfil their promises when it matters most. Trust is fundamental to the insurance proposition, and it is earned through action, not messaging. Every claim settled promptly, every commitment honoured and every positive customer experience strengthens confidence in the industry”, he said.

He cited Heirs Insurance Group’s claims performance as evidence of the role claims fulfilment plays in building credibility and encouraging wider adoption of insurance.

World.title: ADC Campaign Condemns APC’s ‘Cruel Mockery’ of Amaechi, Says Tinubu’s Govt Has Failed Nigerians
World.content:
The African Democratic Congress (ADC) Presidential Campaign Council has condemned a statement by the All Progressives Congress (APC) National Publicity Secretary, Felix Morka, concerning former Minister of Transportation, Rotimi Amaechi, describing it as a “display of political cruelty.”

The ADC PCC, in a statement signed by its Director of Strategic Communications, Phrank Shaibu, on Sunday, said a mother’s death and a family’s grief should never be turned into material for partisan ridicule.

“Felix Morka’s statement is a display of political cruelty, not an answer to Nigeria’s problems,” the statement said.

It added: “If Rotimi Amaechi says he struggled to afford his mother’s medication, the humane response is compassion. The political response is to ask why millions of Nigerians are also being priced out of medicines, food and basic necessities.”

The ADC PCC also faulted Morka for calling Amaechi a “loafer” for struggling outside public office, saying the remark reflected the APC’s “contempt for ordinary people.”

“That insult says more about the APC’s contempt for ordinary people than it says about Amaechi,” the statement said.

According to the council, “Nigerians who cannot afford treatment, keep the lights on or travel safely on their roads are not loafers. They are citizens living through the consequences of a government that has failed them.”

The ADC PCC further criticised the state of the country’s infrastructure, economy, electricity, security and welfare.

“The reality is plain: the roads are bad, the economy is bad, electricity is bad, security is bad and the welfare of the people is bad,” it said.

It added that “Tinubu’s name is increasingly associated with poverty, insecurity and hardship,” arguing that “no amount of mockery can make those conditions disappear.”

The council also challenged Morka to explain why Nigerians continue to face dangerous journeys on roads meant to connect communities and support trade.

“The roads in the East, the region he comes from, are in such a deplorable state that travelling on them feels like taking a route to Lucifer’s kingdom,” it said.

The ADC PCC asked: “How many overturned trailers, near-collisions and desperate journeys must Nigerians endure before this government admits that the country’s roads are in crisis?”

It also criticised the APC over public spending, saying the party “cannot boast about trillions in public spending while Nigerians lack safe roads, reliable electricity and affordable healthcare.”

“It cannot blame one politician’s personal circumstances for hardship being felt in homes across the country,” the statement said.

According to the council, “The test of government is not how viciously its spokesmen can insult their opponents. It is whether people can live safely, afford treatment and earn a decent living.”

“On that test, Tinubu’s government has failed,” it added.

The ADC PCC said Morka owed Nigerians an explanation for the government’s record and Amaechi’s family “the respect that grief deserves.”

It also urged Nigerians to make 2027 “a turning point,” saying the poverty and insecurity associated with Tinubu’s rule should not become the country’s future.

World.title: ADC Campaign Council Faults Zulum Over Alleged Threat to Arrest ‘Tinubu Must Go’ Protesters
World.content:
The African Democratic Congress (ADC) Presidential Campaign Council has criticised Borno State Governor Babagana Zulum over a viral video in which he allegedly ordered the arrest and detention of anyone caught expressing “Tinubu Must Go.”

In a statement signed by its Director of Strategic Communications, Phrank Shaibu, on Sunday, October 4, 2026, the ADC PCC said the video, in which Zulum speaks in Hausa, “raises grave questions about his respect for citizens’ democratic rights.”

The council said the development was particularly troubling because Zulum had recently denied ordering the arrest of people wearing “Tinubu Must Go” T-shirts.

“He must explain the fresh video and reconcile its contents with that denial. Nigerians deserve clarity, not contradictory messages about whether peaceful critics will be arrested,” the statement said.

The ADC PCC argued that no governor had the authority to criminalise peaceful political opinion.

“A slogan, a T-shirt or a call for a president to leave office is not, by itself, a crime,” it said.

“Borno State is not a political detention centre, and its citizens must not be threatened into silence for opposing President Tinubu.”

The council said that if the authorities had credible evidence of a separate offence, they should present it in court and allow due process to take its course.

“They must not use other allegations as a cover to punish citizens for their political views,” it added.

The ADC PCC called on Governor Zulum to withdraw any directive targeting peaceful protesters and guarantee that no one would be arrested solely for expressing opposition to President Tinubu.

“A government confident in its record answers criticism with evidence and performance—not threats of arrest and detention,” the statement said.

World.title: NHIA Urges Early Detection as FG Steps Up Cancer Response
World.content:
*NHIA-Roche initiative cuts cost of selected drugs by 80%, expands support for radiotherapy, diagnostics

James Emejo in Abuja

The National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) has urged Nigerian women to prioritise early detection of breast cancer, while expanding financial protection for insured patients facing the high cost of oncology treatment.

The call comes as the country joins the global community to mark Breast Cancer Awareness Month, with the latest Nigeria-specific estimates putting annual new breast cancer cases at 32,278 and deaths at 16,332, according to the federal government and Nigerian cancer stakeholders from the Global Cancer Observatory.

Breast cancer remains the most commonly diagnosed cancer among Nigerian women and one of the country’s leading causes of cancer deaths.

The federal government also disclosed in July that Nigeria accounts for about 10.5 per cent of Africa’s cancer burden, placing the country among the three most affected on the continent.

NHIA, under its Director General, Dr. Kelechi Ohiri, is seeking to strengthen the role of health insurance as a buffer against the financial shock associated with serious illnesses.

For many families, the cost of comprehensive cancer care can quickly exceed household income, while treatment abroad remains beyond the reach of most Nigerians.

A key intervention is the expanded partnership between the NHIA and pharmaceutical company Roche, which is designed to reduce the cost of selected oncology medicines for eligible insured patients.

Under the arrangement, Roche absorbs 50 per cent of the cost of selected medicines, the NHIA contributes another 30 per cent, while the patient pays the remaining 20 per cent.

The cost-sharing structure effectively removes 80 per cent of the medicine cost from the patient’s direct financial burden, potentially making the difference between treatment being sustained and being interrupted for households already under economic pressure.

The authority had also introduced additional support for radiotherapy, ranging from up to N400,000 to full coverage for eligible patients, while maintaining benefits covering key cancer-related diagnostics.

These include mammography, CT and MRI scans, bone scans and laboratory investigations, alongside radiotherapy and other elements of cancer care covered under applicable benefit packages.

The broader package also provides for components of screening, surgery, chemotherapy and follow-up care, depending on the patient’s eligibility and the applicable insurance benefits.

For Ohiri, the interventions point to a shift in how the effectiveness of health insurance should be measured — away from enrolment figures alone and towards the extent to which coverage protects families when they face expensive illnesses.

He said, “The critical measure of the insurance system should no longer be the number of Nigerians carrying insurance records, but whether those records provide meaningful protection when illness strikes.”

Over 23 million Nigerians are currently enrolled in the national health insurance system, giving the NHIA a growing platform for scaling financial protection against cancer and other high-cost diseases.

The NHIA measures form part of the wider health reform agenda of the President Bola Tinubu administration, coordinated by the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare under Professor Muhammad Ali Pate.

Cancer prevention and control have been elevated as national priorities under the administration’s health agenda, with the Federal Government implementing the Nigeria National Cancer Control Plan 2026–2030.

The plan covers prevention, early detection, diagnosis and treatment, as well as patient navigation, survivorship, research, data management and expansion of the oncology workforce.

The government is also upgrading six Oncology Centres of Excellence across the country. According to the Federal Ministry of Health, centres at the University College Hospital, Ibadan; University of Benin Teaching Hospital, Benin City; University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital, Enugu; and Ahmadu Bello University Teaching Hospital, Zaria, are already fully operational, with specialised equipment including brachytherapy machines.

Other interventions include the Cancer Access Partnership programme, which provides 27 anti-cancer medicines in 48 formulations across 14 federal tertiary hospitals, as well as the Cancer Health Fund for indigent patients suffering from breast, cervical and prostate cancers.

Together, the measures are aimed at addressing different points along the cancer-care chain — from prevention and early detection to diagnosis, treatment and financial protection.

But the NHIA said the interventions should be viewed as steps towards a broader response rather than a completed solution.

As breast cancer awareness month gets underway, the authority urged women to pay attention to unusual changes in their breasts, seek medical attention promptly and take advantage of screening opportunities where available.

It stressed that reducing Nigeria’s breast cancer burden would ultimately depend on detecting the disease earlier, expanding access to effective treatment and ensuring that the cost of care does not push patients and their families into financial distress.

Beyond the human toll, the disease can impose prolonged financial pressure on households, particularly when diagnosis comes late and treatment requires surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, specialised medicines and repeated diagnostic investigations.

World.title: Free Zones: Preserving Nigeria’s Industrial Advantage
World.content:
Nigeria’s free-zone regime is approaching a critical policy test. As the Federal Government moves to tighten tax and customs administration, it must also guard against weakening one of the country’s few established mechanisms for attracting large-scale, export-oriented investment, writes James Emejo

Nigeria’s ambition to build a $1 trillion economy will ultimately be measured in factories, exports, jobs and the volume of long-term capital committed to production—not in the number of policy documents it produces.

That places the country’s free-zone regime at an important crossroads.

The emerging debate over proposed changes to the fiscal and customs treatment of free-zone enterprises is ostensibly about revenue, tax compliance and closing loopholes. But beneath the technical provisions lies a much bigger economic question: can Nigeria tighten oversight without weakening the incentives that make its special economic zones attractive to investors in the first place?

That question assumes greater significance against the backdrop of the federal government’s $1 trillion economic ambition, which depends heavily on expanding productive capacity, attracting foreign direct investment, increasing exports and deepening manufacturing.

The draft Nigeria Export Processing Zones (Domestic Sales, Fiscal Alignment and Customs Treatment) Regulations, 2026, obtained for this report, offers an insight into the proposed framework.

Issued under the Nigeria Export Processing Zones Act and the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, the draft says its objectives include improving investor confidence, protecting government revenue and enhancing the global competitiveness of the zones.

Under the existing free-zone architecture, approved enterprises enjoy exemptions from certain taxes, levies, duties and foreign-exchange restrictions, alongside other incentives designed to attract investment and support export-oriented production.

The proposed regulations retain several of those incentives but introduce new conditions around domestic sales.

Under the draft, an enterprise would qualify for tax exemption on profits where at least 75 per cent of its annual turnover comes from exports and not more than 25 per cent from sales into the Nigerian Customs Territory.

More significantly, from January 1, 2028, profits arising from sales into the Nigerian Customs Territory would become fully taxable, irrespective of the proportion of domestic sales.

For investors making long-term commitments, that is not a minor administrative adjustment.

A refinery, petrochemical complex, automobile plant, pharmaceutical facility or export-processing operation can take a decade or more to recover its capital. Investment decisions are therefore based not only on today’s tax rate but on the credibility and durability of the rules under which capital is committed.

This is where the government faces a delicate balancing act.

There is a legitimate case for preventing abuse of free-zone incentives. Companies that divert duty-free goods into the domestic market outside approved arrangements should not be permitted to use the zone regime as a mechanism for avoiding legitimate duties and taxes.

The draft itself provides for consequences for unauthorised movement of duty-free goods, including customs duties, import VAT and other applicable charges, administrative penalties, seizure and possible prosecution.

The issue, therefore, is not whether government should enforce compliance. It should.

The more consequential question is whether enforcement can be strengthened without progressively eroding the economic proposition that distinguishes a free zone from an ordinary industrial location.

That distinction matters because incentives are not supposed to be an end in themselves. Their economic justification is that they help Nigeria attract productive capital that might otherwise go elsewhere.

The Dangote lesson

Nigeria already has a powerful domestic example of what such an investment proposition can produce.

The Dangote Refinery and Petrochemical complex is located within the Dangote Industries Free Zone in Lekki, Lagos. The project illustrates the scale of industrial investment that can emerge where infrastructure, fiscal incentives, customs arrangements and regulatory support converge.

The facility’s economic significance extends beyond its physical size. A project of that scale has implications for domestic refining capacity, petrochemicals, foreign-exchange demand, industrial supply chains, employment and the country’s ability to retain more value from its energy resources.

That experience raises a fundamental investment question for policymakers: if the fiscal and regulatory advantages of free zones are substantially reduced, what would persuade the next investor considering a $500 million, $1 billion or $5 billion project to locate inside one?

Nigeria is competing for capital with jurisdictions that deliberately construct specialised investment environments around taxation, customs, infrastructure and regulation.

The country therefore needs to measure the free-zone regime not only by revenue forgone but also by the investment, employment, exports, technology transfer and industrial capacity generated in return.

Reform without policy rupture

The proposed changes also bring the question of policy consistency into sharper focus.

An investor entering Nigeria today is making a decision based partly on the rules currently in force. If those rules change substantially after capital has been committed, the economic effect extends beyond the immediate tax liability.

Investor confidence is particularly sensitive to policy predictability because industrial capital is relatively immobile.

A government can amend a tax regulation quickly. A company cannot relocate a refinery, factory or processing plant with the same speed.

The draft recognises this problem to an extent. It provides that enterprises enjoying incentives validly granted before the commencement of the new Act may continue to enjoy them for the unexpired portion of their statutory approval period, subject to applicable law and the terms of their original approval.

That transitional principle is important.

Government can distinguish between incentives granted to existing investors under established legal arrangements, new incentives for future investors and benefits that should be withdrawn from enterprises that breach their obligations.

Such differentiation would allow fiscal reform without creating unnecessary uncertainty around investments already made in reliance on government-approved arrangements.

Who regulates the zones?

Another critical issue is institutional coordination.

The draft provides that the Nigeria Export Processing Zones Authority (NEPZA) shall remain the exclusive regulator for licensing, operational oversight, supervision and non-tax administration within the zones.

The Nigeria Revenue Service would have responsibility for tax administration, while the Nigeria Customs Service would retain responsibility for customs control and enforcement.

On paper, the division is logical.

The problem arises when separate mandates become competing centres of authority.

A free zone requires a regulator capable of coordinating the commercial and operational realities of the zone while allowing tax and customs agencies to perform their statutory responsibilities.

That makes the institutional strength and clarity of NEPZA particularly important.

The Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment has maintained that the reform is intended to improve fiscal accountability while preserving the competitiveness of free zones. Minister Jumoke Oduwole has also said the reform process involved NEPZA and the Oil and Gas Free Zone Authority and that the agencies would retain licensing and operational responsibilities.

The next step should therefore be greater transparency around how the proposed framework was developed, including the inputs received from NEPZA, operators, workers and other stakeholders and how those submissions influenced the final provisions.

The concerns raised by workers and unions also deserve consideration, particularly where they relate to employment, investment flows and the operational sustainability of the zones.

But those concerns should be tested against evidence.

The government should publish the economic assumptions behind the reform: how much additional revenue is expected, what investment impact is anticipated, how many jobs could be affected and what happens to exports and new capital under the proposed regime.

That would move the debate from competing assertions to measurable outcomes.

The bigger problem: an outdated law

There is an even more fundamental issue that should not be lost in the tax debate—the age of the legislation governing NEPZA.

The NEPZA Act, enacted in 1992, predates the current structure of global supply chains, digital commerce, modern special economic zones, contemporary investment financing and many of the regulatory standards now used to compete for international capital.

Its limitations have increasingly become part of the investment challenge.

Modern investors require legal frameworks capable of dealing with complex ownership structures, infrastructure financing, public-private partnerships, dispute resolution, cross-border transactions, technology partnerships and evolving international trade arrangements.

An outdated statutory framework can create uncertainty even where the underlying commercial opportunity is attractive.

That suggests that the immediate debate over tax treatment should ultimately lead to a broader legislative reform.

Rather than repeatedly modifying an old framework through administrative and fiscal interventions, the government could pursue an executive bill to replace the existing NEPZA Act with a modern Special Economic Zones law designed around contemporary investment realities.

Such legislation could establish clearer rules for licensing, governance, incentives, customs treatment, infrastructure development, investment protection and regulatory coordination.

A national economic strategy

There is also a case for stronger coordination of the country’s special economic zones.

Free zones cut across taxation, customs, trade, ports, infrastructure, investment promotion, manufacturing and foreign exchange. Their success therefore cannot depend entirely on the priorities of one ministry or agency.

A coordinated national framework involving NEPZA, OGFZA, the finance and industry ministries, the Nigeria Revenue Service, Customs, the Central Bank, port and infrastructure agencies and private-sector operators could provide a more coherent strategy.

The objective should not be to create another layer of bureaucracy, but to prevent conflicting policy objectives from undermining one another.

Nigeria’s economic challenge is ultimately larger than the question of how much tax a free-zone company should pay.

The more important question is what kind of productive economy the country wants to build.

Factories create jobs. Export industries generate foreign exchange. Petrochemical plants create downstream industries. Industrial parks create supply chains. Large-scale investments expand the tax base over time.

That is why the fiscal value of free zones should be assessed alongside their wider economic returns.

Government has a legitimate interest in revenue mobilisation. It also has a legitimate interest in preventing abuse of tax and customs incentives.

Those objectives do not necessarily conflict with maintaining a competitive investment regime.

The policy challenge is to design a system that is tough on abuse, rigorous on compliance and predictable for legitimate investors.

For Nigeria, the test of the proposed reform should therefore extend beyond the tax ledger.

If the new framework produces greater revenue while attracting more factories, exports and capital, it will have strengthened the economic case for free zones.

If it increases the immediate tax take but makes long-term investors more hesitant to commit capital, the country may simply be transferring revenue from tomorrow’s productive economy to today’s fiscal accounts.

That is a calculation worth making before the rules are finalised.

Nigeria’s $1 trillion ambition requires productive capacity at a scale the conventional economy has struggled to generate. Free zones can form part of that strategy—but only if the incentives, regulation and institutions surrounding them are credible enough to support long-term investment.

The answer, therefore, may not be to weaken NEPZA because its framework requires reform, but to modernise the law, clarify institutional responsibilities, strengthen enforcement and make the investment proposition more predictable.

The country needs a free-zone system that protects public revenue without taxing away the very industrial ambition it was created to attract.

World.title: NOSC Selects Dear Ajayi as Nigeria’s Official Submission for 99th Oscars
World.content:
Vanessa Obioha

‘Dear Ajayi’, a 2026 film directed by Damilola Orimogunje, has been selected as Nigeria’s official submission for the Best International Feature Film category at the 99th Academy Awards.

The Nigerian Official Selection Committee (NOSC) announced the selection in a statement, saying the film emerged after a review of eligible entries and will be submitted to the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences for consideration.

“We congratulate the filmmakers behind ‘Dear Ajayi’ on their selection,” said Stephanie Linus, Chairperson of the NOSC. “We look forward to presenting the film for the Academy’s consideration and wish the team every success in the next stage of the process.”

Set in 1990s Nigeria, the film follows two estranged sisters forced to live together while caring for their paralysed mother. It had its world premiere at the 23rd edition of Giornate degli Autori (Directors/Authors’ Days), an independent sidebar of the Venice Film Festival.

The Nigerian-German co-production was produced by Nigeria’s 2o9ine Films with Depth and Optics Productions, and Germany’s Mayana Films.

Bimbo Akintola and Tosin Adeyemi star as the two sisters.

The 99th Academy Awards ceremony is scheduled to take place on March 14, 2027, at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood, Los Angeles.

World.title: RIP Dewald Naude: Cause of death revealed
World.content:
Dewald Naude cause of death has been revealed. Images via Facebook

Paarl Boys High Old Boy Donald Dewald Naude – who played for the Bulls under 21 side and Tuks rugby squad that lifted the Varsity Cup – died on Saturday, 3 October after a battle with brain cancer.

The 31-year-old player was diagnosed with a brain tumour earlier this year at his club at the HBU Sandy Bay in Hong Kong.

He leaves behind a wife, Annabel.



DEWALD NAUDE DIES AFTER BATTLE WITH BRAIN CANCER

In a statement, HBU Sandy Bay confirmed Dewald Naude had died on Saturday, 3 October, after a battle with brain cancer.

The Hong Kong club paid tribute to the South African player, sharing: “Those who knew him will remember how effortlessly he could put a smile on somebody else’s face and make them forget their worries.

“He had a genuine heart for serving others, and even during the most difficult period of his own life, Donald continued to put those around him first.

“Through all of it, he faced his illness with extraordinary courage, carrying the same optimism and positivity he always had. It never changed the person we knew and loved”

Dewald Naude’s loved ones appealed for public donations earlier this year after he was diagnosed with a brain tumour.

In the time that passed, Dewald underwent an 8.5-hour “awake” craniotomy operation to resection the tumour.



WIDOW: ‘SO PROUD OF YOUR BRAVERY AND STRENGTH’

In an Instagram post, Dewald Naude’s wife, Annabel, shared a touching tribute.

She shared: “What a privilege and honour it has been to be your wife and soulmate. I have been blessed with the best husband. You have taught me to always have courage, determination, perseverance, strength, and, most of all, self-belief.

“Through your bravery, I have learnt to remain positive even through the darkest of times. Thank you for always making me feel loved and for being my calm. I am so proud of your bravery and strength”.

Dewald Naude’s final Instagram post was dedicated to his wife on her birthday in August

“I’m truly blessed & grateful to have you in my life”, he shared.

World.title: Ramaphosa’s ankole bags record R6,4 MILLION at auction
World.content:
President Cyril Ramaphosa has sold the most expensive Ankole in South Africa. Images via X

A pregnant Ankole cow named Queen Arusha was auctioned off for a whopping R6,4 million, becoming the most expensive cow of any breed sold in South Africa. The heifer was sold by Ntaba Nyoni Ankole, a cattle breeding company owned by President Cyril Ramaphosa.

The farm is located at his Phala Phala farm, near Bela-Bela, in Limpopo.

The president is believed to own more than 100 of the unique breed, which is indigenous to African countries such as Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, and parts of Tanzania.



CYRIL RAMAPHOSA BAGS R6.4M FROM RECORD ANKOLE SALE

On Saturday, 3 October, Cyril Ramaphosa’s Ntaba Nyoni Ankole company netted a record-breaking sale at an auction at his Phala Phala farm.

A female heifer, Queen Arusha, sold for a whopping R6,4 million to an anonymous buyer. The Ankole was born in 2023 and is already in calf.

The sale reportedly set a South African record for a female animal across all cattle breeds, not just Ankole.

It’s not the first time the president has netted a small fortune for his pedigree cattle.

In 2022, his Ankole heifer, Fafa, was sold at auction for R2.1 million to businessman Patrice Motsepe, his brother-in-law.

In 2024, another pregnant heifer, Khethiwe, was sold for R1.8m at his auction.



WHY IS QUEEN ARUSHA SO EXPENSIVE?

Queen Arusha is a stud female, making her valuable primarily as a breeding animal and for her elite genetics.

Her R6,4 million price tag is attributed to the following:

Genetically valuable

Queen Arusha comes from a highly sought-after Ankole bloodline. She is the full sister of Optimus Prime, an Ankole bull whose horns measure about 68 inches. During the auction on Saturday, President Ramaphosa’s Ntaba Nyoni Ankole company bought two vials of Optimus Prime’s semen for R250 000 each.

Pregnant, and breeding potential

As a stud female, Queen Arusha has an enormous breeding potential through producing calves and embryos. Her genetics can potentially be multiplied through artificial insemination and embryo transfer.

The Ankole is also an in-calf heifer, meaning she is pregnant with her first calf.

Ankole is a niche market in South Africa.

According to the Ankole Cattle Breeders’ Society, there were only about 1,792 registered Ankole cattle, of which 1,198 were Fullblood, in its 2025 figures.

Hardy breed

Ankole – known for their long horns – produce lean meat, rich milk, and quality leather. Their horns are also considered a hot commodity. The breed is known to be “hardy cattle” and can live up to 30 years, relying on limited food and water.

AN AVID ANKOLE FARMER

In 2004, Cyril Ramaphosa—then an astute businessman—bought 43 Ankole cattle from Uganda, but they had to be brought into South Africa via artificial insemination.

The embryos of the cows were implanted in surrogate cows.

In his 2017 coffee table book, Cattle of the Ages, Ramaphosa described his fascination with the breed.

He said, “They each had long, white, beautiful horns glinting in the African sun. I suddenly became fixated and couldn’t stop looking at them. I was intrigued and in awe and fell in love with these creatures immediately”.

He now owns more than 750 elite cattle, including breeds such as Bonsmara, Boran, Nguni, and Wagyu.

World.title: Cape Town areas to experience 11-hour water shutdown
World.content:
The City of Cape Town has confirmed that some areas will experience a 10-hour water shutdown on Wednesday,

The Water and Sanitation Directorate said the planned maintenance forms part of ongoing efforts to upgrade critical infrastructure and improve water supply across the city.

CAPE TOWN AREAS SET TO EXPERIENCE WATER SUPPLY DISRUPTION

The City of Cape Town said planned maintenance work, including pipe and valve installations, repairs, and replacements, will result in water supply disruption to these areas:



Part of Grassy Park – The water supply to Dieman Road, Iris Road and possibly surrounding streets in Grassy Park will be shut off temporarily on Wednesday, 7 October 2026, from 08:00 until 19:00. This will allow the maintenance teams to safely connect the newly installed pipelines to the existing water supply infrastructure in the area.

“These streets and possibly surrounding streets will experience no water during this period,” the municipality said.

Parts of Woodstock – The City of Cape Town will start with the pipe replacement project that will affect the water supply intermittently to parts of Woodstock from Monday, 5 October 2026 until Friday, 30 April 2027.

The metro municipality said this will result in the water being shut off in Ravenscraig Road, Woodlands Road, Pine Road, Queens Road, Beyers Road, Warwick Street, Salmon Street, Coventry Road, Duke Road, Park Road, High Street, and possibly surrounding streets in Woodstock temporarily from 08:00 until 17:00 daily.

“This will allow the maintenance team to safely carry out the pipe and valve replacement in the area using trenchless technology, which is less of an inconvenience to residents and motorists. These streets and possibly surrounding streets will experience no water during this period and will be notified in advance when they will be affected,” the municipality said.

Parts of Strand – Similarly, the City of Cape Town will shut off the water supply to parts of Broadlands Road, from the vicinity of the Strandfoam Group (Pty) Ltd to the N2, Lwandle Helderberg Industrial and possibly surrounding streets in Strand temporarily on Wednesday, 7 October 2026, from 09:00 until 18:00. This will allow the maintenance team to safely carry out a new connection to the 300mm-diameter water main in the area. These areas and possibly surrounding streets will experience no water during this period.



ZERO-PRESSURE TESTS

Additionally, the City of Cape Town said it will conduct zero-pressure tests (ZPT) and conditional assessments on the water supply network, resulting in water supply disruptions in the following areas:

Wednesday, 7 October 2026, 09:00 to 16:00: Martinville – Bizweni.

Martinville – Bizweni. Thursday, 8 October 2026, 09:00 to 16:00: Helderzicht, Lourensia Park, Paardevlei, Victoria Park, Silvertas, Garden Village and Carey Park.

Helderzicht, Lourensia Park, Paardevlei, Victoria Park, Silvertas, Garden Village and Carey Park. Thursday, 8 October 2026, 09:00 to 16:00: Da Gama Park, Welcome Glen and Scala Road.

Residents have been advised to store water in advance as a precautionary measure in clean, sealed containers for domestic use during this period.

World.title: ‘Heist of the century’: Fans react to Orlando Pirates’ R20.2m court bid
World.content:
Orlando Pirates supporters have reacted after the club launched an urgent court application to freeze R20.2 million allegedly diverted from its accounts.

The matter was filed in the Johannesburg High Court, with the funds reportedly linked to hundreds of unauthorised transactions allegedly involving former finance manager Darryl Joselowsky.

According to reports by Sowetan, Pirates is seeking to freeze four bank accounts allegedly linked to Joselowsky, which have a combined balance of R20.2 million.



The club is also seeking further information from Standard Bank to establish where the money went and who ultimately benefited from the transactions.

Orlando Pirates, however, stressed that the court application does not constitute a finding of wrongdoing.

“The application is not a finding of wrongdoing and should not be interpreted as one. The individual concerned is cooperating, and the Club is committed to a fair process for everyone involved,” the club said in a statement.



The allegations have sparked plenty of reaction among football supporters on social media, with some questioning how a club of Pirates’ stature could allegedly lose such a substantial amount of money through unauthorised transactions.

Fans react to Orlando Pirates ‘losing millions’

@SpholaM6 wrote: “For such a big institution to have these weak internal controls when it comes to its banking process is shocking…”

@Deeflowwd4 added: “They were busy swearing at Pitso and Modiba while a heist of the century was in place.”



Meanwhile, @SundownsOGs joked: “Darryl Joselowsky won’t see heaven. So the whole Betway Premiership prize money is gone.”

“He is very brave. Pickpocketing the Iron Duke?” tweeted @S_Gwiliza.

Orlando Pirates are in action this coming weekend against Mamelodi Sundowns in the MTN8 final.



What’s your take?

World.title: IFP leader calls for no bail and life sentences for convicted rapists
World.content:
Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) leader Velenkosini Hlabisa says people accused of rape should not be granted bail and those found guilty should receive life sentences without parole.

Hlabisa made the remarks while addressing party members at the Greyville Racecourse in Durban on Sunday, 4 October, where the party launched its eThekwini manifesto.

IFP CALLS FOR TOUGHER ACTION AGAINST RAPE

During his address, Hlabisa urged men to join the fight against gender-based violence (GBV) and femicide, emphasising their responsibility to protect women and children.



“Once you are arrested on a case of rape, the person must not be given bail until the case is finalised. When found guilty, the person must be given a life sentence without parole because rapists and murderers are monsters in our society who must be removed once and for all,” said Hlabisa.

Hlabisa’s comments come amid continued concerns about GBV and femicide in South Africa, with political parties calling for stronger action against perpetrators.

SIBIYA FACES RAPE AND OTHER CHARGES

IFP leader Velenkosini Hlabisa’s remarks also come as suspended Deputy National Police Commissioner Lieutenant-General Shadrack Sibiya faces six charges, including rape, sexual grooming of a minor, human trafficking and negligent handling of a firearm.

Sibiya is accused of raping an 18-year-old woman and sexually grooming a 16-year-old girl. He has denied the allegations, telling the Randburg Magistrates’ Court that his sexual encounter with the 18-year-old was consensual.

His bail application is ongoing, with the state opposing his release. The matter was postponed to 7 October.

World.title: Summer came early: Cape Town beach irks local residents
World.content:
An influx of crowds at Saunders' Rock Beach in Sea Point, Cape Town has sparked mixed views. Images via IG

A recent Cape Town heatwave saw residents flocking to the beach – Saunders’ Rock in Sea Point – in particular, much to the annoyance of local residents.

The warmer temperatures – attributed to the El Niño weather phenomenon – have brought dry and windy weather conditions.

PACKED CAPE TOWN BEACH IRKS LOCALS

In photos posted on its social media account, Cape Town Getaway revealed that beachgoers had flocked to the shore during hot, dry weather.



The lifestyle company shared a look at Saunders’ Rock Beach in Sea Point, where visitors can enjoy a swim in a rock pool.

In the pics, the beach attracted a large crowd, who sunbathed, swam and socialised with each other.

In the comments section, residents of the Atlantic Seaboard area expressed their frustration and annoyance.



Comments read as follows:

“Tourism really has ruined Cape Town. What a shame. It’s gone from being manageable to an overrun, chaotic mess in the summer. Book your summers elsewhere, people”

“This used to be a nice, quiet, secluded spot until everyone with a social media account blurted out its existence”



“There goes another summer of no space, no booking reservations and the city absolutely overrun”

“Too peoplely!”

Others commented that beaches were public places that were for all South Africans and tourists to enjoy.



WARMER DAYS AHEAD: THE EL NIÑO EFFECT

In recent weeks, the Western Cape has received little rainfall and experienced warmer-than-normal temperatures due to fewer winter cold fronts reaching the province.

Instead, Cape Town and its surrounds have experienced a dry spell with little to no rainfall.

According to experts, the El Niño condition has contributed to the strange weather patterns.



The condition – where sea surface areas are warmer than usual – has its strongest effect on summer rainfall in South Africa.

In recent weeks, fewer rain-bearing cold fronts have hit the Western Cape, increasing the chances of a drier and warmer winter.

El Niño weather pattern is expected to contribute to hotter and drier conditions and an increased risk of wildfires across the province.



With summer around the corner, Cape Town residents can expect more traffic to local beaches.
