World.title: Coming Home to Heal: Liberian American Surgeon Bringing Global Team to Treat Patients and Train Health Workers
World.content:
Monrovia – Dr. Carolyn Baindu Moore built her career in the United States as a robotic thoracic surgeon, operating on the chest with some of medicine’s most advanced tools. In December, she is bringing a team home to Liberia, where some counties have no specialist surgeon at all.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Moore is CEO and founder of the Liberia Global Health & Surgery Consortium (LGHSC), which officially launches in the country from December 1 to 15. Over two weeks, the group plans to operate on patients, train 250 people in emergency care, screen 100 market women for cancer and hold its first fundraising dinner in Monrovia.



She says she doesn’t want this to be a one-time trip.

“Our goal is to leave a lasting impact through compassionate care, practical training, and partnership with Liberian healthcare teams,” she said.

The gap

Liberians who have had to travel to Monrovia for an operation, or wait weeks for one, know the problem well. The civil war emptied hospitals and drove doctors and nurses abroad. Ebola came a decade later and killed health workers the country could not afford to lose. Liberia has been rebuilding ever since.

The most recent nationwide count of surgical staff, published in the World Journal of Surgery, found 286 surgical providers in Liberia in 2018. Only 67 were accredited specialists. That is 1.6 specialist surgeons, anaesthetists and obstetricians for every 100,000 people. The Lancet Commission on Global Surgery says a country needs at least 20. At the time, Liberia had three specialist anaesthesiologists for the whole country.

Most of those specialists work in Montserrado. In the poorest counties, the study counted 0.7 per 100,000 people.

Women pay much of the price. A UNFPA policy brief drawn from the 2022 national census puts Liberia’s maternal mortality ratio at 854 deaths per 100,000 live births, roughly one mother lost for every 117 babies born alive. The sub-Saharan African average is 536. The global target is under 70.

Then there is cervical cancer. The ICO/IARC Information Centre on HPV and Cancer estimates that 656 Liberian women are diagnosed with it each year and 469 die, about nine women every week. Most of those deaths can be prevented, because screening can catch the disease before it turns deadly. But many women are never screened, and by the time they reach a doctor, little can be done.

Who is coming

The visiting team is made up of five surgeons, six nurses, four global health partners and two medical students. On the ground, they will join five Liberian surgeons, 15 nurse volunteers and 17 Consortium volunteers. The Consortium says it works in partnership with the Ministry of Health, and that its plans were drawn up with Liberian hospital leaders, county health teams and community representatives.

In the operating room

From December 7 to 11, visiting and Liberian surgeons will operate side by side. Where equipment and facilities allow, that will include laparoscopic surgery, sometimes called “keyhole” surgery. Instead of one long cut, the surgeon works through a few small openings with a camera. Patients generally hurt less, heal faster and go home sooner. Few Liberian hospitals offer it now, and teaching it is one of the main reasons for the mission.

The hospital where the operations will take place, and how many patients will be treated, have not yet been confirmed. Local clinical teams will screen patients.

Learning to save a life

The same week, at the Liberian Learning Center at Paynesville Town Hall, the Consortium plans to train 250 people in Basic Life Support and Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support. The courses teach CPR and what to do when a heart stops, the kind of emergency where a few minutes decide whether someone lives.

Not all the trainees are medical workers. Doctors, nurses, residents and emergency medical staff will sit alongside ordinary citizens. Some will be trained to teach the course themselves, so the skills keep spreading after the visitors leave. The team is also donating automated external defibrillators, or AEDs, the portable machines that can shock a stopped heart back into rhythm. They are still hard to find in Liberia.

For the women who feed the city

On December 14 and 15, a mobile clinic will set up in the Rock Church community in Duazon for 100 market women. They will get health education, consultations, breast and reproductive health checks, and screening for cervical cancer and high-risk HPV. The Consortium’s pathology team will process the samples, and its OB/GYN workgroup will work with local health authorities to make sure women who need further care are referred.

The choice of market women is deliberate. They keep homes running and children in school, often on what they earn in a single day. Taking a day off to sit in a clinic queue means losing that money, so many simply don’t go. This time, the clinic is coming to them.

A dinner and a longer plan

On December 12, the Consortium will host its founding fundraiser banquet at Afro Beach, Thinker Village, from 6:00 to 10:30 p.m. Dr. Deddeh E. P. Supuwood will give the keynote address, and Mr. Leo Lekpele Nupolu-Johnson will be master of ceremonies. Money raised will go to patient care, training, equipment, and community outreach.

Medical missions to Africa have a mixed reputation. Too often, a team flies in, operates, takes pictures and flies out, leaving behind patients with no follow-up and local staff no better prepared than before. LGHSC, which now counts more than 120 members in more than 16 workgroups on four continents, says it is trying to do the opposite. It wants to work through Liberian teams, keep mentoring them, and keep checking on patients long after December.

Whether that works will only be clear after the visitors fly home. It will show in the nurse in Paynesville who can now run a resuscitation, the surgeon who can do a keyhole operation without help, and the market woman in Duazon whose results come back in time.

“Our measure of success,” Moore said, “is the quality of care we provide and the knowledge, confidence, and capacity that remain long after we leave.”

Those wishing to volunteer, partner, or support the launch can contact [email protected] or visit www.libghsc.org. Donations can be made at https://givebutter.com/XYetak.

World.title: Liberia: House Honors Fallen Former Bong County Lawmaker Ranney Jackson
World.content:
Monrovia – The leadership and members of the House of Representatives on Thursday paid their final respects to the late Dr. Ranney B. Jackson Sr., a former Bong County lawmaker and veteran public servant, during a State Funeral held at the Capitol Building in Monrovia.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The ceremony brought together members of the Legislature, government officials, family members, friends, former colleagues, and well-wishers who gathered to honor Jackson’s decades of service to Liberia.



Speaker of the House Richard Nagbe Koon, speaking on behalf of the leadership and members of the House, extended condolences to the bereaved family and recognized Jackson’s contributions to the Legislature and the Liberian state.

Speaker Koon said the presence of the House leadership and members at the funeral reflected the institution’s respect for those who have served the Liberian people under its mandate.

Members of the House joined the Speaker in a moment of solemn reflection and paid their final respects to their former colleague.

Dr. Jackson’s public service career spanned local government, the Legislature, national administration and public policy.

He served as a member of the National Transitional Legislative Assembly (NTLA) from 2003 to 2005, representing Bong County during a critical period in Liberia’s post-war transition.

During his two-year tenure, Jackson chaired the NTLA’s Post and Telecommunications Committee. His work on the committee included efforts that contributed to reducing the cost of SIM cards from US$65 to US$15 in 2005.

Following his service in the transitional legislature, Jackson remained active in national politics and public administration. He made three unsuccessful bids for the Bong County senatorial seat, contesting the elections in 2005, 2011 and 2014.

He later served as Superintendent of Bong County during the first administration of former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf. During Sirleaf’s second term, he was appointed Deputy Minister for Operations at the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

Jackson’s public service continued under President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, who in 2024 appointed him Co-Chairman of the Assets Recovery and Property Retrieval Core Team, where he served alongside Chairman Cllr. Edwin Kla Martin.

At the Assets Recovery and Property Retrieval Task Force, Jackson was recognized for his experience in governance, public administration, finance and public policy as the government intensified efforts to trace, recover and safeguard public assets.

Before his death, Jackson had also recently earned a Ph.D. in Public Policy and Administration, specializing in Local Government Management and Sustainable Communities, from Walden University in the United States.

His career reflected a progression through several levels of public service—from county administration and the transitional Legislature to senior positions within the national government and public policy.

Dr. Jackson died at the John F. Kennedy Memorial Hospital in Monrovia on August 22, 2024, at age 74, following a brief illness.

According to the obituary, the body will be taken to Bong County on Friday, October 2, for a night of wake-keeping, followed by the funeral service and burial on Saturday.

World.title: Liberia: FPA Report Triggers Action as China Union Assesses Pollution, Road Damage in Mining Communities
World.content:
MARGIBI COUNTY — A FrontPage Africa investigation into alleged environmental damage and deteriorating living conditions in communities surrounding China Union’s mining concession has prompted the company and Margibi County District Four Representative Emmanuel O. Yahr to conduct a joint field assessment of affected areas.

By Yawah Y. Jaivey

Bangli, a subsidiary of China Union, which is engaged in iron ore extraction around Bong Mountain in Bong and Margibi Counties, joined Rep. Yahr’s office over the weekend to inspect communities where residents have raised concerns about water pollution, damaged farmland, deteriorating feeder roads and other impacts they associate with mining activities.



The assessment followed an FPA report published two weeks ago documenting complaints from residents of several villages bordering the China Union concession.

Residents alleged that mining activities have contributed to the pollution of waterways and farmland, deposits of mud and mining debris, excessive dust and damage to roads used to transport agricultural produce and access essential services.

Following the publication, Rep. Yahr conducted an initial assessment of the affected communities and engaged residents about their concerns before bringing the issues to the attention of Bangli management.

During the latest joint assessment, representatives of Bangli and Rep. Yahr’s office visited several communities to examine the allegations firsthand, including claims involving contaminated water sources, damaged crops and deteriorating farm-to-market roads.

At the conclusion of the assessment, Bangli management committed to addressing concerns raised by the affected communities and taking appropriate measures going forward.

Residents, meanwhile, commended Rep. Yahr for responding to their complaints and expressed hope that the company would follow through on its commitments.

The affected communities include Neitasue, Gboryourmue, Benmue and Jack Village, with residents estimating that more than 2,000 people across the communities are affected by the reported conditions.

During an earlier FPA tour of communities near the Bangli mining area, residents described what they said were worsening environmental and living conditions.

An FPA reporter observed deposits of mud and iron ore debris covering sections of vegetable gardens and rice fields. Some waterways and surrounding farmland also contained visible sediment and mining-related debris.

Residents said the situation becomes particularly severe during heavy rainfall, when muddy water and sediment reportedly flow from mining areas into creeks and other water sources used by surrounding communities.

Residents Complain of Water Pollution

Moses Kollie, Town Chief of Gboryourmue Village in Margibi County, said residents have increasingly struggled to access what they consider safe drinking water since mining activities intensified.

“In our villages, we ran out of drinking water. After the mine started, most of our backwaters have been polluted,” Kollie said.

He also alleged that pollution has affected agricultural production by reducing the amount of land residents can effectively cultivate.

“All our farming lands and waters have been polluted. Dust has covered all our plants. Productivity of the land is reduced. There’s less cultivable soil available,” Kollie told FPA.

Residents said the reported conditions are threatening household food security and their ability to generate income from farming.

Tamba Philip, a resident of Neitasue Village in Fuamah District, Bong County, said a water source once used for drinking, bathing and washing clothes has become increasingly muddy.

“This is where we get drinking water, wash our clothes, and bathe, but now it has turned murky. There are already sediments, which were not here when there were no mining operations up in the mountain,” Philip said.

He said the problem becomes more pronounced during periods of heavy rainfall.

“You visit us here when there’s rain and see our body of waters. Murky water will go to several neighboring villages,” Philip said.

Mud, Mining Debris Affect Road Access

Residents also blamed mining-related runoff and sediment for worsening the condition of a feeder road linking some of the affected villages to surrounding communities.

According to residents, large quantities of mud and iron ore debris carried downstream from the mining area have accumulated along sections of the road, making transportation difficult and, at times, nearly impossible.

They said the deteriorating road has made it harder for farmers to transport produce to markets and for residents to access health care, schools and other essential services.

Samuel K. David, a resident of Gboryourmue, said China Union resumed mining operations nearly four years ago and alleged that the renewed activities have coincided with increased pollution of creeks and farmland.

David said residents have repeatedly requested assistance, including the installation of hand pumps and rehabilitation of damaged roads, but alleged that their concerns have not received adequate attention.

Blasting Raises Health, Structural Concerns

Residents have also raised concerns about loud blasting they associate with mining operations.

Some alleged that blasting, particularly at night, has disrupted sleep and created anxiety among people living near the mining areas.

Residents further claimed that repeated blasting has caused cracks in some houses. However, determining whether mining activity caused the reported structural damage would require an independent technical assessment.

Amara Tate, a Gboryourmue resident, said the combination of water pollution and blasting has heightened anxiety among residents.

“With the blasting that’s going on, our backwaters are not just polluted, but our houses are being damaged and we, especially those with hypotension, are left to endure those loud explosions. So, we’re mostly concerned about our health,” Tate said.

Residents Question Social Development Benefits

Beyond environmental concerns, residents say they have yet to see what they consider meaningful social and economic benefits from the company’s presence in their communities.

David alleged that communities directly affected by mining activities have not benefited sufficiently from social development initiatives associated with the concession.

He cited what he described as inadequate access to basic services, including clinics, safe drinking water, schools and employment opportunities.

According to David, communities affected by mining should receive tangible development benefits, particularly where their farmland, waterways, roads and livelihoods are affected.

Activist Calls for Accountability

Social justice activist Ambassador Joseph Orland Beyan has also called for greater accountability in the management of Liberia’s mineral resources, arguing that resource development should not come at the expense of communities living in mining areas.

Beyan said the Mineral Development Agreement between the Government of Liberia and China Union should protect the lives, dignity, health and livelihoods of people living within and around the concession.

He said he finds it difficult to believe that the Liberian government would knowingly enter into an agreement that places citizens at risk.

“Yet, the reality on the ground is deeply troubling. Our brothers and sisters living around the company’s operational areas are facing serious challenges. Their farmlands, sources of water, crops, homes, roads, and overall health and well-being are being affected, while many communities continue to live in conditions that deserve urgent attention,” Beyan said.

He urged authorities and the company to treat the concerns as issues affecting real communities rather than merely administrative matters.

“These are not just statistics or issues written on paper. These are our people. These are families. These are communities whose lives and livelihoods matter,” he said.

Beyan called for affected communities to have a meaningful platform to seek redress.

“We cannot remain silent when the people who are supposed to benefit from our natural resources are instead left struggling to protect their land, homes, health, and future,” he said.

He added that his group was preparing what he described as a new advocacy approach focused on accountability and the peaceful pursuit of justice for affected communities.

“Our natural resources must not come at the cost of the lives and dignity of our people,” Beyan said.

World.title: Integrity Watch Warns Liberia Must Verify Its Mineral Wealth Before Signing Major Deals
World.content:
Monrovia – Integrity Watch Liberia Executive Director Harold Marvin Aidoo is calling on the government to move cautiously in developing Liberia’s emerging critical-mineral sector, warning that the country could repeat its long history of exporting valuable resources while mining communities remain poor and little wealth is retained domestically.

In a detailed policy commentary released Thursday titled “Liberia Must Not Miss the Critical Minerals Moment,” Aidoo said growing global demand for minerals used in batteries, electric vehicles and renewable-energy technologies presents Liberia with another opportunity to turn its natural resources into long-term economic gains.

But he cautioned that the opportunity could become another resource curse if the government fails to establish the country’s actual mineral potential, strengthen oversight and negotiate investment agreements with enforceable benefits for Liberians.



Aidoo recommended that the government publish the non-confidential findings of a China-supported mineral survey and commission an independent geological verification before making major commitments to potential investors.

The survey has reportedly identified indications of lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, rare-earth elements and other strategically important minerals.

Aidoo, however, cautioned against treating mineral indications as proof of commercially viable reserves.

“Liberia has another chance to turn mineral wealth into lasting prosperity,” he said, arguing that the first step must be establishing exactly what minerals Liberia possesses, where they are located, their commercial value and whether they can be extracted responsibly.

Learning From Iron Ore

Aidoo pointed to Liberia’s experience with iron ore as a cautionary lesson.

He traced commercial iron-ore production to Bomi Hills in 1951, noting that the industry has generated exports and government revenue but has historically had limited connections to the wider Liberian economy.

“Railways and ports moved ore abroad, while the knowledge and industrial capacity needed to transform the wider economy remained insufficient,” he said.

He warned that the global transition toward cleaner energy could reproduce that pattern if Liberia becomes primarily a supplier of raw materials for green technologies manufactured elsewhere.

“The energy transition could reproduce that pattern,” Aidoo said. “Liberia might supply minerals for cleaner technologies overseas while absorbing environmental damage and receiving only a modest share of the value.”

He added: “A green product does not guarantee a fair supply chain.”

Global Competition Creates Leverage

Aidoo said growing competition among major economies for critical minerals could give Liberia greater bargaining power, provided the country approaches potential investors from a position of knowledge and strategic planning.

He cited China’s strong position in mineral processing and efforts by the United States and its partners to diversify their supply chains.

Liberia, he said, should engage China, the United States, Europe and other potential partners, but any agreements should be transparent and aligned with the country’s development priorities.

“The question for every partnership should be practical: what will Liberia gain beyond the export of ore?” he asked.

He recommended that future mining agreements contain measurable commitments covering Liberian employment, skills development, local procurement, shared infrastructure and environmental protection.

“Political friendship cannot substitute for a sound commercial bargain,” Aidoo said.

Verify Mineral Wealth, Strengthen Institutions

Aidoo identified geological knowledge and institutional capacity as immediate priorities.

He called for publication of the non-confidential findings of the mineral survey and independent verification of the country’s mineral potential.

He also urged the government to build institutions capable of interpreting geological data and independently assessing proposals from mining companies.

“Negotiating without that capacity places the country at a disadvantage before discussions even begin,” he said.

Aidoo further recommended a national critical-minerals strategy linking the sector to Liberia’s electricity, education, industrial and trade policies.

He argued that Liberia’s existing legal and policy framework—including the 2000 Minerals and Mining Law and 2010 Mineral Policy—predates the current global competition over minerals critical to the energy transition.

Any reforms, he said, should translate policy objectives into enforceable obligations.

Transparency in Mining Deals

Aidoo called for mineral licensing to be conducted transparently and competitively, with the beneficial ownership of companies seeking mining rights disclosed.

He also urged the government to make mining contracts publicly accessible and provide lawmakers responsible for ratifying agreements with independent technical advice.

Commitments on local procurement, training and mineral processing, he said, should include clear deadlines, measurable targets and consequences for non-compliance.

“Local procurement, training and processing commitments need deadlines, measurable targets and consequences for non-performance,” Aidoo said.

He also called for stronger safeguards to protect government revenue, including the capacity to independently verify mineral quality, production volumes and export values.

Such capacity, he said, would help the government detect under-invoicing and abusive pricing arrangements involving related companies.

“Without these safeguards, apparently attractive agreements can still leave the country collecting far less than it should,” he warned.

Value Addition Without Unrealistic Promises

While advocating greater domestic value addition, Aidoo cautioned against assuming that every mineral discovery should automatically lead to a refinery or processing plant.

“Liberia cannot demand a refinery for every deposit without considering electricity costs, water availability, environmental risks and markets,” he said.

Instead, he recommended that Liberia initially focus on retaining more geological, engineering, maintenance and logistics work associated with mining while gradually developing capacity for commercially viable processing.

Reliable and affordable electricity, he said, will be critical to that effort.

Major mining investments, Aidoo argued, should also contribute to electricity and transportation infrastructure that can benefit surrounding communities and other businesses.

“Shared railways, ports and transmission infrastructure can create economic opportunities well beyond the mine,” he said.

Skills, Jobs and Communities

Aidoo placed particular emphasis on developing Liberian technical expertise.

He called for greater investment in universities and vocational institutions to train geologists, engineers, laboratory technicians and environmental specialists.

Mining agreements, he said, should finance apprenticeships and recognized qualifications while creating opportunities for women and young people from mining-affected communities.

“Counting Liberians on payrolls is insufficient if technical knowledge and managerial authority remain elsewhere,” Aidoo said.

He said mining development should therefore be measured not only by the number of Liberians employed but also by whether Liberians acquire the technical knowledge and decision-making experience necessary to assume senior positions in the sector.

Aidoo also urged the government to ensure that communities affected by mining have a meaningful voice in decisions that could affect their livelihoods and environment.

Water protection, community consultation, accessible grievance mechanisms and adequately funded mine-closure plans, he said, should be enforceable requirements.

“Development cannot be measured only by export earnings when families lose farmland, fisheries or safe drinking water,” he said.

‘What Remains After the Minerals Are Gone?’

Aidoo further encouraged Liberia to work with neighboring countries to develop regional markets and industrial capacity around critical minerals.

While Liberia may not be able to manufacture every finished product domestically, he said the country can participate in African processing and manufacturing chains instead of remaining dependent on raw-material exports.

For Aidoo, the most consequential decisions will be made before mining licenses and long-term sales agreements are signed.

He urged the government to use the current period to establish the scale and commercial viability of Liberia’s mineral potential, strengthen regulatory institutions and define the benefits investors will be required to deliver.

“The decisions taken before licences and long-term sales agreements are signed will shape what Liberia retains for decades,” Aidoo said. “We should use this period to verify our mineral potential, strengthen institutions and define the benefits investors must deliver.”

He said Liberia’s success should ultimately be measured not simply by the volume of minerals exported or government revenue generated during individual projects, but by what remains after the resources are exhausted.

“Minerals are finite. Skills, productive infrastructure and capable institutions can outlast them,” Aidoo said.

“Liberia’s goal should be to turn the resources beneath our soil into the capacity to build prosperity long after the mines close.”

World.title: Holiness Revival Movement Brings Call For Righteousness, Heaven and Biblical Truth to Liberia
World.content:
Monrovia – A Christian ministry known as the Holiness Revival Movement is calling on Liberians to return to what it describes as the Biblical teachings of righteousness, holiness and preparation for eternity.

By Anthony Gray

Speaking ahead of a four-day conference scheduled for October 1–4 in Congo Town, outside Monrovia, Pastor Paul Rika said the movement is in Liberia to “revive holiness” and encourage Christians and non-Christians to embrace what he described as the truth of the Gospel of Jesus Christ.



Pastor Rika said the non-denominational movement was established as a means of bringing Christians together around Biblical teachings, emphasizing that human beings will ultimately face judgment.

According to him, the world is not a permanent place and people must therefore prepare for what comes after life.

He said Jesus Christ came and died for humanity so that people could have access to God, urging Christians to take seriously the teachings contained in the Bible.

Pastor Rika also linked some of the social problems and corruption in society to what he described as a decline in the preaching of biblical truth and the fear of God.

He referenced the Biblical instruction to observe the things written in Scripture, arguing that stronger adherence to Christian teachings could help promote moral discipline and responsible living.

The preacher further challenged those who question the existence of heaven and hell, saying Christians should take seriously the Bible’s teachings about life after death and divine judgment.

Meanwhile, Evangelist Linda Paul Rika shared her personal testimony, recounting what she described as a dramatic transformation from a lifestyle she considered contrary to Christian teachings.

She said that before encountering Jesus Christ, she struggled with alcohol, multiple relationships, drug use, tattoos, what she described as “naked dressing,” and visits to herbalists for charms.

Evangelist Linda said her experience eventually led her to embrace Christianity and dedicate herself to spreading a message of repentance, righteousness and holiness.

She also warned that, in her view, Satan is blinding people to the seriousness of sin and the consequences associated with it.

The Holiness Revival Movement says its Liberian campaign is intended to serve as a catalyst for Christians from different denominations to come together and renew their commitment to Biblical teachings.

Pastor Rika, who is currently on a tour of Liberia, said the campaign seeks to bring what he called “the life of the truth of Jesus Christ” to the Liberian people.

The conference is scheduled to run from October 1 to 4 with morning sessions beginning at 8:00 a.m. at the Oldest Congo Town, opposite SATCOM

Organizers are expecting large numbers of people to attend and are inviting Liberians from across the country to participate in what they describe as a life-changing Christian gathering focused on repentance, holiness and faith in Jesus Christ.

World.title: Sisters of the Child Jesus celebrate 100 years of existence in Kasama
World.content:
Apostolic Nuncio to Zambia and Malawi, Gian Luca Perici, has described the 100 years of existence of the Sisters of the Child Jesus (SCJ), as a testimony of God’s faithfulness and unwavering dedication to serving humanity.

Most Reverend Perici says the congregation’s journey from a humble beginning a century ago to its current position is a story of courage, sacrifice and total trust in God.

The Vatican Ambassador to Zambia and Malawi said this during the centenary celebration of the Sisters of the Child Jesus at Chilubula Mission in Kasama yesterday.

“We are here to celebrate a great milestone. 100 years ago, this congregation began from a humble beginning. Throughout this period, the Lord has guided your journey which has not been easy,” Archbishop Perici said.

The Nuncio disclosed that despite numerous challenges over the decades, the Sisters have remained steadfast and have continued to be a visible sign of God’s love, especially to the most vulnerable people in society.

“Despite numerous challenges, you have continued to show God’s love,” he said.

The Nuncio, who is the Pope’s representative, paid special tribute to the founding members of the congregation, describing them as brave women whose vision and faith laid a strong foundation for the works being seen today.

“We thank God for the brave women who started this mission. We thank the women who have stood firm for this organisation. Your work in health and education is commendable, you have always remembered the poor, giving them comfort,” he said.

He added that the centenary celebration is not only a moment to look back at the past with gratitude, but also an opportunity to look at the present with joy and to the future with hope.

“As we celebrate the present, we see how God continues to bless your congregation. God has sustained you and He is still doing great things through you. I encourage you to stay united. Continue to live out your calling with love, serve the people with total dedication, do not be afraid of what lies ahead,” he said.

Meanwhile, Archbishop of Kasama Archdiocese, Ignatius Chama, called on members of the Sisters of the Child Jesus to continue supporting and appreciating one another as they fulfill God’s work.

Archbishop Chama urged the Sisters to rediscover their vocation of love and to remain true to their identity.

“To find your vocation of love, look, it is who you are,” Archbishop Chama said.

He said the Sisters should remain rooted in love, unity and service which defines their congregation.

Archbishop Chama also thanked the Apostolic Nuncio for accepting to celebrate the milestone with the Sisters of the Child Jesus.

The Sisters of the Child Jesus are a diocesan congregation founded in Chilubula, in the Archdiocese of Kasama in 1926 by Bishop Étienne Larue, a Missionary of Africa.

World.title: President Hichilema reiterates call to preserve culture
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has reaffirmed the government’s recognition of the importance of traditional ceremonies in preserving Zambia’s cultural heritage, national identity, unity and social cohesion.

President Hichilema said traditional ceremonies such as the Lukwakwa, provide an important platform for communities to preserve and showcase their culture and heritage.

He said this in a speech read on his behalf by Northwestern Province Permanent Secretary, Grandson Katambi at the 2026 Lukwakwa traditional ceremony of the Mbunda- people of Manyinga and Kabompo Districts.

President Hichilema said the government will continue supporting the hosting of traditional ceremonies and working with traditional leaders to preserve cultural heritage.

He said the government will also continue working with traditional leadership to accelerate development in their chiefdoms.

“Government has supported various developmental projects in the chiefdom, including the drilling of boreholes, construction of health facilities, classroom blocks and science laboratories, provision of desks and construction of a local court,” he said.

He explained the projects were aimed at improving service delivery to the people of Manyinga district.

He has since called on traditional leaders, Members of Parliament and Ward Development Committees to work together in identifying and planning developmental projects which should be financed through the Constituency Development Fund (CDF).

The Head of State has meanwhile cautioned Ward Development Committees against frustrating government’s development efforts, saying successful implementation of projects required cooperation among stakeholders.

President Hichilema said Ward Development Committees should be scrutinised and strengthened to ensure that projects are successfully implemented.

He said partnerships among traditional leaders, local authorities, government and communities were important in advancing the Grow Zambia Agenda.

The President has therefore appealed to traditional and local leaders to encourage young people to participate in skills training, particularly entrepreneurship programmes.

He said the responsibility of empowering young people required all stakeholders to come on board.

The Head of State has further encouraged young people to be proud of their identity, tribes and origins and advised them not to be ashamed of speaking their traditional languages.

And speaking at the same event, Lukwakwa Traditional Ceremony Organising Committee National Chairperson, Ndandula Livingi, has called for the protection and promotion of Mbunda cultural heritage.

Mr Livingi said culture should not be reduced to dancing but must instead encompass the broader values, traditions, language, history and practices of the Mbunda people.

He has since called on organisers and participants to reduce dances that were not part of Mbunda heritage in order to give prominence to authentic Mbunda cultural practices.

Mr Livingi also urged the people to support efforts aimed at transforming the Lukwakwa traditional ceremony into a major cultural and tourism event.

He said the ceremony had great potential to attract tourists and contribute to the promotion of the Mbunda culture.

“Lukwakwa is a big ceremony which, unfortunately, has been a sleeping lion, but eventually we will start seeing tourists coming to the ceremony,” Mr Livingi said.

He said the people belonging to the Mbunda tribe should take ownership of their culture and ensure that cultural materials and practices showcased during Lukwakwa reflected their heritage.

Mr Livingi said the transformation of the ceremony required collective support from traditional leaders, government, local communities and other stakeholders.

He further urged the people to embrace and promote the Mbunda culture so that it could be preserved for future generations.

The Lukwakwa traditional ceremony is an annual gathering of the Mbunda people of Manyinga and Kabompo districts aimed at showcasing and preserving their cultural heritage.

World.title: Heads of departments urged to prioritise Grow Zambia Agenda
World.content:
Muchinga Province Deputy Permanent Secretary, Brian Sichande, has urged provincial heads of government departments under head 88 in Muchinga to plan and budget deliberately to support the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Mr Sichande noted that it is imperative for the Heads of Departments to identify practical interventions within their respective mandates that will enable them to contribute to national aspirations of the Grow Zambia production targets.

He further advised them to ensure that they also align the identified targets to National Development Plan and provincial priorities.

Mr Sichande said this when he addressed Heads of Department during the planning and budgeting meeting to prepare for the 2027-2029 medium term budget plan held in Chinsali district.

The Deputy Permanent Secretary disclosed that the Muchinga Province Administration Head 88 has been given an indicative budget ceiling of K124 million for the 2027 budget.

He added that with the constrained fiscal requirements given, the ceiling requires discipline in prioritisation in order to obtain maximum value from every Kwacha allocated.

Mr Sichande further said departmental submissions should prioritise statutory and legal obligations, realistic costing of tasks and operations, and provision for operational costs of key programmes.

World.title: ECZ trains DVEC, VEFs in Kanchibiya ahead of by-election
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) has commenced training for the District Voter Education Committee (DVEC) and Voter Education Facilitators (VEFs) in Kanchibiya district ahead of a by-election in Lubaleshi Ward.

The by-election was caused by the death of United Party for National Development (UPND) aspiring Councilor for Lubaleshi Ward in the August 2026 general election, Evans Chileshe, who passed away immediately after filing his nominations.

The training workshop for DVEC and VEFs is being held at Kanchibiya Town Council’s new Civic Centre.

Kanchibiya District Electoral Officer, Julius Katuka, urged participants not to be complacent but proactive in their approach to voter education ahead of the by-election.

Mr. Katuka acknowledged that the district’s vast terrain often proves to be a challenge for Voter Education Facilitators hence the need for them to devise effective strategies for undertaking the voter education exercise.

“A lot of things happen in the field and we must strive to ensure we are professional as we carry out activities that will help facilitate the coming by-election,” Mr Katuka said.

He said every member of the committee has a part to play and must play it well.

Meanwhile, DVEC Coordinator, Chrispin Chishimba urged members to participate fully in the workshop so as to be well equipped for the coming by-election.

Mr Chishimba thanked members for attending the meeting promptly and urged them to demonstrate the same zeal towards the by-election that they have shown in previous electoral exercises.

And DVEC member, Ernest Kambindi, said the committee stands ready to carry out activities for the by-election.

Mr Kambindi said the by-election is of great importance to Kanchibiya district as Lubaleshi Ward is the district’s largest ward.

World.title: President Hichilema asks Zambians to unite to achieve Grow Zambia Agenda
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has called on Zambians to embrace unity, discipline and hard work to drive the newly unveiled Grow Zambia Agenda.

Speaking when he graced the Samu Lya Moomba Traditional Ceremony of Chief Choongo in Monze District, President Hichilema said the values demonstrated by freedom fighters and traditional leaders during the struggle for independence remained critical to Zambia’s development.

He said Zambians should emulate the spirit of unity and hard work as the country pursues economic development.

“Freedom fighters and traditional leaders of old demonstrated unity and hard work that earned the country its independence,” President Hichilema said.

And President Hichilema reaffirmed the government’s commitment to increasing power generation, saying a thermal power plant would be established in Chief Choongo and Chief Hamusonde’s chiefdoms as part of the target to generate 10,000 megawatts.

“We will continue investing in power generation, including establishing a thermal power plant in Chief Choongo and Chief Hamusonde’s chiefdoms as part of our 10,000 megawatt target,” he said.

President Hichilema also challenged traditional leaders to support the government’s one-billion dollar beef export target by promoting livestock disease control and increased production.

“We need our traditional leaders to support the one-billion-dollar beef export target by ensuring that livestock disease control is strengthened and production is increased through effective management of grazing areas,” President Hichilema said.

The President also called for the preservation of historical sites to ensure that young Zambians understand the country’s liberation struggle.

“We must preserve our historical sites like Samu Lya Moomba and many other sites across the country so that our young people can understand and appreciate the struggles that brought us our freedom,” he said.

The President further called for concerted efforts to curb bush burning in the plains and other parts of the country.

The President has meanwhile urged councils to prioritise water-related programmes in preparation for the projected 2026/2027 El Niño weather conditions to ensure communities continue accessing water during dry periods.

“Councils must prioritise water-related programmes so that our communities can continue accessing water during the dry periods that may arise from the anticipated El Niño conditions,” President Hichilema said.

And President Hichilema has assured farmers who supplied grain to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) that the government was making progress towards settling all outstanding payments.

“Government is making progress towards ensuring that all outstanding payments to farmers who supplied their crops to the FRA are settled,” President Hichilema said.

He also urged farmers to retain sufficient maize for household consumption and not to sell all their produce.

The President said the government was rehabilitating and constructing maize storage sheds, while encouraging cooperatives to invest in their own storage facilities, which could also generate income.

Meanwhile, Minister of Green Economy and Environment Gilbert Siame said the government was working to ensure communities likely to be affected by the projected El Niño conditions were adequately prepared.

And Acting Southern Province Permanent Secretary, Gift Monde, said the province was well prepared and had adequate information on the anticipated weather conditions.

“Government and stakeholders in the province are working to ensure that communities are adequately prepared to mitigate the possible effects of the weather phenomenon,” Mr Monde said.

The ceremony was also attended by 71 traditional leaders from across the country, government officials, 40 United Party for National Development (UPND) Members of Parliament and hundreds of people from the local community.

World.title: Copper Queens Jet Out for Uganda Showdown
World.content:
Smarting from a disappointing WAFCON campaign, the Copper Queens have left for Kampala on a redemption mission – with Coach Charles Haalubono vowing to deliver Olympic qualification.

The Senior Women’s National Team left Kenneth Kaunda International Airport aboard RwandAir around 14h00, with eight foreign-based stars expected to join the camp in Uganda to complete the 25-member squad ahead of Thursday’s crucial first leg against the Crested Cranes.

The team is expected to land in Kampala at 03h00 on Monday morning.

Zambia faces Uganda in round two of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic qualifiers on October 8, a tie that offers a chance to heal the wounds of failing to qualify for the World Cup at the WAFCON.

Haalubono admits his charges started clumsily but says five days of intense training have sharpened the team.

“So far, the response has been very good. They all looking good now. The start was not all that good. They looked clumsy but after five days of training we saw a bit of change. Now starting this week, they are sharp; their reactions are up to that level,” Haalubono told FAZ Media.

The Green Buffaloes trainer said lessons from WAFCON have been harsh – Zambia can keep possession but concedes too many goals. Defence and movement on the ball have been the focus in training.

“We have got a big duty ahead of us to give the nation what it deserves because we failed to qualify to the World Cup. So we have another chance of amending our mistakes so we are supposed to qualify for the Olympics,” he declared.

“We are here to work and to deliver; so it’s not something that we should even try to shun away. On my part I’m ready to work and deliver.”

Haalubono described Uganda as an athletic side that relies on direct football and long balls which Zambia must counter, but insists Zambia’s experience from the last two Olympics will count.

He also thanked FAZ for reinforcing his bench with seasoned women’s football coaches Florence Mwila and William Zulu.

World.title: Mundubile And Zulu Taken To Solwezi For Sedition Plea As Mpundu Challenges Militia Evidence
World.content:
Brian Mundubile, the presidential candidate of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), and his running mate Makebi Zulu are being transported by road to Solwezi by prison authorities and the police for a court appearance on Monday. They are due to take a formal plea in a sedition case, and the trial could begin.

On their last appearance, the two NRPUP leaders were before Principal Resident Magistrate Mambwe Mukonde. The case was adjourned to 5 and 6 October for a formal plea and the possible start of the trial.

The case stems from social media posts made after the tense 13 August election. Mr Mundubile is accused of making a Facebook post claiming that the NRPUP was leading the presidential race, based on Parallel Vote Tabulation (PVT) data. The post also demanded that the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) resume vote counting and announce the results. Mr Zulu is accused of posting that Mr Mundubile would shortly address the nation, and urging the public to remain on standby.

The ECZ suspended the counting and announcement of results nationwide on 14 August, saying the decision followed reports of violence targeting polling staff and, in some cases, the theft of marked ballot papers. The commission later lifted the suspension. The European Union Election Observation Mission said the suspension was followed by a deterioration in the transparency of the tabulation process.

As the two leaders head to court, TONSE Alliance presidential affairs chairperson Binwell Mpundu has challenged the authorities to produce the evidence behind the alleged militia activities in a separate treason case involving Mr Mundubile, Mr Zulu and other opposition figures. Mr Mpundu questioned why investigations that he said began in 2023 have yet to produce tangible evidence sufficient to take the matter to court.

“So in this case they have been investigating an imaginary militia for four years, but they still have not gotten any tangible evidence. But when they address the nation, they speak with authority and conviction that they picked evidence including high-grade military weapons,” Mr Mpundu said in a social media post.

His remarks follow government statements that persons linked to alleged militia activities had been under surveillance for between three and five years before a joint security operation at a property in Kabulonga. Government said the operation led to the recovery of restricted military equipment and the arrest of several people. A statement from Secretary to the Cabinet Patrick Kangwa said Mr Mundubile was also found at the scene.

Mr Mpundu disputed the government’s account and questioned the evidence presented publicly in support of the allegations. He also challenged claims that security officers came under fire, saying the authorities had not publicly shown the evidence he believed should accompany those claims.

“They claim they were shot at when they raided Brian Mundubile’s house, but they have failed to show any gun they retrieved, let alone the exchange of fire with our militia. No one was hit, but they managed to kill Hon Mutotwe Kafwaya, who was just in the house, at close range,” he said.

Government has maintained that the operation followed intelligence on individuals considered a national security threat, and that officers were met with gunfire, resulting in an exchange of fire. Authorities said former Cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was fatally wounded during the operation. Mr Mundubile has separately rejected that account and said Mr Kafwaya was shot inside his residence.

In his social media post, Mr Mpundu also said people connected to Mr Mundubile were being targeted in an effort to obtain statements implicating the opposition leader and his associates. “They are now out abducting anyone connected to Brian Mundubile and taking them to torture chambers and forcing them to implicate Mr Mundubile and team so that they can be freed,” he said. He called on the authorities to end what he described as an unnecessary act, and to release Mr Mundubile and his colleagues.

Other political leaders have also raised concerns. Socialist Party (SP) president Dr Fred M’membe said the tensions that followed the election, including the sweeping arrests of opposition members, “cannot be swept under the rug in the name of ‘moving forward’.” He called for an end to the weaponisation of the criminal justice system against political opponents.

Former Cabinet minister Given Lubinda asked how long treason suspects can be held before they are presented before a court. He said the State told the nation it had followed the matter for years, and he wants the Director of Public Prosecutions to say what the law allows.

For the two NRPUP leaders, the next step is the court in Solwezi. The matter is before the court on Monday, with 5 and 6 October set for a formal plea and the possible start of the trial.

World.title: “What Public Interest Exists?” Chansa Questions Archbishop Banda Prosecution
World.content:
Chansa Urges State To Drop Archbishop Banda Case, Says Prosecution Is Not In The Public Interest

Movement for Economic Emancipation (MEE) president Given Chansa has urged the State to discontinue the prosecution of Archbishop Alick Banda over a motor vehicle he received as a gift, saying that continuing criminal proceedings against a prominent clergyman cannot serve the public interest. In a statement, Mr Chansa said the State should weigh that test before pressing ahead, even where it believes it has enough evidence to charge.

He said prosecutorial discretion requires authorities to ask whether pursuing a criminal case is in the public interest, and described that test as a fundamental feature of the discretion the State holds. Mr Chansa tied the test to the way cases are brought. “You have to remember that criminal prosecutions are carried out in the name of the public via the state institutions, hence why most cases are versus the State,” he said. “That principle requires that even where there’s enough evidence to prove a criminal offence, a prosecution should only proceed if it is required in the public interest.”

Applying the test to the Archbishop’s case, Mr Chansa put a direct question to the State. “Now I ask, what public interest exists in prosecuting a high-profile, well-known clergy over a motor vehicle gift he received?” he said.

He said a less drastic route is open to the authorities. If investigations had established that the vehicle gifted to the Archbishop was unlawfully obtained, the State could recover it instead of continuing with a criminal case. “If it has been established that the motor vehicle he was gifted was unlawfully obtained, couldn’t the public interest be better served by asking him to surrender the motor vehicle and for him to be advised to be extra careful when accepting high value gifts?” he said.

Mr Chansa also questioned whether there is evidence that Dr Banda knowingly took part in the alleged unlawful acquisition of the vehicle. He said it is hard to find anyone in Zambia who genuinely believes the Archbishop connived to steal a motor vehicle from the Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA), and he asked what other records of such behaviour exist from him.

He ended with a direct appeal to the State. “I urge the State to exercise the prosecutorial discretion principle of public interest test and discontinue this case whose continued prosecution could not possibly be in any public interest,” he said.

Mr Chansa is not the only voice to speak on the case. The Association of Catholic Bishops’ Conferences of Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe and the Zimbabwe Catholic Bishops’ Conference have separately called for a fair, transparent and lawful process for the Archbishop. The bishops said the Church upholds the rule of law and recognises the role of state institutions, but insisted that judicial procedures must respect the rights of those involved.

Former Cabinet minister Given Lubinda, who acted as Patriotic Front president, said in an interview that Dr Banda is not above the law. He said, however, that the officers handling the case have the ability to assess a person’s vulnerability and risk of flight. Mr Lubinda said it is hard to imagine a man of fixed abode, charged over property believed to have been stolen, leaving his followers to run away, and he said he believed the Archbishop’s passport had already been taken. “Where can Dr Alick Banda hide?” he asked.

The Archbishop appeared before the Drug Enforcement Commission (DEC) on 28 September, then was arrested and appeared before the Lusaka Magistrates’ Court. He pleaded not guilty and was released on bail, and his case continues before the Lusaka Magistrates’ Court

World.title: Sudan: WFP Strongly Condemns Attack on Trucks in South Kordofan, Killing One Driver
World.content:
Abyei and Southern Kordofan are key areas in the dispute between north and south Sudan.

Khartoum — The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) strongly condemns an aerial attack that hit two contracted trucks carrying WFP food commodities in South Kordofan in the early hours of Saturday, 3 October 2026.

One driver was killed in the air strike. We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends and colleagues.

The contracted trucks were en route from Dilling to Kadugli and clearly marked as humanitarian vehicles. Additional details regarding the circumstances of the incident, including the extent of the damage to the food cargo, are still being collected.

WFP calls for a prompt and impartial investigation into this incident and for those responsible for any violations to be held accountable.



This latest attack comes only one day after a WFP truck struck an explosive device in Dilling, South Kordofan, after delivering lifesaving food assistance.

WFP urges all those involved in the hostilities to respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, and ensure the safe and unimpeded movement of humanitarian personnel and cargo.

These incidents underscore the increasingly challenging security environment in Sudan and the risks that aid workers face when delivering life-saving assistance to communities in need. WFP remains committed to safely delivering life-saving assistance to millions of women, men, and children who depend on humanitarian support across Sudan.

# # #

The United Nations World Food Programme is the world’s largest humanitarian organization saving lives in emergencies and using food assistance to build a pathway to peace, stability and prosperity for people recovering from conflict, disasters and the impact of weather extremes.

World.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopia Captures Tigray Capital As Its Regional Rivals Meet in Egypt
World.content:
Ethiopian federal forces have regained control of the Tigray rebels' regional capital, local sources said on Sunday, while Ethiopia's regional rivals gathered in Egypt to discuss the risk of a wider war.

The capture of Mekelle, capital of Tigray, deals a major blow to the opposition alliance that rules the northern region.

The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which leads the alliance, said in a statement posted on Facebook it had retreated from the capital and that the regional government would be "temporarily moved out of Mekelle and operate from somewhere else".



The TPLF launched a fresh offensive against the federal government last month, drawing counterattacks and sparking fears of a return to the devastating civil war of 2020-2022.

As concerns grow that the violence could spread beyond Ethiopia's borders, the presidents of Egypt, Somalia, Sudan and Eritrea were set to meet in the Egyptian city of Alamein on Sunday to discuss the conflict.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of directly backing the Tigray rebels, with the support of Sudan and Egypt, which all three countries deny.

Rebels flee

A source close to a pro-government militia, the Tigray Peace Forces, told Reuters its fighters entered the centre of Mekelle on Saturday afternoon, followed by the Ethiopian military.

Federal troops were patrolling Mekelle and manning key institutions on Sunday, a local journalist told French news agency AFP, as communications were restored for the first time in more than a week.

"We have taken control of Mekelle and we are marching forward," a commander with a pro-government militia said.

Businesses and shops remained closed, with owners moving stock to safer locations ahead of time, fearing looting and vandalism.

"There are no police. Last night, we had to organise ourselves and take care of security," one resident told AFP.

A local business owner, Filmon Equar Hailu, told the Associated Press civilians looted government offices and hauled away equipment from police headquarters as rebel fighters withdrew.

He said he heard celebratory gunfire overnight into Sunday morning as small groups of pro-government fighters entered the city.

Renewed fighting in Tigray raises risk of a wider regional war

Egypt talks

The TPLF has long been the dominant force in Tigray, ousting a government-appointed administration earlier this year. It was also the dominant group in a coalition that ruled Ethiopia between 1991 and 2018.

Since it launched its campaign against the federal government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on 23 September, a counteroffensive has seen Ethiopian forces push deep into rebel-held territory.

Analysts say the fighting threatens to escalate into a wider regional conflict.

Sunday's mini-summit in Alamein - taking place on the sidelines of an African Business Forum - was set to bring together Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, Somalian President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Sudanese Armed Forces head Abdel Fattah al-Burhan.

Before the talks, Sisi urged "dialogue, not confrontation".

Ethiopia's new rebel war redraws alliances across the Horn of Africa

Eritrea, which shares a long border with the Tigray region, is most directly involved in the conflict.

It accuses landlocked Ethiopia of planning to invade and seize access to its coastline. Analysts say it has backed the rebels in Ethiopia in a bid to keep the conflict away from its border.

Close 

The African Union has urged restraint, warning that renewed tensions threaten the 2022 peace agreement that ended the previous hostilities in Tigray.

The TPLF's war with the federal government killed some 600,000 people between 2020 and 2022, according to AU estimates.

The TPLF also pulled out of Mekelle during that conflict, apparently to spare the city from destruction.

The rebels' leader Debretsion Gebremichael implied this week that the group would continue guerrilla-style attacks, as they did last time Mekelle fell. "We operate under a strategy to strike the enemy wherever we choose," he said.
