The U.S. Coast Guard says it's searching a debris field off the coast of Nantucket, Mass., linked to an air ambulance that went missing after it disappeared on Oct. 3. Authorities say neither the six people on board – including four Canadians – nor the plane's black box have been found.

World.title: 'This is home for me': Amber Marshall reflects as 20th season of Heartland set to begin
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Amber Marshall has played a ranch girl in the fictional town of Hudson, Alta., for nearly 20 years on the long-running drama series Heartland. In conversation with CBC’s Ian Hanomansing, the Ontario-born actor talks about actually living that dream on a ranch just outside of Calgary and bringing the beauty of Western Canada to the world.

For nearly 20 years, Amber Marshall has lived, in some ways, the life of Amy Fleming.

She was 19 when she began playing the horse-loving teenager at the centre of Heartland, the CBC drama about a family ranch in the Alberta Foothills.

Marshall has been riding since she was five, got her first horse at 10 and had long imagined a future surrounded by animals.

A young Amber Marshall learns how to ride a horse. (Submitted by Amber Marshall)

"I knew that that's who I wanted to be when I grew up," Marshall, now 38, told CBC's Ian Hanomansing in a new interview. "I wanted to be Amy Fleming."

Nearly two decades later, the distinction between actor and character has become unusually difficult to draw.

Marshall, who is from London, Ont., lives on a ranch of her own. She is surrounded by horses and cows, fosters dogs and has made Alberta her home. She moved there during Heartland’s second season.

"I can never see myself relocating again. This is home for me," she said.

Heartland, which begins its 20th season on Sunday, is the longest-running scripted drama in Canadian television history.

Based on the books by Lauren Brooke, it began airing in 2007 and has grown from a Canadian family series into an international phenomenon — with viewers in countries ranging from England and France to Australia and the United States.

Marshall rides a horse during the filming of Heartland's 20th season, which begins Sunday. (David Brown/CBC/Seven 24/Dynamo)

The series follows Amy and her family as they work to keep their ranch operating while navigating growing up, relationships, grief and financial pressures.

Amy has married, become a mother and been widowed following the sudden death of her husband, Ty Borden (Graham Wardle). Her sister, Lou (Michelle Morgan), has built a career and raised a family, while their grandfather Jack (Shaun Johnston) has remained the family patriarch.

The characters have aged and changed, allowing viewers to grow up with them.

Marshall has met fans who were babies when the show began and have followed it through childhood and adolescence.

Some have told her that Heartland helped them through difficult periods in their lives.

"It’s special to know that a show can resonate with someone who's never been to Canada, that's never been to Alberta," she said, "and they can watch it and feel a connection to those characters and to that Heartland family."

A family story that resonates beyond Alberta

That connection was on display at a fan event in Alberta on Aug. 11, when viewers travelled from all over the globe.

Sarah Metcalf and her daughter, Riva, came from Manchester, England. Riva first encountered Heartland through a schoolbook when she was nine, then began watching the series after relatives in Canada sent the family DVDs.

"We watched one episode and it would leave on a cliffhanger, and then you'd have to watch the next one," Sarah said. "It’s a very special series, and we're very lucky that we came across it.... It’s a special part of us."

Leanne and Ayla Gale travelled from Brisbane, Australia. Ayla says the show’s performances and cinematography inspired her own interest in film, while her mother, Leanne, was drawn to the Alberta scenery. "I love Canada. I love the Rockies, the scenery, the mountains, pine trees, ranches,” Leanne said.

Heartland is filmed in the scenic Foothills of southern Alberta. (David Brown/CBC/Seven 24/Dynamo)

Marshall agrees that the landscape is central to the show. "The Heartland vista has become a character of its own," she said.

Fans often ask whether the Foothills are real or the product of green-screen effects. Marshall said they are and that the scenery has inspired some viewers to visit Alberta.

"It’s just a beautiful part of Canada," she said. "People want to feel and experience what they see on TV, and I don’t think they’re disappointed."

Marshall said visitors can experience the region’s western lifestyle, nature and "calming presence," becoming fully immersed in the Alberta Foothills.

She told Hanomansing that Alberta’s slower pace has taught her to resist the constant rush she notices when she returns to Ontario.

"I love being able to walk out in the field, say, 'You know what, I probably should be doing something else, but I'm just going to really enjoy this nice day,'" Marshall said.

Horses keep everyone present

That calm has shaped the Heartland set, where horses are central to the production. Marshall said their unpredictability keeps the series realistic and forces the actors to remain present.

"Horses are just living in the moment," she said. "They don't read the script, they don't know what's going on.”

Horses are shown on the set of Heartland. (David Brown/CBC/Seven 24/Dynamo)

The animals also require a quiet, relaxed workplace.

"You cannot have a tense set with animals and expect them to perform,” she said. "We have to be quiet. We have to be relaxed. We have to be calm."

Marshall's commitment to animals began long before Heartland. As a child, she wanted to become a veterinarian and volunteered at an animal shelter from the age of 10. She now runs the Foothills Animal Support Society, which helps animals and their families who might need access to veterinary care.

She has also spoken out against opening protected areas of the Rocky Mountains to coal mining, saying she has seen the damage caused to landscapes, water sources and animals.

"I do believe that we have a moral obligation to protect this beautiful place," she said.

'I'll do Heartland till I die'

Marshall said she believes Heartland endures because it offers something increasingly rare: wholesome, intergenerational television that leaves viewers feeling better instead of more anxious.

"It makes you feel very complete,” she said. "It makes you feel settled. It makes you feel like you've done something right for your mind and body."

Marshall, shown in Calgary, says she wants to do Heartland for many more years to come. (Turgut Yeter/CBC)

She said the show is not confined to a particular era or stage of life. Its characters can continue to grow as new people arrive, others leave and families change.

As for how many seasons remain, her answer was immediate: "Oh gosh, another 20."

"I’ll do Heartland till I die," she said. "This is my life. I love being in Western Canada. I love being on a ranch. I love being surrounded by my animals."

World.title: After Trump’s Venezuelan oil deal, those living on polluted lake in oil country wait for change
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Jessica Partida, 42, needs a $30 US ultrasound for her kidneys, which she can’t afford.

Her husband, Enrique Olivares, fishes on Lake Maracaibo, and for days the oil in the water has prevented him from catching the shrimp he uses as bait. Without bait, he cannot fish, and when he doesn’t fish, he doesn’t make money.

“I left the hospital because my husband hasn’t been able to fish because of the oil,” she said.

Jessica Partida, 42, lives in a block home on the shores of Lake Maracaibo. She and her husband have been unable to afford a $30 US ultrasound for her kidneys. (Camille Rodríguez Montilla)

Partida’s family of six lives in a block home in Cabimas, about 500 km west of Caracas, on the shore of one of the country’s largest oil-producing regions. Just over a century ago, a Royal Dutch Shell subsidiary first struck oil here. The lake (technically an estuary) served as a symbol for Venezuela’s oil wealth for decades.

But today, the water is dotted with rusting rigs and pumpjacks. Most of them are out of use and some leak oil and gas into the water. Now, the lake that once embodied Venezuela’s oil bonanza has come to symbolize the industry’s collapse.

Venezuela holds the largest proven oil reserves in the world, with an estimated 303 billion barrels, but accounts for only about one per cent of global supply. Oil output has fallen by about two-thirds since the early 2000s.

The decline began under former president Hugo Chávez, when state oil company PDVSA fired around 18,000 skilled workers following a 2002-2003 strike. Revenues were diverted away from maintenance, and much of the oil infrastructure has been left to decay. U.S. sanctions imposed in 2017 and 2019 compounded the problems.

An idle pumpjack is seen on a platform on the waters of Lake Maracaibo. Much of the oil machinery on the lake has fallen into disuse. (Camille Rodríguez Montilla)

“We don’t feel the oil wealth,” Partida said. “We don’t sell the oil, we don’t do anything with it. It just sits there, going to waste.”

Oil fields in the Maracaibo Basin, where the lake is located, are part of the sweeping energy deal reached in late August between the United States and Venezuela’s interim authorities. It grants private company North American Blue Energy Partners a 100-year concession over 17 oil fields around the country. The company has promised to double oil production in two years.

While many in the community surrounding the lake welcome promises to revitalize the oil sector, they also have a more immediate demand: clean up the polluted lake.

Fishing despite spills

The oil shifts with winds and currents, but fishermen say it often drifts toward them in the early afternoon, just when they would normally head out to collect shrimp to use as bait for the following morning.

“When there’s a lot of oil, we don’t do anything,” said Gregory Díaz, 36, who has fished the lake for 20 years. “When we throw our nets, they become covered in oil, and if the nets get damaged, we have nothing to work with.”

Carlos Rodríguez, left, and Gregory Díaz have fished the water of Lake Maracaibo for decades. Díaz estimates catches have dwindled by 40 per cent in recent years due to frequent oil spills. (Camille Rodríguez Montilla)

“The oil companies used to come clean the shore but stopped,” said Olivares, who has fished on the lake for over a decade. “Used to, PDVSA would replace our nets when they were damaged, but they haven’t done that in years.”

Data on oil spills in Venezuela are outdated. The Observatory of Political Ecology of Venezuela, which tracks pollution events across the country, counted more than 80 oil spills in 2022, the last year for which figures are available. Most were located in the western part of the country near the lake.

Those who live along the lake say the spills haven’t stopped, and many describe dozens of large ones each year.

“This one just exploded a few weeks ago,” said Carlos Rodríguez from his fishing boat as he steered toward a pumpjack that was leaking gas and covered in sticky crude, which was also dripping into the water. There was a heavy smell of gas for several metres around the machine.

Fishermen push a boat out of the water on the shore of Lake Maracaibo, with a ring of slimy black residue from oil pollution on the lake. (Camille Rodríguez Montilla)

The crude oil covers every surface in contact with the water, leaving a black slimy residue.

Many say the constant smell and contact with the oil has impacted their health.

“There are people who suffer from asthma and it chokes them,” said Rodríguez. “Most have left because the oil chokes them so much and they would rather live somewhere else.”

“The kids go swimming and come out stained with oil,” Partida said.

Children swim in Venezuela’s Lake Maracaibo, which is contaminated with oil. (Camille Rodríguez Montilla)

No cleanup scheduled

Neither the U.S. nor Venezuelan authorities have mentioned cleanup of the lake as part of the new oil deal. Venezuelan authorities have made several unfulfilled promises in recent years to clean up the water and shore, most recently in 2023, when the Environmental Ministry promised a “national team” to clean 600 beaches by the lake.

The government’s communication ministry didn’t respond to a request for comment.

One local environmental organization, Azul Ambientalistas, has demanded that five per cent of revenue from new oil output go to efforts to clean the lake.

Cleaning up the lake is the first thing many residents want, so they can fish. But many say they would also welcome the chance to work with the oil, instead of only alongside it.

“If they call me, I’ll go to work,” Olivares said.

Enrique Olivares has lived on the shores of Lake Maracaibo his entire life. He fishes for a living to support his family of six but says he'd also work in oil if the industry does grow again in his region. (Camille Rodríguez Montilla)

So far, he says they haven’t felt any economic change since the new oil deal was announced.

Díaz, who has two daughters, ages five and seven, says a job on land “could change your life.”

“Here we depend on fishing. If we catch something, we eat. If we don’t, we don’t have money,” he said.

Their catches have dwindled by 40 per cent in recent years due to the oil in the water, he estimates.

A fisherman holds a recently caught fish on the shore of Lake Maracaibo. (Camille Rodríguez Montilla)

Some residents say a company recently came through the neighbourhood collecting names, phone numbers and addresses should new jobs open up. Olivares says he is on the list, but so far no one has called.

For Partida, the ultrasound of her kidneys will have to wait until her family’s economic situation improves. She says she’s hopeful the new oil money will soon be felt.

“I believe it, but sometimes I have doubts, because time passes and there are still gas leaks and oil spills,” she said.

World.title: The King will never live at Buckingham Palace. What does that mean for the monarchy?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hello, royal watchers and all those intrigued by what's going on inside the House of Windsor. This is your biweekly dose of royal news and analysis.

For quite a while now, it's been clear that King Charles is quite happy living at Clarence House and has little interest in moving out of that stately home and going down the road to reside in Buckingham Palace.

So it was perhaps not a huge surprise when word emerged that he would never live in that historic central London landmark — even though in ways it has become the most high-profile and visible symbol of the monarchy itself.

While there have been efforts to emphasize that the palace will continue to be the working and ceremonial headquarters of the monarchy, the confirmation that the King won't be living there could also be sending signals about the institution and its future.

"It's a real shift away from what we expect from the monarchy and … it's an example of perhaps slimming down," Craig Prescott, a constitutional expert and lecturer in law at Royal Holloway, University of London, said in an interview.

With fewer senior members of the Royal Family, there is perhaps a move to start to "rationalize some of the properties," he said.

The shift in emphasis for the palace could also be a harbinger of a more subtle but noteworthy shift in focus for the House of Windsor as the monarchy, an institution steeped in tradition, tries to fortify its relevance in a modern world.

From left, Queen Camilla; King Charles; Prince Louis; Prince William; Prince George; Catherine, Princess of Wales; and Princess Charlotte stand on the balcony of Buckingham Palace during Trooping the Colour in London on June 14, 2025. (Alberto Pezzali/The Associated Press)

"The King will, in effect, use Buckingham Palace … as his office and in a sense go to work every day," said Prescott, who sees it as part of a potential distinction emerging between the institution of the monarchy and the person who holds the role of monarch at any given time, effectively becoming a custodian.

"There seems to be a shift, which perhaps is more modern thinking, because with Elizabeth II, she was the monarchy — the two were totally sort of one in the same, whereas perhaps we're teasing out a distinction between the monarchy and the monarch at any particular time."

Buckingham Palace was built in 1703 and converted into a royal palace in the 1820s.

While it had been the home of every monarch from Queen Victoria up to Elizabeth, no monarch had actually lived there since the COVID-19 pandemic. At that time, Elizabeth moved to Windsor Castle, just as a 10-year, 369-million-pound ($692 million Cdn) refurbishment project at the palace was also underway.

When Charles started his cancer treatment in 2024, there were also some advantages to the royal residence and the royal office being in separate places, Toronto-based royal historian Carolyn Harris said in an interview.

"At a time when there was an enormous amount of concern about King Charles III's health and the aftermath of his cancer diagnosis, the fact that he had a short commute from Clarence House to Buckingham Palace had the effect of keeping him in the public eye without a need for formal public occasions," she said.

"Some of the symbolism that came out of that moment might also have informed this decision."

King Charles waves as he and Queen Camilla leave their Clarence House residence by car in London on Feb. 6, 2024. Buckingham Palace announced the previous evening that the King had begun outpatient treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer. (Frank Augstein/The Associated Press)

A shift in royal residences has precedents.

"There have been many periods where an established royal residence that seemed as though it would always be a royal residence — it didn't necessarily suit the needs of the next dynasty or the next generation in the Royal Family," said Harris.

"George III refused to live at Hampton Court, which had been a royal residence all the way from Henry VIII to his grandfather George II, because he didn't have good memories of that palace. He remembered his grandfather … boxing his ears there."

Still, the move away from the monarch calling Buckingham Palace home feels significant.

"In the 21st century, this is being treated as a seminal moment as Buckingham Palace is so closely associated with the Royal Family today that we sometimes forget about palaces that no longer exist or mostly no longer exist, such as Whitehall or Greenwich, [which] were at one time the centre of royal power," said Harris.

With the monarch no longer living at Buckingham Palace, it remains to be seen what effect — if any — that will have on public perceptions of the monarchy.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, left, speaks with King Charles, right, during an audience at Buckingham Palace on March 16. (Aaron Chown/Getty Images)

"So many people — when they visit London, [they] visit Buckingham Palace and peer through the gates, watch the changing of the guard … always hoping they might catch a glimpse of a member of the Royal Family," said Harris.

"So it'll be interesting to see if what Buckingham Palace symbolizes transcends whether there are royalty in residence or not, or whether we see … more interest in some of the other royal residences."

Harris isn't writing off Buckingham Palace just yet.

"I think Buckingham Palace's name recognition, its appeal as a tourist destination, I think there's still going to be a lot of interest."

An 'unusual' royal phone call with Canada

Prince William, left, laughs with his wife Catherine, then Duchess of Cambridge, after they both competed in a dragon boat race in Dalvay-by-the-Sea, P.E.I., on July 4, 2011. It was their first overseas visit after their marriage. (Phil Noble/Reuters)

As far as royal phone calls go, there don't seem to be many precedents — at least not any calls that get public attention drawn to them.

After Prince William and Prime Minister Mark Carney were on the phone together the other day, their spokespeople let it be known they'd had a chat.

The Prime Minister's Office didn't share any details of what they talked about, but a Kensington Palace spokesperson said the heir to the throne "discussed the enduring strength of the U.K.-Canada relationship" with Carney.

William also expressed his "longstanding affection for Canada and its people," the spokesperson said.

The call "certainly seems to be unusual," royal historian Justin Vovk said via email.

"In most situations like this, the prime minister would be speaking directly with the King as sovereign."

King Charles, left, takes a video call with Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau during a virtual audience at Buckingham Palace on March 6, 2024. (Victoria Jones/AFP/Getty Images)

It's also rather unusual that the PMO would release a statement announcing that a phone call had taken place and then provide no details of what was discussed, Vovk said.

"We know that William will not speak about the conversation, so without more information, we have to assume that the PMO disclosed this conversation as an optics exercise and a reminder that Canada maintains close ties with the United Kingdom in no small part because of our shared monarchy."

The call, says Harris, shows that William's diplomatic role is expanding and he's building a "strong rapport" with political figures in the Commonwealth realms along with the United Kingdom.

Harris also noted the public reference to William's feelings toward Canada, a country he first visited as a child with his parents and younger brother, going up the CN Tower in Toronto and visiting Niagara Falls.

Diana, Princess of Wales, right, enjoys a ride on the Maid of Mist in Niagara Falls, Ont., in October 1991 with her sons Prince Harry, left, and Prince William, centre. (Hans Deryk/The Canadian Press)

"Canada was the first country William and Catherine visited as a married couple and during this visit William quoted his great-grandmother Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother in 1939, who stated: 'Canada made us.'"

Traditionally, Harris said via email, the heir to the throne has built relationships with Commonwealth prime ministers through royal tours and official engagements.

But there might have been another factor at play in the call between William and Carney.

"There is a personal connection between Prince William and Prime Minister Carney," Harris said.

"Prime Minister Carney's brother, Sean Carney, is chief operating officer at Kensington Palace."

Back to the U.S. and Canada

Prince Edward, Duke of Edinburgh, talks to a Revolutionary era re-enactor during a tour of Mount Vernon, the estate of George Washington, in Virginia on Thursday. Washington led the Continental Army to win independence from British rule and became the first U.S. president. (Tierney L. Cross/Reuters)

After spending several days in New York and Washington, D.C., this week, Prince Edward was in Toronto Friday, drawing to a close a North American visit that focused on areas of particular interest to the Duke of Edinburgh.

Youth opportunities and the arts were front and centre in the visit that was scheduled to take him to the Lassonde Art Trail in Toronto, along with engagements supporting the Duke of Edinburgh Awards.

Edward planned to meet with educators, award providers and students at Queen's Park Friday. The Ontario government recently announced it is investing $4 million and expanding access to the award program in schools across the province.

"Talent is everywhere; opportunity is not," Fouzia Younis, British consul general to Toronto, said in a release. "This investment into young people delivers just that: opportunity."

Earlier in the week, Edward was at the Metropolitan Opera in New York meeting representatives of the city's cultural sector. In Baltimore, he visited Western High School, the oldest all-girls public high school in the U.S., as they became a new partner school for the Duke of Edinburgh Award.

Dr. Lindsay M. Chervinsky, executive director of the George Washington Presidential Library, gives Prince Edward a tour of the library at Washington's Mount Vernon estate on Thursday. (Tierney L. Cross/Reuters)

While in the Washington area, Edward also visited Mount Vernon in recognition of the 250th anniversary celebrations in the U.S. this year.

Edward's U.S. visit follows the high-profile trip there earlier this year by his elder brother, King Charles.

Edward is a more frequent royal visitor — he was last in both the U.S. and Canada in 2025.

A brother's swan song for his sister

Copies of Charles Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, my sister, are displayed at a bookshop in London on Sept. 22. (Jack Taylor/Reuters)

There is little doubt that Charles Spencer's recent book about his late sister Diana, Princess of Wales — published amid a mad swirl of headlines around its more incendiary claims — adds to the debate and interpretation of her legacy.

Beyond those claims — perhaps the most incendiary being that King Charles said his former wife would soon be forgotten after her death — the book offers new anecdotes and insights into Diana, particularly in the early years she shared with her little brother.

More broadly, Swan Song: Diana, my sister raises more questions over recent history within the upper echelons of the Royal Family, and ultimately reflects the impossibility of ever fully knowing what Diana thought or felt.

To read more of my review and analysis of the book, click here .

click here Listen to Matt Galloway's interview with Charles Spencer for CBC Radio's The Current.

WATCH | Charles Spencer doubles down on King Charles claims: Diana's brother doubles down on scathing King Charles allegations | Duration closed caption 1:55 Princess Diana's brother Earl Spencer doubled down on his allegation King Charles sounded elated on the night she died in a BBC interview promoting the release of his book Swan Song: Diana, my sister.

Royally quotable

"I created my Reading Room simply because, like all of us here, I love books and their life-enhancing power and I want to share that love with others."

— Queen Camilla, in a speech at the Queen's Reading Room Festival at Chatsworth House.

Queen Camilla, second from right, views exhibits in the Chatsworth's House of Stories exhibition during a visit to The Queen's Reading Room Festival at Chatsworth House, near Bakewell in northern England on Sept. 19. (Aaron Chown/AFP/Getty Images)

Royal reads

King Charles plans to tour Caribbean countries beginning this month, and will "not shy away from" what he has called the "darkest days" of colonial rule and slavery, Buckingham Palace announced, but is not expected to apologize. [Guardian and ITV]

Police are investigating after two men, believed to be photographers, were seen surveilling the British school that Harry and Meghan's children attend. A spokesman for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex called the incident "extraordinarily reckless." [ITV]

Charles Spencer has apologized to Piers Morgan for incorrectly claiming in his new book about Diana, Princess of Wales, that the former tabloid editor was behind the publication of intrusive photos of the late royal in the mid-1990s. [The Guardian]

Catherine, Princess of Wales, enjoyed a morning outdoors as she joined people recovering from drug and alcohol addictions for a gardening session for Addiction Awareness Week. [The Daily Mail]

The Prince and Princess of Wales laughed with Tom Cruise as the royal couple were greeted by the movie star at the premiere of his new film Digger in London. [The Standard]

Prince Harry fought back tears as he gave a speech on stage at a children's charity that is very close to his heart. [ITV]

World.title: 'The Night of the UFOs': Remembering the Oct. 4, 1967, skies over Nova Scotia
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Chris Styles was just 12 years old on a clear night when he looked out his bedroom window and spotted a strange light moving along the shoreline a few blocks from his house.

He grabbed his grandfather's binoculars to get a better look and then ran out of the house, much to his dad's dismay, down to the water's edge.

"There's this huge sphere and it was a very dull orange, and it was glowing just like a poker in a fireplace," said Styles about what he saw on Oct. 4, 1967, around 10 p.m. AT.

While that date is best known for a UFO sighting in Shag Harbour in southwestern Nova Scotia, Styles was in Dartmouth, N.S.

Primarily between the Halifax area and southwestern Nova Scotia, people recorded seeing things in the sky that night, which has led ufologists to call it "The Night of the UFOs."

"If you were outside that ... night and you looked up, and for some hours afterwards, you would have seen something," said Styles. "It was a clear night. People were seeing the faintest stars without binoculars."

Chris Styles has written or co-written three books about UFO sightings. (Submitted by Chris Styles)

Styles has written or co-written three books about UFO sightings, including Impact to Contact: The Shag Harbour Incident. He said coverage of Shag Harbour meant other sightings fell out of the press, such as what the crew of the MV Nickerson saw in the waters off Sambro.

Around 9 p.m., Capt. Leo Mersey said he spotted an object with three flashing red lights. The object, which showed up on radar, was about 25 kilometres away.

"It was very clear that night and we could see the lights of Halifax," Mersey said in a statement he filed with the RCMP.

The radar also showed three objects about 10 kilometres away, but he could not see them.

Around 11 p.m., the object he could see went into the air, but by then had only one red flashing light.

This is the statement the RCMP took from the captain of the MV Nickerson, regarding something he and his crew saw in the sky on Oct. 4, 1967. (Submitted by Chris Styles/RCMP)

"I had never seen anything like that before but it sounds like the thing they are looking for down off Shelburne or Barrington Passage," Mersey said in the statement, which was taken Oct. 7, 1967.

The RCMP statement, taken by a corporal with the Lunenburg detachment, noted: "Capt. Mersey is considered to be a reliable type individual and bears a good reputation in his community."

But Shag Harbour has long remained the focus, said Styles, in part because of the large witness pool, what authorities said at the time, and the subsequent paper trail left behind.

In Shag Harbour, an object with flashing lights crashed into the waters off the tiny fishing village.

Besides the many eyewitnesses, adding credence to the account was that a responding RCMP officer, Const. Ron O'Brien, described seeing a light from the object floating about 800 metres offshore.

"It was being carried out to sea by the tide and disappeared before we could get a boat to it," he told the Chronicle-Herald in an Oct. 7, 1967, article.

An Oct. 6, 1967, memo by a National Defence official describes some of the details surrounding the Shag Harbour UFO incident. (Public Archives Canada)

Styles said RCMP officers commandeered two fishing boats to see what was in the water and if there were any survivors, assuming a plane had crashed. They were joined on the boats by local fishermen and other residents.

He said depending on who you talk to, the object either disappeared or submerged, but there was a yellow foam on the water that some say smelled of sulphur.

On Friday, Oct. 6, a naval diving team was brought in, and seven divers searched through the weekend, but reported finding nothing.

This CBC News footage shows the search in the days following the Oct. 4, 1967, Shag Harbour UFO incident. (CBC)

The investigation reached the highest levels of National Defence.

An Oct. 6, 1967, memo by Col. W.W. Turner, the director of operations at National Defence headquarters, noted: "The Rescue Co-ordination Centre conducted [a] preliminary investigation and discounted the possibilities that the sighting was produced by an aircraft, flares, floats, or any other known objects."

His son, John Turner, told CBC News his father often mentioned to the family that he received reports of alleged UFO sightings.

"Many were easily discounted as photos of a Frisbee or a hubcap, but he often said others simply could not be explained," Turner wrote by email.

The Shag Harbour investigation was the cover story in the Oct. 7, 1967, Chronicle-Herald. (Oct. 7, 1967, Chronicle-Herald)

Styles wasn't the only person to see something in Dartmouth on Oct. 4, according to the Chronicle-Herald on Oct. 7, 1967. The newspaper reported that a woman on her way home from work saw a bright, round object in the sky moving from the Halifax-Dartmouth ferry terminal.

"She described it as brighter, more vivid than a star, with an orange hue like a halo around the circumference," the reporter wrote.

The woman looked at it through binoculars when she got home and saw it was not a star.

The newspaper checked with CFB Shearwater's control tower to see if anything was on the radar during the window the woman described. Control tower personnel said no one was monitoring the radar at the time.

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Canada's spy agency shakes up hiring process to 'meet operational needs': documents
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian Security Intelligence Service is shaking up its hiring process to meet operational needs, internal emails show — a signal the service continues to face recruitment issues.

CSIS brought in a suite of changes earlier this year to "meet operational needs and emerging demands," according to documents obtained by CBC News through an access to information request.

"These changes represent a shift in how we recruit, classify, deploy and empower our people," reads one of a series of emails sent to managers at CSIS.

"These developments and initiatives will enable us to be more efficient and effective … and better positioned to meet the demands of our changing, more challenging environment."

Most of the changes are aimed at addressing "structural bottlenecks," increasing external hires and making changes to shorten the time between recruitment and operational deployment, according to the documents.

That includes setting up a new team dedicated to external recruitment to bring in people "efficiently and responsibly," the documents say.

As of March 2026, CSIS's hiring ratio is 85 per cent internal appointments to 15 per cent external hires, the documents show. The emails tell managers to strongly consider external talent for certain skilled positions.

Unlike other government positions, most jobs at CSIS require enhanced top secret clearance — a rigorous process diving deep into a candidate's personal background, character, family history and financial history that can take 12 to 18 months.

CSIS looking to outsource more tasks

While sections of the documents were heavily redacted, they also show a push to accelerate deployment.

Changes would see candidates apply directly to their region of choice which CSIS says would enable targeted hiring for regional vacancies. It's also bringing in adjusted official language requirements "where appropriate," and shortening training classes," according to the documents.

"It will empower us to recruit individuals who can fill critical vacancies in regions that will augment our operational capacity," reads one of the emails.

The documents show the secretive and often insular agency is looking to outsource recruitment steps including some screening, targeted recruiting and psychological assessment services.

WATCH | Canada's security screening questioned after alleged spy arrested: Canadian NATO spying suspect raises questions about country’s security screening | Duration closed caption 10:35 A CBC News investigation has identified Biwei Zhang as the Canadian woman recently arrested on suspicion of spying at NATO’s military headquarters in Belgium. According to her online resume, Zhang previously worked for both the Canadian Space Agency and Statistics Canada prior to her NATO internship. The case has raised questions surrounding Canada's security screening process for sensitive government roles.

The service has already increased its use of outsourced, standardized written testing tools to streamline the testing process. It's also restructuring how it bridges co-op students into full-time positions, it said.

CSIS is looking at acquiring new technology that "enables recruitment," but there are few details about what that could look like.

The service didn't answer questions about how many employees it needs to hire but said it's seeking to fill vacant positions for intelligence officers, engineers, analysts, IT and communications professionals "and more."

"CSIS faces growing demands due to evolving security threats, including espionage, foreign interference and terrorism," said spokesperson Magali Hébert.

"To date, CSIS has continued to have high levels of qualified applicants for its work, and recruitment efforts have garnered positive results."

Staff shortages pose risk: former analyst

Stephanie Carvin, a former CSIS analyst and now an assistant professor at Carleton University, said recruitment and retention "has for a long time been a priority concern" at the service.

"Its unique value is that it has human intelligence officers going out, speaking in the community, getting information, developing relationships, developing sources. It can't do that without people," she said.

"When you have staff shortages, you have people working overtime, they burn out, they get tired and that is a risk for the organization."

CSIS Director Dan Rogers has made culture change one of his top priorities at the spy agency. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

As an intelligence agency and Five Eyes partner, onboarding at CSIS is always going to be a long and "demanding" process, said Carvin, but "attempts to find efficiency are welcome."

"Someone can quit with two weeks' notice, but at the same time, it can take somewhere between a year and two years to replace them given the security requirements," she said.

"The demands on the service have probably never been greater, but at the same time, the ability to bring people in largely the same as they were in the 1980s."

A further sign the agency is worried about its staffing is its initial move to bar employees from taking the government's early retirement incentive. As CBC News reported in April, CSIS and other security agencies like the Communications Security Establishment, signalled to employees that it wouldn't accept applications citing "continued operational pressures and growth requirements."

The National Post reported that Privy Council Clerk Michael Sabia then stepped in, leading to both agencies walking back their approach. According to a source who spoke to the Post, Sabia sees the early retirement offers as "a golden opportunity to breathe fresh air into the mid- to senior-levels of the public service and promote younger bureaucrats."

CSIS Director Dan Rogers, who took the reins in late 2024, has made culture change one of his top priorities.

As part of changes to the service, he brought in a new executive lead in recruitment and staffing in February, the emails shared with CBC News show.

"Welcome to the new role, I hope I didn't scare you off earlier today :)," Rogers wrote in an email.

"Given that context, you've got a very important job for the service — so glad you decided to take it on."

World.title: Can I get AI face? Plastic surgeons say AI-generated inspiration is more than meets the eye
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

AI might be finding its way into surgeons' waiting rooms. Patients are taking in AI-generated images of the results they are hoping for from plastic surgeries. So, what could this mean for the medical community?

Dr. Ian MacArthur is accustomed to dealing with new trends in cosmetic surgery, but he's starting to see more patients coming into his Ottawa clinic with expectations that aren't entirely realistic.

Some clients, he says, bring in "fairly stylized" images generated with artificial intelligence, seeking results that may not even be "physically possible."

The experiences he's had so far motivated him to share a few cautionary thoughts on his Instagram page.

But it's a trend that plastic surgeons are dealing with more often.

The British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (BAAPS) recently warned about the rise of "AI face" — flawless, AI-enhanced images of patients' own faces that they believe can be recreated surgically.

The concern, says the organization's president, is that AI could also lead some people to put their desire for an unachievable look ahead of their own safety and well-being.

"The less realistic the image, the more dangerous that becomes if someone says, 'Yes, I can do it,'" Dr. Nora Nugent told CBC News.

More than meets the AI

BAAPS surveyed about half its roughly 350 members about how often they're seeing instances of AI face during consultations, Nugent said, with about 15 per cent of them responding that it's happening more often.

It's not that people are asking for anything unusual, she says. It's that the chatbot may have made other enhancements that it doesn't immediately disclose, such as a sharpened jawline or smoothed-out skin.

CBC News uploaded a photo of a journalist's face to three commonly used generative AI platforms — the free versions of OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google Gemini's Nano Banana and Anthropic's Claude — and prompted them to show the outcome of a rhytidectomy (a facelift).

Claude would not complete the task, responding that it wouldn't generate "realistic manipulated images of actual people."

Nano Banana did complete the task. When prompted, the chatbot explained that in addition to simulating the rhytidectomy, it also reduced loose neck skin and applied dermatological treatments like laser resurfacing or a chemical peel. (It also appeared to shave off facial hair).

It would not, however, create a medical before-and-after image comparison, encouraging consulting with a certified plastic surgeon for a realistic assessment.

ChatGPT did not hesitate to produce a visualization, as well as a side-by-side comparison. Like Nano Banana, it actually simulated multiple procedures — including what appeared to be an eyelid lift, brow lift and neck lift. ChatGPT said it smoothed out the forehead.

The chatbot did not immediately recommend consulting with a surgeon but later said the outcomes depend on one's anatomy, goals and doctor.

Pixels, not human tissue

Nugent says it's important for anyone seeking cosmetic surgery to know that AI can't account for an individual's anatomy.

"[AI] works in pixels, not human tissue," she said.

"Some tissue intrinsically is stronger, has more collagen, maybe thicker skin, and will hold a lift better," she said, adding that there are limits to "what's structurally safe to do" with a person's face.

"If you make a nose too small and too narrow, that person won't be able to breathe properly through their nose," she said. "If you take too much skin from an eyelid, someone can't close their eyes properly and that creates a medical problem."

On top of that, a patient's age, weight and lifestyle are also factors in the outcome.

WATCH | Real doctors appearing in AI deepfakes peddling unreal medical advice: AI deepfakes of prominent Canadian doctors are coming for your money | Duration closed caption 1:56 Health officials are warning Canadians about hyper-realistic AI deepfake videos of prominent doctors selling products or pushing bad advice. Victims are urged to contact the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre, but doctors warn the videos are hard to take down.

Nugent says people can likely recognize the "more extreme changes" as unrealistic.

"But it's the mild to middle changes that they might think are realistic," she said.

Karen Rowa, a psychiatry and behavioural neurosciences professor at Hamilton's McMaster University, says it could also worsen problems for those who struggle with their appearance or have body dysmorphic disorder.

AI chatbots tend to "please the person they're talking to," she says. Asking them to fix something a person doesn't like about their face or body may "reinforce a problem that may not actually exist."

An unachievable risk

Dr. Michael Weinberg says he hasn't consulted any patients who have used generative AI tools to simulate their cosmetic surgery outcomes, but he's not entirely against the idea.

Weinberg, a plastic surgery division lead at Ontario's Trillium Health Partners, says AI may help a patient visualize their own goals in advance of an appointment. A surgeon can then help them determine what's possible and what's not.

He says plastic surgeons have already been using digital 3D simulation tools in their consultations for some time — for procedures like breast augmentations or eyelid lifts.

"If it's used wisely and judiciously with realistic results, then it is great because it can show you what you can look like," he said.

What he worries about is doctors who overpromise on what can be achieved — whether it's due to inexperience, pressure from the patient or unscrupulous business practices.

"There's a lot of bad plastic surgeons," he said, and a patient's desire to meet AI-generated expectations may lead them to seek less reliable options if they're told that their goals aren't achievable by a more responsible doctor.

He says "tourist plastic surgery" is another issue, with some people travelling abroad for aesthetic procedures.

That comes with a big risk, Weinberg says, of returning with the "absolute worst complications" that can require additional surgeries and months of care.

LISTEN | Just how dangerous is AI — and what we should do about it: Front Burner 33:35 Why are AI leaders calling for a slow down?

But Ottawa surgeon MacArthur says most patients are reasonable and aren't looking to go to any extremes. He says those who turn to AI tools may be doing so because they want to better communicate their wishes.

As long as he's clear with them about what is achievable, he says, they're generally understanding. But he does think some people have unrealistic expectations, and that AI could "be like gasoline on the fire."

World.title: Colombia’s top corporate lobbyist resigns over reported tensions with president
World.content:
The director of one of Colombia’s most powerful business associations, Bruce Mac Master of the ANDI, resigned amid tensions with President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a letter to the ANDI, Mac Master said that “it is time for me to step down from my role as head of the National Association of Entrepreneurs of Colombia.”

According to the former ANDI boss, “unexpected and troubling circumstances” made working for the association “particularly complex” and ‘multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously.”

In recent weeks, unexpected and troubling circumstances have arisen that have made the Association’s operating environment particularly complex, with potential adverse effects on its members and staff. Multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously. In the face of these challenges, I have sought to act with firmness and prudence, always prioritizing institutional channels and placing the interests of the ANDI above any personal considerations, in an effort to resolve this situation. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master’s resignation followed news suggesting that De la Espriella instructed his cabinet of boycotting the ANDI chief.

According to political news magazine La Silla Vacia, the rift between the ANDI and the government was because De la Espriella’s law firm was never allowed to join the ANDI and the association’s donations in response to the august 10 earthquake bypassed the First Lady’s newly founded and very controversial foundation.

“The General Board of Directors, its Executive Committee, and I did everything in our power to facilitate a solution and create conditions that would allow the Association to fully fulfill its role, seeking to keep channels of dialogue open and to continue contributing,” but “all of those attempts were unsuccessful.”

I deeply regret this, because I have always believed in collective intelligence and in the need for the government, the private sector, and institutions to work together—even in the face of differences—with respect, independence, and a sense of national responsibility. We tried, but we were unsuccessful. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master said that he hoped that his resignation would restore “collaboration between the national government and the business community—as represented by the General Board of Directors, the members, and the various divisions of the Association.”

The former ANDI chief had been trying to represent the business interests of its approximately 1,600 members since 2013.

World.title: Colombia seeks to tighten checks on public protests
World.content:
Colombia’s government published a draft decree that seeks to tighten regulations on public protests.

The draft was published weeks before labor unions and social organizations plan regional anti-government protests ahead of a national strike that is set for November.

The draft seeks to update the Decree #3 of 2021, which was issued months before a national strike that was violently repressed by the police and the military.

In an attempt to prevent another bloodbath, the decree seeks to regulate authorities’ response to protests and the coordinated use of force in response to acts of vandalism and violence.

The decree regulates dialogue between the protesters and law enforcement authorities to promote the peaceful nature of protests.

The decree additionally limits the use of police intelligence against those organizing and participating in the protests.

Last but not least, the decree seeks the effective prosecution of those arrested during protests through increased surveillance and a permanent police presence.

The decree comes amid social tensions that surged after the far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August and announced counterrevolutionary measures that seek to undo reforms by his leftist predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro.

Swelling student protests have been publicly accused of being fueled by insurgencies and De la Espriella has warned that police may enter universities if they find evidence they are used to prepare acts of vandalism or terrorism.

World.title: Colombia breaks diplomatic ties with Iran
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that it had broken diplomatic ties with Iran and designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization.

The foreign ministry made the announcements in two separate statements that were published in its website.

In the first statement, the government claimed that the decision claimed to defend “national and hemispheric security, and the fight against transnational crime.”

According to the foreign ministry, the Iranian government has “alleged ties to international terrorist groups and other narco-terrorist groups that threaten [Colombia’s] security.”

Colombia also took into account the documented human rights violations committed by the Iranian government on its territory, the verified attacks against countries not involved in the Middle East conflict, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the authorities’ obstruction of the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) efforts to verify the scope of Iran’s nuclear program. Foreign Ministry

In regards to the IRGC, the foreign ministry claimed that the Iranian armed force “poses a serious threat to international peace and security” through “covert operations beyond Iran’s borders.”

“Colombia will strengthen its control and security measures to prevent individuals associated with the IRGC from entering its territory,” said the foreign ministry in a second statement.

In his 2017 book “Watch Your Backyard,” Foreign Minister Omar Bula claimed that “Iran and Islamic extremist groups such a Hezbollah and Al Qaeda have profusely penetrated Latin America.”

As part of his foreign policy, President Abelardo de la Espriella has renewed ties with the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

In a response, the Iranian government said that the accusations of the De la Espriella government go “against the principles of mutual respect” and damage both countries’ “interests and benefits.”

“It is clear that none of the arguments put forward by the Colombian government to justify this decision are valid or logical, and that this measure was adopted solely under the influence of the Zionist regime and the United States,” said Iran’s foreign ministry.

World.title: ACSN extends lockdown of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to Friday morning
World.content:
Santa Marta-based organized crime group ACSN said Wednesday that the lockdown it has imposed on parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast will be lifted on Friday morning.

In its first formal statement, the ACSN said that “the armed strike announced for 72 hours will end at 7:00AM on Friday 25 September 2026.”

The lockdown, which was initially called for 48 hours on Monday, has devastated the legal economy in the port city, particularly after ACSN assassins uploaded videos of them opening fire at stores that ignored the order to social media.

The online videos and half a dozen burnt buses and taxis all but cleared the streets of Santa Marta, which became a ghost town on Tuesday.

“We have never seen anything like this,” one Santa Marta resident told news program El Reporte Coronell.

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the militarization of Santa Marta, but this was barely visible in the city’s downtown area and in the majority of Santa Marta’s neighborhoods.

“There are no police or soldiers in the streets, the people feel unprotected and are in panic,” said journalist Javier Manjarres on social media platform X.

“The current situation is a consequence of the behavior of the security forces and the decisions taken by the National Government in regards to our organization,” the organized crime group said in their statement.

The ACSN admitted that the clandestine lockdown was the result of the killing of Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” one of its commanders in the region around the Sierra Nevada mountain range just outside the city.

According to the group, security forces executed Cholo in front of his wife after his arrest.

An 18-year-old farmhand with no ties to the organization was also executed by the security, his family told media.

The lockdown has been imposed throughout the Magdalena and La Guajira provinces, a region where the group dominates organized crime and controls drug trafficking route to the Caribbean.

World.title: Colombia withdraws support for ICJ genocide case against Israel
World.content:
Colombia has withdrawn its participation in South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Tuesday.

In a statement, the court in The Hague said that Colombia’s government “decided to withdraw the Declaration of intervention that it had filed… on 5 April 2024 in the case concerning Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip.”

The decision of the administration of President Abelardo De la Espriella is part of a wider attempt to restore ties with Israel and its main sponsor, the United States, and appease its Evangelical Christian support base.

In response to the ongoing genocide in Palestine, former President Gustavo Petro took a leading role in diplomatic efforts that sought to isolate Israel and seek justice for Israel’s victims through the world court.

In a response, the US Government put Petro on a blacklist and actively campaigned for the election of De la Espriella to prevent another leftist victory in elections earlier this year.

The new president, who took office in August, immediately restored diplomatic ties to Israel and lifted a ban on coal exports to the country in West Asia.

World.title: ACSN crime group shuts down parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast
World.content:
Santa Marta-based crime group ACSN shut down parts of the city and the surrounding region after Colombia’s armed forces killed one of their commanders.

Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” and six of his comrades were killed during an offensive on Monday.

The son of Fredy Castillo, a.k.a. “Pinocho,” who is one of the alleged bosses of the crime group, was reportedly among those killed during the operation.

Shortly after, a pamphlet that was signed by the ACSN ordered an “armed strike” of 48 hours because of the “the fierce attacks that the government has been launching against our organization in the Sierra Nevada since this afternoon.”

Multiple buses were incinerated in the region around Santa Marta.

We hereby declare a 48-hour armed strike throughout the province of Magdalena, particularly along the Troncal del Caribe highway, in the city of Santa Marta, and in the banana-growing region. We do not want any businesses to remain open for a period of 48 hours. ACSN

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who traveled to the city, “they are trying to intimidate the public by promoting an armed strike.”

“I will not allow any criminal organization to subjugate citizens through threats and terror,” the president added.

Notwithstanding, multiple shop owners in Santa Marta and along the highway kept their shops closed on Tuesday, afraid to challenge the authority of the local crime bosses.

The district government closed public schools in neighborhoods where the ACSN is believed to have a strong presence. Public transport was suspended as videos of armed men opening fire on shops that failed to close voluntarily were posted on social media.

The ACSN control much of drug trafficking to the port of Santa Marta and to the coastline of the neighboring La Guajira province.

De la Espriella ended attempts to negotiate the group’s surrender and ordered a military approach after taking office in August.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal warns ICC that De la Espriella supports “worst attack in history”
World.content:
Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP said that it would warn the United Nations and the International Criminal Court about plans of President Abelardo de la Espriella to cut its budget.

In a statement, JEP president Alejandro Ramelli raised the alarm warned about a pending proposal by far-right Senator Enrique Gomez (National Salvation) to reduce the tribunal’s budget by COP100 billion ($31.6 million), which received De la Espriella’s support.

A second proposal by another far-right party, the Democratic Center, sought to push all sentences against members of the security forces to military justice for revision.

According to Ramelli, the two bill proposals “prove the existence of a strategy to block the JEP’s functioning” and called on the international community to “put a stop to this effort to dismantle our financial system and calls for the essential resources needed for our operations to be guaranteed.”

These initiatives constitute a combined strategy of economic strangulation and the subjugation of the JEP to military criminal justice. It is the most serious attack we have ever faced against our independence and autonomy. JEP president Alejandro Ramelli

The president , who vowed to get rid of the JEP on campaign, said that the 2027 national budget “does not constitute any threat to any judge, it’s the Constitution at work.”

I do not have a policy of retaliation against the JEP. I have a duty to manage spending, demand results, and allocate the State’s limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone, not to a court that part of the country perceives—for reasons debated in Congress and in public opinion—as a system of privileges rather than an effective end to impunity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Since March of 2018, the JEP has played a key role in clarifying crimes committed during the armed conflict that erupted in response to the insurgency of the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC.

Among other things, the JEP found that the guerrillas recruited more than 18,000 children and that the security forces assassinated more than 7,800 civilians to inflate their combat kills.

Hundreds of former guerrillas and former members of the armed forces are taking part in a transitional justice system that seeks to solve as many as possible of the hundreds of thousands of crimes committed during the decades-long armed conflict.

World.title: Colombia pulls out of international LGBT coalition
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella pulled Colombia out of the international Equal Rights Coalition, which promotes the rights of sexual and gender minorities around the world.

The Foreign Ministry announced its departure from the coalition in a letter addressed to the organization of which Colombia was co-president until February next year.

According to Caribe Afirmativa, a gay rights NGO that was part of the international initiative, warned that the decision was “a serious setback in foreign policy and commitments to LGBTIQ+ rights.”

We also view this action as a snub to the international community, a break from the leadership role Colombia had established, and an unequivocal political signal regarding the place the current government is willing to grant to the rights of LGBTIQ+ people. Caribe Afirmativa

De la Espriella has appointed multiple prominent far-right figures in his government and has vowed to wage a “Culture War” against what it considers “gender ideology.”

On top of this, De la Espriella and multiple of his cabinet members oppose the right of gay couples to adopt children and reportedly sacked the newly appointed planning chief because he and his gay partner had adopted a child.

World.title: Know your Mexico City neighborhood: Historic center of Coyoacán
World.content:
Borough: Coyoacán

Established: 1521, as Villa Coyoacán

Location: 10 km south of the Angel de la Independencia



Pre-Columbian inhabitants: Colhuas, Tepanecs and Mexica

Who lives here

The Historic Center of Coyoacán comprises several smaller neighborhoods, including Villa Coyoacán, Del Carmen, Santa Catarina and La Concepción. Its bohemian lifestyle attracts young families and artists, while its proximity to UNAM makes it a hub for students. According to government data, 23% of the borough’s inhabitants are between the ages of 25 and 49. There is a notable mix of newcomers and families that have lived here for generations, adding to the area’s eclectic feel.

A litany of colorful characters have lived in Coyoacán’s Historic Center, notably Frida Kahlo, León Trotsky, Octavio Paz and Rufino Tamayo — as well as at least three Mexico News Daily staff members.

A brief history of Coyoacán

The Colhuas of Culhuacan transformed the future Coyoacán into an urban center, settling here in the 7th century. In the 15th century the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco arrived, displacing the Colhuas and establishing the area as a center of trade, agriculture and commerce. At some point, the settlement acquired its current Nahuatl name, which is most often translated as “place of coyotes.”

Coyoacán’s strategic position on Lake Texcoco caught the attention of the Mexica, who soon seized the area from the Tepanecs. Plazas, residential zones and temples were constructed to the chagrin of the conquered Tepanecs, the majority of whom detested the Mexica. In 1521, Hernán Córtes and his allies launched their campaign against the Mexica Empire, they chose Coyoacán as their headquarters, establishing the town of Villa Coyoacán. A strategic location, abundant agricultural resources and local support made the cultural hub an ideal place to become the first capital of New Spain.

Coyocán remained its own municipality until 1857, when it was officially incorporated into the Federal District. It retained its small-town and semi-rural character until sometime in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when it was swallowed up by the urban sprawl of what is now Mexico City. The borough of Coyoacán, taking its name from the ancient town, was designated in 1928, and is still the physical heart of Mexico City, sitting dead in the center of the metropolis.

A guide to Coyoacán today

Today, the quaint Barrio Mágico is known for its cobblestone streets, colonial architecture and vibrant cultural scene. The weekends are especially lively. Expect streets lined with food carts selling everything from churros to esquites, live music in Plaza de La Conchita and various amusement park-style rides for the little ones. Don’t miss the neighborhood dance party on Sunday evenings at the Jardin del Arte Allende.

The Saturday art market in Plaza Allende is smaller than its more famous cousin in San Ángel, but still worth checking out if you find yourself in the area.

Coyoacán is great if: You love Spanish colonial architecture, colorful facades, traditional festivals and an authentically Mexican community.

What to do in Coyoacán

Frida Kahlo Museum: Also known as the Casa Azul, this is the former home of Mexico’s most iconic female artist. Reservations must be made in advance.

Church of San Juan Bautista: This 16th-century church is the spiritual center of Coyoacán

Leon Trotsky Museum: The house where the exiled Russian revolutionary lived and met his unfortunate demise by way of ice pick.

Plaza Hidalgo and Plaza de la Conchita: Two lively squares surrounded by cafes, restaurants, street performers and food carts. The church in the center of the square is said by some to be Mexico’s oldest. The two are linked by Calle Higuera, believed to be the first street laid down by the Spanish during the early days of the conquest. Visit weekend mornings for a chance to jam with unofficial resident band KoolBananas, while enjoying coffee and cake from one of the coffee shops that dot the square.

Jardín Centenario: Home of the famous Coyote Fountain.

Avenida Francisco Sosa: A charming, tree-lined street with colonial-era architecture and art galleries. Attractions include the Casa Alvarado — the last residence of Nobel prize winner Octavio Paz, now home to the National Sound Archive — and some of the best coffee and wine stores in the city.

National Watercolor Museum: Tucked down a side street a stone’s throw from the Casa Alvarado, the museum hosts an array of works from across the country.

Viveros de Coyoacán: A 39-hectare park and tree nursery with trails and — you guessed it — trees. Thousands of them. Keep in mind that food is not allowed in the park, and security searches bags at the gate.

Honorable mentions: Though not in the Historic Center proper, any visitor to the borough of Coyoacán should see the Anahuacalli Museum, which houses Diego Rivera’s personal collection of pre-Columbian art, and the central campus of the National Autonomous University of Mexico, a Unesco World Heritage Site since 2007. The surrounding area is also home to major sports teams, notably soccer giants Club América and rugby titans Coyotes.

Where to eat in Coyoacán

Tostadas de Coyoacán: A stall in the Coyoacán Market known for crispy tortillas topped with ceviche or cochinita pibil.

Mercado de Comida de Coyoacán: Located at the tip of Calle Higuera, on the corner with the main square, visitors can make the most of a genuinely authentic street food market.

Tacos Chupacabras: A legendary taco stand known for its special “Chupa Cabra tacos,” which are a mix of chorizo and carnitas, garnished with various toppings.

Mi Compa Chava: The second branch of chef Salvador Orozco’s Sinaloan-style restaurant is never not packed with seafood lovers. The ambience alone is worth the wait for a table.

Los Danzantes: The sister restaurant to Oaxaca’s legendary Michelin star winner is located opposite the Coyote fountain.

Coyoacán hidden gem

The Callejón del Aguacate, or Avocado Alley. Legend has it that in the 1930s, a uniformed soldier was sauntering down this tiny alley when a young boy, captivated by the soldier’s appearance, asked to play with him. The boy was so insistent that the soldier lost his head and killed the boy.

His regret mounted so much that he did what any repentant murderer would do: supervise the construction of a Virgin Mary statue at the site of the child’s death. In this way, all future visitors to the alley could be given the opportunity to clean their sinful slates by offering prayers to the statue. Some say, if you tune in, you can feel the boy’s spirit wandering the alley.

Have we missed any must-see sights in out Coyoacán guide? Let us know down below!

Bethany Platanella is a travel planner and lifestyle writer based in Mexico City. She lives for the dopamine hit that comes directly after booking a plane ticket, exploring local markets, practicing yoga and munching on fresh tortillas. Sign up to receive her Sunday Love Letters to your inbox, peruse her blog, or follow her on Instagram.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Guanajuato residents mistake arrival of French acrobats for third ‘French Intervention’
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

GUANAJUATO, Guanajuato — Civic vigilance reached a 160-year high in the historic capital of Guanajuato on Saturday evening after local residents, observing a group of French performers scaling public buildings and suspending high-tension ropes across historic plazas, mistakenly believed the French Republic had launched a third military intervention in Mexico.

Members of the Paris-based Chaillot National Theater, who arrived in the city to perform a collaborative aerial circus piece titled “Vértigo” for the 54th International Cervantino Festival, were met with suspicious glances and immediate defensive maneuvering from municipal historians, local shopkeepers, and neighborhood watch organizers who recalled that previous French arrivals had resulted in imposed monarchies and six-year occupations.

“We saw men in fitted performance gear deploying cables across Plaza Allende and securing anchor points near the Cervantes Theater,” said local historian and retired educator Don Héctor Morales, who admitted to briefly scouring his cellar for period-appropriate artillery. “Naturally, given the diplomatic history of 1838 and 1862, we assumed the French government was once again attempting to collect unpaid bakery debts or institute an unconstitutional monarchy. It turned out they were just balancing on a wire to live ambient jazz.”

The diplomatic confusion mounted when highliner Jean-Claude Moreau walked across a slackline suspended decades above the cobbled streets, an act interpreted by several onlookers as an attempt to establish aerial dominance over the state’s historic center. Public concern was only eased when municipal officers confirmed that France was merely participating as the festival’s invited guest nation to celebrate 200 years of mostly peaceful diplomatic relations.

The production, which combines contemporary dance, live music, and aerial arts, required local authorities to release a clarification confirming that highliners hanging mid-air were engaged in artistic expression rather than strategic reconnaissance. Organizers assured the public that despite the visible presence of French acrobats hovering near historic architecture, no foreign princes would be installed in Chapultepec Castle as a result of the performance.
