World.title: USA defeats error-prone Mexico, hands Márquez first loss as boss
World.content:
This one is going to hurt for a while.

El Tri face-planted in the first real test of the Rafa Márquez era, producing a handful of blunders that a grateful U.S. team converted into a 3-0 rout on Saturday night in Arizona.

TRES A CERO IN THE DESERT! 🇺🇸 https://t.co/CI3plLNTrD — U.S. Soccer Men’s National Team (@USMNT) October 4, 2026

Worse than the self-inflicted wounds that left Márquez screaming in frustration, the bloopers by key players might produce significant line-up juggling for Tuesday’s game against Chile.

Multiple errors by goalie Raúl Rangel, fullback Mateo Chávez and defender Diego Campillo might not cost them roster spots for next month’s Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals, but a loss of confidence is surely a possibility.

Mexico pressed forward during the opening 25 minutes, creating three scoring opportunities though failing to get a shot on target.

Then, against the run of play, El Tri was caught napping.

With two Mexico defenders hard against the sideline, U.S. midfielder Gio Reyna charged into the vacated space well ahead of his marker, Orbelín Pineda.

Reyna got deep into the box before sending a low cross that Rangel should have handled. Instead of corralling the ball, the Chivas goalie watched it clank off his right foot and bounce into the path of Julian Hall who, left unmarked by Campillo, simply poked the ball into the net.

Fifteen minutes later, Santi Giménez had a chance to equalize, but was unable to redirect a deflected pass on net from the back side.

Though Mexico enjoyed 60% possession, El Tri went to the locker room trailing 1-0.

Chávez came on to start the second half, but was off-tune from the outset. He turned the ball over the first two times he touched it and was out of position on two other occasions.

In minute 62, Rangel committed a howler. Looking to pass out of the back while outside the goalie box, he passed it straight to Cavan Sullivan and the 17-year-old forward calmly chipped the embarrassed Rangel for a 2-0 lead.

Before Mexico could regain equilibrium, Chávez lost his cool, unnecessarily fouling Yunus Musah before lashing out at Sebastian Berhalter and earning a red card.

Sebastian Berhalter got right in Mateo Chávez’s face after the foul on Musah, refused to back down, and ate a two handed slap that earned Mexico the red. Some will say he lost control and left his teammates exposed in a rivalry scrap, but that sending-off left El Tri with 10 men and the USMNT closed it out 3-0. Mateo Chávez should have controlled himself and better still fall to the immediately he was pushed https://t.co/wme6irdsN1 — @DailyFootyTakes (@DailyFootyTakes) October 4, 2026

El Tri spent the remaining 23 minutes chasing shadows, but was unable to prevent further damage.

In minute 84, Campillo allowed a back pass to roll into the box while trying to shield the ball from Malik Tillman, but the U.S. midfielder circled him and blasted a left-footer into the net past a helpless Rangel.

After this latest gaffe, cameras caught an exasperated Márquez turning toward the El Tri bench, venting his incredulity that the culprits were players expected to be stalwarts in the run-up to the 2030 World Cup.

Rangel, 26, starred for Mexico during the just-completed World Cup, posting four shutouts, while Chávez, 22, appeared to be the heir apparent at left back, scoring a goal in his only World Cup start (against Czechia). Campillo, 24, is bidding to stake claim to a spot in the defensive rotation.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: 6 Mexican comfort foods to warm you up this autumn
World.content:
As cold weather sets in across most of the Northern Hemisphere, bringing heavy coats and low temperatures, the seasonal change in Mexico is a subtle shift marked by increasingly chilly mornings and nights alongside mild days.

It might not be cold enough to break out winter coats, but it is chilly enough to whet the appetite for steaming broths, warm tortillas fresh off the comal, and other comforting flavors.

From north to south, here are six dishes from across Mexico to whet your autumn appetite.

Apapacho de mamá – cheese soup

El Mejor Caldo de Queso Estilo Sonora

Watch this video on YouTube

Hailing from the northern cattle-ranching state of Sonora — characterized by freezing winters in its highlands — this cheese soup is a simple yet comforting dish that feels like an apapacho de mamá (“warm hug from mom”).

The broth features tomato, onion, garlic and chiles, into which cubes of queso fresco or regional cheese are added. Unlike other cheese soups around the world, these cheese cubes do not melt — rather, they soften without completely losing their shape. Depending on the specific recipe, the soup may also include potato, zucchini, corn, cilantro and fried tortilla strips for added texture.

A nourishing dish – milpa soup

Milpa is a pre-Hispanic crop-growing system in which several plants were cultivated together, with maize as the central element.

Farmers in present-day Puebla, Tlaxcala, Mexico City, Hidalgo and central Mexico overall would prepare a broth incorporating all ingredients of the milpa, primarily corn kernels, onion, squash blossom and chilies.

Following the Spanish conquest, crops grown in the milpa diversified, and chicken broth became the base of the soup.

Today, milpa soup represents an accessible, balanced and nourishing meal that will keep you going through the colder months.

The Mexican paella – morisqueta

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Michoacán (@visitmichoacan)

Think of paella, but make it Mexican — that is morisqueta, one of the most cherished dishes of Michoacán’s Tierra Caliente region.

This humble yet classic dish is full of flavor, featuring cooked white rice served with pot-style beans and topped with a red sauce made from tomatoes, chili peppers, onion and garlic. In some households, it is garnished with queso fresco and may also include pork, dried meat and eggs.

Some scholars suggest that its name reflects the cultural syncretism that occurred after the Spanish conquest. It is derived from the Spanish words Moros (Moors) and Cristianos (Christians), referencing the combination of rice — introduced to Spain by the Moors — and beans, which were grown in present-day Mexico.

A hearty soup, not a taco – birria

View this post on Instagram A post shared by @sabor_casero29

Birria has taken the world by storm, with many restaurants abroad featuring birria tacos on their menus. However, few people know that authentic birria is mostly consumed as a soup rather than a taco.

Originally from the western state of Jalisco, birria is a traditional slow-cooked stew served in a deep bowl with its hot broth or consommé, making it more akin to a hearty soup than a taco filling.

The classic version is prepared with goat meat marinated in adobo made from dried chiles, garlic, onion, vinegar, tomato and spices such as cumin, oregano, cloves, pepper and cinnamon.

It is served with warm tortillas and garnished with cilantro, onion and a few drops of lime.

A comforting breakfast – huevos motuleños

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Tasos Mitselis (@tasos_mitselis)

Huevos motuleños is an iconic breakfast dish originally from Motul, Yucatán, a town located in the north-central region of the state.

This heartwarming dish features a fried corn tortilla topped with refried black beans and fried eggs, covered by a warm tomato sauce made from onion, diced ham and peas. It is often garnished with queso fresco and fried plantain.

The combination of ingredients encapsulates Yucatecan cuisine, which is characterized by Caribbean flavors (plantain), pre-Hispanic ingredients (corn) and Spanish elements (eggs and pork).

Sopa de lentejas

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Karina Valladares (@kari.receta)

Although lentils are typically associated with Middle Eastern dishes, this ancient crop found a place of its own in Mexican cuisine following its introduction during the viceregal era.

In southern Mexico, including the states of Chiapas, Tabasco and Oaxaca, lentils are cooked in a base of tomato, onion and garlic, and may include ingredients such as carrot, potato, chili pepper, epazote or cilantro. It can also be enriched with bacon, smoked pork chop and chorizo, infusing the warm dish with deeper flavors and protein.

In Oaxaca specifically, the soup is garnished with fruit, including southern staples such as plantain and pineapple.

Gabriela Solís is a Mexican lawyer turned full-time writer. She was born and raised in Guadalajara and covers business, culture, lifestyle and travel for Mexico News Daily. You can follow her lifestyle blog Dunas y Palmeras.

World.title: From jungle to wildflowers: How Mexico made me a botanical artist
World.content:
It all started with a twisted scarlet seedpod … such a beautiful, unexpected thing lying at my feet. Then curiosity set in, and I began to notice the plants around me.

Mexico’s amazing plants eventually inspired not just curiosity, but creativity. Thus, for the first time in 30 years, I picked up a sketchbook again. That was two and a half years ago. Today, my third sketchbook is almost complete.

1 of 6

Pages are filled with huge leaves, wildflowers and edible treasures like tejocote, mamey and nance; plus, seedpods of all shapes and sizes. Native plants, edible plants, healing plants … I’ve sketched them all, plus the pollinating creatures they attract: butterflies, metallic green bees and beetles.

Now, I am an artist. Bel the Batty Botanist. I deeply thank Mexico for this.

A passion for natural beauty

The medicinal healing properties of native plants have become a passion, as have edible plants. Enjoying edible treasures like Jamaican cherries that taste like cotton candy. Or the crunchy delights of pepino kat, a long, ribbed cucumber-like fruit.

It seems every time I step outside, something delights me. The cheery yellow of Mexican prickly poppies, the plant of resilience and endurance, waving in the sunshine. The smell of vanilla from beach spider lilies after a swim.

These botanical beauties inspire my art. I sketch in black ballpoint pen or fine-line markers, with watercolor pencils and paints and on different-colored papers. Which, I must say, really makes a white subject shine.

Inspired by seeing a chicalote, a native white poppy in the Central Highlands, I looked for ways to capture its brilliance. Soft gray paper for a dreamy, romantic feel seemed right. Because, to me, poppies are dreamy.

1 of 6

Sometimes it’s nice to sit quietly. As seen on my passionflower page. Within 20 minutes, while sketching, I witnessed a Gulf fritillary butterfly lay eggs. I saw its spiky orange caterpillars varying from tiny to huge, ready to form their chrysalis … mature butterflies pollinating the flowers. An entire life cycle was revealed to me on a single vine.

Other times, a collection of found treasures inspires something new. Hurricane Beryl two years ago, for example, brought down a bounty of botanical treasures for me to paint.

So, who knows what I’ll find tomorrow. Something as beautiful as that twisted scarlet seedpod, I hope. But I bet it will be magical.

Mexico Correspondent for International Living, Bel Woodhouse is an experienced writer, author, photographer and videographer with 500+ articles published both in print and across digital platforms. Living in the Mexican Caribbean for over seven years now, she’s in love with Mexico and has no plans to go anywhere anytime soon.

World.title: Remembering the Tlatelolco student massacre of 1968
World.content:
The Tlatelolco student massacre of 1968 — one of the most pivotal events in modern Mexican history, one that the renowned National Security Archive organization has called “Mexico’s Tiananmen Square” — all began with a fracas between two rival public vocational high schools that erupted into an out-and-out brawl in a Mexico City marketplace built for the upcoming 1968 Olympics.

The next day, riot police arrived at the two schools, wielding clubs and beating anyone within reach, attacking students and faculty with equal brutality. The following day, students took to the streets in protest of the previous day’s beating, which then, in turn, drew the police out for more violent confrontations.

How protests escalated into the 1968 Tlatelolco Massacre

“Those protests provoked more repression, which provoked more protests,” journalists Julia Preston and Samuel Dillon explained in their 2005 book, “Opening Mexico: The Making of a Democracy.”

By the fourth day of protests, tensions escalated. To express solidarity with their fellow teenage protesters, the students of the prestigious high school, San Ildefonso Preparatory — officially known as the National Preparatory School — declared a strike. When Mexican President Gustavo Díaz Ordaz learned that the students at the prestigious government-run school were on strike, he ordered the Mexican army to take the campus.

Soldiers in Jeeps and small tanks moved across the city, aiming to confront the students of San Ildefonso. When they arrived at the campus, they found the entrance locked, so soldiers blew the school’s ornate 18th-century wooden door, hand-carved by Indigenous craftsmen, to bits.

The soldiers rampaged through the school, beating anyone they could find. They then turned on other high schools, and even attacked unsuspecting pedestrians they encountered on surrounding streets.

“By the end of the day, 400 people had been hospitalized and 1,000 arrested,” Preston and Dillon noted.



“Through the military occupation of the San Ildefonso School, the government elevated the situation from a local, primarily police matter to an issue of national security,” wrote Mexican historian Enrique Krauze, author of the seminal book “Mexico: Biography of Power.”

A history of government repression

For most Mexicans, government repression was nothing new. In 1959, railroad workers who went on strike, asking for better working conditions and a modest pay increase, were viciously put down, a pattern well-established with striking miners, doctors, nurses and even teachers. Strikers were routinely either beaten into submission or cajoled into joining a newly created government-run union. But this episode — the government violently attacking a high school — stunned most Mexicans.

In response, on July 31, Javier Barros Sierra, the politically moderate rector of the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) — which was in charge of San Ildefonso Preparatory and is the largest and most prestigious university in Latin America — led a dignified, peaceful march of 50,000 faculty and students through Mexico City’s leafy suburbs.

That Barros had the temerity to lead such a protest earned him the enmity of Díaz Ordaz; later that summer, it cost him his job. That march, however, moved the center of protests against the government from Mexico’s high schools to its universities.

Taking inspiration from the U.S. civil rights movement and the earlier 1968 student protest movements in Paris, West Germany, Czechoslovakia, Poland and Japan, the Mexican university student activists had happened upon an issue that already deeply resonated with the general Mexican public: government brutality.

Students stand up in dissent

Raúl Álvarez Garín, a 27-year-old physics student from Mexico’s National Polytechnic Institute, emerged as one of the student leaders. Álvarez came from a family steeped in a tradition of protest and of standing up for its beliefs. His grandfather was an aide to Mexican Revolutionary General Álvaro Obregón. His parents were communists. His wife was the daughter of one of the leaders of the aforementioned railroad workers’ strike of 1959.

Álvarez helped draw up a modest list of demands: The government should release the recently jailed students, as well as the railroad union leaders still imprisoned since 1959. They should also compensate the families of injured protesters, disband the riot police and repeal vague laws used to jail anyone who dissented with the government.

Álvarez and his fellow activists weren’t advocating regime change or overthrowing the government. They were advocating that the political process in Mexico become more tolerant, open and democratic. But, for Díaz Ordaz, this was beyond the pale. The government never responded to the demands.

In the face of government silence, the student activists decided to hold a march from the southern suburbs to the Zócalo. They set the date for August 13, hoping to attract a few followers. On that day, by the time they reached the Zócalo, there were 200,000 people in tow. While many were students and families of students, there were also nurses, teachers, and every kind of worker in the city in the crowd. Speeches were delivered, and the event was entirely peaceful. As Preston and Dillon pointed out, “The unexpected size of the crowd proved that the students were voicing frustrations felt by Mexicans of all ages in a modernizing Mexico.”

A warning to protesters

The students then planned another march to the Zócalo for August 27, and this time, 400,000 people showed up. On this occasion, though, some students congregated under the balcony of the National Palace, the building from which Mexican presidents traditionally preside over annual Independence Day celebrations, standing on a balcony. Those students then started chanting, “Sal al balcón, chango hocicón” (“Come out to the balcony, you big-snouted monkey”) — referring to Díaz Ordaz’s pronounced buckteeth and frequent comparisons to a monkey.

As nighttime fell, most protesters left, but at the approach of midnight, a few thousand stragglers continued to mill around. At that point, a dozen armored personnel carriers rolled into the Zócalo; the army mercilessly beat any remaining protesters.

Then on September 1, Díaz Ordaz delivered his annual State of the Union address, essentially offering a warning.

“We can’t allow our legal order to continue to be ruptured so inexcusably,” the president declared in his speech. “We wouldn’t like to find ourselves in a situation where we would have to take measures we don’t want to. But we’ll take them if we must. We’ll go as far as we have to.”

Unfortunately, the students did not recognize the warning.

Politician and ex-education minister of Mexico City Salvador Martínez della Roca, one of the student leaders from UNAM at the time, told U.S. journalist Mark Kurlansky, “It was a threat, but we didn’t really listen.”

By September 24, “Mexico City was living under a barely camouflaged state of siege,” Krauze explains.

Mexican military mobilizes against campuses

On that day, the army seized the National Polytechnic Institute (IPN), known colloquially as the Politécnico; government forces had already occupied the UNAM campus. IPN students fought the army for hours, but there was only so much that unarmed civilians could do against tanks.

Although the army withdrew from both campuses on September 30, the message had been sent. Unfortunately, students failed to recognize that, for Díaz Ordaz’s government, a hard-and-fast deadline was quickly approaching: the 1968 Olympic Games, scheduled to begin in Mexico City on Oct. 12.

The Olympics were seen by many in the nation as Mexico’s moment to shine: The world no longer saw it as a chaotic, strife-ridden backwater nation but as the “Mexico Miracle” — with a powerful economy and a newly minted middle class. From the 1950s through the 1960s, Mexico’s economy had grown at 6% per annum (8% in 1968). In 1968, Mexico had the strongest economy in all of Latin America, with an inflation rate lower than the United States.

Díaz Ordaz was not about to let a bunch of long-haired students, whom he viewed as spoiled, ruin the opening of the Olympic Games and Mexico’s moment of glory.

President Díaz Ordaz sees conspiracies everywhere

Much like former U.S. president Richard Nixon, Díaz Ordaz was a tremendously insecure man, about his appearance and when interacting with others. “Ever since he was a little boy, the sense of being ugly had tortured him,” Krauze explained. “His mother would freely say to anyone, ‘But what an ugly son I have!’ It would take its toll on his life.”

And much like Nixon, Díaz Ordaz saw conspiracies everywhere. If students were protesting, it must be at the behest of French communists or Cuban agitators. In reality, this seems unlikely; even the CIA station chief in Mexico City, Winston Scott, doubted it.

“Although the [Mexican] government claims to have solid evidence that the Communist Party engineered the fracas of 26 July, and reportedly had indications of Soviet Embassy complicity, it is unlikely that the Soviets would so undermine their carefully nurtured good relations with the Mexicans,” Scott told CIA headquarters at the time.

It never occurred to Díaz Ordaz that it was, in fact, his policies — or his overreaction to a minor skirmish — that spurred the student protests.

After a few more protests, at which some buses were set on fire, the student leaders scheduled a rally to be held on October 2 at the Plaza de las Tres Culturas. This plaza sits in the Tlatelolco neighborhood on the north side of Mexico City. Perhaps more than any other site, it best represents Mexican history: Aztec ruins there are flanked by a Franciscan church.

In the 1960s, the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) government built a housing project there, one building of which was Edificio Chihuahua. The third floor of the Edificio Chihuahua had an open-air hallway with a three-foot wall overlooking the plaza. It was from this third-floor balcony that the speakers decided to address the crowd on October 2.

The day of the Tlatelolco Massacre

By 8:30 a.m. that morning, the army had taken up positions in each corner of the plaza — not necessarily unusual — as the army often posted soldiers at protest rallies. But something about this day seemed off: Witnesses later mentioned seeing men with short haircuts in civilian clothes, all wearing a white glove on one hand.

Myrthokleia Gonzáles Gallardo, a 22-year-old Politécnico student, had been chosen to introduce the speakers that day, even though her parents warned her not to go, fearing something might happen with the increased military presence.

Myrthokleia described her entry into the Plaza:

“As I approached the Tlatelolco with the four speakers, I was introduced, and we were warned to be careful, as the army had been seen nearby. But I wasn’t afraid, though we decided to make it a short meeting. There were workers, students, and families coming into the plaza, filling it up. We didn’t see any [soldiers] in the plaza.

“We took our place on the third floor and started our speeches. Suddenly, off to the left, over the church, were helicopters with a green light. Suddenly, everyone down in the plaza started falling. And then men with white gloves and weapons appeared, maybe from the elevator. They ordered us down to the ground floor, where they began beating us.”

Gunfire erupts and continues for hours

Raúl Álvarez Garín was also whisked down to the ground floor and made to stand facing a wall as government forces beat him relentlessly. Álvarez remembered the sound of automatic gunfire continuing for a full two hours. Other witnesses remember sporadic gunfire until 11 p.m.

The next morning, journalist Elena Poniatowska arrived at Tlatelolco at dawn. There were tanks and soldiers everywhere, yet no one tried to impede her strolling around the plaza. She had heard from a friend that bodies covered the plaza, but by morning, they all had been taken away.

In the newspaper Excelsior, Poniatowska learned that Italian journalist Oriana Fallaci was in Mexico to cover the Olympics and had been wounded while attending the rally. Poniatowska tracked down Fallaci in a hospital and interviewed her.

“What savagery!” Fallaci told her. “Police dragging students away by the hair. I saw many people get hit — until I was hit too. I lay in a pool of my own blood for 45 minutes.”

Shocked by what she heard, Poniatowska wrote an article detailing the events. Her editor immediately rejected it.

“There’s an order,” the editor announced, according to Preston and Dillon. “We’re going to concentrate on the Olympic Games. We’re not printing anything more about Tlatelolco.”

The legacy of the Tlatelolco Massacre

The Tlatelolco student massacre was a tragic and immensely consequential event in Mexican history. The Olympic Games may have gone off without a hitch, but at what cost? Over 400 people were murdered in cold blood by government troops. Hundreds more simply disappeared, never heard from again. Hundreds more were imprisoned for years. Hundreds, if not thousands, went into hiding, fearing retaliation for simply expressing their ideas about the nature of their society.

Before 1968, most Mexicans felt proud of their nation’s economic achievements. During the Mexican Revolution, one leader after another had been brutally assassinated. In the wake of the Revolution, the PRI provided stability and economic growth, and Mexico had become a modern nation. In 1959, American academics conducted a poll and found that while most Mexicans were tired of their country’s endemic corruption, they were generally proud of their political system and its achievements and felt their presidents were, for the most part, benign. After 1968, however, most middle-class Mexicans felt disillusioned, resentful and utterly distrustful of their government.

Perhaps the students’ National Strike Council (CNH) final statement, issued in December 1968 upon its dissolution, summed it up best:

“Democracy in Mexico is just a concept, another formalism,” it announced. “Politics is carried out behind the backs of the popular majorities and of their aspirations, interests and demands.”

While the student movement of 1968 was neutralized, the Tlatelolco massacre has had a long-lasting impact on Mexican politics and history: More than 50 years later, October 2 is commemorated every year across Mexico with civilian demonstrations. Films and documentaries and countless books have been written about it — in Mexico and around the world.

Groundwork laid in 1968 also spawned a generation of the nation’s activists and political leaders, who were involved in Mexico’s electoral reform in the 1980s, which ultimately led to the end of the PRI’s uninterrupted rule over Mexico for 70 years in 2000, with Vicente Fox’s election as president.

Kurlansky, in his book “1968: The Year that Rocked the World,” commented: “But very much in the same way that the invasion of Czechoslovakia was the (beginning of the) end of the Soviet Union, Tlatelolco was the unseen beginning of the end of the end of the PRI.”

Robert McLaughlin, Ph.D. is a historian specializing in Cold War Latin American history.

World.title: Flávio Bolsonaro Leads Brazil Election Count at 51%
World.content:
Live tonight Follow Brazil’s vote count live The official TSE count with every candidate’s share, the state map and what a runoff would mean, updated through the night. Open the live results →

Flávio Bolsonaro leads Brazil’s first-round count, but only 36.60% of polling stations have reported, and several states where Lula leads are far from fully counted.

Key Facts The count: 36.60% of polling stations counted as of 18:32 Brasília time (17:32 US Eastern, 22:32 Lisbon), according to the electoral court (TSE).

Flávio Bolsonaro: 50.63% of valid votes (21,383,323 votes). He is a senator for the conservative Liberal Party (PL).

Lula: 41.23% of valid votes (17,411,527 votes). He is the leftist president, from the Workers’ Party (PT).

The rest: Augusto Cury 2.95%, Ronaldo Caiado 2.39%, Renan Santos 2.30%, Romeu Zema 0.28%. Six other candidates are each below 0.2%.

Why it matters: A candidate needs more than 50% of valid votes to win outright. If nobody gets there, a runoff follows on Sunday 25 October.

What it means for you: Brazil’s stock market is closed on Sundays and reopens on Monday 5 October. Treat tonight’s shares as a partial picture.

Where the Count Stands

Brazil’s electoral court, the TSE, showed Flávio Bolsonaro ahead with 50.63% of valid votes at 18:32 Brasília time (17:32 US Eastern, 22:32 Lisbon). Lula had 41.23%. The gap was about 4.0 million votes, or 9.4 percentage points. A share above 50% at the end of the count would avoid a runoff, and the count has a long way to go.

Only 36.60% of polling stations had been counted. That is 182,745 of 499,248 sections. The TSE had not declared a result.

The rule is simple. A candidate wins in the first round with more than half of the valid votes. Blank and null ballots are not valid. Flávio Bolsonaro is above that line for now, but the line applies to the final count, not to a partial one.

Behind the two leaders, Augusto Cury has 2.95%, Ronaldo Caiado 2.39%, Renan Santos 2.30% and Romeu Zema 0.28%.

Why the Early Count Is Not the Result

States report at different speeds. In the TSE’s state tables at about 22:40 Lisbon, the Federal District, Paraná and Mato Grosso do Sul were 82% to 95% counted. Flávio Bolsonaro led in all three.

Bahia, Pernambuco and Ceará were each no more than 29% counted. Lula led them with roughly 60% to 65%. São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, two of the biggest electorates, were each under 34% counted.

The national shares will therefore move as those states report. The final polls had pointed to a different order. Datafolha, in a poll published on 3 October, had Lula at 45% and Flávio Bolsonaro at 42% of valid votes, with a margin of error of two points. A poll is not a result, and neither is a partial count. Read more in our final polls report.

Who Is Who

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) is a senator for Rio de Janeiro and the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. His Liberal Party sits on the political right.

Lula (PT) is Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the president since 2023. He also governed from 2003 to 2010. His Workers’ Party is on the left, and his running mate is Vice President Geraldo Alckmin.

Augusto Cury (Avante) is an author and psychiatrist. Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) is a conservative politician from Goiás. Renan Santos (Missão) represents the newer Missão party. Romeu Zema (Novo) represents a free-market party.

Why It Matters for the US

Brazil is the largest economy in Latin America, and US investors hold it through stocks, bonds and funds. The B3 exchange in São Paulo is closed on Sundays. The first market test comes on Monday 5 October.

US-listed shares of Petrobras and Vale, and the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ), trade during US hours on Monday. The real, Brazil’s currency, will also react. A clear first-round result would remove three weeks of uncertainty. A runoff would keep it alive until 25 October.

The winner will also set the tone of Brazil’s relations with Washington, including trade. Our guide on what the election means for US investors covers the market angle, and our election explainer covers the rules.

What Happens Next

The TSE keeps publishing as more stations report. The share counted should rise through the night, and the leaders’ percentages will change with it.

If nobody ends above 50% of valid votes, the top two meet in a runoff on Sunday 25 October 2026. If someone does, the TSE would declare a first-round winner once the count is complete. We update this article as the TSE numbers change, and our live results page carries the state map.

What Is Not Known

We do not know whether the lead will hold as Bahia, São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and other states report. We also do not know whether a runoff will be needed. Only the TSE count answers that.

Sources Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), Resultados portal, presidential count, data of 4 October 2026, 18:32 Brasília time.

TSE, state results tables, 4 October 2026.

Datafolha poll published on 3 October 2026.

More on Brazil: Brazil hub. Live: Brazil election results.

Frequently Asked Questions Who is leading Brazil’s presidential election count? At 18:32 Brasília time (17:32 US Eastern, 22:32 Lisbon), the electoral court (TSE) showed Flávio Bolsonaro of the conservative Liberal Party (PL) with 50.63% of valid votes and President Lula of the leftist Workers’ Party (PT) with 41.23%. Only 36.60% of polling stations had been counted, so the shares will move. Has anyone won Brazil’s election yet? No. The TSE has not declared a result. A candidate wins in the first round only with more than half of the valid votes once the count is complete. Blank and null ballots do not count as valid. If nobody passes that line, the top two meet in a runoff. Why can an early count change so much? Brazil’s states report at different speeds, and the early numbers come from different places. In the TSE’s state tables at about 22:40 Lisbon, the Federal District, Paraná and Mato Grosso do Sul, where Flávio Bolsonaro leads, were 82% to 95% counted, while Bahia, Pernambuco and Ceará, where Lula leads, were each no more than 29% counted. When is a runoff, and where can I follow the count from the US? A runoff would be held on Sunday 25 October 2026. The official count is on the TSE’s Resultados portal at resultados.tse.jus.br, and The Rio Times live results page shows every candidate’s share and the state map.

AGRICULTURE · PANAMA

Key Facts — The country Panama. The main drought zone is the Arco Seco: Herrera, Los Santos and parts of Veraguas and Coclé. Panama uses the US dollar.

— What happened On 28 September 2026 the Agriculture Ministry (MIDA) put a US$8.2 million plan into action for small and medium producers hit by El Niño drought and heavy rain.

— The numbers US$2.45 million for water systems (1,158 producers), US$2.4 million for cattle feed (3,106) and US$636,000 for crop inputs (1,345), per MIDA on 28 September.

— What it means for you The minister has projected rice output 15–20% lower; he also says rice stocks are sufficient. Watch rice, onion and beef prices into 2027.

— Still open Delivery dates, how farmers apply, and how the unpriced machinery and Bocas del Toro items fit into the total.

Panama has put a US$8.2 million emergency plan into action for small and medium farmers hit by El Niño. The Ministry of Agricultural Development (MIDA), led by Roberto Linares, announced the measures on 28 September.

The money targets two opposite problems: drought in the Arco Seco and too much rain in Bocas del Toro. It is the agriculture slice of a wider US$80 million national emergency fund approved in August.

Where the Money Goes

The largest item, US$2.45 million, pays for water. It covers collective reservoirs, 2,500-square-metre irrigation kits for fodder grass, small pumps and repairs to masonry mini-dams for 1,158 producers.

Another US$2.4 million buys feed for 3,106 cattle farmers. The list includes hay bales, haylage, maize silage, rice straw, molasses and alfalfa.

Itemised parts of MIDA's US$8.2 million El Niño plan for farmers, in US$ million: water systems 2.45, livestock feed 2.40, crop inputs 0.64; machinery and Bocas del Toro items were not priced. Source: Ministry of Agricultural Development (MIDA), 28 September 2026.

A further US$636,000 goes on fertiliser, seed, tool kits, small nurseries and greenhouses for about 1,345 producers and families. MIDA will also buy tools and machinery for some 600 producers, without giving a price.

In Bocas del Toro, on the Caribbean side, the plan supports 1,050 producers and 100 families. It provides seed for maize, rice and beans and aims to reach more than 2,400 hectares of crops.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Drought in the Arco Seco, Floods on the Caribbean

The Arco Seco, or “dry arc”, covers Herrera, Los Santos and parts of Veraguas and Coclé. It is Panama’s driest region, and MIDA lists it among the areas most vulnerable to El Niño.

In early September Deputy Minister José Aníbal Rincón set out a first split, La Prensa and TVN reported on 3 September. About US$6.7 million would fight drought, and US$1.5 million would repair flood damage in Bocas del Toro and Puerto Armuelles.

Part of a US$80 Million Emergency

The Cabinet created the wider fund by Resolution No. 80 of 25 August 2026, La Estrella de Panamá reported. The Economy Ministry runs it through a National Bank trust, with emergency contracts allowed until 30 June 2027.

Both newspapers put MIDA’s share of that fund at US$8.2 million, roughly a tenth. It comes on top of a ministry investment budget of about US$120 million.

The ministry says it has already spent about US$1.2 million on machinery, spare parts and veterinary supplies. The National Assembly’s budget committee also approved US$2.3 million for three deep-well drilling rigs.

Doubts in the Assembly

Lawmakers questioned on 3 September whether US$8.2 million is enough. Linares himself noted that about US$10 million had reportedly gone to an earlier Azuero drinking-water emergency, which more than a year later is still unresolved, TVN reported.

Linares told deputies that rice output could fall 15–20% and onions about 15%. He also said Panama holds sufficient rice stocks, and that impacts differ by region and crop. Our earlier report shows how El Niño splits Latin America into winners and losers.

Water has long been contested in this region, as our report on farmers resisting Panama Canal water projects showed. MIDA says regional agro-climatic panels brief producers on forecasts every quarter.

What Is Not Yet Known

As of 4 October, MIDA has not published delivery dates or an application process for farmers. The three priced items total about US$5.5 million, and the ministry has not costed the rest.

It is also unclear how long El Niño will last or how far harvests will fall. Linares has promised to report spending on the ministry’s website.

Sources: Ministerio de Desarrollo Agropecuario (MIDA) press release (28 September 2026); La Estrella de Panamá (28 September 2026) and La Estrella de Panamá (4 September 2026); La Prensa (3 September 2026); TVN (3 September 2026).

POLITICS · JAMAICA

Key Facts — The country Jamaica keeps King Charles III as head of state. Its final court of appeal is still the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London.

— What happened On 4 October 2026, Justice Minister Delroy Chuck told the Jamaica Observer the final court “should be a Jamaican appellate court”, not the Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ).

— Who is involved Prime Minister Andrew Holness’s government; Opposition Leader Mark Golding of the People’s National Party (PNP); opposition justice spokesperson Zuleika Jess.

— What it means for you Nothing changes in the courts for now. Chuck said the Privy Council stays Jamaica’s final court until Jamaicans agree on a replacement.

— Still open Whether Golding answers a letter from Holness sent last year, and when the stalled republic bill returns to Parliament.

Jamaica Justice Minister Delroy Chuck says the country’s eventual final court of appeal should be Jamaican. He ruled out, for now, giving that role to the Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ), a regional court in Trinidad and Tobago.

His comments came in an interview with the Jamaica Observer published on Sunday 4 October. Until the two main parties agree, he said, the Privy Council in London remains Jamaica’s court of last resort.

What Chuck said

The Jamaica justice minister, who also handles constitutional affairs, said there is “a general consensus” among most Jamaicans and within government. The final court, he said, “should be a Jamaican appellate court and not a Caribbean court of justice.”

He called the CCJ “basically a part of a political system that doesn’t exist”. With no Caribbean political system, he argued, Jamaica is not agreeing to the CCJ as its final court “at this present moment”.

He noted that Jamaica has signed on to the CCJ’s original jurisdiction, which handles disputes under the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) treaty. Swapping the Privy Council for the CCJ, in his view, would only replace one external court with another.

He said the Privy Council is the court “we have been using and will continue to use” until Jamaicans agree on a final court. That leaves the current system in place for every pending appeal.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

A stalled move to a republic

The remarks are the latest round in a long dispute between Holness’s Jamaica Labour Party government and the opposition PNP. At stake is which court should sit at the top of the system as Jamaica tries to become a republic.

A 2024 republic bill to remove the British monarch has been tabled but not passed. Chuck urged MPs to revisit it in a debate on 10 June 2026, according to the Jamaica Information Service (JIS), the government news agency.

On Sunday he accused the PNP of using accession to the CCJ as a tactic to delay constitutional reform. He said Opposition Leader Mark Golding has not answered a long letter Holness sent him last year.

Chuck suggested Golding pass the file to Zuleika Jess, the opposition justice spokesperson, so she and a team could meet him. He called it “most inappropriate” that no such meeting between the two sides has been organised.

Room for a middle path

The government’s stance still leaves space on who would sit on the bench. In June, Chuck pointed to Hong Kong, whose top court mixes local and international judges.

He told Parliament he would not mind if “five Caribbean court judges sit” on a Jamaican final court, according to JIS. “But it must be a Jamaican final court,” he added.

He has also said the court question will go to the public through constitutional town hall meetings. On Sunday he urged the opposition to form a parliamentary team to find areas that could be agreed and implemented.

The Privy Council remains central to Jamaican legal life, as the recent reparations petition referred to the Privy Council shows. For wider political context, see Jamaica Explained.

What Is Not Yet Known

The Observer report carried no response from the PNP. It is not clear whether Golding will answer Holness’s letter or name a team for talks.

No date has been announced for the town hall meetings or for a debate on the republic bill. Any change to the final court would require amending the Constitution, which needs broad agreement between the parties.

Sources: Jamaica Observer, interview with Justice Minister Delroy Chuck, 4 October 2026; Jamaica Information Service, “Justice Minister Urges MPs to Revisit Bill to Make Jamaica a Republic”, 12 June 2026; Caribbean Court of Justice.

ECONOMY · URUGUAY

Key Facts — The country Uruguay has had no IMF lending programme for more than 20 years, Finance Minister Gabriel Oddone said on 28 September. Like every member, it is still reviewed annually.

— What happened IMF mission chief Raphael Espinoza told El País on 4 October 2026 that growth averaging 1.2% since 2016 is too slow, and that “stability alone” cannot fix it.

— The numbers IMF forecasts of 24 September: growth of 1.3% in 2026 and 2.4% in 2027; inflation at the 4.5% target; a primary surplus of 0.5% of GDP urged for 2029.

— What it means for you Investors get a stable, low-risk Uruguay with slow growth. The IMF wants cheaper energy, logistics and licences, plus a review of decades-old tax incentives.

— Still open Whether the central bank raises its 5.75% policy rate at its meeting this week, as some market pricing suggested on 29 September.

The IMF mission chief for Uruguay, Raphael Espinoza, says the country has room to be more ambitious. In written answers published by the Montevideo daily El País on Sunday 4 October, he argued that stability alone will not deliver the growth Uruguay needs.

The interview follows the International Monetary Fund’s annual review, which ended on 24 September. Its staff noted that growth has averaged only 1.2% since 2016, too little to converge with rich-country incomes.

Why the Fund Expects a Rebound

The Fund’s mission, in Montevideo from 14 to 24 September, cut its 2026 growth forecast to 1.3% because last year’s drought hit farm output. It expects 2.4% in 2027.

Espinoza explained that optimism to El País. Leaving aside the pandemic of 2020–2021 and the historic 2023 drought, he said, the economy has grown about 2.1% a year.

Uruguay's growth: 1.2% average since 2016, about 2.1% excluding the pandemic and 2023 drought, and IMF forecasts of 1.3% for 2026 and 2.4% for 2027. Source: IMF staff concluding statement, 24 Sep 2026; Raphael Espinoza to El País, 4 Oct 2026.

He pointed to consumption, about 80% of GDP, growing at 2.5%. Fixed investment rose 9.5% year on year in real terms in the second quarter of 2026.

He also called monetary policy “accommodative”, which should help output reach its potential. Finance Minister Gabriel Oddone called the IMF’s reading “adequate” on 28 September, Subrayado reported.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Uruguay markets Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

A Tighter Fiscal Target Than the Government’s

The government aims for a primary deficit of 0.1% of GDP in 2029, covering central government and the BPS, the state social-security agency. The IMF urges a surplus of 0.5% instead.

Espinoza said debt to GDP stays broadly stable in the Fund’s baseline, so the aim is a falling path. The extra effort could be phased in gradually, he added.

His options are reviewing tax incentives, many set decades ago, moderating the public wage bill and spending reviews in health and education. He said such reviews should be gradual and evidence-based.

On the pending pension bill restoring retirement at 60, he cited BPS actuarial work showing a negligible effect. A full judgement needs the final text, he said.

Where Uruguay Could Be More Ambitious

Espinoza welcomed the competitiveness bill, saying licences to operate or import take far longer in Uruguay than elsewhere in the region. About one firm in five cites access to finance as a major obstacle.

Logistics and energy costs are not in the bill, he acknowledged, though the government has them on its agenda. He also urged state-company reform, with wages tied to productivity and cost-based pricing.

He defended Uruguay’s consensus politics as a source of durable policy. “Stability by itself cannot generate the increase in growth” the country’s social model needs, he said, urging “calculated risks” with discipline.

The Rate Decision Ahead

The IMF expects inflation to settle at the 4.5% target, with a gradual rise in the policy rate to a neutral level. The central bank (BCU) rate committee meets this week, Ámbito reported on 29 September.

On 28 September, 28-day BCU bills cleared at 5.94%, above the 5.75% policy rate, hinting at a 25 basis-point rise. Analysts polled by the BCU see one such increase within six months.

What Is Not Yet Known

The IMF board has not yet discussed the staff report, and the full document is not public. The final shape of the pension bill is also still open.

It is unclear whether the BCU moves this week or holds. Earlier coverage of the IMF’s 1.3% forecast set out the government’s more upbeat view.

GOVERNANCE · DOMINICAN REPUBLIC

Key Facts — The country Dominican Republic. OMSA (Operadora Metropolitana de Servicios de Autobuses) is the state-run metropolitan bus operator based in Santo Domingo.

— What happened On Friday 2 October 2026 the Comptroller General published an OMSA audit covering 16 August 2020 to 30 June 2024, flagging accounting, payroll and asset failures.

— The numbers A RD$107.9 million (about US$1.8 million) fuel balance gap and RD$47.5 million (about US$797,000) in undocumented per diems, per the report as cited by Diario Libre and N Digital.

— What it means for you No change to bus services has been announced. The findings concern how public money was recorded and are audit observations, not criminal charges.

— Still open Whether prosecutors will review the findings, and how far fixes have gone. OMSA told auditors most issues were being corrected.

The Dominican Republic’s Comptroller General has flagged accounting gaps running into hundreds of millions of pesos at OMSA, the state-run bus operator. The OMSA audit, published on Friday 2 October, covers 16 August 2020 to 30 June 2024.

The best-attested figure is a RD$107.9 million (about US$1.8 million) gap in the fuel balance at the Las Caobas depot. Diario Libre and N Digital both reported it, and conversions here use RD$59.59 per US dollar (2 October close).

What the Auditors Found

The Comptroller General (Contraloría General de la República) is the government’s internal auditor. Diario Libre, quoting its report, said inventory movements differed from the ledgers by RD$204.9 million (about US$3.4 million).

At Las Caobas, spare parts were also off by RD$2.7 million on top of the fuel gap. Fuel dispatches were logged by hand, and the person measuring tank levels also handed the fuel out.

Largest individual amounts flagged in the Comptroller General's OMSA audit, August 2020 to June 2024, in RD$ million; items overlap and should not be added. Source: Contraloría General de la República audit, via Diario Libre and N Digital, 2–4 Oct 2026.

Both outlets cite RD$55.3 million (about US$928,000) in transport sold to three ministries in early 2024 but never booked as income. A further RD$96 million (about US$1.6 million) in supplier debts was overdue at the end of June 2024.

Auditors also found RD$43.7 million (about US$733,000) booked as legal representation costs, although the money paid for generator rental and mechanical services.

The books still carried RD$45.8 million (about US$769,000) for construction on buildings already demolished. Of nine plots OMSA occupies, only one was registered with the tax authority, Diario Libre reported.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on the Dominican Republic Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Payroll, Per Diems and Contracts

The OMSA audit found RD$47.5 million (about US$797,000) in per diems, paid from September 2020 to June 2024, lacking result reports. Severance payments showed a calculated distortion of RD$126.8 million (about US$2.1 million).

In a physical check of 338 employees, 45 could not be located, Diario Libre reported. Fifteen staff also drew state pensions, and 15 more appeared on other public payrolls.

N Digital, citing the report, said ten contracts from a sample of 37 tenders went to firms run by serving military personnel. Diario Libre did not report this point, so it rests on one outlet’s reading.

How OMSA Responded

In its reply to the auditors, OMSA said most observations were “in the process of being corrected”, according to Diario Libre. It committed to fixing its accounts, regularising property and vehicle titles, and moving payroll onto the state personnel system.

The audit period falls within the tenure of Radhamés González, who led OMSA from August 2020 to August 2025, Diario Libre noted. No public comment from him had been reported by Sunday evening.

Why These Audits Are Public Now

The OMSA report was among audits released after President Luis Abinader ordered their publication. He acted after Diario Libre revealed that hundreds of audit reports had been kept out of public view.

The same release showed the migration agency could not find 150 vehicles, as covered in Dominican Migration Audit Cannot Find 150 Vehicles. Publishing the reports gives voters and lawmakers material they previously lacked.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is unclear whether the Public Ministry, the national prosecution service, will review the OMSA audit. Audit observations are administrative and do not establish that anyone broke the law.

The figures come from detailed accounts by two outlets, since the full report could not be retrieved directly on Sunday. It is also unknown how far OMSA’s promised corrections have advanced since mid-2024.

Sources: Contraloría General de la República audit of OMSA (16 August 2020 to 30 June 2024), published 2 October 2026, as reported by Diario Libre (3 October 2026) and N Digital (4 October 2026); Remolacha (4 October 2026).

World.content:

ENERGY · PUERTO RICO

Key Facts — The country Puerto Rico, a US territory that uses the US dollar, ships in the liquefied natural gas (LNG) burned at its San Juan and Palo Seco power plants.

— What happened The LNG tanker Amur River missed its planned 06:00 entry to San Juan Bay on Sunday 4 October 2026. It first reached the bay on 17 September (El Nuevo Día).

— Who is involved Supplier New Fortress Energy and its subsidiary Genera PR, which runs the plants; the Energy Bureau regulator; the state utility AEE; and the 3PPO procurement office.

— What it means for you San Juan units 5 and 6 have burned diesel instead of gas since mid-September. Genera put the extra fuel cost at about US$14 million on 28 September.

— Still open Whether the regulator revises its 30 September order deferring US$17.6 million (El Nuevo Día), and when the tanker docks. Lawmakers hold a hearing on 6 October.

A Puerto Rico gas tanker, the Amur River, did not enter San Juan Bay on Sunday 4 October 2026 as planned. Its supplier, New Fortress Energy, blamed a 30 September order from the island’s energy regulator for creating uncertainty over payments.

The ship carries LNG for power plants that have been short of gas since mid-September. Until it docks, the San Juan plant burns costlier diesel. Background: Puerto Rico Natural Gas Dispute Could Add US$48 a Month to Power Bills (29 September).

What the Regulator Ordered

On 30 September the Energy Bureau, the island’s electricity regulator, deferred about US$17.6 million in gas-related payments, El Nuevo Día reported. The deferral fed into the fuel charge behind the higher electricity rate in force since 1 October.

In a letter on Friday 2 October, New Fortress said the order breached its contracts with the AEE (Electric Power Authority), the state utility that owns the plants. It said it could not commit any LNG to Puerto Rico going forward. The Energy Bureau posted the letter on its website on Sunday afternoon.

The company set two conditions for supplying again. The regulator must revoke or modify its order, and the AEE must confirm it will pay outstanding debts under the contracts.

Dollar figures on the record in Puerto Rico's gas supply dispute: LUMA's estimate of charges for unused contract gas (US$67 million, 28 Sep), the Energy Bureau's deferred payment (US$17.6 million, 30 Sep order) and Genera's estimate of extra fuel cost (US$14 million, 28 Sep). Source: Metro Puerto Rico, 29 Sep 2026; El Nuevo Día, 4 Oct 2026.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Puerto Rico Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How the State Answered

The Independent Procurement Office (3PPO), which handles the island’s energy contracts, replied the same Friday. It warned that stopping supply could amount to wilful misconduct and deliberate abandonment of the contract.

The office gave New Fortress 24 hours to confirm in writing that supply would continue. El Nuevo Día could not establish whether the company did so.

Late on Friday the AEE filed an urgent motion asking the regulator to address the company’s claims. It said it would comply with the deferral unless the regulator instructed otherwise.

The utility warned that the order, as New Fortress reads it, could deepen reliance on diesel. The next move sits with the Energy Bureau.

Courts, Pilots and the Coast Guard

Payment is the newest hurdle for the Puerto Rico gas tanker. It first reached San Juan on 17 September but could not berth amid a dispute with harbour pilots over vessel size, El Nuevo Día reported.

On Thursday 1 October federal judge Silvia Carreño-Coll authorised the ship to enter and berth, Telemundo Puerto Rico reported. Her conditions include two standby tugs paid by New Fortress and manoeuvres only in winds of 10 knots or less.

On Saturday the US Coast Guard raised objections over the vessel’s dimensions. It later said these concerned the company’s navigation study rather than the planned delivery, El Nuevo Día reported.

What It Means for Power Bills

San Juan units 5 and 6 have run on diesel and heavy fuel oil for nearly two weeks, said legislator José Hernández. Hernández, who chairs the House transport committee, said this raises generation costs and, in turn, household bills.

Genera PR told a 28 September regulatory hearing that the extra fuel could cost about US$14 million. Grid operator LUMA put possible charges for unused contract gas at about US$67 million, Metro Puerto Rico reported.

Neither estimate has been approved. Genera vice-president Iván Báez said on Sunday it would keep generating with the fuel it has.

For now the shortage shows up as cost rather than lost supply. All sides say they want the Puerto Rico gas tanker unloaded.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is not known whether New Fortress met the 3PPO deadline, or when the regulator will rule. No new entry date had been announced by Sunday evening.

On Tuesday 6 October at 09:00, the House transport committee will question the Ports Authority, the pilots and New Fortress under oath.

Who finally pays for the diesel, and for contract gas that never arrived, remains open. The US$17.6 million figure rests on El Nuevo Día’s reading of the order and is not independently confirmed.

Sources: Metro Puerto Rico, 4 Oct 2026; Metro Puerto Rico, House hearing, 4 Oct 2026; Metro Puerto Rico, 29 Sep 2026; El Nuevo Día, 4 Oct 2026; El Nuevo Día, Coast Guard, 3 Oct 2026; Telemundo Puerto Rico, 4 Oct 2026.

SECURITY · TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO

Key Facts — The country Trinidad and Tobago, a twin-island Caribbean state off Venezuela’s coast, where firearms were used in 82.5% of murders from 2018 to 2024 (Global Crime study, TTPS data).

— What happened Of 279 guns recovered in 2025 and traced by the US firearms agency, 204 (73.1%) were US-sourced, up from 52% in 2020 (Trinidad Guardian, 4 October 2026).

— The numbers From 2020 to 2025, 1,116 of 1,777 traced guns (62.8%) were US-sourced. Handguns made up 246 of the 279 traces in 2025 (Trinidad Guardian, 4 October).

— What it means for you Homicides fell to 265 in January to September 2026, from 275 a year earlier (TTPS, 2 October). Tracing aids police, but nearly half of US trails went cold.

— Still open The data do not show who smuggled the guns or by which route. For 100 of the 204 US-sourced guns, the first buyer was never identified.

Nearly three in four traced crime guns from Trinidad and Tobago in 2025 were US guns, the Trinidad Guardian reported on Sunday. The figure comes from a Guardian Media review of six years of US trace data.

Police submitted 279 recovered firearms to the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) for tracing last year. The agency classed 204 of them, or 73.1%, as US-sourced.

A Six-Year Rise in US Guns

The share has climbed steadily. In 2020, 155 of 298 traced firearms were US-sourced, or 52%, according to the Guardian review.

Across 2020 to 2025, 1,116 of 1,777 traced guns came through the US market. That is 62.8% over the six years.

US-sourced share of firearms recovered in Trinidad and Tobago and submitted to the ATF for tracing. Source: Trinidad Guardian analysis of US ATF trace data, 4 October 2026.

“US-sourced” covers guns made in the United States and foreign-made guns legally imported into the US market. In 2025 the split was 104 US-made and 100 imported.

The classification does not show who smuggled a gun into the country or which route it took. It only shows the weapon passed through the US commercial system.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Trinidad and Tobago Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Mostly Handguns, and Many Trails Go Cold

Pistols (183) and revolvers (63) made up 246 of the 279 traces in 2025, or 88.2%. The rest were 17 rifles, eight shotguns and eight other firearms.

The ATF identified the first US retail buyer for 72 of the 204 US-sourced guns. Another 32 were traced to a foreign government, dealer or other entity.

For the remaining 100, the first purchaser could not be found. The ATF cites incomplete records, missing details, filed-off serial numbers and guns too old to trace.

The agency also warns that traced guns are not a random sample. Not every crime gun in Trinidad and Tobago is sent for tracing.

Guns Behind Most Murders

A 2026 study in the journal Global Crime, using police data, found firearms in 3,072 of 3,723 murders from 2018 to 2024. That is 82.5%, the Guardian reported.

Police seized 1,064 firearms in 2017 but 656 in 2024, the same study showed. The researchers cautioned that fewer seizures do not necessarily mean fewer illegal guns.

A 2024 report by Parliament’s Joint Select Committee on National Security put the average black-market gun price at TT$17,429. That is about US$2,586 at 6.74 Trinidad and Tobago dollars per US dollar (2 October close).

Killings Fall as Police Lean on Tracing

The Trinidad and Tobago Police Service (TTPS) recorded 265 homicides from January to September 2026, its third-quarter appraisal shows. That compares with 275 a year earlier and 475 in 2024.

Homicides recorded January to September, 2024 to 2026. Source: TTPS Third Quarter 2026 Public Performance Appraisal, via Trinidad Guardian, 4 October 2026.

The appraisal, released on Friday 2 October, also showed serious reported crime down 13.3% on 2025. Kidnappings for ransom rose from six to seven, the Guardian reported.

Deputy Commissioner of Police Junior Benjamin said tracing helps police see how guns enter the country. “It helps us in a lot of ways,” he told Guardian Media.

Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar raised illegal gun flows at the UN General Assembly days earlier. She said the country would use its coming UN Security Council term to push for stronger tracing.

The fall in killings comes after months of emergency rule. In September the government revived its zones of special operations bill. Police also burned seized drugs worth US$249 million in late September.

What Is Not Yet Known

The ATF data cover only guns police chose to submit, so the US share of all crime guns is unknown. The routes and smuggling networks behind the US guns traced in 2025 have not been published.

It is also unclear how many of the 265 homicides in 2026 involved firearms. The TTPS appraisal, as reported, did not break down killings by weapon.

Sources: Trinidad Guardian, “US gun trail grows in T&T: Nearly three-quarters of traces now linked to America” (4 October 2026), Guardian Media analysis of US ATF trace data; Trinidad Guardian, “TTPS appraisal: Homicides, serious crime down” (4 October 2026), citing the TTPS Third Quarter 2026 Public Performance Appraisal.

World.title: Uruguay Teacher Unions Win Both Elected Seats on National Public Schools Board
World.content:
RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only â every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesCost of living, safety, visas across Latin America › RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. × Best for expats Cost of living Safest places Easy visas Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

EDUCATION · URUGUAY

Key Facts — The country Uruguay runs its public schools through ANEP, the National Public Education Administration. Two of the five seats on its governing council, the Codicen, are elected directly by teachers.

— What happened In the vote on Saturday 3 October 2026, union-backed lists won both seats. The tally was 27,768 votes to 7,109 (Electoral Court primary count, 4 October).

— The numbers 45,660 of 50,782 eligible teachers voted, about 90 percent. Blank ballots fell to 6,163 from 10,570 in 2021; annulled ballots rose to 4,613 from 2,039 (Electoral Court, 4 October).

— What it means for you Uruguay teacher unions keep a formal voice on the body that sets public school policy for the next five years. The three government appointees still hold the majority.

— Still open The figures are from the primary count, not a final proclamation. The new councillors take their seats in February, La Diaria reported; the reason for the jump in annulled ballots is unconfirmed.

Uruguay teacher unions won both elected seats on the board that runs the country’s public schools on Saturday 3 October. Their lists took 27,768 votes against 7,109 for the only rival banner, according to the Electoral Court’s primary count.

Pablo Macedo and Limber Santos will sit for teachers on the Codicen, the governing council of ANEP, the National Public Education Administration. They replace Julián Mazzoni and Daysi Iglesias, who also ran with union backing.

How the vote broke down

Five lists ran under two banners, known in Uruguay as lemas. The union banner, “In Defence of Public Education”, grouped the lists of the CSEU, the education federation of the PIT-CNT, Uruguay’s national union confederation.

List 11, headed by Macedo and promoted by the secondary teachers’ union Fenapes, came first with 11,792 votes. List 22, led by Santos, a primary school teacher, took 8,438.

List 30, headed by Marcos Correa and Andrea Touzet, added 6,745, so the union lists filled the top three places. Under the rival banner, list 3 won 3,743 votes and list 1 won 3,159.

Votes per list in the election of two teacher representatives to Uruguay's Codicen on 3 October 2026; lists 11, 22 and 30 ran under the union banner. Source: Corte Electoral primary count, via Montevideo Portal and Uypress, 4 Oct 2026.

Turnout was about 90 percent: 45,660 of 50,782 eligible teachers voted across 171 polling circuits. The Electoral Court also counted 6,163 blank and 4,613 annulled ballots.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Uruguay Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What each side campaigned on

Union candidates promised more support for classroom teachers and backed UNED, a planned national university of education, La Diaria reported. Santos also pledged more channels to make teachers’ daily work visible.

The rival banner, “Teaching Commitment, Educational Future”, opposed the UNED project. List 1, headed by Víctor Pizzichillo, a former president of the teacher training council, criticised what it called “legal uncertainty” inside ANEP.

That list named five priorities, including better learning results, higher status for teachers and decentralisation, Diario La R reported. List 3, from the Alternativa Docente group, focused on teachers’ mental health and inclusive education.

Why the two seats matter

The Codicen has five members. Three are appointed by the executive with Senate approval, and two are elected by teachers.

The elected pair cannot outvote the government appointees on their own. They do give organised teachers a formal place where national school policy is set, for a five-year term.

ANEP president Pablo Caggiani congratulated Macedo and Santos and called the vote a “very important” space for participation. He stressed that it was a secret ballot organised by the Electoral Court.

The result adds to a busy season for organised labour in Uruguay. In parliament, a Colorado Party bill seeks seven working days’ notice for strikes.

A wider margin, and more spoiled ballots

The union lead has widened since 2021, when its lists won almost 25,000 votes against about 8,600, La Diaria reported. Blank ballots also fell, from 10,570 five years ago to 6,163.

Annulled ballots, however, more than doubled from 2,039. El Observador linked part of the rise to a campaign among teachers urging colleagues to put their own slip in the envelope.

Blank and annulled ballots together made up nearly a quarter of the votes cast. That points to a sizeable minority of teachers who backed neither banner.

What Is Not Yet Known

The results reported on Sunday come from the Electoral Court’s primary count, not a final proclamation. Macedo and Santos take their seats in February, La Diaria reported, and candidates framed their programmes for 2027 to 2032.

There is no breakdown of how many of the 4,613 annulled ballots came from the campaign El Observador described. How the new pair will work with the three government appointees on UNED remains to be seen.

Sources: Electoral Court (Corte Electoral) primary count, as reported on 4 October 2026 by El Observador, La Diaria, Montevideo Portal, El País and Uypress; campaign positions from La Diaria (union candidates, List 1, List 3) and Diario La R.
