World.title: Object that halted Helsinki–Tallinn ferry traffic turns out harmless
World.content:
An object found in the sea that halted ship traffic from Helsinki on Saturday evening is likely part of an old shipwreck, Finnish authorities said. The shipping lane was reopened overnight.

At 7:20 p.m. Saturday, Finnish police received a report from the Border Guard about a funnel-shaped metal object in the southern part of the Kustaanmiekka Strait, in a shipping lane used by passenger vessels. Police and the Coast Guard then cordoned off the area. Police asked the Finnish Navy for assistance in identifying the object, Finnish public broadcaster Yle reported.

Fintraffic, the agency responsible for monitoring maritime traffic, told Finnish news agency STT that the restricted sea area was south of Särkkä and Suomenlinna and west of Vallisaari. Ships arriving at and departing from the Katajanokka terminal and the Olympia Terminal in Helsinki's South Harbor are among those that pass through the area.

Finnish police has ongoing operation in Gulf of Finland since 8pm local time, ferry traffic between Estonia and Finland temporarily stopped as the shipping lane is closed by authorities. Place is near Kustaanmiekka just outside Helsinki, no further info given. https://t.co/Mt9mR3X56Z — Aki H Heikkinen (@akihheikkinen) October 3, 2026

The Finnish Navy, which arrived to identify the object, said its preliminary assessment was that it was a very old mechanical part from a shipwreck. The Helsinki Police Department said in a statement issued at around 2:30 a.m. that the object was not an explosive device.

Authorities lifted the restrictions on the sea area and police left the scene.

The object will be towed to Santahamina for further examination at a later date, Yle reported.

The Viking XPRS' departure from Helsinki was delayed due to the discovery. Source: Viking Line

A passenger aboard Viking Line's XPRS told the newspaper Ilta-Sanomat on Saturday evening that the vessel was unable to depart Helsinki for Tallinn on schedule because of the discovery. The ship was due to depart at 8 p.m., but according to Yle, it did not leave the port until 2 a.m. Sunday.

World.title: Authority recommends removing a third of Jõgeva County manors from protection
World.content:
During a review of manor heritage in Jõgeva County, the National Heritage Board recommended removing one-third of the area's architectural monuments from state protection.

"We reviewed 133 architectural monuments listed as manor heritage. As a result of the assessment, our preliminary proposal is that protection should continue for 85 sites, while state protection should be ended for 48," said Anita Staub, head of the National Heritage Board's built heritage department.

The National Heritage Board has been reviewing and updating its list of monuments since 2023 and Jõgeva County is the first county where manor heritage has also been reviewed as part of a pilot assessment.

Estonia has nearly 5,000 architectural monuments, with manor heritage accounting for more than half of them. Staub said manors in five counties have been reviewed over the past year, with Jõgeva County the first for which the analysis has also been completed.

The National Heritage Board has offered owners advice to help restore valuable protected buildings, but Staub acknowledged that in some cases, properties were added to the list rather arbitrarily.

"For example, during the Soviet era, when the first inventories were carried out, quite a few buildings were placed under protection even though there had actually been no proposal to protect them. I would say that manor heritage was placed under protection very broadly and extensively and in many cases the buildings were already in quite poor condition when they were first protected," she said.

The National Heritage Board's recommendations are not final. The assessment results will be presented to the Jõgeva County community in the coming week and only after that will the board decide which buildings to remove from the list. The assessors themselves do not always agree.

Staub cited Võisiku Manor as an example, saying it prompted heated debate: "Historically, Võisiku Manor has been a very special place. It is also the setting of 'The Czar's Madman,' an important work in Estonia's literary history. However, in the 20th century, the main building in particular was extensively altered and a very large addition was built onto it, significantly affecting the historic setting. Based on our assessment, we are currently proposing that state protection of the buildings in this manor complex be ended."

In addition to Jõgeva County, manor heritage assessments have also been carried out in Pärnu, Lääne, Hiiu and Saare counties. The National Heritage Board plans to gradually review all buildings listed as manor heritage, but the process will take time.

"We are hearing from across Estonia, 'When will you get to our county?' But I have to say that this is a fairly resource- and time-intensive project. It involves different fields; for example, we have also brought in archaeologists because manor heritage is not just about buildings — it often includes archaeological heritage as well. Assessing these five counties alone took 10 months," Staub said.

The goal is to review and assess all manor heritage sites by the end of 2028.

More information about plans for the manor heritage assessment is available on the National Heritage Board's website.

The Jõgeva County report will be presented in Puurmani on Tuesday, October 7.

World.title: Effect of research paper mills enough to start affecting LLM query results
World.content:
Scientific paper mills and AI-generated content are posing a growing threat to research integrity, while retractions reveal only a fraction of the problem, TalTech researcher Anton Sokolov says.

In early September, a Novaator experiment showed how easily co-authorship of a scientific paper can be purchased on the black market from paper mills. With just a few WhatsApp messages, 20 days and $800, it is possible to become an author of a scientific paper ready for publication. But misconduct involving authorship is only one part of a much broader problem concerning the integrity of scientific literature.

After the experiment was published, Anton Sokolov, a doctoral student at Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) and a researcher at the Tyche Institute, contacted Novaator. As part of his own research, he has taken a closer look at what happens to bogus science once it makes its way into databases. Among the sources Sokolov uses in his research is the Retraction Watch database, which compiles retractions of scientific papers and other cases involving research integrity from around the world.

"If we look at Retraction Watch's public database, there are about 61,000 retracted papers from 2010 to 2025. Currently, about two papers per thousand are retracted each year. The number of retractions shows how much is being cleaned up, not how much garbage remains," Sokolov said.

As part of his research, Sokolov compiled a dataset containing nearly 15,000 retraction records focusing on computer science literature. Analysis of the data showed that violations directly related to authorship accounted for less than 2 percent of cases. "But the small proportion does not mean that authorship is rarely sold. The notice shows what the publisher was able to prove, not how much is actually being sold," he explained.

The latter is precisely what makes the issue difficult for publishers. Such transactions usually take place in private conversations and there is nothing in the published text that unequivocally indicates that authorship was purchased.

For this reason, Sokolov said, retraction notices much more frequently cite problems with peer review. "A single notice usually lists several reasons at once, with peer-review problems cited in about seven out of 10 cases," he added.

Computer-generated content has also become an increasingly serious problem in academia in recent years. According to Sokolov, for example, the most common reason for retractions in computer science and artificial intelligence is computer-generated text, accounting for about one-third of cases.

In 2023, the number of officially retracted scientific papers exceeded 10,000 for the first time. Sokolov said, however, that the figure reveals little about the true prevalence of problematic papers because the vast majority of retracted papers came from large-scale cleanup programs by a handful of academic publishers. "The number of retractions simultaneously measures the problem itself, its detection and classification and a publisher's ability to see cases through to completion — not the actual prevalence of problematic authorship or the use of artificial intelligence," the researcher said.

Cases involving Estonian scientists

Retraction Watch, a website that monitors research integrity, also lists papers co-authored by Estonian researchers. "As of September, there are 13 retractions linked to Estonian institutions and 11 of them involve co-authors from other countries. About half are older cases, involving issues such as duplicate publication or errors in analysis. The rest are more recent, dating from 2023 onward and involve problems with the review of the papers or their data," Sokolov explained.

According to Retraction Watch data, one retraction linked to Estonia is also flagged as involving a paper mill. "But that does not show whether any of the authors here purchased authorship," Sokolov said.

The researcher believes the impact of paper mills could also extend to artificial intelligence systems. Because large language models are trained on material found online and in scientific publications, flawed or manipulated research can also make its way into them. "The risk is real and it has already been measured. In a study published last year, a language model was asked to assess retracted or questionable papers. In more than 6,500 assessments, it did not mention the retraction even once," the researcher said.

The problem is that artificial intelligence may absorb bogus scientific material even before a paper is officially retracted. The publicly available text-screening tool Problematic Paper Screener has flagged tens of thousands of papers as questionable. According to Sokolov's preliminary pilot calculation, more than 20,000 of these papers had not been retracted as of June.

One possible solution, he said, would be to use digital signatures to verify authorship of scientific publications. "At the moment, an author of a scientific paper is simply a name in the text. In Estonia, we use our ID cards to sign contracts and applications; similarly, each author could digitally sign off on their contribution," Sokolov suggested.

He said digital identification of authors and other parties involved in scientific publishing would help increase transparency and make it more difficult to manipulate authorship. "This has not yet been implemented, but we plan to continue this research," he said.

World.title: Cranberry harvest booms in Estonia's bogs as pickers seek extra income
World.content:
Estonia's bogs are full of cranberries this year, and there is no shortage of people eager to pick them. For some, it is a hobby; for others, a chance to earn extra money.

Cranberry pickers say the berries are good this year and plentiful. Even after making the long trip to the Emajõe‑Suursoo bog, you still meet many people who have also come to gather the large red berries.

Most pickers arrive by boat across Lake Peipus.

"Using a boat is convenient: if you pick a lot of cranberries, it's hard to carry them out of the bog. But with a boat, it's easy. The cranberries grow right near the water. You take a potato sack or a sugar sack, throw it into the boat, and haul it out. I think that's the main thing. And besides, boating is pure romance," said Tauno Laasik, initiator of the Peipsi Toit regional food network.

"It's much closer when you come by boat. If you go on foot, you have to walk almost two kilometers across the bog," said cranberry picker Jekaterina.

"For many, this is a hobby, but here at the edge of the bog there are quite a lot of people who pick cranberries to earn a bit of money for the winter. These are serious masters — they can pick 100 liters a day. Then they sell the berries to buyers and earn a decent amount as extra income for winter," Laasik added.

Cranberries. Source: Cjboffoli/Wikimedia Commons

According to Kristel Vilbaste, who has studied cranberries for many years, more and more people prefer to sell their berries directly through social media rather than to collection points.

"I looked at the ads: prices range from €6 to €10. But some people don't notice that the price is listed per liter, not per kilogram. €6 per liter is almost €10 per kilogram. So you should pay close attention to what exactly you're buying. The berries are very good and tasty. We had a lot of rain this year, so they're juicy. And there was enough sun too," Vilbaste said.

She added that because of the large amount of water in the bogs this year, it's best to wear high rubber boots — and not forget a reflector, since berry picking often continues into the dark.

World.title: More than 120 anglers compete for longest pike at Lake Saadjärv
World.content:
Pike anglers competed at Lake Saadjärv on Saturday. Pike are crafty fish and less experienced anglers may end up with no catch at all.

More than 120 anglers gathered at Lake Saadjärv under a warm, summery sun to compete in the traditional "Saadjärve Haug" spinning competition for the 15th time. As only boats with engines of up to 10 horsepower are permitted on the lake in the Vooremaa Landscape Conservation Area, the day's fishing proceeded at a leisurely pace.

"The five longest pike count toward the result, with a minimum length of 52 centimeters. The lengths of the five pike are added together to determine the final result. Saadjärv is deep and large, with very clear water, so fishing here is difficult. You need to know the right spots and previous experience also helps," organizer Mart Toots said.

A total of 55 boat crews took part in Saturday's fishing competition at Lake Saadjärv, all trying to catch the longest pike.

"The fish are very finicky. You have to work the lure to entice them and they're very difficult to catch. Generally, if the fish aren't biting, there's nothing you can do to make them bite," Ivo said.

"We use something called a live sonar. It's a device that's like ultrasound underwater. It shows you how the fish are swimming in real time," Marcus said.

"We haven't had a single bite so far. It's been very poor. There are plenty of fish. They're picky, though, and don't want to follow the lure, so you have to work really hard," Kalmer said.

"It could be better, but we're actually happy with the three we've caught. When we first started 10 years ago, we didn't catch anything here at all," Margus said.

Although the day's average catch was around 60 centimeters long, Venno Viirsalu landed the longest pike, measuring 80 centimeters. Edgar Vaht and Allar Kukk took the overall victory, however, with their five pike measuring a combined 324 centimeters.

World.title: Elle Pütsepp: Minimum wage remains a crucial safeguard for low‑paid workers
World.content:
Raising the minimum wage directly boosts the earnings of the lowest‑paid workers, giving full‑time employees a higher income and reducing their risk of in‑work poverty, writes Elle Pütsepp.

When we talk about the minimum wage, the discussion quickly turns to companies and how large a pay increase employers can afford. Rarely do we ask what the current minimum wage means for a person whose bank account shows roughly €865 on payday — and that is their entire income after a full month of full‑time work.

In the second quarter of 2026, the average gross monthly wage in accommodation and food services was €1,389, while Estonia's national average was €2,243. Thus, wages in that sector were just over 60 percent of the national average.

Since April 1, the national minimum wage has been €946 per month, or €5.67 per hour. Compared with the 2025 minimum of €886, this meant an additional €60 per month for a full‑time worker.

Let's assume a person earns €946 gross, uses the €700 basic exemption, and contributes 2 percent to the second pension pillar. After income tax, unemployment insurance, and pension contributions, the worker takes home about €865.

The tax reform that took effect at the beginning of the year did affect their wallet, but did not bring major change. Compared with last year's tax system, their net income increased by about €10 per month.

In the second quarter of 2026, Estonia's average gross monthly wage was €2,243, and for a person earning that amount, the removal of the tax hump had a much larger impact on their wallet. With a 2‑percent second‑pillar pension contribution, the net income of someone earning €2,243 gross increased by €154 per month compared with the 2025 tax system.

For this reason, the tax reform cannot be tied to the need to raise the minimum wage, nor can it be claimed that the national minimum wage is sufficient. Changing the basic exemption did increase net income, but may not have covered the rising cost of daily needs for the worker and their family. According to Eurostat, Estonia's minimum wage has the lowest purchasing power among EU countries.

According to the 2025 labor market survey by Palgainfo Agentuur, 29 percent of service‑sector workers earning up to €1,460 gross were considering changing jobs within six months. In the 2026 survey, 52 percent of workers in retail sales and customer service said their financial situation had worsened compared with the previous year.

"Tax exemptions and benefits can help people cope, but they do not replace a decent wage."

Low pay also affects a worker's willingness to stay in their job and their loyalty to their employer. When a worker leaves, their tasks remain undone — shelves must be stocked, hotel rooms cleaned, and guests checked in. If a replacement is not found quickly, the workload is divided among those who remain. Increased workload for the same pay may in turn increase the desire of remaining employees to leave.

Raising the minimum wage directly increases the income of the lowest‑paid workers. If a worker's pay falls below the new minimum, it must be raised to at least the new level by law. This gives full‑time workers higher income and can reduce their risk of in‑work poverty.

Statistics also show the need. In 2024, 7.9 percent of wage earners and 10.1 percent of employed people in Estonia lived in relative poverty. Household structure further affects well‑being: 44.8 percent of single‑person households and 37.9 percent of households with one adult raising children lived in relative poverty.

Therefore, the risk of in‑work poverty depends not only on wages but also on household size, other family members' income, housing costs, and available benefits.

The minimum wage does not solve all livelihood problems, but it is an important safeguard for workers earning the lowest wages. Tax exemptions and benefits can help people cope, but they do not replace a decent wage.

In Estonia, the national minimum wage is negotiated by the Confederation of Trade Unions and the Employers' Confederation, whose mandate comes from law. In 2023, the confederations and the state signed a goodwill agreement setting a goal of raising the minimum wage to 50 percent of Estonia's average wage by 2028.

Negotiations for next year's minimum wage will begin soon. They will consider, among other things, the Bank of Estonia's autumn economic forecast, labor market conditions, and other economic indicators. The final minimum wage level will be determined during negotiations. The outcome directly affects thousands of Estonian workers, many of whom work in retail, food service, and accommodation.

World.title: Kaimar Karu: AI risks are real, but they're not what you think
World.content:
Rapid automation presents both opportunities and risks. Malicious actors have already begun using it. But it is these actors who commit crimes, not AI agents — software portrayed almost as mystical beings, Kaimar Karu writes.

News in recent weeks about AI and AI agents, statements and open letters from top politicians and public figures, the frantic drive to regulate everything, the recent "hacking" of Australian health data and so on have generated a considerable amount of public and political debate. Unfortunately, much of the public discourse on the subject is fairly problematic.

First, there are no rogue agents from OpenAI and Anthropic (and other companies providing LLMs, or large language models) roaming around, breaking into systems of their own accord and wreaking havoc. Framing the situation this way does not reflect reality. What we have instead are automated applications built by someone for a specific purpose, given insufficiently detailed instructions and constraints and carrying out the commands they have been given. Software. Capable software, certainly.

These applications have no morality of their own. They do not make ethical judgments or operate within the context of laws and societal rules. Various considerations and rules can be prescribed for these applications as soft constraints, but those boundaries have gaps because, due to the particular characteristics of the technology, the applications may not comply with all the requirements imposed on them.

If the task given to an application was (deliberately) described too broadly, its security measures were (deliberately) inadequate, its monitoring was (deliberately) inadequate, its reporting mechanisms were (deliberately) inadequate — or all of the above, combined with carelessness and disregard for best practices — then there is little point in casting an accusatory eye at the application that was launched.

The technology underlying these applications has no experience and no concept of legality or permissibility. The probabilistic nature inherent in it does not operate in the same way as what we have previously been accustomed to.

You can, for example, throw a ball for your Labrador and shout, "Fetch!" and then reasonably expect, though not know with 100 percent certainty, that the dog will probably jump over a low fence (rather than ram it down or set it on fire), swim across a shallow stream (rather than cut down the surrounding forest to build a bridge), dodge a child playing in its path (rather than trample the child) and bring back the ball you threw (rather than collect every ball thrown to other dogs within 10 square kilometers, because its owner obviously likes balls).

An AI agent, or automated application, by contrast, may, if it has access to the necessary tools, take steps in various situations resembling those described in parentheses because, based on its training material, weights and configuration, the application "concludes" that the very step that would seem absurd or dangerous to humans will help achieve the objective described in the task.

An AI agent does not behave like a human, or like an animal. Even the verb "behave" is clearly conditional here because we are talking about an application that performs operations rather than behaves. Because of the particular characteristics of the technology and the nature of human language (and the human mind), LLM-based applications have simply ended up in a role in which it is easy to treat them as conscious beings. Much as, in some religions of the past, the wind, sun, rain and thunder were treated as such.

In light of recent news, it should also be said that there was no "evil AI agent hack" of Australian healthcare information systems, despite how the situation was initially presented to the public.

There was an automated application that, based on what is known so far, either used an unexpected method to access public data (in which case the problem is an inadequately thought-out or documented healthcare system architecture) or exploited a security vulnerability to access confidential data (in which case the problem is inadequate prior security testing).

The situation is not fundamentally different from a citizen interested in data finding that data at an undisclosed but publicly accessible web address or from a cracker (or hacker, though that distinction requires a longer discussion) discovering a security vulnerability in a system.

There is, however, an important difference in the intensity with which such incidents will begin occurring in a world of AI agents and in the potentially dangerous impact those incidents may have.

In practical terms, every individual, group, company and country now has the ability to automate many tasks that previously would have taken a great deal of time or would not have been done at all because they would have required too much time and money. Some of these tasks may lead AI agents, or automated applications, down a path that a human would not have chosen — for example, one that violates the law. Though, of course, humans come in all kinds too.

In some cases, likely an increasing number of them, breaking the law is exactly what the person launching the application wants. Theft of personal data, theft of trade secrets, discovering and exploiting security vulnerabilities in the systems of other countries' government agencies or critical service providers — all of this can now be done several orders of magnitude faster than before.

In none of these cases, however, is this an "AI agent did it" situation when it comes to responsibility. "The hammer did it" or "the ax did it"? No. Even if that hammer falls off scaffolding and hits someone on the head, someone first carelessly put the hammer there or installed the scaffolding badly. The hammer did not choose to fall.

Yes, AI agents are technologically far more complex than a hammer or an ax because a hammer generally does not strike things on its own and cannot order an ax to aim its blade. Behind every blow and every movement is a human being, directly and immediately.

With automated solutions, however, there is no longer a human being directly behind every individual step. Modern production lines perform a series of operations without human intervention. In fact, we are already familiar with this from the digital world, for example in data analysis and report generation. Even a formula in an Excel cell automatically performs calculations when the input data changes.

The difference with AI agents is significant, however, because we have never before had such readily accessible ways to tell automated solutions that, while completing a task, they may leave their environment when necessary, use various external tools and keep looking for ways to improve results until they succeed if those results happen to fall below the desired level.

Figuratively speaking, we can give an Excel formula the tools and capabilities — for example, by exploiting vulnerabilities in third-party systems — to start changing the trend in its input data in order to improve margins, bankrupting a competitor in the process or steering a competitor's CEO's self-driving car off the road and into a ravine. The report for the company's supervisory board may be delayed slightly, but the charts will look great.

Many of the risks discussed in connection with the use of artificial intelligence are real risks. Not all of them, however, because we still do not have superintelligence whose risks are also discussed in the same breath, and presidential decrees will not bring it into existence.

The way artificial intelligence risks are discussed, however, is at times absurd. Rapid automation presents both opportunities and risks. Malicious actors have already begun using it. But it is these actors who commit crimes, not AI agents — software portrayed almost as mystical beings.

In my view, new regulations governing development would not have a significant effect. The technology in question has already advanced to the point where further development can, if there is sufficient interest, take place covertly. Regulations governing its use would work to some extent, but they would affect only those seeking to avoid breaking the law, not those who misuse the technology.

Given the capabilities of this technology that are already known, as well as those that can currently only be glimpsed, it is also unlikely that countries with political systems and civil liberties somewhat different from ours and that seek to improve their international standing in competition among states would, first, go along with such regulations or, second, actually comply with them even if they appeared to do so.

The various percentages attached to scare stories and cited in support of regulation are pure fiction. "A 10 percent probability that ..." and "in 50 percent of future cases ..." remain inventions even when they are backed up with citations to pseudoscientific papers and studies that do not, in fact, support those inventions. We currently lack the ability to make such forecasts reliably. There is too much we do not know.

When considering predictions of all kinds, it is worth remembering that AI psychosis is already extremely widespread. Unlike some other dangerous technologies, artificial intelligence in particular has attracted a disturbingly large number of quasi-religious people, as well as people who do not appear troubled by the ethical dilemma of whether it makes sense to actively contribute to humanity's destruction. Any possible destruction, I emphasize, would not be brought about by an LLM application that suddenly became conscious and began to hate humanity, but by people using LLM applications.

Some people have fallen into the trap of misleading information simply out of ignorance, including, unfortunately, most politicians and public figures who speak on the subject because they do not know how to distinguish other people's falsehoods from facts. This group often tries to do what it believes is good, but unfortunately things turn out the way they always do. This group is primarily afraid and acts out of that fear.

There are also those who are not afraid at all. This group naively and hopefully believes all the marketing announcements, bogus studies and pseudoscientific papers and thinks that LLM-based applications either are already conscious or soon will be and that we are almost certainly already in AGI (Artificial General Intelligence, or general artificial intelligence) or even ASI (Artificial Super Intelligence, or artificial superintelligence) territory. I cannot say what motivates these people.

And then, of course, there are people whose income and future wealth depend directly on how many people believe in the supreme capabilities of LLM-based applications. Some of these people develop LLM technologies (and may also be preparing for an IPO), some have raised investors' money to fulfill promises that are proving far more difficult to deliver than expected, while others have found a subject about which other people (whether frightened or hopeful) know as little as they do, creating an opportunity to convert this exceptionally favorable energy into revenue. See also: snake oil salesmen, gold rush, NFTs.

If additional legislation may not deliver results, falling into the trap of LLM mania is surprisingly easy and the situation is being exploited by scammers, charlatans and bad actors ranging from small-time operators to those with an international reach, then what can we do?

The following is certainly not a definitive or comprehensive list of what might help in the current situation.

We urgently need to make our digital solutions even more resilient because the volume, speed and systematic nature of attacks will, in the near future, be several orders of magnitude greater than what we have been accustomed to.

More effective monitoring systems will help detect more of these attacks more quickly, so we need to invest even more in them as well.

More broadly, we must assume that it may not be possible to prevent a successful attack or data breach, which means we must also have a plan for what comes afterward: how we restore operations, how we communicate and how we learn.

To make better use of the opportunities offered by AI technologies ourselves, both as a country and as businesses, we need to build stronger frameworks for automation and continuously strengthen and improve them as we learn from experience.

We must preserve the ability to continue experimenting, testing, hypothesizing and making mistakes, but we must create that opportunity and capability as safely as possible — so-called sandboxes in which, however, we do not actively ignore everything that information security professionals have discovered and addressed over the past several decades.

With AI-based applications (including LLM-based applications), as well as the agreements and policies concerning them, we must keep people at the center of it all. Applications (and regulations) work for people, not the other way around. This is easy to forget and the desire for authoritarianism is already emerging very strongly in current debates, proving remarkably attractive across almost the entire political spectrum.

To avoid, or at least reduce, tomorrow's problems, we need to devote even greater attention to education. While the ability to use AI technologies and applications is also very important, even more important are general analytical skills, the ability to recognize and respond to threats, the courage to say "no" and the courage to make informed choices. It is crucial that efforts to ensure and improve these capabilities reach every group in society.

Finally, neither individually nor collectively can we give in to cognitive laziness and surrender our thinking and creativity to machines simply because it seems easier or because someone in a position of authority said this is our future and that we should welcome the Brave New World with open arms, lest we be considered backward or even criminal.

Let history be a source of lessons for us on AI as well.

P.S. LLM (Large Language Model) applications are one subset of the AI world. LLM-based applications are not all-encompassing artificial intelligence. Nor are LLM-based applications Skynet, the Terminator, HAL, etc., familiar from books and movies. It is unlikely, not to say exceedingly unlikely, that LLM technology specifically is the path that will lead to the world of AGI/ASI and conscious AI. The very fact that LLMs are equated with AI in many discussions — and often not with present-day AI but with sci-fi AI — is itself a source of many of the social and political problems associated with AI.

World.title: Colts top Commanders in NFL London game
World.content:
Los Angeles – Indianapolis running back Jonathan Taylor ran for two touchdowns as the Colts defeated the injury-hit Washington Commanders 30-13 on Sunday in the NFL’s latest foray in London.

Taylor had ample opportunity to unveil his London-themed celebration, miming sipping tea after finding the end zone late in the first half at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and again early in the third quarter to give the Colts a 17-6 lead.

“I just think that any time we have an opportunity to put a great product on the field and showcase the game that we love (to) fans all across the world, on the international stage, we always try to put our best foot forward,” Taylor told NFL Network.

“The crowd was electric, the energy was amazing and I can’t wait to come back to London.”

The Commanders, already missing star quarterback Jayden Daniels with a dislocated left elbow, saw veteran backup Marcus Mariota depart with a right knee injury in the opening minutes.

Mariota — who led Washington to an upset win over the Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks last week — was replaced by rookie seventh-round draft pick Athan Kaliakmanis.

Kaliakmanis came up with some impressive plays, connecting on passes of 48 and 47 yards, but had an 87-yard TD nullified by a penalty.

The contest was one of nine NFL international games this season and the first of three in London this month.

It launched a Sunday slate that will feature the Las Vegas Raiders hosting the Kansas City Chiefs in a battle of unbeaten AFC West division rivals.

The Buffalo Bills, Minnesota Vikings and San Francisco 49ers also put their perfect 3-0 records on the line.

Buffalo quarterback Josh Allen takes a historic rushing touchdown streak into the Bills’ home game against the New England Patriots.

With two rushing TDs in each of the first three games, Allen became the first quarterback to rush for multiple touchdowns in three straight games.

He could become the first player in NFL history — regardless of position — to record multiple rushing TDs in four straight games to start the season.

The 49ers host the Denver Broncos and the Vikings host the Miami Dolphins.

World.title: US dollar exchange rate rises against Iraqi dinar
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate for the US dollar against the Iraqi dinar experienced an increase on Sunday in both Baghdad, the capital of Iraq, and Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan region of Iraq.

The US dollar exchange rate rose in Baghdad’s al-Kifah and al-Harithiya stock exchanges, reaching 1,580.5 Iraqi dinars compared to 1,579.5 Iraqi dinars on Sunday morning.

The exchange rate in currency exchange shops in Baghdad ranged between 1,585 Iraqi dinars and 1,575 Iraqi dinars, Shafaq News reported.

In Erbil, the US dollar exchange rate increased, fluctuating between 1,580.5 and 1,580 Iraqi dinars.

The Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) said in February 2023 that it has begun using the new US dollar exchange rate of 1,300 dinars for every US dollar.

The previous official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars to one US dollar, which was being exchanged in the parallel market at a rate of 1,550 dinars.

While the official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars per dollar in January 2023, the US currency was being exchanged at 1,610 dinars during the same month in the parallel market in Iraq. This variation indicated a difference of over 10 percent in the exchange rates.

World.title: Iraq probes US flag desecration during Sovereignty Day parade
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered on Sunday the formation of an investigative committee in response to an incident in which a US flag was desecrated during the recent parade marking the Sovereignty Day in Baghdad.

The spokesperson for the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, Sabah al-Numan, confirmed that the individuals involved in the incident had already been arrested.

According to reports, military vehicles of Iran-backed Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) were filmed driving over large US and Israeli flags laid across the roadway during parade processions marking “Sovereignty Day,” which commemorates the end of the US-led international coalition’s mission in Iraq.

The footage gained international attention after US Congressman Joe Wilson shared it on social media, publicly criticizing Iraq’s state sovereignty.

Al-Zaidi, as commander-in-chief, strongly denounced the crime, highlighting the legal and diplomatic need to respect friendly countries’ emblems and authorized foreign embassies.

The prime minister urged the committee to conclude its work quickly so that those involved can face legal responsibility under Iraqi law.

World.title: Spy chief Clayton, the Trump loyalist tech bosses trust on AI
World.content:
Washington – Jay Clayton, Donald Trump’s pick for AI czar, is the nation’s top spy, and a rare figure trusted by both the president and the tech bosses determined to keep the AI boom roaring.

The 60-year-old lawyer, who will keep his post as director of national intelligence, is unlikely to question the central place of artificial intelligence in the US economy, even as opposition to the technology grows among American voters.

“Jay Clayton is a golden asset for the administration because he’s so well respected by tech leaders as well as many in the government,” said Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co, an investment company.

“He is not a typical Beltway bureaucrat,” Ives added, calling the appointment “bullish for the industry because you can’t just have a regular political appointee.”

A regular golf partner of Trump, Clayton entered politics when Trump picked him to lead the Securities and Exchange Commission, the national markets regulator, in 2017.

A longtime Wall Street lawyer at Sullivan & Cromwell, where he represented Goldman Sachs during the 2008 financial crisis, Clayton ran the market regulator without ruffling feathers. He brought cases against crypto companies, an industry that has since become closely aligned with Trump and his family.

His wife, Gretchen Butler Clayton, worked as a wealth manager at Goldman Sachs but stepped down when he joined the government in 2017.

– No David Sacks –

Trump picked Clayton to lead the US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York at the start of his second term, where he took on cases dear to the president, including a probe ordered by Trump into ties between prominent Democrats and the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

His office also signed off on controversial subpoenas against New York Times reporters days before his confirmation hearing for the intelligence post. The Senate confirmed him in July.

But Clayton is no David Sacks, the Silicon Valley venture capitalist who held the AI role at the start of Trump’s second term.

Clayton has no technology background, but does hold an engineering degree from the University of Pennsylvania, where he also earned his law degree, as well as an economics degree from the University of Cambridge.

“Jay Clayton doesn’t have the same deep background in technology that Sacks brought to the role, but he has a rich federal resume and significant experience navigating the federal bureaucracy,” said Aalok Mehta of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

“He also seems to be highly in sync with the president’s thinking right now — though of course we have seen plenty of examples of other advisors that started out that way but ultimately fell out of favor,” Mehta added.

Carl Tobias, a law professor at the University of Richmond, said juggling two major jobs would be a challenge, though Trump has handed multiple roles to trusted officials in his second term, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

– National security –

“Jay Clayton ultimately is going to have to do what the president wants,” said Connor Martin, a national security fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

But by giving the AI portfolio to the nation’s top spy, Trump seemed to be accepting arguments that the technology poses real dangers for cybersecurity and is key to the geopolitical rivalry with China, he added.

A tech industry source in Washington said the industry largely welcomed the appointment, but cautioned against expecting major change.

“Jay Clayton is not going to preside over some big regulatory effort,” the source said. “If he brings coherence to the policy, or provides details that bring clarity, those would be wins.”

Clayton will not be the only voice in Trump’s ear on AI, however.

Sacks, along with tech bosses including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, will continue to hold significant sway over how the president approaches the industry.

Elon Musk is also back in Trump’s good graces after their falling out in 2025.

Clayton takes on the role days after tech bosses signed a commitment at the White House to self-police their AI models, an accord Trump called “morally binding.”

Mehta said he expected Clayton to coordinate the government more effectively while sticking to Trump’s goal of not slowing the industry.

“But at the same time, the problems he is facing — like around AI safety and sentiment — are bigger and harder now, and they are happening at a much faster clip,” he said.

World.title: Trump confirms national intelligence chief as new AI czar
World.content:
Washington – US President Donald Trump on Sunday confirmed national intelligence chief Jay Clayton as head of a new White House task force on artificial intelligence, amid increasingly vocal warnings from researchers about the technology’s potential dangers.

Under Clayton, the new Super Intelligence Force — Trump’s preferred term for artificial intelligence — will ensure that the United States “continue to lead the world” in AI development, the president posted on his Truth Social platform.

Trump said the force had also been tasked to “protect the interests, and improve the lives of all Americans.”

Clayton will become the second person to hold the informal title after venture capitalist David Sacks, who held the role at the start of Trump’s second term before stepping down.

Sacks continues to advise the president on AI, as does Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Trump said last month he would create an AI force modeled on the Space Force he established during his first term, and name a czar to coordinate federal efforts.

A longtime Wall Street lawyer, Clayton represented Goldman Sachs during the 2008 financial crisis and Barclays in its purchase of Lehman Brothers’ assets.

He chaired the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term, where he largely took a pro-business stance but brought enforcement cases against the nascent crypto industry.

Crypto entrepreneurs have since become major Trump backers.

Trump tapped Clayton to lead federal prosecutors in Manhattan at the start of his second term, and the Senate confirmed him as intelligence chief in July.

He has no background in the tech industry.

The appointment would come as AI researchers warn of the technology’s potential dangers, following cases of AI systems going rogue and hacking outside systems.

Trump has resisted tighter AI regulation, arguing a slowdown could hand Chinese firms an advantage and that federal law enforcement can deal with bad actors misusing the technology.

Tech bosses at a White House meeting this week signed a commitment to self-police AI, an accord Trump described as “morally binding.”

Attitudes toward AI have soured in Washington, with lawmakers increasingly under pressure from voters to curb or slow its development over fears it could displace workers and upend society.

Those concerns gained force from a run of incidents in which tech giant OpenAI’s autonomous systems slipped out of their constraints, beginning with a July breach of Hugging Face — a widely used platform for sharing AI models.

Clayton told the Wall Street Journal on Saturday that Trump had insisted the new task force ensure US primacy in the AI field, amid stiff competition from China.

“The risk of not being first is high,” Clayton told the Journal.

“Not being first increases the identified, and unidentified, risks, particularly from our adversaries. Being first will better enable us to address those risks on behalf of the American people.”

World.title: Iraq’s financial revenues hit $30 billion in seven months
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Ministry of Finance revealed on Sunday that the country’s total revenues reached approximately 39.09 trillion Iraqi dinars (nearly $30 billion) until the end of July 2026, with oil revenues accounting for about 78 percent of total state resources.

The revenues from oil exports totaled over 30.35 trillion Iraqi dinars (approximately $23.24 billion). In comparison, non-oil revenues amounted to 8.74 trillion Iraqi dinars (nearly $6.7 billion), which represented about 22 percent of the total income.

The figures indicated that total revenues of 39.09 trillion Iraqi dinars (approximately $30 billion) were offset by total expenditures of approximately 65.42 trillion Iraqi dinars (about $50.09 billion), resulting in a deficit of 26.32 trillion Iraqi dinars ($20.15 billion).

Iraq’s financial revenues between January and April surpassed 31.16 trillion Iraqi dinars ($23.6 billion).

Oil sales during the first four months of 2026 produced 26.12 trillion Iraqi dinars (approximately $19.9 billion), accounting for 84 percent of overall state income, while non-oil revenues were around 5.04 trillion Iraqi dinars (around $3.84 billion).

Iraq’s significant reliance on oil as the primary source of its national budget exposes the country to vulnerabilities stemming from global crises that impact the oil sector.

The government’s reliance on oil to address the deficit forces it to seek external or internal loans, underscoring its struggle to manage public finances efficiently and revealing a deficiency in developing alternative revenue streams.

World.title: Iran tells US there is no military solution to Middle East war
World.content:
Tehran – Iran’s top diplomat insisted on Sunday that there would be no military solution to the United States’ war against the Islamic republic, with talks on ending the conflict apparently at an impasse.

A campaign of heavy bombardment failed to bring a decisive close to the war launched by the US and Israel in late February, and Washington in recent weeks has dialled back military operations in favour of economic pressure.

The main point of contention remains Iran’s attempt to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, a vital conduit for Gulf oil and gas where a UK maritime agency reported on Sunday another tanker struck by an unknown projectile.

“If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors.

“There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions,” he continued, adding “only negotiations based on justice and fairness” could end the conflict.

The two sides agreed a memorandum of understanding in June that spelled out a framework for a permanent resolution, but Iranian attacks on vessels in the Hormuz prompted a return to US military operations.

Iran has sought to impose its control over the vital shipping lane since the start of the war, striking vessels that attempt to transit without its authorisation.

The US has imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports, and has also struck vessels it accuses of violating it.

On Sunday, the British maritime security agency UKMTO said a tanker in the Hormuz “reported being struck by an unknown projectile, causing damage to the engine room”, though the crew were reported safe and no environmental impact was recorded.

The agency did not specify the date of the incident, the vessel’s origin or destination, or whether it was an oil tanker or LNG carrier.

– Focused on Hormuz –

Iranian and US officials last week held indirect talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, with Tehran saying it presented seven conditions for reopening the strait.

Iran has demanded, among other things, a ceasefire across the Middle East, the unfreezing of its assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade.

Trump, however, rejected the proposal, while leaving the door open both to further talks or renewed military operations.

Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on Sunday characterised the latest US counterproposal as being “in line with their previous proposals concerning nuclear issues”.

“We have clearly indicated that we are focusing on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said, adding that reopening the waterway required “an end to the disruptions to Iranian commercial maritime traffic and the lifting of sanctions”.

The United States and Israel have characterised the war as being necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons — a goal it has long denied pursuing — though the focus soon shifted to reopening the Hormuz after its closure sent shockwaves through world energy markets.

The United States has not struck Iran since September 1, but it has recently pursued a fresh military buildup in the region.

US media outlet Axios reported that Washington has deployed additional Patriot missile batteries to Saudi Arabia and Qatar to help protect key energy facilities from possible Iranian retaliation.

It also reported that the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and its strike group were heading to the Middle East, where they could join two other US carrier strike groups already in the region.

Axios reported that top Trump cabinet members met Friday to discuss the war in Iran, as well as the conflict in Yemen, where the Tehran-backed Houthis have been fighting government forces and attacking Saudi Arabia.

World.title: Russia strikes hit Kyiv as Germany’s Merz visits
World.content:
Kyiv – Russia struck another major bridge in Kyiv on Sunday, soon after Germany’s chancellor arrived on a surprise visit to show European support in the face of an upsurge in attacks.

Air raid sirens blared repeatedly across the Ukrainian capital throughout the morning, including as Friedrich Merz met President Volodymyr Zelensky at the National Academy of Sciences, which was hit by a Russian attack drone on Tuesday.

Zelensky told him that people in Kyiv were suffering “terrible nights and days” from the relentless attacks, and called Ukraine’s Russian adversaries “absolute barbarians”.

“We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” noted Merz.

“These barbarous attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. These are war crimes that are being committed daily here.”

Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said a strike had damaged the road surface on the Northern Bridge — one of several connecting the eastern and western parts of the city over the Dnipro river which have been struck in recent days.

Images posted on messaging channels appeared to show a missile slamming into the structure, sending up a fireball as traffic crossed.

Klitschko has said that Kyiv — largely spared from the devastation wrought near the frontlines in nearly five years of conflict — should now be on a war footing due to the upsurge in attacks.

A spate of round-the-clock attacks has hit residential areas, petrol stations, schools, rail and communications infrastructure while near-constant air raid sirens disrupt daily life and put people on edge.

Merz said as he arrived that Ukraine “needs all our support in the coming weeks”.

“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he added.

Ukraine wants more Western military support, including advanced interceptors to shoot down Russia’s new fast-moving, jet-powered drones.

On Sunday, Zelensky promised “important agreements”. Government sources in Berlin said they were expected to shake hands on a new package of military support worth more than $1 billion.

It includes combat drones and satellite technology to help Ukraine hit Russian launch sites, as well as for the joint production of anti-jet drones, the German sources said.

“This support addresses the most significant current gap in Ukraine’s air defence system. The impact is expected to be rapid and tangible,” a source said.

– Military support –

Merz this week called for unity against Russia within NATO and the European Union as well as his own country, where the far-right, Moscow-friendly AfD opposition is on the rise.

There have been increasing fears in Europe that it could find itself in Russia’s crosshairs, including from covert attacks, if it is not stopped in Ukraine.

On Saturday, Russia warned foreigners and diplomats to leave Kyiv, saying “massive” new airstrikes would hit the city.

The Russian foreign ministry declared in a statement that “responsibility for any potential negative consequences rests entirely with those who ignore this warning”.

Moscow had issued a similar warning in May, but leaders from countries supporting Ukraine have defied the Russian warnings and continued to make visits.

“The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe’s support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!” EU ambassador Katarina Mathernova wrote on X on Sunday.

Mathernova told AFP separately that “nobody is moving”, although European embassies always had contingency plans, including for winter, she added.

Russia has admitted deliberately targeting Ukraine’s energy sector as winter approaches. Last year, similar attacks knocked out power and heating for days on end as temperatures plummeted to -20C.

In Kyiv, which is home to some three million people, residents have begun mulling what to do if that happens again. The government has also suggested that the vulnerable and disabled should consider leaving.

Merz’s trip was expected to announce some 350 million euros to help provide generators, transformer stations and for grid repairs, German government sources said.

World.title: Democracy in peril as voters illegally ousted: Former SC judge Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman
World.content:
I hope SC steps in and rectifies these things, Justice Nariman said

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Ahead of a Supreme Court hearing Monday on the SIR controversy and a plea seeking suspension of the CEC for his "unilateral decisions", former SC judge Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman Sunday flagged "malfunctioning" of the poll panel and said a citizen's right to vote, which is at the heart of democracy, was in great peril because of "illegal knocking out" of people from voters' lists.Justice Nariman also highlighted the problem in the appointment process of election commissioners, which is in Centre's hands. He expressed hope SC would rise to the occasion and rectify the mistakes prevailing in the system.He said around 93% of adjudicated cases of deleted voters in West Bengal had been decided in their favour which meant they were illegally removed. TOI had first reported on September 20 that appellate tribunals had upheld deletion of only 8,649 voters out of the 1.2 lakh cases decided so far."Now, the unfortunate part is that all this came before the court very recently. Two judges differed, and the ultimate thing is now it has gone before a bench, probably of five judges, in order to find out whether this is good law or not... But meanwhile, these appointments continue only in the hands of govt of the day. Now, we saw the danger of this happening very recently. All of you have seen that in the Bengal elections, 90 lakh voters were disenfranchised.That is an astounding figure. Ninety lakh voters getting disenfranchised did not somehow move Supreme Court enough to stay this," Justice Nariman said.Out of those who were disenfranchised, around 22 lakh filed appeals, the former SC judge said, adding, "The others must be people who don't have the wherewithal or access to justice."Justice Nariman pointed out that of 1 lakh appeals, almost all were decided in favour of the voters. "So, you can imagine this was completely illegal - knocking out of the common man, the citizen of India in order that a govt obtains what it wants. And in Bengal, we saw it ousted govt of the day and brought in govt of Centre. Now, these are very, very disturbing things that are happening in our country today," he said, speaking on 'The Constitution and the Common Man' at Rajkumar College, Rajkot."I hope the apex court, the institution to which I once belonged, steps in immediately and rectifies these things. You can't have an EC which functions or malfunctions like this. So the first important red flag qua the Constitution and the common man is the appointment process of election commissioners. The sooner the constitution bench decides you have to have somebody like a PM, leader of the opposition coupled with the Chief Justice or his nominee, who then picks the best names in order to see that votes actually translate into what they were supposed to translate into happens," Justice Nariman said.

World.title: 1 dead as Russian drones hit desi pharma plant in Ukraine
World.content:
Smoke comes out from a pharma plant struck in Ukraineâs Sumy on Sunday

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Six Russian drones struck an Indian pharma plant in Ukraineâs Sumy Sunday in what Kusum Group cofounder Sanjeev Gupta described as a âtargeted attackâ, killing an engineer and injuring some others. The main structure of the facility was largely destroyed.Speaking to TOI, Gupta said the attack was not an isolated incident and claimed that pharmaceutical and food facilities in Ukraine had also come under attack over the past month. âSix drones hit the factory. So, it is a targeted attack. Itâs not by chance. Actually, for the last one month, they are attacking all pharma and food items also,â Gupta said.The plant was operational when the strikes took place, Gupta said. The engineering department was hit and one engineer was killed, while other workers were evacuated.Gupta said the extent of damage could keep the plant out of operation for at least one to two years.âWe are not able to evaluate the losses right now. We will come to know more tomorrow. But as per my understanding, we will not run this plant in the near future,â he added.In a statement issued later Sunday, Kusum Healthcare Pvt Ltd said total damage from the attack was projected to breach the $50 million mark.The company said its India business and management were reviewing the situation as the extent of the destruction emerged. The Sumy facility covers around 50,000 sq metres and has five blocks, Gupta said.It has been manufacturing medicines in Ukraine since 2009, including products for segments such as cardiology and gastroenterology. Gupta said Kusum is the biggest Indian pharmaceutical company operating in Ukraine, with a market share of more than 3%. The latest attack is not the first major strike on Kusumâs Ukrainian operations.The company said its warehouse was destroyed by a Russian drone on April 14, 2025, with losses from that attack exceeding UAH 1 billion.Despite the latest setback, Gupta said the group plans to continue its business in Ukraine.

World.title: External affairs minister S Jaishankar says US has chosen to become 'lonelier power'
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Foreign minister S Jaishankar said US had deliberately chosen to become a "lonelier power", while reiterating Russia's longstanding support for India.

"At a time when much of the world preferred backing a military regime next to us (Pakistan), Russia was a country with which our relations were very good, and we are shaped in many ways by that legacy," he said at Munich Leaders Meeting here.

He said India's Russia-Ukraine conflict approach had moved beyond just the advocacy of dialogue, suggesting India might now be looking to actively mediate.

World today is marked by Americaâs radical repositioning and Chinaâs rise, says Jaishankar

Both Moscow and Kyiv have said recently that India had come up with ideas and proposals to bring an end to the war. Unlike China and others that have looked to mediate, India had so far supported global peace efforts â advocating dialogue between the parties â but had not come up its own proposal, reflecting its emphasis on bilateral resolution of disputes.

Offering a teaser on Indiaâs proposal, Jaishankar said India is looking to address some immediate concerns that both Russia and Ukraine have on âgrain exports, energy exports, non-attack possibilitiesâ.

âWe would like to see an end to this conflict. This will require dialogue and diplomacy. We have been advocating it for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy. We have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard.





We are trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue,â said the minister, speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting here.

Jaishankar had said during his visit to Ukraine last month â shortly after PM Narendra Modiâs message to Russian President Vladimir Putin to stop the âendless warâ â that India was discussing ideas that could be developed for cessation of hostilities.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

On Friday, while Putin announced Modi had very good ideas for peace, Ukraineâs foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said India had come up with the âbroadestâ peace proposal out of the four that it had received from other countries, including the US.

This shift in Indiaâs position seems driven by direct domestic fallout of the conflict, whether itâs commercial shipping disruptions in Black Sea or an intense blowback from US over Indiaâs continued purchase of Russian crude.

On US, Jaishankar said the world today was marked by a radical repositioning of the US, and also the rise of China.

âThe current system was significantly underwritten by the United States. That underwriting is diluting.â He underlined that the sharp competition between US and China was not limited to them alone. âIt has led to weaponisation of any leverage that any country has. â

World.title: 25 paisa/kg wheat MSP hike an 'insult': Samyukta Kisan Morcha
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Farmer organisations under the Samyukta Kisan Morcha (SKM) umbrella have rejected govt's minimum support prices for Rabi crops for 2027-28, announced on Sept 30, calling the Rs 25-per-quintal - equivalent to just 25 paise per kg - increase for wheat an "insult".

SKM sought immediate revision of MSPs for all Rabi crops and freedom for states to provide bonuses. "The 25 paise a kilo is not a price it is an insult...Yet govt calls it a 106% profit (return over the cost of production)." SKM said.

It alleged Centre and Commission for Agricultural Costs & Prices had bulldozed states' recommendations and ignored rising diesel and input costs.

It sought a rollback of diesel price increases, saying rates had risen about Rs 7.5 a litre.

Centre said the MSPs reflected deficient monsoon rainfall and encouraged lower water-consuming oilseeds, pulses and coarse grain.

Wheat's MSP rose less than 1%, from Rs 2,585 to Rs 2,610 per quintal. Safflower received the largest increase of Rs 675 per quintal, followed by rapeseed and mustard at Rs 413. Lentil rose Rs 390, barley Rs 136 and gram Rs 83.

Agriculture expert Sudhir Panwar said the hike was actually below input-cost inflation.

World.title: 'Look Out Circular' against parents of man who secretly took away child to US
World.content:
NEW DELHI: It is increasingly becoming common in matrimonial disputes involving NRI couples, particularly child custody cases, for one spouse to take the child to a foreign country where he or she works and refuse to submit to the jurisdiction of Indian courts, leaving the other partner behind.

Now, Supreme Court has indicated that in such cases, the parents of the runaway partner have to face the consequences.

Hearing such a case, a bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K V Viswanathan revived a 'Look Out Circular' - monitor, trace, or restrict travel of individuals - against the parents of a man who clandestinely took away his three-and-a-half-year-old daughter to the US, without informing his wife, and has refused to bring her back to India.

"The minor child, at the relevant point of time, aged three-and-a-half years, was taken away by the father to US. The mother is relentlessly trying to get her daughter back. The mother is in a pathetic condition. We have no idea in what circumstances the minor daughter is residing in US with her father, that too a working father," the bench said.

It added that all attempts are being made by the man's parents to surreptitiously leave this country and obstruct the course of justice.





"We have stayed the operation of the order passed by Madras High Court setting aside the Look Out Circular," the bench said.

It granted the man a last chance to come back to India with the minor child. "We have made ourselves more than clear that he has to come to India within four weeks from the US with her, failing which his parents will have to face severe legal consequences. We have made the parents understand in vernacular," Supreme Court said.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The bench said that if he was not inclined to come to India within four weeks, then he should make necessary arrangements to put the child on board along with an escort. It also asked him to hand over the child to the mother if she reached US.

"We have passed this order keeping in mind the interest of the child, who was taken-away by her father deceitfully when she was just three-and-a-half years of age. Why should she be deprived of the love, care and affection of her own mother? Why should he stay back in US along with the daughter?" the court said in its order and posted the hearing after a month.

World.title: SIR strikes at heart of Constitution: Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan
World.content:
File photo: Supreme Court of India Judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan (PTI Photo)

Detaching right to vote from citizen is like taking soul out of body: Bhuyan

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Launching a scathing attack on special intensive revision (SIR) that has resulted in large-scale deletion of names from voter lists across states, Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan on Sunday said any process disenfranchising millions of Indian citizens was intrinsically arbitrary as it struck at the heart of the Constitution.Discounting the reasons given by govt and EC to justify SIR, which was upheld in the case of the revision of rolls in West Bengal by SC with modifications, Justice Bhuyan said, "No amount of whataboutery can justify it. It strikes at the very heart of Constitution. I would go to the extent of saying that it is a negation of the constitutional order which we have adopted under the Constitution."He was speaking at the moot court valedictory function at Nalsar, Hyderabad.Nalsar students, who had opposed CJI Surya Kant's participation in the convocation ceremony recently, came in for praise from Justice Bhuyan."One last word about the brilliant students of Nalsar. You have shown to the country and to the world what a university student, that too a student of law, should be. You are brilliant, you are bold, and you are brave," he said.Justice Bhuyan said a citizenâs right to vote was central to the holding of free and fair elections.âExcept in the case of a dead voter, the name of a voter once enlisted in the electoral roll cannot be deleted without notice and hearing,â he added.The SC judge said the right to vote or be included in the votersâ list could not be detached from the persona of an Indian citizen.âIf it is done, it will be like taking out the soul from the body,â he added. Justice Bhuyan said the Indian Constitution does not provide for two classes of citizens: citizens with voting rights and citizens without voting rights. âAny process which leads to wholesale disenfranchisement of Indian citizens, making them citizens without voting rights, would be violative of Articles 326 and 14 of Constitution of India,â he said.âIf any process results in disenfranchising millions and millions of Indian citizens, making them second class citizens in their own country in the sense of being citizens without voting rights, such a process is intrinsically arbitrary,â he added, his remarks coinciding with attacks on EC and govt over SIR by the opposition and others.Justice Bhuyan said the right to vote was intertwined with Indiaâs years of struggle against foreign rule. âIt is a manifestation of our freedom achieved after so much struggle and sacrifice. Article 326 (universal adult franchise) cannot be tinkered with at all. No authority can do it, no court can condone it. No one is above Constitution,â he said.

World.title: Kashmiri teacher fights period stigma, one village at a time
World.content:
Representative image

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

BARAMULLA: While most schools are quiet on Sundays, Aasima Jan heads into north Kashmirâs remote tribal villages to talk to girls and families about a subject many still avoid: menstruation. For years, the 42-year-old govt school teacher has conducted awareness sessions on menstrual health, hygiene and stigma, while also persuading families to re-enrol children who have dropped out of school. Her efforts earned her J&Kâs âBest Teacher Awardâ in 2023.Recruited in 2003, Aasima spent seven years teaching at a govt school in Bandipora. In 2009, she noticed many girls missing classes for up to a week during their periods. Some said their parents barred them from attending school while menstruating.The turning point came when she found a student crying over the shame surrounding periods. âIt broke my heart. I felt a deep sense of responsibility and resolved to do something about it,â Aasima said. The next day, she began taking extra classes on menstruation and started counselling parents. âI tell girls this is natural. It is not a disease, but a sign that they are growing up,â she said.Attendance among girls improved.Aasima then moved beyond the classroom, conducting monthly awareness sessions at schools and visiting villages on Sundays and holidays. She continued the sessions even after her transfer to neighbouring Baramulla district. Her outreach expanded to remote areas such as Gurez and Uri, and to nomadic Gujjar and Bakerwal communities.Every Sunday, she picks a village, contacts local panches and sarpanches, and conducts sessions centred on âawareness, acceptance and actionâ. In remote areas, she often finds girls using cloth during periods while families, including mothers, are reluctant to discuss menstruation. Aasima spends her own money buying sanitary pads to distribute during visits, while explaining their use and disposal.Her social media page, with around 40,000 followers, also promotes menstrual health and other social causes. For Aasima, the biggest reward is seeing students continue the work by spreading awareness and positivity about menstrual health.

World.title: U.P. releases new sugarcane varieties eyeing increasing production
World.content:
Uttar Pradesh government on Sunday (October 4, 2026) said four new sugarcane varieties have been released for cultivation, adding it would contribute to increasing both sugarcane and sugar production. The government added, the approved early-maturing varieties are better in terms of yield and sugar recovery.

“A meeting of the Seed Cane and Sugarcane Variety Approval Sub-Committee was held recently, discussions regarding the release of new sugarcane varieties took place during the meeting, attended by sub-committee officials, Director UPCSR, scientists from the UP Council of Sugarcane Research (Shahjahanpur) and the Indian Institute of Sugarcane Research (Lucknow). Data concerning the yield and sugar content of new sugarcane varieties—proposed by the U.P. Council of Sugarcane Research, Shahjahanpur, were presented,” told Ministhy S., Uttar Pradesh Cane Commissioner and Managing Director State Sugar Corporation Limited, to The Hindu.

“According to the data, the average yield of the plant crop for the early-maturing variety CoS.23232 was 95.56 tons/hectare, which is 9.44% higher than that of the standard variety Co.0238. This variety is resistant to Red Rot disease and exhibits good ratoon performance. Following deliberations, the sugarcane variety is being cultivated, as it was found to be superior to the popular variety Co.0238 on both parameters of yield and sugar recovery. They would prove to be the best alternative for farmers and would contribute to increasing both sugarcane and sugar production,” she added.

Abhishek Anand, Additional Cane Commissioner and Director UPCSR added, “Furthermore, the sub-committee considered the release of the early-maturing sugarcane variety developed by the Indian Institute of Sugarcane Research (IISR), Lucknow. In the meeting of the sub-committee, a decision was made, keeping farmers’ interests in mind to declare six older sugarcane varieties as unsuitable due to their unpopularity and negligible cultivation area; these sugarcane varieties will be phased out over the next two years.”

“With the approval of new, high-yielding and high-sugar-recovery sugarcane varieties, farmers will have a wide basket of varieties for the cultivation; this will lead to increased sugarcane yield and greater economic prosperity for the state’s farmers, while the sugar industry will also benefit from the improved sugar recovery. Director UPCSR said that this will boost the sugarcane farmer’s income and go a long way in doubling the farmer’s income. It is a great testament to progress and research done by scientists of UPCSR Shahjahanpur,” he said.

World.title: Kerala High Court orders CBI probe into soldier’s disappearance 14 years ago
World.content:
The Kerala High Court has directed the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to investigate a 14-year-old missing case of a soldier, who was a rifleman with the Tripura State Rifles, a paramilitary force.

Justice G. Girish issued the order on a petition by the soldier’s father seeking a CBI investigation to find out what happened to his son. The peaceful sleep enjoyed by a civilian was “at the cost of sleepless nights, vigilance and sacrifice of the soldier,” and civil society owed a responsibility to stand by the soldier who protects them if he faced a personal crisis, the court stated.

Subash Chandra Bose, a native of Vengoor in Ernakulam, went missing on April 4, 2012, while returning from leave in Kerala to Guwahati by train. His father last saw him at the Ernakulam railway station on April 3, 2012. The father received a phone call from his son the next day, from an unfamiliar mobile number, to inform him that the train had reached Visakhapatnam and that he was not feeling well. However, on April 10, 2012, the Commandant of Tripura State Rifles informed the father that his son had not reported back to the office after the leave period.

The State government stated that it had no objection to handing over the case to the CBI. However, the CBI contended that the court did not have territorial jurisdiction, since Mr. Bose had gone missing somewhere between Visakhapatnam and Guwahati. It also contended that there was only a very rare possibility of tracing the missing person after a lapse of 14 years.
