World.title: US marine arrested on suspicion of murder and robbery in Japan's Okinawa
World.content:
Japanese police have arrested a 20-year-old US marine over the alleged robbery and killing of a woman in Japan's Okinawa prefecture.

It is the latest criminal case on the southern island where the heavy American troop presence has remained a sensitive issue.

The Okinawa prefectural police said on Sunday they arrested a marine from the Futenma Air Station on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old local woman at a hotel in Naha, Okinawa's capital city, and taking her wallet and backpack in the early hours of Saturday.

Kyodo News agency, citing the police, reported the woman's body was found in her hotel room and she appeared to have been strangled to death.

Police said security camera footage showed the suspect entering the hotel with the victim and coming out alone.

An officer arrested the suspect after spotting him walking alone on a street in Naha's entertainment district late Saturday, Kyodo said.

There have been several protests against the US military base in Okinawa. (Reuters: Kyodo)

"The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to US bases," newly elected Okinawa Governor Genta Koja told reporters.

" It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged. "

"I must say, discipline and troop education are not working at all," said Mr Koja, referring to the US military's measures taken in response to past criminal cases.

Some 50,000 US troops are deployed in Japan under a bilateral security pact, about half of them on Okinawa, whose strategic role is seen as increasingly important for the Japan-US military alliance amid growing tensions with China.

Okinawans have long complained about noise, pollution and crime related to US bases, with crimes involving US service members on Okinawa complicating ties between Japan's central government and the Okinawa administration.

The latest case comes as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's cabinet pushes to further fortify its Japanese military presence on Okinawa and work more closely with the US military.

"The occurrence of the heinous crime is extremely regrettable," Ms Takaichi said in her message on X.

She said her government had strongly protested to the US side and demanded maximum cooperation with the Japanese authorities in the investigation, as well as tougher discipline for US service members and preventive measures.

The US Marine Corps said in a statement the suspect was assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force on Okinawa and that it was fully cooperating with Japanese authorities.

"The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behaviour," it said.

Crimes committed by US personnel in Okinawa have created anxiety among locals in Okinawa. (Reuters: Kyodo)

Futenma base, located in a densely populated area in central Okinawa, has been a sore spot for many Okinawans for decades, who demanded its relocation.

Despite protests, the central government green-lit construction to relocate the base to Henoko on Okinawa's eastern coast, though the project has faced massive delays.

A high-profile 1995 rape of a 12-year-old girl by three US service members sparked massive protests against the heavy US troop presence on Okinawa.

The number of arrests related to US service members and their families exceeded 100 last year, according to prefectural police.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Live: AFL trade period officially opens as stars eye blockbuster moves
World.content:
Do you think Geelong would be willing to send Jay Polkinghorne and pick 14 to Moorabbin as part of a trade for Rowan Marshall, possibly also with pick 8, given that St Kilda need a key forward and are insisting on getting a player in return? - Adam

(Getty Images)

First of all to set the scene, reports emerged last night that St Kilda was looking for Geelong's pick 14 AND a player for ruck Rowan Marshall.

That to me seems like obvious overs, and the Cats won't be doing that. Also don't think the Saints will be too keen to part with pick eight and certainly not for Jay Polkinghorne in this instance.

Geelong's first two picks are currently 14 and 34. The Cats probably say 14 is too much and the Saints would say 34 isn't enough. The answer might have to be in the middle, but how do they make that happen?

The Cats are also on the hook for Jordan Ridley from Essendon, and it sounds like they will be offering future picks for that deal. They are going to have to come up with something (and give up something) to get both of those deals done.

World.title: What to look for during the AFL trade period
World.content:
Footy never truly sleeps. Just days after the final siren sounded in one of the most chaotic AFL grand finals in memory did the competition begin once again.

The trade period can help sides find the missing pieces in their side, while the draft provides young footballers the opportunity to play on the biggest of stages.

Seventeen clubs are looking to catch the reigning premiers, while Brisbane is doing its best to stay ahead of the pack. No games are won during the off-season, but a good period can set sides up for years to come.

The names of countless players and draft picks have been discussed by the list managers in earnest over the last year, all ahead of the two weeks to come. These are the key themes to watch out for as the AFL enters its silly season.

A star-studded crop

This time of year lives and dies on the star power of the names linked to new clubs. If the trade period is about hope, then only the best in the game truly drives that optimism.

On achievements alone you would be hard pressed to find a trade period where more highly credentialed players have found new clubs.

Already a two-time Brownlow Medallist with three flags, Lachie Neale has found his way to his third club, Collingwood. He's set to replace AFL games record holder Scott Pendlebury in the Pies midfield. Pendlebury is set to finish his career like many future Victorian retirees do; on the sunny sands of the Gold Coast.

Elsewhere, GWS games and goals record holder Toby Greene has found his way to Geelong, and fellow former GWS teammate and Coleman medallist Jesse Hogan is set to join his fourth club, Collingwood. These players are joined by several others who have achieved plenty across their careers already.

But despite the list of greats looking for another club, one younger star has grabbed the lion's share of the headlines. Unlike the names listed above, Zak Butters, firmly in his prime and off a top 10 finish in the Brownlow Medal, is poised to move east if Port declines to match a contract offer from the Western Bulldogs.

Butters will attract top Band 1 compensation, but other high-profile moves have not. Compensation is tied to last year's salaries of players across the league. The sharp jump in the total player payment cap in recent years saw inflated compensation as a result.

Those effects have now dissipated, with the likes of Lachie Neale and Toby Greene attracting lower compensation picks than they may have a year or two ago.

These stars are far from the only players that will be discussed heavily over the coming 10 days. It's expected up to 40 trades involving about 30 players will be made during the player movement period, with many negotiations already firmly underway.

Beyond the list of vested greats, there's an uptick in the number of rucks and key position players expected to find new homes. As the league trends back towards multiple key forwards and an extended bench, clubs lacking depth are searching for answers.

No surprise about number one

In many — if not most — years there's intrigue about who is likely to be the number one pick in the November draft. Recruiters and scouts alike are scouring over player videos and stat profiles, trying to separate the wheat from the chaff.

But not so much in 2026.

Thanks to a recent rule change from the AFL, Essendon are heavily incentivised to pick a player tied to a club via the father-son or academy rules. If it does, it'll give itself (plus up to four other clubs) an extra high-end draft pick.

"We're certainly planning for Dougie to be bid on at one," Port Adelaide list manager Jason Cripps told Trade Radio last week.

"I'm happy to share that Essendon has told us that as well."

This year that player is almost certain to be Dougie Cochrane. The young key position player from South Australia is the son of former Port player Stuart, and brother of current Port midfielder Tom.

However, Dougie isn't eligible for the father-son process, and is instead tied to Port via its Next Generation Academy (NGA). He is set to become the second NGA player to be chosen at pick one after Jamarra Ugle-Hagan.

Cochrane has missed almost the entire year with injury, but his 2025 junior season was incredibly impressive. If there was a fully open draft there may be questions about whether he would go first, but under the current rules there's little doubt.

The new rule seeks to better aid lowly clubs seen as missing out on top talent and it may also address some reluctance by clubs with early picks to actually bid on high-value tied players.

The new scheme is a de facto priority pick system for bottom five clubs. With the introduction of Tasmania and years of compromised drafts ahead (more on that later), this could be a handy leg-up to strugglers. This bonus draft pick disappears if the original is traded, so only lopsided trade offers are likely to be entertained.

A bleak draft future?

Last week the Tasmania Football Club unveiled its first eight players to the football world. For many list managers it acted as an alarm that tough times were coming on the draft front.

Each club values the crop of each draft in different ways. Some drafts have stronger top ends, but weak depth. Others are even throughout. While last year's draft fell away sharply after the early picks, this year is considered to be deeper throughout the pack.

That's a key reason that this year's picks are being considered to hold a premium on their usual value, but it's not the only one. This year's draft will be the last majorly uncompromised for at least two seasons. This is due to the list concessions awarded to Tasmania on entry to the competition.

"We've obviously got Tasmania coming in who are going to dominate the next three drafts." Melbourne list boss Tim Lamb told Melbourne Media last week.

Like GWS and the Suns on their entry to the league, the Devils have been awarded a generous set of list-building tools to construct their first side. These include access to elite players in their pre-draft year, $5m in signing bonuses to established players, extra draft picks to both use and on-trade, and mini-draft picks to auction off. All in all, as few as nine of the top 25 players in next year's draft will be untouched by Tasmania's entry.

That's before considering the expected strong crop of both father-son and academy talents across the next two drafts, including some available to Tasmania under its academy, structured like those in NSW and Queensland.

As a result, many clubs are looking to prioritise picking up talent in this year's draft unless they have academy or father-son talent in the coming two years. It could mean that the value of future draft picks is significantly lower than in previous years, with clubs struggling to see eye to eye on what's fair.

With a strong crop of draft talent this year (even after excluding tied players), teams may spend relatively large amounts to secure any available picks for this draft. These factors, when combined, might make trading for talents such as Zach Merrett and Rowan Marshall even harder than in years' past.

World.title: NT government scrambles for Batchelor dialysis options ahead of YiSSA closure
World.content:
The Northern Territory government has been exploring dialysis treatment options in the remote town of Batchelor, despite assurances it would not shift medically vulnerable YiSSA residents away from their services.

It is less than a week before the expected closure of Darwin's largest short-stay accommodation centre, the Aboriginal-run YiSSA facility, on October 11.

The accommodation has been relied on by vulnerable Territorians, including dialysis patients, homeless residents and families fleeing violence.

The NT government is setting up an accommodation facility in Batchelor. (ABC News: Dane Hirst )

The NT government rejected a $3.5 million shared-purchase offer from the federal government to keep the centre open and announced it was instead shifting some of YiSSA's residents to Batchelor, a town 100 kilometres from Darwin.

Correspondence provided to the ABC reveals a senior NT Health bureaucrat reached out to renal health service Purple House last week about the possibility of using its "Purple Truck" for treating dialysis patients in Batchelor.

The Purple Truck is used in Central Australia. (Supplied: Western Desert Dialysis)

The bureaucrat asked for written confirmation "that Purple House does not currently have the capacity to provide mobile haemodialysis services for individuals relocating to Batchelor who may require treatment in the coming weeks, following the closure of YiSSA".

"Having this confirmed in writing would be helpful in informing our planning for alternative arrangements," the bureaucrat said.

The email chain included Purple House chief executive Sarah Brown and one of her staff members.

"Purple House does not have the capacity to provide dialysis in Batchelor via the Purple Truck mobile unit," the staff member said in response.

"The truck is currently in Alice Springs and limitations re staffing, and the oncoming build up and wet season will make providing service from the truck over the next four- six months very difficult.

"Our priority in staffing is to maintain our existing permanent sites."

The Purple Truck dialysis unit travels to remote communities for weeks at a time. (Supplied: The Purple House Facebook)

The Purple House staff member then explained why moving dialysis patients to the Batchelor facility was "not advisable on several levels".

The reasons outlined include a lack of access to dialysis, reliable return transport to Darwin, proximity to aged care, disability services and the Darwin and Palmerston hospitals "as dialysis patients are unfortunately frequent flyers to acute care".

It would create "further dislocation and destabilisation to an already extremely vulnerable patient group that require a high level of medical and social services support", the email said.

The NT Health bureaucrat thanked Purple House for its advice: "This information will help inform our planning and advice to executive leadership," the bureaucrat said.

Minister had ruled out Batchelor move

During a press conference announcing the decision to relocate YiSSA residents to Batchelor, Children and Families Minister Robyn Cahill said NT Health was working to find dialysis patients accommodation close to services in Darwin.

In response to a direct question about whether dialysis patients would be moved to accommodation in Batchelor, Ms Cahill replied "No".

Despite several requests from the ABC, the NT government has not confirmed whether there are now plans to accommodate dialysis patients at the Batchelor site or how many dialysis patients resided at YiSSA and required alternative accommodation.

The YiSSA accommodation facility has been relied on by vulenrable Territorians. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

In a statement to the ABC last week, a spokesperson for the NT government said "where residents require dialysis or other ongoing treatment, the service providers will work with NT Health to ensure appropriate transport and accommodation arrangements are in place so people can continue to attend their medical appointments".

"The government has been working with residents to support them into suitable alternative accommodation, and no resident who needs medical care will be left without a way to reach it," they said.

Government urged to keep YiSSA open

Since the announcement of the YiSSA closure, support workers for dialysis patients have spoken about fears some patients could miss treatments and become unwell after being forced into "unsafe" overcrowded homes or onto the streets.

Last month, the board of the Aboriginal-run Purple House wrote to NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro and all other NT government ministers, urging them to reconsider their negotiations with the federal government over YiSSA.

"Investing in services such as YiSSA enables Aboriginal people from remote communities to receive the care they need with dignity, safety and cultural support," the board members wrote in the letter seen by the ABC.

"The closure of this service would create significant barriers to healthcare for some of the Northern Territory's most vulnerable residents and place additional pressure on hospitals, community organisations and other accommodation providers."

Dialysis patients among residents forced out of YiSSA Charlie Yebarrarr Dhamarrandji and Evonne Mitja Wunungmurra need dialysis in Darwin every week, but the short-stay accommodation facility where they have sought refuge is about to close its doors.

In a letter responding to the Purple House board, Ms Cahill wrote that negotiations regarding the site had not been straightforward and the federal government had insisted on a "movable feast" of conditions.

Ms Cahill said they ranged from a "requirement for the Northern Territory government to relinquish ownership of the infrastructure to a third party to committing to engage in a long-term agreement with a specified third party, with no capacity for discussion or negotiation".

World.title: Opal miners, whip crackers and teddy makers eye Olympic stage
World.content:
As Queensland irons out the finer details of the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games, outback artisans and entertainers are putting up their hands to get involved.

The pitch by the state government that the Games would be "for all of Queensland" has been taken to heart, even by those more than 1,000 kilometres away from the main host city.

Opal miner Daniel Black said it would be a "dream" to see the famed Australian gems on the world stage.

Australia is the world's major supplier of opal, its national gemstone. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

"Whether that's within gifts to dignitaries that might come over for the games, whether that's within our medals or even within the torch itself," he said.

With Australia supplying more than 90 per cent of the world's opals, Mr Black, who is also the Queensland Boulder Opal Association president, said it was a fitting inclusion.

Daniel Black is a fourth-generation opal miner in remote Queensland. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

"A lot of people don't actually understand where opal is found or where specific types of opal are found," he said.

"And I think it actually provides a great international platform to make sure that people know."

Mr Black said he had already been in early talks with the government about how opals could be used and how that could benefit many small western towns.

Olympics a chance for outback performance

Remote Queensland kids are learning how to crack stock whips with hopes of performing at Games ceremonies. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

In Winton, co-founder of comedy and circus troupe The Crackup Sisters, Amanda Lyn-Pearson, is helping to train a team of whip crackers.

"Rather than having little city kids run around with whips, we're working on taking a mob of kids to the city to do the opening and closing ceremonies," she said.

Amanda-Lyn Pearson shares her larrikin brand of comedy and circus from The Crackup Sisters' arts precinct in Winton. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

Outback performers boost hope as tourism slumps The grand opening of an outback theatre has put on a show for a town hit hard by tourist cancellations.

The 17-strong crew, aged four to 58, have performed at Winton's Dustarena and believe they are ready to take to the Olympic and Paralympic stage.

"I could see it definitely as an opener. Or even when events going a little boring, let's whip it up a gear," she joked.

Ms Pearson said including Australian outback art forms would add an authentic touch of Queensland to the Games.

The Australian stock whip was developed in the 19th century. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

"Stock whip cracking, the knockabout acrobatics, hula hoop, the kelpie dogs, larrikin humour and big characters with a real nice blunt, dry sense of humour," she suggested.

"Tourism and audiences, they're actually after that genuine thing. They don't want the crap that you think that they might want."

Teddy makers ready to put needle to sheepskin

Tambo Teddies was founded in 1993 to support the wool industry after the wool market crashed. (Supplied: Tambo Teddies)

The team at Queensland toy producer Tambo Teddies have pitched a koala mascot for the Games.

"We put him out to our social media, to our world, and said, 'name him'. And yeah, Bunji came back, because Bunji means friendship," co-owner Alison Shaw said.

Bunji the koala was created as a potential mascot for the Brisbane Olympics. (Supplied: Tambo Teddies)

Ms Shaw said their facility in Toowoomba was ready to create merchandise, including for the Games' cockatoo-inspired emblems that were accidentally revealed in full on Friday.

"The new symbols and mascots, we want to make them," she said.

" Whether it's made of sheepskin or made of another fabric, there's no reason why we can't be the manufacturers here in Queensland. "

Co-owners Tammy Johnson and Alison Shaw hope they can help produce merchandise. (Supplied: Tambo Teddies)

She said the Games needed to be for all of Queensland, not just its south-east corner.

"It's an opportunity for the likes of us to be in there making something to share the love all around. Everyone gets a bit of the pie," Ms Shaw said.

Outback tourism industry set to benefit

Tony Rayner is advocating for remote Queensland businesses and towns to benefit from the Olympics. (ABC Landline: Cameron Lang)

Longreach Mayor Tony Rayner said there were challenges of supplying an event on the scale of the Olympics.

Weathering the season in Birdsville Birdsville, a pilgrimage point for outback travellers, navigates the ripple effects of flood, fuel fears and the cancellation of a massive music festival, when the surrounding country has rarely looked so green and alive.

"It's important that planning starts early, and then if the opportunity is there,they can bid to have that put in," he said.

"The big one for us obviously is visitation from tourists that are both international visitors coming over for the Olympics and equally those that might want to leave Brisbane and head to the quiet of the bush."

Brisbane 2032 was contacted for comment.

World.title: Former foster child's NDIS plan didn't prepare him for adulthood
World.content:
Coby spends almost all of his time on his computer, either playing games or writing code.

It's the only place where the 19-year-old feels safe and content.

But while his computer skills are improving rapidly, his independent living skills need work.

" I want to get more skills at cooking, money handling … I'm wasting my money on stupid things. "

Coby has level two autism, ADHD and an intellectual disability; he needs to be prompted to prepare food for himself and take medication.

He lived with foster carers until just before his 18th birthday, when he was relocated into a supported independent living house in suburban Hobart where he lives with two others.

"I get the help and support that I need … I know most of the workers that come, I get along with them," Coby said.

Billions slashed from NDIS packages as reassessments lead to more cuts As NDIS participants brace for cuts to community supports, documents show the agency running the scheme has been slashing packages overall.

" If I had to move, my mental health wouldn't be good because I would lose all of that. "

But moving is something he has been forced to contemplate four times this year — including into public housing — at the suggestion of child safety.

He now fears that if he leaves the house, he won't be allowed to return.

So he stays at his computer.

Staff acknowledge support issues

Coby missed out on critical support to develop independent living skills as a teenager.

It was the responsibility of the Child Safety Services to ensure Coby's National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) plan included this as he prepared to transition to adulthood, but his plan changed very little from age 10 to 17.

The NDIS plan is how these supports would have been funded.

Child Safety workers and support staff recognised this issue, in emails sent to his foster parents, and seen by the ABC:

"… I am sorry that [a review] has not occurred for three years … his needs would definitely be different to what they were three years ago"

"… the plan has been rolled over multiple times with limited updates, resulting in outdated goals and potentially misaligned funding allocations"

"… completely out of whack with his current wants and needs"

There were also severe funding and resource constraints, which child safety workers said limited their ability to respond to his foster carers' concerns:

"… unfortunately the ongoing lack of resourcing in [Child Safety Services] and [Out of Home Care] makes it very difficult for us to respond quickly … there are so many demands on our time"

"… [Out of Home Care] isn't currently able to offer much proactive support for carers"

"… [Child Safety Services] acknowledged the frequency of visits had decreased due to … a shared care management model and staffing numbers being lower than normal at present"

His foster carers feared what would happen when Coby turned 18, after their calls for supports in his NDIS plan did not eventuate.

They received a government form to sign, which stated the department would no longer be his legal guardian when he turned 18, and that it "does not have any legal responsibility for the young adult".

Coby was moved into supported independent living — but his housing issues were far from resolved.

Case manager raised 'couch surfing' as an option

While waiting to see if his new living arrangement would get NDIS funding and approval from the provider, Coby started to receive offers of other housing from government agencies.

Coby was offered two public housing properties as a potential solution to his housing issues. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Two of these were for public housing, where he would get about four hours of care support a day.

He rejected them.

"They think they're trying to help me by wanting me to live on my own, when I've learnt nothing," Coby said.

His rejection prompted an email to his foster parents from his case coordinator, who had been engaged by Child Safety through a non-government organisation:

"I have asked he consider his options for accommodation — your home, shelter or couch surfing," they wrote.

But Coby's choice was backed up by multiple reports from concerned medical practitioners.

One wrote that he needed 24-hour supervision until he gained critical independent living skills.

"Without this he will be taken advantage of, engage in unsafe, unhealthy and eventually criminal practices," they wrote.

Another report strongly urged that he remain in the supported independent living house.

"[He requires] structure, consistent staffing, and trauma-informed supports to maintain his safety, participation, and wellbeing," it reads.

A report this year questioned why the other medical practitioner reports had not been fully followed.

"… such an attitude can place him at risk of harm which can be seen as neglect," it reads.

Some of these reports were provided to the department before it decided to offer him public housing.

Coby to stay for now, but can't trust agencies

Coby's NDIS plan was ultimately updated to allow him to stay at the supported living home until 2028.

But the uncertainty over his housing and the way his support has been managed has left him distrustful of government agencies, and he no longer returns their phone calls.

Changes to NDIS eligibility have created new concerns for his future, particularly if he has to live independently in a few years.

It could make it more difficult for him to receive more than a few hours of support per day.

Recent reforms to the NDIS system have created widespread eligibility and funding concerns. (ABC News)

His former foster parents said if Child Safety Services had "followed the NDIS guidelines and started to do the appropriate assessments for adult needs at 16 years … we wouldn't be here today with this issue".

The family was asked to send a list of grievances to the department, and received a response that "there was no mismanagement of his [NDIS] funding", with further apologies for issues they faced as carers.

Coby is not the only foster child in Tasmania who has faced significant uncertainty during the transition to adulthood, Foster and Kinship Carers Association Tasmania (KFAT) chief executive officer Kim Backhouse said.

Dr Kim Backhouse said supporting Coby's transition to adulthood should have started far sooner. (ABC News: Carla Howarth)

"It's disappointing to learn that a foster carer placement with a young adult broke down through poor planning on behalf of the department around a complex matter," she said.

"The transition should have occurred way earlier in the journey, or support should have been put in place for him to be able to stay with foster parents by the government up until at least 21 years of age.

" There is a gap in supports to transition young adults from Out of Home Care to the NDIS system in terms of their wellbeing. "

Department says funding has been increased

The Child Safety Services faced extensive scrutiny in 2021 during Tasmania's commission of inquiry into child sexual abuse in institutional settings.

Commissioners described "chronic underfunding" in children and families services as limiting its ability to carry out its role.

Tasmania's commission of inquiry into government responses to child sexual abuse in institutional settings highlighted a range of issues with the out-of-home care system. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"One systemic issue that appeared to be causing harm was the unrealistic caseloads that frontline staff have to manage," its final report reads.

Tasmanian Greens MP Cecily Rosol, who is a foster carer, said that such a situation had resulted in a young person's needs being "pushed aside" and expert advice "being ignored".

A Tasmanian department spokesperson said the children and youth system — which includes youth justice services — received $150 million in new funding in the last state budget.

As part of that funding, three disability service navigator roles have been funded.

Powerful testimonies heard at NDIS inquiry The key takeaways from the six-day Senate inquiry into a proposed NDIS shake-up.

The spokesperson said planning for adulthood "occurs well before young people in Out of Home Care turn 18", and departmental staff play "an important role" in advocating for NDIS supports.

The ABC asked the department about whether public housing, with some NDIS-funded carer visits, is seen as a potential outcome for former foster children with disability.

"Young people leaving care have different needs and goals. There is no single housing model that is suitable for everyone," the spokesperson said.

"The most appropriate housing and support arrangements depend on each young person's level of independence, disability support needs, personal preferences and family, community and service connections."

World.title: Dwindling volunteer numbers put seafarers' rights at risk, charity says
World.content:
Ports are heavily regulated for safety and border control, which means in many harbours around the world, seafarers are never allowed to venture off their ships.

For thousands of international seafarers docking in Australia is their only opportunity in months to set foot on land.

Most ships docking in Australia are staffed by foreign workers and Australia has signed a UN charter to protect their rights. (ABC South West Vic: Violette Storm)

In most Australian ports the Mission to Seafarers charity provides international workers with support, including the only transport allowed — a free shuttle bus.

But with its volunteers ageing, regional Mission to Seafarers chapters fear they will not be able to maintain services for much longer.

Shore leave vital

Australia has signed the Maritime Labour Convention (2006), a United Nations charter that states international seafarers should be able to leave their port for time on land.

Mission to Seafarer Portland chapter manager Neville Mason has been working in the port for more than 20 years, driving a shuttle bus to the Seafarer Welfare Centre, which he also runs.

"We have often found crew that have not stepped on land for three months or longer," he said.

"They love Australia.

" Australia is really good with seafarers' welfare — pretty much every port here has a welfare centre, but it's not the case around the world. "

The welfare centre in Portland includes a shop, prayer room and recreation spaces. (ABC South West Vic: Violette Storm)

Seafarer welfare centres are spaces near ports for the crew to relax, socialise, use the internet, get transport into town, currency exchange or access to medical care.

Sailor Paul Gegremosa said the centre have him his only opportunity to relax between months spent at sea.

Paul Gegremosa won't see his family in the Philippines until his six-month contract ends. (ABC South West Vic: Violette Storm)

"During my shore leave, we will be going to the city to access some food, groceries, or anything that relieves stress, like just sightseeing, because on board you will see the same ship, the same cabin," he said.

Sailors enjoy access to fresh fruit and vegetables during shore leave. (ABC South West Vic: Violette Storm)

After a month-long journey from Japan, he has three days in Portland before his ship heads to China.

He said he could not go onshore in Japan and did not know whether disembarking would be allowed in China.

He worried that without the support of the Mission to Seafarers, simple comforts such fresh fruit or internet access could disappear.

"If you are a first-timer, it will be very hard — you must have a strong mentality because most of the time you will be away from your family," Mr Gegremosa said.

Gig responsibility for small town

About 5,000 seafarers come through the Port of Portland every year, and manager Neville Mason said almost all of them make use of the welfare centre.

Many seafarers leave a banknote on a board in the welfare centre and check that it's still there when they return. (ABC South West Vic: Violette Storm)

Aside from Christmas Day, it operates every day from 11am–10pm.

Mr Mason said the Portland chapter once had plenty of volunteers, but these days had fewer than 20, who had an average age of 80.

Two volunteers are needed per shift. One runs the centre and the other drives the bus. (ABC South West Vic: Violette Storm)

"[Volunteers are] also volunteering at the op shop, at the Coast Guard, at the church fete — they're doing multiple volunteer jobs, so it stretches the whole volunteering workforce.

" Volunteers are like gold. "

Portland's most dedicated volunteer is 91-year-old Ern Harrison, who works five six-hour shifts a week.

Mr Harrison believed Australia would not function without the international crew behind the shipping industry.

The Port of Portland is about 2.5km from Portland's city centre. (ABC South West Vic: Violette Storm)

"Australia is a continent with water all around and if those ships come in from the other side of the continent, they've got 30 days sailing," he said.

" I would not like to be locked on the ship for 30 or 40 days and not being able to get off and have a break at the other end of it. "

The shuttle bus operates from 11am to 10pm every day. (ABC South West Vic: Violette Storm)

Calls for federal funding

Australian ambassador for global advocacy group Human Rights at Sea, Paul MacGillivary, said the volunteer model was unsustainable.

Paul MacGillivary has worked in the maritime industry since the 1970s. (Supplied: Paul MacGillivary)

He would like to see Australia to introduce a system similar to New Zealand's, where a portion of the government levies imposed on commercial ships docking is set aside to fund seafarer welfare services.

International seafarers rely on volunteers to help them access services. (ABC South West Vic: Violette Storm)

The NZ system was introduced in 2024 and has contributed about $1 million in grants to seafarer welfare centres and transport services this year.

"We've been proposing now for five years to adopt a New Zealand model and there's been huge resistance to that," Mr MacGillivary said.

He said the support for international seafarers had been left up to a charity organisation for too long.

A spokesperson for the federal transport minister said it was the responsibility of vessels, ports and Port Welfare Committees to ensure workers' rights set out in the Maritime Labour Convention are met.

"The Australian Government recognises the essential contribution international seafarers make to Australia's economy, trade and supply chains, and the vital support provided by seafarer welfare organisations and volunteers," the spokesperson said.

"Strong and active [Port Welfare] committees are critical to coordinating and providing local welfare arrangements and supporting practical delivery of Australia's Maritime Labour Convention welfare framework in ways suited to each port."

World.title: Queensland mother seeks to force inquest into daughter's 2023 Kakadu death
World.content:
The mother of a Queensland woman who died in Kakadu National Park after receiving mental health treatment at Royal Darwin Hospital (RDH) in 2023 has applied for court orders that would force the Northern Territory coroner to hold an inquest.

Jessica Stephens, 35, was missing for almost a week before police found her remains on Burrungkuy Rock, six days after her mother Karon Evans reported her missing on October 18.

At the time, Ms Evans told the ABC her daughter had travelled to Darwin from her home in the Whitsundays, before driving to Kakadu following her discharge from hospital.

Jessica Stephens's body was found on Burrungkuy Rock in Kakadu after an extensive search in 2023. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"I know she wasn't very well when they discharged her, but they deemed her well enough to be discharged," she said in 2023.

" She's obviously just decided to go on to where she was going but we haven't … heard from her since. "

In documents filed with the NT Supreme Court last month, Ms Evans says coroner Elisabeth Armitage formally declined to hold an inquest into Ms Stephens's death in February this year.

"The essential material from Queensland Health, Queensland Mental Health Tribunal and Queensland Child Safety was not fully available or disclosed at the time of the coroner's investigation," Ms Evans's originating motion reads.

"Conflicting statements appear between the coronial findings and the deputy coroner's refusal letter of the 20th [of] February, 2026 regarding what records were obtained."

Mother pays tribute to daughter after remains recovered at Kakadu Human remains, believed to be that of Jessica Stephens, were found by Northern Territory Police on Saturday at Kakadu National Park.

Ms Evans also claims NT Health's own findings detailed in the coroner's report state that the health department "did not follow its own policy and procedures in Jessica's discharge".

"[The] compressed time frames from when the Coroner received the final root cause analysis on the 4th [of] February, 2026 concerning discharge, accommodation and continuity of care failures, raises serious questions [about] if the coroner was able to give a fully and properly considered report before the refusal was given," the documents read.

"NT Health may have withheld documents from the coroner received from Jessica's treating team in Proserpine Queensland. Documents not mentioned in the coroner's report nor NT Health's own disclosure.

" If Jessica had been provided with the correct aftercare as per policy and procedure Jessica would still have been in care with NT Health. "

The documents state that "key evidence" about what happened "can only be compelled via judicial process, such as an inquest" and that "the public interest requires a full, independent examination".

Ms Evans is seeking a declaration that Ms Stephens's death "ought properly to have been treated as a death occurring while in care", triggering a mandatory inquest, or otherwise that the Supreme Court use its discretionary powers to order an inquest regardless.

Jessica Stephens's mother Karon Evans says her daughter had been receiving mental health treatment at RDH before she went missing. (Supplied: Karon Evans)

Judge Armitage's office is yet to file a defence to the lawsuit.

After her daughter's death in 2023, Ms Evans told the ABC her family's hearts were broken.

"Our beautiful Jess has been found, her soul released to the peace of the Dreamtime and heaven," she said.

"The sunset tonight is a reminder of how brief our lives can be.

"We will miss our beautiful daughter, sister, mother and granddaughter."

NT Health has been contacted for comment.

World.title: KPMG Australia mulls seeking $100 million in loans from global firm
World.content:
The Australian arm of embattled consultancy KPMG is considering seeking up to $100 million in loans from the global wing of the firm as it battles with the fallout from a whistleblower scandal that has cost it several marquee clients.

An anonymous KPMG whistleblower warned the firm of a raft of serious allegations in 2024, including that senior partners had misused confidential information to win work, but his claims were dismissed until Senator Deborah O’Neill went public with the allegations in March.

KPMG Australia chief executive John Sams has also presided over major job cuts. Alex Ellinghausen

On Monday, The Australian Financial Review reported that KPMG Australia chief executive John Sams was in the process of asking KPMG’s global network of firms to loan his division up to $100 million, and agree to waive its fee to use the KPMG name and resources, which is worth about the same amount.

KPMG is structured as a network of quasi-independent consultancies that operate in different territories under the ultimate supervision of the global head office.

World.title: Expert cast excels in Doctor Who and Sherlock writer Steven Moffat’s debut play
World.content:
Roslyn Packer Theatre, until October 31

John Cleese once observed that an English person’s greatest fear was embarrassment. This is the premise behind British writer Steven Moffat’s debut play – and what a debut! Moffat, having written scores of TV scripts (including Sherlock and Doctor Who), has turned to theatre with all the assurance of years of crafting characters, plot, dialogue and, here, side-splitting comedy.

The pin around which the whizzing Catherine wheel of laughs revolves is Elsa Jean Krakowski, a middle-aged American who hails (loudly) from Denver. She’s as absurdly optimistic as a golden retriever who can smell a treat, and as garish as a toddler’s vomit after excessive M&Ms. Helen Thomson plays her to the hilt in a performance that guarantees Elsa commands the stage whenever present.

Tim Walter and Helen Thomson in The Unfriend at Roslyn Packer Theatre for the Sydney Theatre Company. Prudence Upton

London couple Debbie (Alex Lee) and Peter Lindell (Tim Walter) have met Elsa on a cruise. She insists they look her up if they’re ever in Denver but a trip to Denver is as likely as either of them murdering someone.

That’s Elsa’s department.

Having extracted Debbie’s email, Elsa announces she’s coming to stay, whereupon Debbie Googles her, to discover she’s the prime suspect in six murders of close family. By poisoning. The Lindells, who have two teenaged children, Alex (Ty Arnott) and Rosie (Brooklyn Davies), are appalled. Or at least Debbie is: Peter struggles to work up much in the way of emotion other than anger over politics. Happiness, he tells Elsa on the cruise, is misinformation.

Once confronted by Elsa’s neon presence, the Lindells’ terror for their children’s welfare is far outweighed by their terror at being embarrassed by saying the wrong thing. Falseness and hypocrisy are their defaults.

Ty Arnott, Helen Thomson and Brooklyn Davies in The Unfriend. Prudence Upton

But Elsa’s a cross between Mary Poppins and a wicked witch. If she kills – about which she leaves only jolly innuendoes hanging in the air – she doesn’t do it without good cause. Meanwhile, she’s equally capable of bringing out the best in everyone. Arnott’s Alex, for example, is the teen from hell: a flopping, farting, parent-scorning, computer-game-obsessed pest, whose default communication is whining – until tamed by Elsa. Rosie is also enchanted out of her perpetual crossness towards everyone.

Directed with phenomenal finesse by Simon Phillips on Isabel Hudson’s eye-popping set, everyone excels in roles to be relished. The expert cast is completed by Huw Higginson as the neighbour who would drive anyone to drink and/or fence heightening, and Ben Wood as the cooper who’s like a bloodhound with a nosectomy.

Moffat is not in the business of judging his characters, but of painting them with equal affection. The comedy spirals in style between early Tom Stoppard (After Magritte, The Real Inspector Hound, say) Monty Python, Carry On movies and David Williamson. In that way, it’s reminiscent of Shakespeare’s ability to pitch humour at all levels of learning, intellect and taste. Sydney Theatre Company just might have a hit on its hands.

World.title: US pulls bomber jets from UK air base after terror plot
World.content:
The US has withdrawn all of its bomber jets from RAF Fairford after the base in south-west England was the target of a suspected terror plot last weekend.

The Pentagon said all B-1 bombers deployed to the base, which US forces have used to strike Iran, have returned to the US.

A British-Iranian dual national has been arrested on suspicion of “preparation of terrorist acts” in connection with an alleged plot to target UK’s RAF Fairford airbase used by the US military. AP Photo/Alastair Grant

Counterterror police are investigating whether Iran was behind the plot. Five British nationals and a UK-Iranian national have been arrested on suspicion of terrorism and explosive offences over the incident. All those arrested have since been bailed.

A Pentagon official told The Telegraph: “While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States.”

World.title: ‘Boots, pompoms’ and premiership bling: Inside Leniu’s kitbag for last Roosters ride
World.content:
SportNRLNRL grand final ‘Boots, pompoms’ and premiership bling: Inside Leniu’s kitbag for last Roosters ride Dan Walsh October 5, 2026 — 8:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Spencer Leniu’s family packed the three premiership rings that were twinkling away on his left hand within minutes of adding a fourth on Sunday night. The polarising Roosters prop told coach Trent Robinson that “I was packing my boots and my pompoms” for what he accepts is most likely his last game for the club. Four to the fore: Spencer Leniu brandishes his premiership bling. Getty Images Leniu proved himself a genuine game-breaker off the Tricolours bench in their 19-18 triumph over Newcastle. He rates his fourth title as “a bit more special” after a trio of Panthers premierships given the dramas of his three-year stint at the Roosters, most notably the racism row involving Brisbane’s Ezra Mam at the start of 2024. The 26-year-old enforcer has a year left on his contract at the club but is set to link with Parramatta. He spoke with an air of finality, as well as warmth for the Roosters and pride in his achievements as he took to the presentation stage, brandishing his quartet of premiership rings and delivering some choice words to the cameras.



“I’m forever indebted to this club; it tells you who your true friends are when you’re at your lowest point,” Leniu said. “I was obviously at my lowest point here at the Roosters at one point of my career, and they stuck by me. Loading “I think this [premiership] is a bit more special to me because I came to this club [when it was] in a sort of rebuild phase. “It didn’t work out exactly how everyone planned it … but at the end of the day, we got a premiership. It’s such a special club, and I would encourage anyone who’s wanting to come here to come experience it because it’s second to none.”



Leniu was the last Rooster to leave the Accor Stadium turf for the dressing rooms on Sunday night, and he spent several minutes taking a knee by himself on the halfway line as cleaners went to work around him clearing away red, white and blue streamers. The Samoan international eventually pointed to the sky and joined his teammates in the sheds and explained that he was fulfilling his regular post-game ritual. “I definitely felt God’s presence today, and I had to give all that glory back to him,” he said. Spencer Leniu celebrates with his former teammates after the grand final. Instagram / @crittaaa_ Leniu also confirmed that his family “always bring my premiership rings in case there’s a win”. So the three mementos from his time at Penrith were slipped straight on as he also caught up with his old Panthers teammates Stephen Crichton, Jarome Luai and Brian To’o in the stands.



His preparation for the decider was anything but ordinary though given he had watched the entire grand final qualifier as an unused bench replacement. Related Article Analysis

NRL grand final The tiny grand final moments turned on a dime by NRL’s biggest marquee buys Robinson lauded Leniu’s response to that uncomfortable scenario after defeating the Dolphins. The four-time premiership-winning coach was again full of praise for Leniu’s 25-minute stint that featured 93-line-bending metres and several heavy shots in defence. “I was definitely a little bit bitter in the sense that I would have loved to feel like I’ve earned my job and earned my way into this grand final week,” Leniu said. “I didn’t get that opportunity, but I learned early in my career that egos are a really bad thing in this game, so I just put that ego aside.



“I told Robbotoo, I’ll pack my boots or I’ll pack my pompoms … then when Robbo told me I was going to play I was just like ‘f--- I just gotta send it. I gotta give everything, empty the tank’. Related Article Live

NRL grand final NRL grand final celebrations LIVE updates: Roosters celebrate NRL and NRLW premierships “Having that feeling last week, I never want to feel that again. I thought I had to just put everything out there. “It gives you a lot of confidence having Gus [Crichton] and Nat Butcher sitting on the bench, we called it the bomb squad. “When we found out that we were going to come on together it was just like ‘there’s no excuses why we can’t impact the game with us three players coming in’, and I think we did a tremendous job.”

World.title: NRL grand final celebrations LIVE updates: Roosters celebrate NRL and NRLW premierships
World.content:
Roosters captain and Clive Churchill medallist James Tedesco addressed supporters gathered outside Easts Bondi Junction in the hours after last night’s grand final, to kick off celebrations following a thrilling victory.

The Roosters players hoisted the Provan-Summons trophy to their adoring fans in the early hours of this morning, when a handful of squad members spoke to the crowd, gathered on the street, from the balcony of the leagues club.

Tedesco, who ran for more than 380 metres in an outstanding grand final performance, dedicated the victory to the Roosters faithful.

“Thank you every single one of you for supporting us all year, whether its at home or away, or out at Homebush you guys turned up, supported us all year, so I can’t thank you enough, let’s celebrate well,” Tedesco said.

Daly Cherry-Evans, who kicked the field-goal that proved the difference on Sunday, thanked the supporters for “making me one of your own this year”.

“It’s been a pleasure, it’s going to be a year I’ll remember for the rest of my life, so let’s celebrate it for the next week,” said Cherry-Evans, who marked his NRL swansong with a premiership.

World.title: Russian drones attack Kyiv as Merz meets Zelensky
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war Russian drones attack Kyiv as Merz meets Zelensky Adam Berry October 5, 2026 — 8:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Russia launched a drone attack on Kyiv while the German chancellor was making a surprise appearance in the city. Two people were injured when the Northern Bridge, over the Dnipro River, was targeted while Friedrich Merz visited Ukraine on Sunday. Loading Brushing off the attack, Merz, who was accompanied by a senior minister and several company executives, said his trip “demonstrates that we will not be intimidated. Nor will we be intimidated by a drone attack occurring at the very time of our visit”. He announced military aid for Ukraine worth about £850 million ($1.6 billion) and a £300 million energy support package.



Video footage showed the drone crash into the bridge, triggering a large explosion and sending a plume of black smoke into the air as cars continued to cross. Other photos showed soldiers inspecting a gaping hole in the highway. The crossing, previously known as Moscow Bridge, connects the densely populated neighbourhoods of Troeshchyna, Voskresenka, Raiduzhny and Obolon, and was already attacked on the previous day. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visit the site of a Russian air strike on Sunday. Bundesregierung via Getty Images The Russian defence ministry claimed the bridge had been targeted as it was used to transport troops and military cargo. In all, Russian assaults since Thursday have forced the full or partial closure of three of Kyiv’s six road bridges as part of Moscow’s latest effort to disrupt life in the Ukrainian capital.



The escalation in attacks comes after Volodymyr Zelensky, the Ukrainian president, pledged to step up the bombing of Russian oil refineries. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war US-Russia talks on Ukraine now involve an oil deal tied to Trump allies Vitali Klitschko, the mayor of the Ukrainian capital, said the Kremlin’s strikes were “tearing Kyiv apart”, but Zelensky was more bullish. “They strike bridges – do they really think we will not respond? I am simply astonished by this animalistic desire to escalate the situation every day,” he said at a press conference. Throughout the day, other areas of the country were also hit by drones, with five people injured in the north-eastern Sumy region when a residential building was hit.



Sirens sounded several times during Merz’s visit, which included a tour of Ukraine’s Academy of Sciences, which was badly damaged by a drone strike that killed two people last week. “We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” noted Merz. “These barbarous attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. These are war crimes that are being committed daily here.” Zelensky and Merz at a memorial for fallen Ukrainian soldiers in Kyiv. AP As well as announcing more military aid for Kyiv, Merz also set out plans for joint Ukrainian-German drone production. He was accompanied by Katherina Reiche, Germany’s minister for economic affairs and energy, and business leaders from firms such as Siemens Energy and Diehl Defence. The visit came a day after Russia warned against foreign delegations travelling to the country.



“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” Merz said. “There are immeasurable consequences for Europe if the German government cannot meet the challenges it faces. I will do everything in my power to ensure it remains stable.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

However, he said the stakes of the inevitable failures that come from that approach are growing along with the technology’s capabilities, citing OpenAI’s failure to prevent its AI from going rogue during testing.

World.title: KPMG Australia mulls seeking $100 million in loans from global firm
World.content:
The Australian arm of embattled consultancy KPMG is considering seeking up to $100 million in loans from the global wing of the firm as it battles with the fallout from a whistleblower scandal that has cost it several marquee clients.

An anonymous KPMG whistleblower warned the firm of a raft of serious allegations in 2024, including that senior partners had misused confidential information to win work, but his claims were dismissed until Senator Deborah O’Neill went public with the allegations in March.

KPMG Australia chief executive John Sams has also presided over major job cuts. Alex Ellinghausen

On Monday, The Australian Financial Review reported that KPMG Australia chief executive John Sams was in the process of asking KPMG’s global network of firms to loan his division up to $100 million, and agree to waive its fee to use the KPMG name and resources, which is worth about the same amount.

KPMG is structured as a network of quasi-independent consultancies that operate in different territories under the ultimate supervision of the global head office.

World.title: Expert cast excels in Doctor Who and Sherlock writer Steven Moffat’s debut play
World.content:
Roslyn Packer Theatre, until October 31

John Cleese once observed that an English person’s greatest fear was embarrassment. This is the premise behind British writer Steven Moffat’s debut play – and what a debut! Moffat, having written scores of TV scripts (including Sherlock and Doctor Who), has turned to theatre with all the assurance of years of crafting characters, plot, dialogue and, here, side-splitting comedy.

The pin around which the whizzing Catherine wheel of laughs revolves is Elsa Jean Krakowski, a middle-aged American who hails (loudly) from Denver. She’s as absurdly optimistic as a golden retriever who can smell a treat, and as garish as a toddler’s vomit after excessive M&Ms. Helen Thomson plays her to the hilt in a performance that guarantees Elsa commands the stage whenever present.

Tim Walter and Helen Thomson in The Unfriend at Roslyn Packer Theatre for the Sydney Theatre Company. Prudence Upton

London couple Debbie (Alex Lee) and Peter Lindell (Tim Walter) have met Elsa on a cruise. She insists they look her up if they’re ever in Denver but a trip to Denver is as likely as either of them murdering someone.

That’s Elsa’s department.

Having extracted Debbie’s email, Elsa announces she’s coming to stay, whereupon Debbie Googles her, to discover she’s the prime suspect in six murders of close family. By poisoning. The Lindells, who have two teenaged children, Alex (Ty Arnott) and Rosie (Brooklyn Davies), are appalled. Or at least Debbie is: Peter struggles to work up much in the way of emotion other than anger over politics. Happiness, he tells Elsa on the cruise, is misinformation.

Once confronted by Elsa’s neon presence, the Lindells’ terror for their children’s welfare is far outweighed by their terror at being embarrassed by saying the wrong thing. Falseness and hypocrisy are their defaults.

Ty Arnott, Helen Thomson and Brooklyn Davies in The Unfriend. Prudence Upton

But Elsa’s a cross between Mary Poppins and a wicked witch. If she kills – about which she leaves only jolly innuendoes hanging in the air – she doesn’t do it without good cause. Meanwhile, she’s equally capable of bringing out the best in everyone. Arnott’s Alex, for example, is the teen from hell: a flopping, farting, parent-scorning, computer-game-obsessed pest, whose default communication is whining – until tamed by Elsa. Rosie is also enchanted out of her perpetual crossness towards everyone.

Directed with phenomenal finesse by Simon Phillips on Isabel Hudson’s eye-popping set, everyone excels in roles to be relished. The expert cast is completed by Huw Higginson as the neighbour who would drive anyone to drink and/or fence heightening, and Ben Wood as the cooper who’s like a bloodhound with a nosectomy.

Moffat is not in the business of judging his characters, but of painting them with equal affection. The comedy spirals in style between early Tom Stoppard (After Magritte, The Real Inspector Hound, say) Monty Python, Carry On movies and David Williamson. In that way, it’s reminiscent of Shakespeare’s ability to pitch humour at all levels of learning, intellect and taste. Sydney Theatre Company just might have a hit on its hands.

World.title: US pulls bomber jets from UK air base after terror plot
World.content:
The US has withdrawn all of its bomber jets from RAF Fairford after the base in south-west England was the target of a suspected terror plot last weekend.

The Pentagon said all B-1 bombers deployed to the base, which US forces have used to strike Iran, have returned to the US.

A British-Iranian dual national has been arrested on suspicion of “preparation of terrorist acts” in connection with an alleged plot to target UK’s RAF Fairford airbase used by the US military. AP Photo/Alastair Grant

Counterterror police are investigating whether Iran was behind the plot. Five British nationals and a UK-Iranian national have been arrested on suspicion of terrorism and explosive offences over the incident. All those arrested have since been bailed.

A Pentagon official told The Telegraph: “While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States.”

World.title: ‘Boots, pompoms’ and premiership bling: Inside Leniu’s kitbag for last Roosters ride
World.content:
SportNRLNRL grand final ‘Boots, pompoms’ and premiership bling: Inside Leniu’s kitbag for last Roosters ride Dan Walsh October 5, 2026 — 8:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Spencer Leniu’s family packed the three premiership rings that were twinkling away on his left hand within minutes of adding a fourth on Sunday night. The polarising Roosters prop told coach Trent Robinson that “I was packing my boots and my pompoms” for what he accepts is most likely his last game for the club. Four to the fore: Spencer Leniu brandishes his premiership bling. Getty Images Leniu proved himself a genuine game-breaker off the Tricolours bench in their 19-18 triumph over Newcastle. He rates his fourth title as “a bit more special” after a trio of Panthers premierships given the dramas of his three-year stint at the Roosters, most notably the racism row involving Brisbane’s Ezra Mam at the start of 2024. The 26-year-old enforcer has a year left on his contract at the club but is set to link with Parramatta. He spoke with an air of finality, as well as warmth for the Roosters and pride in his achievements as he took to the presentation stage, brandishing his quartet of premiership rings and delivering some choice words to the cameras.



“I’m forever indebted to this club; it tells you who your true friends are when you’re at your lowest point,” Leniu said. “I was obviously at my lowest point here at the Roosters at one point of my career, and they stuck by me. Loading “I think this [premiership] is a bit more special to me because I came to this club [when it was] in a sort of rebuild phase. “It didn’t work out exactly how everyone planned it … but at the end of the day, we got a premiership. It’s such a special club, and I would encourage anyone who’s wanting to come here to come experience it because it’s second to none.”



Leniu was the last Rooster to leave the Accor Stadium turf for the dressing rooms on Sunday night, and he spent several minutes taking a knee by himself on the halfway line as cleaners went to work around him clearing away red, white and blue streamers. The Samoan international eventually pointed to the sky and joined his teammates in the sheds and explained that he was fulfilling his regular post-game ritual. “I definitely felt God’s presence today, and I had to give all that glory back to him,” he said. Spencer Leniu celebrates with his former teammates after the grand final. Instagram / @crittaaa_ Leniu also confirmed that his family “always bring my premiership rings in case there’s a win”. So the three mementos from his time at Penrith were slipped straight on as he also caught up with his old Panthers teammates Stephen Crichton, Jarome Luai and Brian To’o in the stands.



His preparation for the decider was anything but ordinary though given he had watched the entire grand final qualifier as an unused bench replacement. Related Article Analysis

NRL grand final The tiny grand final moments turned on a dime by NRL’s biggest marquee buys Robinson lauded Leniu’s response to that uncomfortable scenario after defeating the Dolphins. The four-time premiership-winning coach was again full of praise for Leniu’s 25-minute stint that featured 93-line-bending metres and several heavy shots in defence. “I was definitely a little bit bitter in the sense that I would have loved to feel like I’ve earned my job and earned my way into this grand final week,” Leniu said. “I didn’t get that opportunity, but I learned early in my career that egos are a really bad thing in this game, so I just put that ego aside.



“I told Robbotoo, I’ll pack my boots or I’ll pack my pompoms … then when Robbo told me I was going to play I was just like ‘f--- I just gotta send it. I gotta give everything, empty the tank’. Related Article Live

NRL grand final NRL grand final celebrations LIVE updates: Roosters celebrate NRL and NRLW premierships “Having that feeling last week, I never want to feel that again. I thought I had to just put everything out there. “It gives you a lot of confidence having Gus [Crichton] and Nat Butcher sitting on the bench, we called it the bomb squad. “When we found out that we were going to come on together it was just like ‘there’s no excuses why we can’t impact the game with us three players coming in’, and I think we did a tremendous job.”

World.title: NRL grand final celebrations LIVE updates: Roosters celebrate NRL and NRLW premierships
World.content:
Roosters captain and Clive Churchill medallist James Tedesco addressed supporters gathered outside Easts Bondi Junction in the hours after last night’s grand final, to kick off celebrations following a thrilling victory.

The Roosters players hoisted the Provan-Summons trophy to their adoring fans in the early hours of this morning, when a handful of squad members spoke to the crowd, gathered on the street, from the balcony of the leagues club.

Tedesco, who ran for more than 380 metres in an outstanding grand final performance, dedicated the victory to the Roosters faithful.

“Thank you every single one of you for supporting us all year, whether its at home or away, or out at Homebush you guys turned up, supported us all year, so I can’t thank you enough, let’s celebrate well,” Tedesco said.

Daly Cherry-Evans, who kicked the field-goal that proved the difference on Sunday, thanked the supporters for “making me one of your own this year”.

“It’s been a pleasure, it’s going to be a year I’ll remember for the rest of my life, so let’s celebrate it for the next week,” said Cherry-Evans, who marked his NRL swansong with a premiership.

World.title: Russian drones attack Kyiv as Merz meets Zelensky
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war Russian drones attack Kyiv as Merz meets Zelensky Adam Berry October 5, 2026 — 8:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Russia launched a drone attack on Kyiv while the German chancellor was making a surprise appearance in the city. Two people were injured when the Northern Bridge, over the Dnipro River, was targeted while Friedrich Merz visited Ukraine on Sunday. Loading Brushing off the attack, Merz, who was accompanied by a senior minister and several company executives, said his trip “demonstrates that we will not be intimidated. Nor will we be intimidated by a drone attack occurring at the very time of our visit”. He announced military aid for Ukraine worth about £850 million ($1.6 billion) and a £300 million energy support package.



Video footage showed the drone crash into the bridge, triggering a large explosion and sending a plume of black smoke into the air as cars continued to cross. Other photos showed soldiers inspecting a gaping hole in the highway. The crossing, previously known as Moscow Bridge, connects the densely populated neighbourhoods of Troeshchyna, Voskresenka, Raiduzhny and Obolon, and was already attacked on the previous day. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visit the site of a Russian air strike on Sunday. Bundesregierung via Getty Images The Russian defence ministry claimed the bridge had been targeted as it was used to transport troops and military cargo. In all, Russian assaults since Thursday have forced the full or partial closure of three of Kyiv’s six road bridges as part of Moscow’s latest effort to disrupt life in the Ukrainian capital.



The escalation in attacks comes after Volodymyr Zelensky, the Ukrainian president, pledged to step up the bombing of Russian oil refineries. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war US-Russia talks on Ukraine now involve an oil deal tied to Trump allies Vitali Klitschko, the mayor of the Ukrainian capital, said the Kremlin’s strikes were “tearing Kyiv apart”, but Zelensky was more bullish. “They strike bridges – do they really think we will not respond? I am simply astonished by this animalistic desire to escalate the situation every day,” he said at a press conference. Throughout the day, other areas of the country were also hit by drones, with five people injured in the north-eastern Sumy region when a residential building was hit.



Sirens sounded several times during Merz’s visit, which included a tour of Ukraine’s Academy of Sciences, which was badly damaged by a drone strike that killed two people last week. “We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” noted Merz. “These barbarous attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. These are war crimes that are being committed daily here.” Zelensky and Merz at a memorial for fallen Ukrainian soldiers in Kyiv. AP As well as announcing more military aid for Kyiv, Merz also set out plans for joint Ukrainian-German drone production. He was accompanied by Katherina Reiche, Germany’s minister for economic affairs and energy, and business leaders from firms such as Siemens Energy and Diehl Defence. The visit came a day after Russia warned against foreign delegations travelling to the country.



“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” Merz said. “There are immeasurable consequences for Europe if the German government cannot meet the challenges it faces. I will do everything in my power to ensure it remains stable.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.
