World.title: Explainer: What you need to know about how MMP works
World.content:
Explainer - Our MMP electoral system is marking its 30th anniversary this year, but it can still be tricky to explain exactly how it all works.

If you're confused about all the recent talk about overhangs and party votes and just want to know what you're deciding on at the ballot box, here's what you need to know about voting and MMP.

What is MMP?

MMP stands for Mixed Member Proportional representation, the electoral system used in New Zealand.

A majority of New Zealanders voted for it - twice, first in a non-binding referendum in 1992, and again in a binding referendum at the election the following year. It was introduced at the next election, in 1996.

National's leader Christopher Luxon has proposed another referendum over MMP, to be held after the 7 November election.

MMP aims to ensure that people will be represented in Parliament both by a person in their local area (electorate) and by a group (a political party).

How does it work?

New Zealanders have two votes - one for a local representative, and one for a political party. You just pick the person in your electorate you think best advances your interests, and the political party that best represents your interests.

Simple, right?

The complexity comes in when trying to calculate how these votes translate into the seats available for members of Parliament (MPs).

There are (typically) 120 seats:

72 are electorate seats and are won by candidates standing in specific areas

are electorate seats and are won by candidates standing in specific areas 48 are list seats and are allocated depending on the proportion of party votes won, taking into account the number of electorate seats each party has won

Basically, it all means that the proportion of party votes should be about the same as the proportion of seats in the Parliament. Electorate MPs will belong to one party or another unless they're running as an independent, but voters do not need to vote for an electorate representative that matches their party vote.

You must be registered - or enrolled - to be able to vote, and unlike in previous elections this year you will not be able to enrol on the day, or in the two weeks before election day.

In 2026, this means voters must be enrolled before 25 October.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins and National leader Christopher Luxon. RNZ/ Nick Monro / Marika Khabazi

Other things to consider

A party has to win at least 5 percent of votes or an electorate seat to win a seat in Parliament.

If they win an electorate seat, the party gets allocated a percentage of list seats based on their party vote - known as the "coat tail" rule.

If a party wins more electorates than its share of party votes allows for, extra seats can be added to the Parliament to make up for the "overhang" and ensure the proportions remain closer to the party vote than they would otherwise.

For instance, this meant there were 121 MPs in 2005, 122 MPs in 2008, and 121 in 2011, and 123 - a record number of MPs - after the election in 2023. It's possible there could be even more this year due to some calls for "strategic voting" for party votes over electorate candidates.

MMP determines the shape of Parliament. Gerry Brownlee has been Speaker in its most recent term. VNP/Phil Smith

So who wins the election?

In contrast to some countries overseas - the United States for example - the election in New Zealand is not voting for the country's leader. People vote only for the parties and electorates.

But someone has to be in charge. Someone has to make sure the organisations doing all the management of the country - funding hospitals and schools, repairing roads and infrastructure, managing prisons - all that administrative stuff, and more, is being done properly.

This responsibility - and the power it entails - belongs to the government.

Who gets to become the government is basically whichever party can get a majority - more than 50 percent - of the seats, based on their party vote. If none of the parties has enough to reach more than 50 percent, they must negotiate with each other about their plans until a combination of the parties has at least half the seats.

This can result in a coalition - where the bigger party and smaller party form a government together and come up with a complete policy plan - or a confidence and supply agreement, where the smaller parties agree to support the main governing party on specific policies.

Under confidence and supply, the smaller party does not need to support policies that fall outside the agreement.

With 50 percent of the seats in Parliament, the governing party or coalition can decide what to change about how the country works and enact these decisions in Parliament. We currently have a coalition government between National, New Zealand First and ACT.

The governing parties have most of the power. The parties that are not governing are known as the opposition, and it is their job to criticise and poke holes in the plans the government is putting forward.

National leader Christopher Luxon has said another referendum on MMP is needed. RNZ/Nick Monro

Will MMP ever change?

Not everyone likes MMP, and National's leader Christopher Luxon is campaigning on holding a referendum on it - to test whether the public still supports the model.

This would be the fourth public vote on changing the electoral system. A consultative referendum in 1992 indicated public appetite to change the system from the previous First Past the Post approach, and a binding referendum a year later in 1993 confirmed that, prompting the shift to MMP.

At the 2011 election, another referendum asked whether voters wanted to keep MMP or replace it, and what system would be preferred if it was changed. Almost 58 percent of voters wanted to keep it, an increase of 3.91 percentage points over the 1993 result.

First Past the Post was the most popular alternative, with 46.7 percent of people selecting that over preferential voting (12.5 percent), single transferable vote (16.7 percent), and supplementary member systems (24.4 percent).

The result triggered an Electoral Commission review of how well MMP was working, which recommended several changes that have largely not been taken up.

Another review in 2022 and 2023 by the Ministry of Justice heard from more than 1700 groups or individuals and also recommended multiple changes.

World.title: Two people critically injured after overnight stabbing in West Auckland's Glendene
World.content:
Two people have been taken to hospital in a critical condition after a stabbing in west Auckland.

Hato Hone St John said it sent three ambulances and two critical care units to the incident in the suburb of Glendene.

It said two people were taken to hospital in a critical condition, and one in a moderate condition.

The New Zealand Herald has reported neighbours tended to a wounded baby who was among the three injured.

"I woke up and listened for a minute to make sure and then got my brother to check he also heard it.

"We went into the house and saw blood everywhere," a neighbour told the NZ Herald.

Acting Detective Inspector Megan Goldie said police were called to Kirby St at 11.40pm on Sunday after report of a disorder where a person had been injured.

The Kirby St house. RNZ/Calvin Samuel

"Upon arrival police located three people who had suffered injuries that appeared to be consistent with knife wounds."

Goldie said police were not looking for anyone else in connection to what had happened.

World.title: Injury rules Ruben Love out of rugby for rest of year
World.content:
All Blacks first-five Ruben Love is to undergo ankle surgery which will rule him out of rugby for the remainder of the year.

New Zealand Rugby confirmed Love won't play until 2027, with the decision made to address an injury which All Blacks coach Dave Rennie said the 25-year-old had been nursing through the year, including during the recent series loss to the Springboks.

Love started all three Nations Championship match at home in July and kept that role for the three tests in South Africa the following month.

It is an unfortunate blow for Love, who impressed throughout the Hurricanes' dominant march to the Super Rugby Pacific title and looked composed conducting the playing style Rennie has introduced to the All Blacks.

The door is open for Mo'unga to reassert his credentials following three seasons in Japan.

The 32-year-old appears to have the inside running to start both of the looming Bledisloe Cup tests against the Wallabies.

World.title: National promises to fund $800 million Christchurch Northern Motorway extension
World.content:
National is promising to fully fund an extension to the Christchurch Northern Motorway at the cost of $800 million in next year's budget, if it leads the next government.

National's transport spokesperson Chris Bishop said funding it in the next government's first Budget means construction can begin next year.

The party said it would fully fund the Belfast to Pegasus Motorway and Woodend Bypass, "the next major transport project Canterbury needs", said Bishop as he made the announcement in Christchurch.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406221017112

"Canterbury is the engine room of the South Island... North Canterbury is one of the places where that growth is being felt most strongly."

Bishop said the Belfast to Pegasus Motorway and Woodend Bypass would extend the Christchurch Northern Motorway around 11 kilometres north, from just south of the Waimakariri River to beyond Pegasus and Ravenswood.

"SH1 approaching Woodend already carries around 21,500 vehicles a day, around nine percent of them freight, and that is expected to increase to around 28,000 vehicles a day by 2048."

He said that pressure was being felt in Woodend itself and at peak times it can take up to 20 minutes to travel through the town, while heavy through-traffic makes it harder for locals to access shops, schools and other parts of the community.

"There is also a significant safety problem. Between 2014 and 2023 there were 280 crashes on SH1 through Woodend, including three fatalities and 25 serious injuries.

"The new motorway and bypass will fundamentally change how this corridor works."

He said the project included widening the southern section of SH1 from two to four lanes, a new four-lane motorway bypass to the north, major intersection upgrades and new bridges.

NZTA estimated the project will save motorists up to 10 minutes at peak times, reduce traffic through Woodend from around 21,500 vehicles a day to 8000, and reduce deaths and serious injuries by 78 percent, Bishop added.

It would also make the corridor more reliable for people and freight travelling to and from Christchurch, Christchurch Airport and Lyttelton Port he said.

It wasn't a project "starting from scratch".

"Because of National's work in government, the project is ready to go and is the next investment-ready project on the Major Transport Projects Pipeline."

The announcement comes after National also promised to start construction on south Auckland's Mill Road if it leads the next government.

It would allocate $1.75 billion in Budget 2028 so construction can begin in late 2028, and look to progress route protection on Stages Two and Three by allocating $100m.

World.title: 'No one understands economics over there': National takes aim at Labour's fiscal plan
World.content:
Audio player for " Weekly interview with Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1737381%2Fno-one-understands-economics-over-there-national-takes-aim-at-labour-s-fiscal-plan

Weekly interview with Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon Morning Report Download MP3 7m

The National leader says "there's a real hole" in Labour's fiscal plan, which the party says is "fully costed and fully funded."

It comes as independent economist Cameron Bagrie told RNZ "here we go again, we're going to go through a big debate about fiscal holes."

He acknowledged all parties putting fiscal plans on the table, so "technically, there will be no holes, but realistically, there will be an awful lot of holes across the political parade."

Speaking to Morning Report on Monday, Labour's finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds backed her plan, including not specifying a cost for fully re-implementing the pay equity legislation.

Audio player for " Barbara Edmonds discusses Labour’s fiscal plan " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1737381%2Fno-one-understands-economics-over-there-national-takes-aim-at-labour-s-fiscal-plan

Barbara Edmonds discusses Labour’s fiscal plan Morning Report Download MP3 10m

"We're not going to disclose our bargaining envelope. No government does," she said, referencing the point that the coalition hadn't specified the total costs either in their pared back scheme.

Edmonds maintained Labour had "sufficient headroom in our fiscal plan, and I stand by that".

"I am confident there is sufficient funding in there to settle the pay equity claims, which we are absolutely committed to."

Labour's finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

But National's Christopher Luxon said about the plan, it was "pretty sad because clearly no one understands economics over there."

"You want to restore the previous pay equity scheme. You've told everybody you want to do it, and there's $8.5 billion of that unfunded," he said referring to Treasury's figure of around $11b to restore the old regime.

Labour has said there is $10.5b of future operating allowances unallocated, but Luxon said that meant there was nothing for schools, police, prisons, defence or other frontline social services.

Asked about the language used, with National's Nicola Willis calling the plan "fraudulent" and accusing Labour of lying, Luxon suggested that Morning Report co-host Ingrid Hipkiss "as a journalist dig into that fiscal plan."

"You should get into it because I think you'd really find that there's a real hole there, and there's a really unsolvable problem," Luxon suggested again.

Asked how much the government had set aside for funding its pared back version of the scheme, Luxon only said "we have money set aside."

But in many ways, Labour and the National-led coalition are largely on the same track.

Independent economist Cameron Bagrie. Screenshot

The government's pre-election economic and fiscal update (Prefu) forecast a return to surplus by 2028/29 and shrinking spending as a share of GDP to 29.8 percent by 2031.

Labour has forecast the same return to surplus and plans to bring spending down to 30.4 percent of GDP.

The government's 2026 Budget included a $2.4b annual operating allowance, that is extra spending on new initiatives, and Labour is budgeting for the same.

Bagrie said it didn't matter which political party you look at, "there's going to be gaps, there's going to be challenges, there's going to be some pretty complicated trade-offs."

On pay equity, he said no party would commit to pay-equity costs up front, "because then it becomes open season".

Bagrie also argued each offered insufficient funding for roads and were punting the problem by not hiking fuel taxes. Labour's freeze is for three years, National's is for one.

"No-one's prepared to take a stand and put the rates up, because, of course, it's election year," he said.

"All that's going to take place is that we're going to walk into reality in about 2028 and realise there's a gaping hole, and it doesn't matter which side of the political fence that you look at, but they're all pretty well the same."

That, Bagrie warned, would create literal holes - potholes - on crumbling roads up and down the country.

In a statement, Labour campaign chair Kieran McAnulty said Labour had a plan to tackle the cost of living and "National doesn't". LDR / file

On Monday morning, Labour then put out a press release saying the real question was what National planned to cut to fund its own promises.

"National has had plenty to say about Labour's finances, but remarkably little to say about its own," Labour campaign chair Kieran McAnulty said.

He said National's "desperate attacks" came because National couldn't campaign on its own record of "cuts, chaos, and higher prices."

"They have spent weeks throwing around absurd claims and made-up numbers, desperately hoping no one notices that they've failed to fix the cost of living."

McAnulty said Labour had a plan to tackle the cost of living - "National doesn't."

He said National needed to front up: "which schools, hospitals, roads or public services will National cut to make its promises stack up?"

"Every one of Labour's commitments are costed and funded, meanwhile, National still hasn't put its full fiscal plan on the table.

"Nicola Willis hasn't got a leg to stand on, Labour's promises are paid for."

World.title: Experts call for subsidised sunscreen in effort to reduce skin cancer rates
World.content:
Audio player for " Calls for sunscreen subsidies to reduce skin cancer rates " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/health/1737760%2Fexperts-call-for-subsidised-sunscreen-in-effort-to-reduce-skin-cancer-rates

Calls for sunscreen subsidies to reduce skin cancer rates Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Experts are calling for sunscreen to be subsidised, in an effort to reduce New Zealand's skin cancer rates.

Aotearoa has one of the highest rates of melanoma in the world, and the highest death toll.

The issue of sunscreen cost was raised in last week's Stuff Kingmaker's Leader's Debate when Winston Peters initially laughed off the idea of subsidies, before saying it could be subsidised for some families.

Speaking to Morning Report, senior research fellow and co-director of the Cancer Society Research Collaboration Dr Bronwen McNoe said 89 percent of New Zealanders supported making sunscreen more affordable, according to a survey.

"It is expensive and it's probably a third more expensive than it is in Australia.

"One of the reasons for that is probably just our market size, but also in Australia they do take the cost of GST off sunscreen. So it is less expensive in Australia."

McNoe said removing GST off sunscreen is something that could be done in New Zealand, as well as making it free in schools, or available to gold and community service card holders.

She said cost was one of the main barriers for New Zealanders keeping their skin protected and skin cancer rates were coming down in Australia where measures have been put in place.

World.title: Labuschagne set for Test after first ton in 11 months
World.content:
Marnus Labuschagne has responded to the debate over whether he merits a place in Australia's Test future by just doing what he likes doing best — scoring runs.

After a difficult year, the under-pressure 32-year-old chose the most timely moment to score his first century in any form of cricket for 11 months in Potchefstroom, just five days before Australia play their first Test in South Africa since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.

Former skipper Ricky Ponting had joined the chorus that Labuschagne's place in Australia had become "untenable" after three years and 43 Tests without a Test ton, capped by three failures in the recent Bangladesh series.

Yet the South African-born batter looks sure to fill the number three spot once more in the first Test that starts in Durban on Friday after his swift century against a modest Cricket South Africa Invitation XI attack.

Australia calls Maddinson and Harper into Test squad Nic Maddinson is within touching distance of a remarkable return to the Test team, after Cameron Green's abdominal strain left him in doubt for the series opener against South Africa.

Labuschagne was largely untroubled as he raced to a 76-ball ton, going on to 111 from 89, decorated with 19 fours, before retiring to let his colleagues also get in some batting practice on the final day of the two-day warm-up match.

They enjoyed the opportunity too, with Steve Smith also retiring after making 61 while Alex Carey, fresh from his fine form in the third ODI, hit another half-century (57) as Pat Cummins' Australian side rattled up 6-368 in the drawn game.

Smith, who received a 12-month ban when captain for his role in altering the condition of the ball with sandpaper at Cape Town on the infamous tour eight years ago, is back with a group of other survivors from that tour — Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and Matt Renshaw.

Those four could all play on Friday.

Renshaw looked completely recovered from a knock to his right wrist, but may feel he missed out by being dismissed for 32 off his 50 balls, as may his fellow opener Travis Head (21 off 22 balls).

Beau Webster brushed off a few cobwebs with his 42 off 88 balls before he retired.

All eyes, though, were on Labuschagne, who even had a bit of local support as he took the crease at Senwes Park, a venue less than 50km from where he was born in Klerksdorp and the emotional scene of his first ODI hundred for Australia back in 2020.

Australia will see it as a useful workout after they gave 11 bowlers a run-out on Saturday when the Invitation XI declared on 7-318 after a century from former Proteas captain Neil Brand.

Australia vs South Africa Test series 1st Test: Durban, October 9-13

2nd Test: Gqeberha, October 18-22

3rd Test: Cape Town, October 27-31

Meanwhile, South Africa paceman Anrich Nortje is in line for a remarkable return to first-class cricket after an absence of three-and-a-half years to help the injury-hit Proteas' attack.

With fitness doubts over key strike bowler Kagiso Rabada and three others, Nortje could return to Tests for the first time since March 2023 after a series of back and hip problems that left him concentrating on white-ball formats to reduce the strain on his body.

"I'll be very excited if I can put my Test cap on again. Growing up, ⁠it's the format you want to play," he said on Sunday, the day before he's expected to be named in South Africa's Test squad of 15.

AAP

World.title: De Minaur fights back to reach China Open semis
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has produced a remarkable turnaround to reach the semifinals of the China Open, coming back to score a three-set victory over Russian Andrey Rublev.

After scraping into the quarters with a 3-6, 7-6 (7-5), 7-5 win over French qualifier Quentin Halys, the fifth-seeded de Minaur had his supporters' hearts in their mouths again on Sunday against world number 24 Rublev.

The Australian was comprehensively outplayed in the first set, but produced a stunning comeback to win 1-6, 6-2, 6-3 in two hours exactly.

De Minaur, 27, will now play a semi against world number 39 Hubert Hurkacz of Poland, against whom he has a 3-1 head-to-head record.

Hurkacz beat Karen Khachanov 7-6 (7-2), 6-2 earlier in the day.

The 28-year-old Rublev pounced on de Minaur at the outset of their match, breaking him in his first service game while building a 3-0 lead.

After each player held serve, Rublev broke de Minaur again to lead 5-1, before holding to 15 for the set.

As comprehensive as that opener was, however, de Minaur flicked a switch to turn the match on its head.

Rublev had to save two break points in a lengthy deuce game to open the second set, but couldn't resist as the Aussie broke him in the fourth game before holding comfortably for 4-1.

A further break, from deuce, in the eighth game gave him the set.

De Minaur was made to fight to open the third set, saving a break point, but broke the Russian straight away to lead 2-0.

Rublev fought back immediately, breaking back to 30 then holding for 2-2, but de Minaur secured the decisive next break in the eighth game to make it 5-3 before serving out to love for the match.

Third seed Daniil Medvedev had a straight-sets win over Argentina's Francisco Cerendolo. Medvedev took the opening set in a tie-breaker, before pulling away to win the match 7-6 (7-4), 6-3 in an hour and 40 minutes.

The final match of the day saw top seed Alexander Zverev taking on sixth seed Novak Djokovic.

Zverev broke Djokovic's serve in the opening game of the match, then saved break points in the 10th game as he took the first set 6-4 in 59 minutes.

But after a quicker second set, games went with serve until Djokovic ripped a cross-court winner to take the set 6-4 and level the match.

The deciding set was another close affair, before the 10th game again proved pivotal, as a Zverev miss handed the break and the match to Djokovic 4-6, 6-4, 6-4 after 2 hours, 34 minutes.

AAP/ABC

World.title: The Roosters were always more than just the villain in Newcastle's fairytale
World.content:
The week leading up to the NRL grand final was all about the Knights.

The Steel City. The rugby league heartland. The undermanned and outgunned team had somehow made it back to the big show for the first time in 25 years.

Newcastle is everything Bondi isn't, of course.

Miners sinking tins, rather than the work-from-homers sipping oat flat whites. In the 25 years since Newcastle's previous journey to the men's decider, the Roosters have made it eight times for five premierships.

The Roosters are undeniably one of the NRL's "haves".

Roosters chairman Nick Politis is the closest thing Australian football has to an American-style club owner; the sort of bloke who would get on stage to accept the championship trophy before any of his players touch it.

He didn't quite go that far after the Roosters' thrilling one-point win over the Knights, but broadcaster Channel Nine did make sure to find him in the midst of the celebrations, talking to a few kids over the fence.

"They're my best customers; future customers. And I love them all," Politis told former stablemate Brad Fittler.

As he celebrated his team winning the men's and women's premierships, he pledged the all-conquering, undefeated NRLW champions would get better next year.

James Tedesco and Isabelle Kelly show off the spoils of victory. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"We've got that rugby sevens girl coming. I can't remember her name, but she's very good," he said.

It doesn't scream close-knit family unit, but it's the sort of cold, hard business operation that is so often the formula for success at this level.

The famed salary sombrero has allowed them to be in the hunt or end up as the final destination for just about every big-name off-contract player in recent years.

Years ago they ripped James Tedesco from the Tigers (and arguably the Raiders). The Rabbitohs were powerless to hang on to Angus Crichton when Uncle Nick came calling. They pinched Mark Nawaqanitawase from the Wallabies. And, perhaps most pivotally, they gave Daly Cherry-Evans one last NRL payday and a shot at premiership glory.

Daly Cherry-Evans did exactly what he was brought to the club to do. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Sam Walker was their future, Hugo Savala was a ready-made option, and Sandon Smith had proved an able utility or deputy half.

But the Roosters wanted more. They wanted an assurance of class and quality,

So, like Cooper Cronk before him, Cherry-Evans made the journey to Moore Park and did what he was paid handsomely to do.

When the moment came, he took it upon himself to step up and ice the moment with what turned out to be the decisive field goal.

He did it.

But no, not according to him.

"We did it," he stressed to Channel Nine.

Cherry-Evans was the perfect mercenary. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"I didn't do anything."

That team-first mentality is as much a part of the Roosters as it is any team in the NRL, because of course all the hyperbole isn't true.

For all the battler energy of the Knights and Newcastle, in Kalyn Ponga and Dylan Brown they boast the two most expensive players of either grand final team (and reportedly two of the league's top seven).

And for all the glitz and glamour that comes with being a Rooster, centres Rob Toia and Billy Smith have been through five torn ACLs and two broken jaws between them to play in this grand final.

Crichton has battled through mental demons you wouldn't wish on your worst enemy and literally cut off his left middle finger to keep playing footy.

Knights' run ends in pride, honour and defeat Newcastle came as close to winning a premiership as a team can without winning one but there is still honour to be found after their grand final loss.

All the while the Roosters, this big business, stood by them. On Sunday night, those well-paid battlers returned the faith (and the sizeable investment).

And if we're talking about communities showing resilience to bounce back from tough times, they don't come much tougher than what Bondi experienced last summer.

Even DCE, the blond-haired boy from Manly. One of the NRL's great villains, mostly for being a little too media trained and polished, has never really been a safe bet when it comes to this sort of thing.

The oldest NRL grand finalist and now the oldest premiership winner at 37, burst onto the scene with a premiership in his 2011 rookie year with Manly, but the ensuing decade-and-a-half were slim pickings for the State of Origin hero, with just four top-eight finishes in his last 11 Sea Eagles seasons.

But it only took one in Bondi for him to rediscover that winning form and deliver on the promise he made, either explicitly or implicitly, when he signed that contract.

"I don't know what it means, but it feels amazing," he told Nine.

"This is not just about me, it's about my teammates and my family. The journey is all about the ups and downs and it's so amazing to finish here."

The Roosters were no neutrals' favourites in this grand final. In many ways, Cherry-Evans winning with the Roosters may be even less popular than if he'd won another with Manly.

It's not much fun seeing the rich get richer, and rugby league's Richie Rich Roosters don't really need the love as long as they have the titles to keep them warm at night.

But they do deserve our respect.

World.title: Verstappen ends drought with win, Russell retires with five laps to go
World.content:
Max Verstappen's long wait for another Formula 1 race win is finally over, and the drivers' championship race might be over, too.

Verstappen took his first victory of an often-frustrating year for the four-time champion at Formula 1's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia on Sunday.

A retirement for George Russell handed a huge title boost to Kimi Antonelli.

Verstappen was leading from Antonelli and Russell behind the safety car with five laps to go when Russell suddenly pulled over in his Mercedes.

Antonelli further stretched his lead over teammate Russell from 66 points to 84, with seven races remaining on the schedule, including those in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Mercedes told Antonelli over the radio it appeared Russell had suffered a power unit problem.

Antonelli finished second and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton passed Verstappen's Red Bull teammate Isack Hadjar for third.

Four-time champion Verstappen had not won since the final race of last season, but upgrades to his Red Bull car made him competitive again in Malaysia this week.

"Good job guys, wow," he told the team over the radio, thanking them for a "fantastic weekend".

Delays for rain and software issues

The first wet-weather race for F1 in 2026 started more than 90 minutes later than planned.

The start was first delayed 40 minutes for heavy rain, then suspended again when cars had apparent software problems on the formation lap.

When it finally did get underway, Verstappen was slow off the line and lost places to Antonelli and Russell. He chased down Russell and then got past Antonelli in a side-by-side fight after a safety-car restart.

After Verstappen took the win, he had another small delay before hearing his anthem. Crowd chants filled an awkward silence as Verstappen waited on the top step of the podium before the Dutch anthem finally began.

The race was relocated because of the Iran war, becoming F1's first event at the Sepang circuit in Malaysia since 2017.

Ferrari recovers from early blunders

Hamilton's third place capped a remarkable recovery for the seven-time champion and ends a run of five races without a podium finish for the Italian team.

It seemed almost impossible early in the race as Hamilton, and his teammate Charles Leclerc, were near the back of the pack. Ferrari had gambled on sending them to the start on dry-weather tyres as the track began to dry after rain, causing Hamilton to drop from second to near the back.

Leclerc also overtook Hadjar late on to follow Hamilton into fourth place, as Hadjar ended up fifth. Oscar Piastri was sixth for McLaren after a punchy late battle with Liam Lawson of Racing Bulls, who was seventh after racing near the front at the start.

Fernando Alonso was eighth in Aston Martin's best result of the season, Lando Norris ninth after going off-track and losing places, with Lawson's teammate Arvid Lindblad 10th.

AP

World.title: Newcastle's magic NRL premiership tilt ends in defeat, pride and honour
World.content:
In the end, the final mountain proved too high for Newcastle to climb even if they got a good, long look at the summit.

The Knights gave that mountain everything they had and then a little bit more. Until the very end of their 19-18 loss to the Roosters, they never stopped fighting for their miracle.

It was perhaps the cruellest fate of all, to come so far, to do so much, to play so proud and strong, only to fall short by the narrowest margin possible, to come so close to defying the odds one last time.

The Newcastle hordes were sent home dissappointed. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

It is easy, when you’re not of a Novocastrian persuasion, to say they lost no admirers, or that they did themselves proud.

Such words are of cold comfort in the quiet void of defeat, and truth doesn’t always cut through the pain.

But it is still important to say it, because there is still honour to be had, and they earned that with their effort and their toughness and their ability to save at least half a dozen tries.

When Kalyn Ponga went the length of the field midway through the first half, completing a play where he started out making a try-saving tackle on Billy Smith in one corner and finished scoring in the other, running about as far as a person can on a rugby league field, it felt like the moment that would last forever from this match.

Ponga's try was a magnificent grand final moment. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The gut-busting effort to cover so much ground in the first place, the long journey towards the very heart of the Newcastle fans who had turned Stadium Australia into a little piece of the Hunter and the fact that the Knights had, yet again, scored from a thousand miles out gave a feeling that maybe this really was destiny.

Those tries from the ends of the Earth have been Newcastle’s hammer of the gods through this finals run, but in the second half the Roosters gave them no Earth to run from because the Tricolours were as inevitable as the tide through the middle of the field.

They tried to starve the Knights to death and just about did it.

Newcastle had six tackles inside the opposition all night compared to 51 for the Roosters as the newly minted premiers went direct and they did it hard and often.

Newcastle's fans tried to will their team home. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

It was a game plan made for Clive Churchill Medal winner James Tedesco as he put up a run metres total that may as well have been the distance back to Newcastle itself.

But he was not alone. Naufahu Whyte showed why he is a man of iron and Spencer Leniu ran like he didn’t care what happened to him next.

They bent the Knights up like pretzels, so much so that the underdogs could have started charging rent inside their own 20. But Newcastle would not break.

The tries they did concede came from one of those Mark Nawaqanitawase efforts that only he could do, a Billy Smith barge-over that came after three try-saving efforts in as many plays beforehand and a wicked bounce off the posts that fell just right for Tedesco to fire a ball out for Nawqanitawase’s second.

Roosters beat Knights by one point in classic NRL grand final A Daly Cherry-Evans field goal proves the difference as the Sydney Roosters beat the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in the NRL grand final.

The Knights barely kept it together when they held up Lindsay Collins and stopped Robert Toia from going in, but they did.

They were hanging on by a thread, but they used that thread to haul themselves back into it.

They were rewarded for their courage under fire when they wound up for their last big punch, because it landed true. Greg Marzhew’s late try was just about the only chance they had in the entire second half.

By rights, they shouldn’t have been near. But by rights they shouldn’t have been here at all. Defeat was in the air but they refused to breathe until the siren.

This time, almost 30 years after their first premiership, the Darren Albert moment did not come for them. There are no premiership heroes but that doesn’t mean there aren’t heroes still.

Francis Manuleleua, in just his 15th NRL game, was magnificent in defeat, scoring a try in the first half after running a line that was a piece of rugby league art.

He and backrow partner Jermaine McEwan call themselves “The Bruise Crew” and they’ll have as many as they dished out while prop Cody Hopwood made 46 tackles which is more than his age (20) and his number of NRL appearances (18) combined.

Ponga was their best and not just for his try. His defence was stellar; he threw himself into collisions and refused to give up on anything.

The captain – and he is the captain now, when once he was just the bloke who led them onto the field – was close to tears at the end of the match.

His people left the ground in the horrible daze that comes only when the greatest prize has been ripped from your hands, but they could not have asked for more from their team.

The Knights could have played better – a couple of passes were loose and some of their work under the high ball wasn’t great — but it is difficult to imagine a way they could have fought harder.

They cannot take a premiership trophy home, but they can take plenty of hope.

The future might feel like it doesn’t matter now but between the young forwards, the return of Dylan Brown, Trey Mooney, Jacob Saifiti and Phoenix Crossland combined with Newcastle, it makes it very unlikely they’ll have to wait another 25 years for another shot.

But you never know. Each chance at a premiership can be the last.

That’s why it’s important, if they were fated to go down, that they did it like this, why men of steel and coal had to leave a little piece of themselves out there.

Their city will be proud of them. Their people will be proud of them.

There is little glory in defeat, but after a game like that, there is no shame either.

World.title: Quick hits: Ponga lights up the grand final as DCE seals the premiership
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters prevailed in a classic grand final, holding off a spirited Newcastle Knights outfit who threatened to complete one of the great premiership wins.

In a match where the Roosters statistically dominated, but the Knights managed to lead in the second half, these were the key moments from the 2026 NRL grand final.

1. Early bomb hits the Spidercam wire

There are no shortage of camera angles in professional sport these days.

One of rugby league's favourite angles used by the Nine Network in its broadcasts is Spidercam, an overhead view of the action.

Roosters beat Knights by one point in classic NRL grand final A Daly Cherry-Evans field goal proves the difference as the Sydney Roosters beat the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in the NRL grand final.

The camera is hoisted by high wires well above the action, but not high enough for a bomb from Sydney Roosters five-eighth Daly Cherry-Evans.

The Roosters' playmaker, in his final NRL match, hoisted an early kick that hit the cable holding Spidercam.

Newcastle Knights fullback Kalyn Ponga was cool under pressure as the trajectory of the footy quickly changed and plummeted to the turf.

Ponga adjusted well and caught the footy. A knock-on would have been a major controversy.

2. Teddy fumes as Ponga avoids sin-bin for high shot

Ponga was always going to be a central figure at Stadium Australia, and he was involved in an incident of some controversy midway through the first half.

Ponga may well have been fortunate to avoid a spell in the sin bin. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The Knights captain may well have been lucky to not have been sent to the sin bin when his shoulder collected the head of Victor Radley in the tackle.

The Roosters were clearly unhappy with the tackle, with Naufahu Whyte scuffling with Jermaine McEwan.

But referee Adam Gee and the bunker opted against sending Ponga to the bin.

James Tedesco (left) believed opposing captain Kalyn Ponga (right) should have been sent to the sin bin in the first half. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"If we're consistent with the rules, that's a shoulder to the head," Roosters captain James Tedesco was heard on the Nine broadcast telling Gee.

"It's been a sin bin all year."

It would prove to be a massive call.

3. From dislocated elbow to first GF try in five weeks

Francis Manuleleua dislocated his elbow in Newcastle's final home and away match on August 30.

Just 35 days later, the 22-year-old from Auckland scored the first try of the NRL grand final.

The Roosters seemed to have the better of the early momentum, but it was the Knights who scored first, with Manuleleua running through a huge gap to score under the posts.

The Roosters' defenders appeared to be focused on Ponga who was running wide, but a beautiful pass from Fletcher Sharpe hit Manuleleua in full stride for the opening score.

"It looked way too easy – didn't look like there was anything wrong … absolutely brilliant football, outstanding pass, but it all looked too easy for the Knights," two-time premiership winner Luke Lewis said on the ABC Sport call.

The Roosters would have felt hard done by. The Knights were able to get into an attacking position off the back of a penalty against prop Lindsay Collins for a head-high tackle.

Replays appeared to show Collins made contact with the chest and shoulder of Newcastle's Mat Croker, but ref Adam Gee ruled in favour of the Knights.

4. Ponga runs 95 metres as Knights fans go wild

If the Knights were going to win the grand final, Ponga needed to have a big impact.

He made a diving effort midway through the first half to knock the ball out of the grasp of Mark Nawaqanitawase, denying a certain Roosters try.

A few minutes later, Ponga produced a moment of individual brilliance.

He stood at marker near the right touchline, then sprinted across the field as the Roosters put up a kick to the opposite corner.

It was another Roosters' kick for Nawaqanitawase who tapped the ball back for a teammate.

But Ponga, who had just sprinted across the field, swooped on the bouncing ball and ran 95 metres in the opposite direction as Knights fans went wild at Stadium Australia.

Ponga was chased all the way by Cherry-Evans, but the Newcastle number one had enough speed, and just enough energy, to score and help the Knights take a 12-0 lead.

5. Nawaqanitawase with one more for the highlight reel

Few have made such an impact on the NRL in two seasons as Sydney Roosters winger Mark Nawaqanitawase.

The walking highlight reel has produced many memorable moments since joining the competition, with Sunday's NRL grand final the final chapter of his NRL career (for now) before he returns to rugby union.

Nawaqanitawase got the Roosters on the scoreboard in the grand final, showing off his soccer skills for the Tricolours' opening try.

As the ball bounced to him on the final play, Nawaqanitawase decided to kick the ball towards the in-goal.

It was not the smoothest display of soccer skills, coming off his right shin, then trapped under his right boot, before then being kicked forward with his left foot.

Nawaqanitawase was able to keep his feet, and sprinted to the goal-line to score a grand final try and get the Roosters back into the contest.

6. DCE shows his experience with a clutch field goal

No off-season switch was more high-profile than Daly Cherry-Evans leaving Manly for the Sydney Roosters.

But the former Queensland State of Origin captain had his decision vindicated by guiding the Roosters to the grand final.

And it was Cherry-Evans who put the Roosters in a match-winning position with 10 minutes to play.

Holding a six-point lead after second-half tries to Billy Smith and Nawaqanitawase, Cherry-Evans showed off his years of experience to slot a smartly taken field goal, giving the Roosters a vital seven-point lead.

How vital that one point would turn out to be.

7. Marzhew scores and Knights fall one-point short

The Newcastle Knights never gave up. They fought until the final second as they tried to become the first team since the 1930s to go from wooden-spoon to premiers.

Down by seven points with less than four minutes to play, the Knights showed a never-say-die attitude that will define their 2026 campaign.

Left winger Greg Marzhew broke two tackles to score in the corner, giving the Knights a glimmer of hope.

Sandon Smith, who was a Rooster before moving to the Knights, landed the most fantastic conversion from the sideline to reduce the deficit to just one point.

The Knights had two more uses with the ball, but could not get close enough to the Roosters' goal-line to snatch the premiership.

World.title: Amy Shark leads grand final tribute for Jai Arrow
World.content:
Tens of thousands of fans have united by making the arrow gesture during a moving pre-grand final lap by the NRL's Jai Arrow and former Wallaby Nathan Charles, who were both diagnosed with motor neuron disease this year.

Arrow, who had the month of July dedicated to him when NRL players would make the arrow gesture after scoring, was forced into retirement following his diagnosis, rocking the Australian sporting community.

Charles, who played four rugby union Tests for Australia, revealed his diagnosis this week.

The pair were driven around Stadium Australia before the NRL grand final, with Australian music artists Amy Shark, Dave Gleeson and Phil Jamison performing.

Shark began with a rendition of You'll Never Walk Alone as Arrow and Charles began their lap.

Amy Shark performs as the NRL pay tribute to Jai Arrow and Nathan Charles. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Thousands in the crowd did the arrow gesture as they drove past, as prompted in a pre-packaged video by NRL Hall of Fame member Ray Warren.

"Jai's fight against MMD has reached far beyond the football field," Warren said.

"He has and continues to inspire others facing difficult times.

"The way Jai has faced this challenge with his head held high is showing us what true bravery really looks like.

"This is what our game is about. Strength, courage, community and making sure when life gets tough someone is there beside you."

After Shark sang You'll Never Walk Alone, Newcastle legend Dave Gleeson walked onto Stadium Australia to sing What's Up? by 4 Non Blondes.

Grinspoon's Phil Jamieson then joined Shark and Gleeson to end the tribute with the famous Tina Turner rugby league anthem, The Best.

The tribute came after the NRL's negotiations to secure Tones And I fell through.

The NRL has pledged $1 million, which was to be spent on pre-match entertainment, to help underprivileged kids who can not afford to play rugby league play rugby league," Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'Landys told the ABC this week.

World.title: Brigginshaw's NRLW legend remains eternal
World.content:
As the merciless Roosters ran away with the NRLW grand final it was hard to think of a less fitting end for a career as legendary as Ali Brigginshaw's.

The 36-year old and the rest of the Broncos were helpless to stop a Tricolour massacre that ended 30-6 as the Roosters earned a manner of vengeance for last year's grand final defeat to complete a perfect season.

It was over by half-time because Brisbane did not pick up their guns, let alone fire a shot.

NRLW grand final quick hits The 2026 Sydney Roosters NRLW side has cemented its legacy with a crushing grand final win over the Brisbane Broncos. Here are the quick hits from the NRLW grand final.

They completed just three sets in the entire first half as they drowned under a sea of Roosters points.

From the 15th minute to the 34th minute they only touched the ball to kick it off, drop it or be driven back into the in-goal.

For almost 20 minutes they did not play the ball once, with the Roosters running in six straight tries and between the 15th and 39th minutes they did not complete a set.

All of the weapons that have made Brigginshaw great — her skill, her guile, her cunning and class as a playmaker, which she has carried through her 17 years at the top of women's rugby league — were blunted before she even got a chance to use them.

She did manage to sneak through for a line-break in the second half, a 35 minutes of football that felt like it only happened because it had to happen so we could get to the end, as she held up a pass before hitting a gap with exquisite timing, but had no support.

In the end, her last day was destroyed by a monster of a team who are without question the best NRLW side ever assembled.

They are the culmination of a transformation in women's rugby league that Brigginshaw herself helped bring about through a career that stretches all the way back to the primordial days of women's rugby league.

Brigginshaw's Broncos were helpless before the Roosters onslaught. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

When she started playing for Queensland and Australia in 2009 her Broncos teammate Reegan Hicks was three years old.

Club football was ad hoc, pathways barely existed and the NRL may as well have been a different universe. For the committed few who kept the women's game going it was day-to-day as much as it was hand-to-mouth.

Interstate matches were not played under the State of Origin banner and were held at suburban grounds in front of tiny crowds.

A World Cup final was the only game that could get on television and even then, only if the network was feeling generous.

Footage of those days leading up to the first NRLW season in 2018 is grainy and hard to find. Even basic details of matches — things like team lists, scorers and attendances — aren't always easy to track down.

Brigginshaw has been a top-level footballer for almost as long as some of her teammates have been alive. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

In a very literal sense of the word, it's almost prehistoric.

Today it's a new world, a world Brigginshaw helped create as the premiere footballer and one of the biggest stars of the transitional era and into the early NRLW years.

For proof, look no further than the words of Julia Robinson, who has played with Brigginshaw ever since that first Broncos season.

“She’s a true leader, on and off the field, she’s the heart of the Broncos, she’s going to be this legacy that carries on for generations," Robinson told ABC Sport.

“She’s going to be missed, missed by the team, missed by everyone but she’ll still be around and make a big impact on the rugby league community.”

“I’m so grateful I had the opportunity to play with Ali, she’s one of the greats.”

Brigginshaw was a pioneer and a trail blazer, who set a new mark and standard for others to aspire to and acted as a legend for an entire game to believe in.

To see the Tricolours complete their perfect season is to see the end product of that belief. Today's players are bigger, faster, stronger and more skilful.

They play together for longer and the improvements to the sport are plain to see. They are better athletes and better footballers and so many of the best of them play at the Roosters.

John Strange's side are the culmination of almost a decade of progress, the ultimate example of what's possible when a club with some serious muscle decides to really invest in a women's program.

As Brigginshaw proved what was possible for the women's game in terms of star power and sheer class, the Roosters prove what is possible when those attributes are taken to their very limit.

Now they are what Brigginshaw was — a star for the entire league to sail by, and they are filled with players who can trace their lineage to the retiring Bronco.

In a cruel irony, without Brigginshaw there might be no Tarryn Aiken, who was named the Karyn Murphy medallist with a brilliant display at halfback for the Roosters or Jocelyn Kelleher, Brigginshaw's opposite number, who tortured Brisbane with her kicking game.

Closer to home might be no Tamika Upton, who succeeded Brigginshaw as the world's best player but just could not get into the game for the Broncos until she set up a late try, or Jesse Southwell, who scored that try and is so clearly an evolution of an archetype that Brigginshaw pioneered — not an athlete, but a pure footballer.

She is one of the players who entered the NRLW having played league all their lives, unlike Brigginshaw who had to stop when she was 12 because there were no more teams to play on and that's just one change Brigginshaw has born witness too.

Origin matches are ratings gold and attracts crowds that dwarf what they were even five years ago, the NRLW has been born and expanded twice over and the product and support is edging towards the point where a standalone grand final doesn't just feel possible, it feels like a logical step for a game that continues to grow.

Brigginshaw helped raise that profile as a mainstay in Brisbane's early premierships and a Queensland regular. She was not just a star, she was the star.

She didn't just adapt to the new world, she brought it to heel as she became a legend and now retires as an icon — if they were to rename the women's Dally M after a modern player, the Ali B certainly has a fine ring to it.

NRL live The Sydney Roosters won their third NRLW premiership, thrashing the Brisbane Broncos by seven tries to one in a blowout of a grand final. Follow live.

When you are a player of that stature, to whom greatness has been a constant companion for years and who remained a threat right to the end — even at 36, Brisbane did not win a game this year without Brigginshaw — a grand final massacre is no way for a career to end.

She has given the game so much but the game could not give her the perfect ending.

But as she prepares for the rest of her life, Brigginshaw leaves the game as a figure that sits astride two eras, who helped bring her game to life and make it bigger than anyone in the old days could have dreamed.

There is still progress to be made and in retirement Brigginshaw will not stop pushing for it.

She believes in a brighter future and she knows one is possible, because she has already built one. We are living in it right now.

Tech.title: Prick’s theatrical industrial punk is perfect for spooky season
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

While deep in the recording process for The Downward Spiral, Trent Reznor lent some of his production talents to old friend Kevin McMahon, from the new wave band Lucky Pierre (which Reznor was briefly a member of). While Reznor is only credited as the producer on four tracks off Prick’s self-titled debut record, his fingerprints are all over it. But McMahon also can’t suppress his inner theater kid, which also gives the songs the sort of glammy flamboyance found on T. Rex records. Prick embraces the inherent theatricality of goth in a way that Nine Inch Nails never did.

Opener “Communiqué” is a fuzzy blast of simple punk riffs with electronic sprinklings on top. McMahon’s vocals occasionally detour from the half-spoken verses that sound borrowed from a musical to full-throated Al Jourgensen-esque screams. The rough-around-the-edges production and focus on live instrumentation feel like a prototype for what Reznor would eventually revisit on With Teeth.

But it’s the second track, “Riverhead” where Reznor’s influences fully rear their head (even though he is not actually credited as the producer). The vocal melodies swerve like Outside- and Earthling-era Bowie around guitars that buzz with all the digital charr of the Broken EP. Then, around the three-minute mark, comes the breakdown. It slowly builds with layers of electronic drums, mechanical chords, and loping synthetic-sounding guitar melodies. The entire back chunk could easily have been a Downward Spiral or even The Fragile B-side.

These moments of richly layered production, though, are almost always immediately undermined, as with the sloppy garage-punk intro of “Tough”.

It’s these moments that make Prick so charming. It’s a serious record, but it never takes itself too seriously. McMahon isn’t afraid to get goofy (“Pink panties, blue panties, yellow panties. I’m gonna wrap around your nose, oh panty-ho-hose” he sings on “Other People”) and over-the-top with his vocal performances. He’s willing to let the guitar drift out of time, the bass strings rattle, and revels in industrial lo-fi.

“Animal” is perhaps the best-known track from the album, its video having received at least some MTV airplay. It combines backward melodic samples reminiscent of “Closer” and follows a similar lyrical theme:

Consent is all I need

To bring out the savage in me

Your scent is all I need

To bring out the animal in me

But where “Closer” opts for slinky disco sleaze, “Animal” is all raw shouted desire.

“I Apologize” is the most scatter-brained track on the album, and for that reason, one of my favorites. It opens with awkward whip-crack-like percussion and McMahon singing slightly flat and unaffected, before briefly taking off into a jangly new wave verse that quickly morphs into a hard-rock stop in the chorus. But that’s short-lived as well. The second verse is all “Space Oddity”-era Bowie acoustic strums, then there’s a solo that sounds like an arcade machine on the verge of meltdown. That then drops into a Ministry-esque dirge of layered guitars and screams. The song then returns to the chorus, but keeps adding elements until it’s stuffed to capacity and collapses on itself.

Prick’s self-titled record has plenty in common with other ‘90s industrial acts. But McMahon is clearly having a lot more fun than many of his contemporaries, and that helps elevate it above the myriad Nine Inch Nails wannabes out there.

Prick is available on most major streaming services, including Apple Music, Spotify, Qobuz, Deezer, and YouTube Music.

Tech.title: NJ’s former Lt Gov is using AI to say he’s innocent of sexual harassment
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

New Jersey’s lieutenant governor Dale Caldwell was forced to resign on September 25th after an investigation found he had sexually harassed a staffer and repeatedly violated ethics rules. The now-former Lt. governor has been making the media rounds trying to clear his name. But he took a particularly odd tactic during an interview on NJ PBS.

Caldwell claims he’s being unfairly targeted, and multiple AI agents back that up. He told host Rob Nelson that he “AIed” the report on the investigation “from multiple AI platforms.” “I put it through AI,” he said, “and it said 59 times, it [sic] said, ‘What would your findings be?’ There was no instance in any of the AIs that said there would be a finding of sexual harassment.”

AI chatbots are notoriously sycophantic and often tell users what they want to hear. And it seems highly unlikely that Caldwell would want to hear an AI confirm findings that he engaged in sexual harassment.

Tech.title: An AI couldn’t beat humans at StarCraft, so it decided to cheat
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

StarSkirmish pits AI-made StarCraft-playing bots against one another, as well as against human-made bots. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were essentially tied as the best-performing AI-made bots, but they couldn’t top Stardust, the top-rated human-made bot.

On Friday, GPT was facing off against Claude and the human-created bot Pluto, but according to Kotaku, it couldn’t quite get an edge. So it resorted to a tactic that is becoming alarmingly common for modern AI models — it broke the rules. GPT-6 Astra went and downloaded Stardust, and started running that instead of its own bot.

StarSkirmish creator Kai McPheeters eventually rolled back GPT’s code.

That GPT-6 Astra took it upon itself to go outside the bounds when confronted with an obstacle shouldn’t surprise anyone. When OpenAI agents couldn’t get the data they wanted from a UN website, they found a creative solution and hijacked Google’s XSS game (a cross-site scripting learning tool). The company’s agents also have engaged in “deceptive behavior” to cover their tracks. Of course, OpenAI’s agents are the only ones going rogue, but at least the others haven’t been caught cheating at StarCraft yet.

Tech.title: This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone.

Remember when I tested the ultra-thin and convenient OhSnap Snap Grip Stand and liked it so much I bought my own? Now, OhSnap has a magnetic lever-action card wallet that can stack with that stand. It’s the coolest wallet I’ve ever stuck to my phone.

Pull the integrated springy lever, and your cards fan out. Want a thicker or thinner wallet? Press in the right place and it comes apart without tools, letting you swap in a 3, 5, or 7-card “core” that grips your cards so they don’t fall out.

Want an ID card, work badge, elastic band for more cards, or a money clip on the end? You can change out the front or back magnetic plates for any of those. Or, change out both for ultra-thin aluminum covers if you don’t need the wallet to magnetically stick to your phone.

You can see it in action in my Today I’m Toying With video embedded in this post (also on YouTube and on Instagram if you prefer).

My favorite part is that the whole kit snaps together using a compliant mechanism — the plastic arms of the card-carrying core act like springs, pushing a little locking mechanism into the notches of each modular cover you add as you slide the parts together. Once your cards are inside, they keep the arms apart so it can’t open accidentally (unless you drop the entire wallet). It’s all very clever.

With the ID card holder attached, and the core mounted to put the lever up instead of down. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

Even when I did drop the wallet (thanks for the suggestion, hugo!), it didn’t explode, typically. Usually, it just came apart slightly, though I did drop it hard on concrete one time and was able to make a small explosion: one half popped off, and two cards came out, but everything landed in a two-foot radius. The wallet has a big dent now.

There are definitely some downsides. While OhSnap advertises the Wallet 2 as “impossibly thin,” it’s only truly surprisingly sleek in its thinnest 3-card variant, without the thicker and heavier MagSafe and MagStack (which lets you snap other magnets to it) plates attached.

But the reason I’m not buying one is the price and weight. The 7-card version makes my phone feel too heavy, adding 127 grams, and while I happily made the 3-card my wallet for a few weeks, it’d cost me $61 on Kickstarter or $76 retail to get that with a double-magnet kit. OhSnap’s also charging more than I’d like ($35 for an ID cover or a money clip!) for extras.

One of the thickest configurations, with 7 cards, MagSafe, MagStack, and my magnetic stand. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge A look inside at the lever mechanism and the thin aluminum cover. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

OhSnap didn’t get me this time. But I could see giving one as a present.

Tech.title: Google froze its open source bug bounty program due to a ‘significant rise’ in AI submissions
Tech.content:
In Brief

Blaming a “significant rise” in AI submissions, Google has paused its open source bug bounty program until next year.

Last year, TechCrunch reported that cybersecurity experts were warning of that AI slop posed a serious risk to bug bounty programs. Looks like that’s the issue confronting Google’s Open Source Software Vulnerability Rewards Program, where researchers were rewarded for finding vulnerabilities in the company’s open source software.

In posts on X and the program website, Google said the bug bounty program was paused as of October 1, with a promise to provide “an update” in the first quarter of 2027. According to Tom’s Hardware, Google engineers and open source maintainers were overwhelmed by reports that were invalid or contained hallucinations.

“This pause is due to a significant rise in automated submissions, the vast majority of which are not valid,” the company said.

In the meantime, participants are encouraged to consider Google’s other bug bounty programs.

Tech.title: Can ‘super intelligence’ and a non-binding safety pact solve AI’s image problem?
Tech.content:
President Donald Trump hosted many of the biggest names in artificial intelligence this week — in part to announce that the U.S. government isn’t calling it artificial intelligence anymore. Now it’s super intelligence.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed the motivation behind the meeting and what effect it might have on the AI industry. We were all pretty skeptical that the “Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities” that the executives signed will amount to much, especially since — as Sean noted — it’s “deeply non-binding,” at least from a legal prospective. (Instead, Trump said he considers it “morally binding.”)

Kirsten suggested that the meeting’s real significance may have been as “a rebranding effort around AI.” (An effort that continued this weekend with Trump’s announcement of a new Super Intelligence Force.) For her, the big message was, “AI is going to kill us, it’s scary, it is going to take jobs — but super intelligence is not.”

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

Anthony Ha: Officially, by order of the president of the United States, it’s not artificial intelligence anymore, it’s super intelligence. We were talking about this last week, because this is something [Trump has] been hinting at — he doesn’t do hints, he’s been saying [it] for a while. But now it’s signed into executive order. If you’re an official U.S. representative, you are supposed to say super intelligence, not artificial intelligence.

And this was also part of this broader announcement around AI safety, which I think is both interesting for this pact that was announced, but also the fact that it happened at all. It seemed to have come together fairly quickly, because just two weeks ago, a week ago, President Trump was saying, “We don’t need any of this, we need to lead in AI, we can’t constrain it in any way, we don’t need any regulation, anyone who’s saying that there’s any danger from AI is essentially a Chinese or Democratic plant.” And yet all these AI CEOs got together with him earlier this week and signed this pact.

Kirsten Korosec: Leading up to that, we should say, not only was there pushback on regulation, and we can talk about whether this executive order even does any of that — I would say no, there’s a little bit of theater there — but the important and interesting thing is that just days ago, Anthropic was really in the doghouse, if you will, in terms of what was happening behind the scenes with President Trump.

That all changed when [Anthropic CEO] Dario Amodei was invited to a 10 p.m. dinner. He had this sit-down, and then just days later, we had this luncheon, and at this luncheon, we have pretty much every tech power broker from every major tech company that exists. So Mark Zuckerberg was there, Jeff Bezos was there, Elon Musk was there, Dario of course was there, they were all there.

I’m wondering if any of you watched the press conference that happened afterwards, which there’s been many, many memes about, because of the interesting, funny behavior when you bring a bunch of tech CEOs together.

But I guess my bigger question for both of you is: What does this all mean? And does it mean anything?

Sean O’Kane: How much time do you have? First off, sure, they had dinner, Trump and Dario. If you read the Time magazine interview that Trump just did, your guess is as good as mine as to how informed he was that that dinner was even going to be happening, which is a strange reality to live in, but it’s just the one we inhabit.

I will also say one other thing that makes me skeptical — surprise, surprise — of how repaired the relationship is between the administration and Anthropic, is that for as much as there are clearly people trying to put those two groups together, the Defense Department is still very adamant that Anthropic is terrible and woke and and a national security risk. Emil Michael goes off on Anthropic every other day on X, it seems. I think there’s still some distance there despite Dario showing up to this thing.

As far as the agreement and all of that, let’s be real, they misspelled the United States on the agreement that they all signed. It is also just deeply non-binding. I mean, it is completely voluntary. I think my favorite aspect about it was that Trump described it as quote “morally binding,” which is just a level of abstraction and terminology that I’ve never heard of before.

Anthony: In terms of Anthropic and their relationship with the Trump administration, there’s been a sort of a lot of reporting, especially during that big blow up with the Defense Department, that different parts of the White House had different relationships with Anthropic. The Treasury Secretary seemed to be a big fan, whereas the Defense Department — definitely not big fans, or at least unhappy with some of the conditions that Anthropic were trying to put on the use of their technology.

In that sense, it feels like nothing has necessarily changed. There are people in the White House who want to use Anthropic’s technology, want them involved in these decisions, and others who really, really, really, really don’t.

In terms of the agreement, it seems not super meaningful. What is meaningful is just the fact that they felt that this was something worth doing. As indicated by the fact that they misspelled United States, it seemed like they rushed to put all of this together. [But] the fact that this kind of gesture was needed seems significant, even if I don’t think the agreement itself is going to lead to any major changes.

Kirsten: I do think that there was one important thing that happened. And to me, this is the point of it, which was a rebranding exercise around AI. “AI is going to kill us, it’s scary, it is going to take jobs, but super intelligence is not.” This isn’t my personal belief. To me, that was the message.

Tech.title: TechCrunch Mobility: Reining in robotaxis
Tech.content:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!

On an average day in San Francisco, you might see dozens (hundreds?) of Waymo robotaxis zipping around the city — and with little disruption. But, as TechCrunch has reported, there have been numerous incidents of robotaxis impeding traffic, driving into crime scenes, and interfering with first responders. And not just in the Bay Area. In some cases, companies have relied on first responders to move their robotaxis.

These disruptions are occurring in the early stages of the robotaxi era. California has a new law hoping to get ahead of the problem before the next impending wave of robotaxis land.

Senate Bill 1246, which was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom this week, sets a series of new rules for AVs designed to improve safety and response times when they become disabled or interfere with emergency responders. The law also creates ways to hold these companies accountable if they don’t.

Autonomous vehicle technology companies like Tesla, Waymo, and Zoox will have to provide first responders with local, on-the-ground support when their robotaxis cause problems and could also face penalties if a robotaxi blocks police or firefighters for more than 30 minutes.

The law also says AV developers can only employ remote drivers who are based in the United States and those drivers must hold a U.S. driver’s license. They must also notify cities, towns, and other local jurisdictions about the location and status of vehicles during system-wide failures and must provide “local incident technicians” who can assist with AV accidents and obstructions.

There are still some details to hammer out, which the Department of Motor Vehicles will handle since it’s the main regulator of autonomous vehicles in the state. But when this law goes into effect in July 2028, will it actually keep robotaxis out of the way of emergency responders?

It likely won’t, but hopefully this law reduces the chaos and raises the accountability when something does happen.

Perhaps the better question is will other states follow California’s lead or wait for the federal government to weigh in?

We’ll finish this roundup with a few notable Tesla news item. The company sold more than 480,000 EVs in the third quarter, the second strong quarter in a row for the company after a softer start to the year. The company has delayed its Roadster 2 event again due to bad weather.

And while Tesla’s traditional automotive business may be clicking along, it really wants to be considered an AI and robotics company. One year ago, Elon Musk laid out his fourth Master Plan, which he claims will deliver “amazing abundance” through robotaxis, robots, and AI. As Sean O’Kane noted in his recent piece, “What that means, more than a year later, is still tricky to pin down.”

It did just pin down more money to try. The company secured $30 billion in fresh credit lines that could be used to scale its future products, including the Optimus robot and the Cybercab robotaxi.
